Having come to Magnesia, when the month of January was already halfway through, and this having passed, with February coming into its fifth day, one of the couriers stood before him, swift as an eagle, putting into his hands a letter securely sealed. Having opened it and read it, he learned of the death of his father. The letter had been sent by the viziers, both Halil and the others. It disclosed the death of his father and instructed the reader not to delay, but if possible to mount a winged Pegasus and arrive in Thrace before the announcement of the ruler’s death was heard by the surrounding nations. Which he did; at that very hour he mounted one of his swift Arabian horses. He said nothing else to his magnates than, "He who loves me, let him follow me." He departed quickly, having before him his own slave archers, and swift runners, all ambidextrous giants, all on foot; and behind them the swordsmen and javelin-throwing horsemen. And in two days from Magnesia he crossed the strait and arrived in the Chersonese. After waiting in Gallipoli another two days for those who were accompanying him to gather, he sent one of the couriers to Adrianople, announcing his arrival.
Since a frequent murmuring and rumor spread everywhere that the ruler was in Gallipoli, so that the rabble might not become disorderly and go rampant—for it was their custom to incite sedition during the changing of rulers; that is why they often concealed a death and told the people that the ruler was sick, and they do this because one who is about to take his place is not found in the place where the one who is dying exists. After he had departed from Gallipoli, many crowds flocked to pay homage to him. And when he drew near to the field, the whole order of the government went out, the viziers, and the satraps, and the governors, and the mayors, and the mystagogues and teachers of their impure religion, and those skilled in sciences and arts, and a large portion of the rabble in order to meet him. When the crowd had arrived in front of the ruler, at a distance of one mile in a line, they all dismounted their horses and walked on foot toward the ruler. But the ruler and those with him remained mounted. When they had arrived within a half-mile, with extreme silence on their lips, they stopped abruptly and raised a great lamentation with tears. Then he also, dismounting from his horse along with those under him, did the same, filling the air with cries and wailing. And it was possible to see great mourning and lamentation on that day from both sides. When they had come together and approached one another, the magnates paid homage to the leader, kissing his hand. And mounting their horses, they entered the city as far as the gate of the palace, and the ruler having entered, each withdrew to his own home. On the next day, a great assembly having taken place according to custom (and even more so, as the ruler was still young and had just recently entered into power), sitting on his father’s throne (as, would that it had not happened, but it occurred by the permission of God for our sins), all the satraps and the viziers of his father, Halil Pasha and Isaac Pasha, stood opposite him at a distance. But his own viziers, Siachin the eunuch and Ibrahim, stood by him according to custom. Then the ruler Mehmed asked Siachin his *mesazon*: "Why do the *mesazontes* of my father stand at a distance? Call them, and tell Halil to return to his accustomed place. But let Isaac depart to Brusa with the remaining leaders of the East, to consign the body of my father to burial. Let him also have the care of the eastern provinces." Having heard these things, they immediately ran according to custom and kissed his hand; and while Halil remained *mesazon*, Isaac, having taken the corpse of the ruler with many leaders and great provision, departed to Brusa and buried him in the shrine built by him, having distributed a vast amount of coins to the poor at the funeral.
Morates indeed did not die after a long and grievous illness; rather, he succumbed to fate, but he was far less troubled by pains and afflictions than his father. This, it seems to me, was a tribute granted to him by the decree of God, to whose human nature the kindly disposition and compassion of this man toward the poor were manifest. For he not only kept inviolate and undefiled the sworn treaties which he made with those bound to him by race and impious superstition, but he also stood by the covenants made with Christians. If ever the conditions of peace were violated by the Christians, and the treaties confused, they did not escape the eye of God, to whom nothing is hidden, and having been justly punished by Him, the very avenger, for the injuries received, the extent of His wrath did not stretch long; but immediately after the victory, the barbarian did not pursue them. He did not thirst for the total annihilation of any nation he happened to defeat; but as soon as the vanquished considered sending embassies for peace, he readily received them and dismissed the envoys in peace, hating battles and loving peace. And the Father of peace measured out the end of the barbarian in peace, and not by the sword. There were but four days in all of his sickness. Having left the palace with a few young companions, he crossed to the island which the rivers, splitting near the city, render spacious, and where, the land being fertile, pastures and green fodder for the dumb beasts grow. For in it are kept mares, and mules, and the proud horses of the leader, and buildings are constructed, most excellent for both warmth and pleasure as the season demands, and whatever else is useful for enjoyment. He wished to spend many days there, living privately with a few intimates for the sake of recreation and relief from the cares and toils of the wedding that had passed. Having crossed, therefore, and having spent one day there, enjoying himself not as he was accustomed, he ordered on the next day to be taken to the palace, saying that he was oppressed by a heaviness in his head and the rest of his body was numb. Having lain down, therefore, and being ill for three days, he fell into a coma and died on the second day of the month of February of the year 6959. It is said [..] D
that after the wedding, and before he departed for the island, he saw a vision of this kind one night: that a terrible man stood before him; the man who appeared took him by the hand, for he was struck with fear, and he wore on the right hand a gold ring on the thumb. The one who appeared then took the ring [(16)] off the great finger of the ruler, and placed it on the index finger, which is next to the thumb; then, having removed it from the index finger, he fitted it to the middle finger, and after this to the one next to the middle, and again to the last, the little finger. After this, the one who appeared removed the ring and vanished. The ruler, having awoken from his sleep, called for his soothsayers and told them what he had seen. They interpreted the ring as the principality itself, and the fingers: the first as himself, and the others as those after him who would rule from him. Others secretly and in silence interpreted the thumb as the last time of his life, and the removal of the ring as the loss of rule. They compared the insertions and removals of the other four fingers through the ring to the fingers of those who were to rule after him, and the number of the years of the rule, and then the tyranny will have an end. But let us return again to the narrative, and let us see what this bloodthirsty beast destroyed in his days, and consumed, and reduced to nothing. Having sent the body of his father to Bursa for burial, he began to search the treasuries and the paternal riches, and having found them filled with countless silver vessels, with gold, with precious stones, and with coins of great value, he sealed them with his own seal and placed them back in the treasury; then he found an infant [(17)] son of his father, born of his father's wife, a daughter of the ruler of Sinope.
Ismaelis Bullialdi notes
. And without a crown, the ring refers to the confirmation of the kingdom. For often kings, even without a crown, are understood by it. And below: Generally, the ring, with respect to those who manage and administer affairs, indicates power and the kingdom. To men of private condition, however, it foretells joy, children, and a wife. [(16)] Having removed it, therefore, the one who appeared took the ring. And having sought to grasp the stone in it, he found it shattered into many pieces, so that it was useless, and there was breathed into him all the events of fifty-five days. A ring is judged for the confirmation of a kingdom. For often kings are judged from it, even without a crown. In general, the ring is thus judged for those who are doing—that is, exercising power or reigning; but for those who are not, it signifies joy and a child with a wife. [(17)] Then finding the child. Leunclavius calls this boy Cuizug-Achmet, and does not relate that he was killed by his brother; rather, he says that of the children of Morates, only Mehemet survived. This is what Phrauzes also wrote in express words, book III, ch. 2. At Laonicus he teaches that this child, having been shut off, was killed. But he was born from the daughter of Spendiar, or Isfendiar, as Leunclavius testifies in the cited passage; and the words of Ducas, who relates that Mehemet was born of a maidservant, refute Remeccius and Philippus Lonicerus, who wrote that he was born of Maria, the Georgian wife, and was imbued by her with the dogmas of the Christian religion. But if the matter had been so, it is not credible that she, after Morates died, would have been sent back to her father.
from the daughter of the governor of Sinope, a legitimate wife; for he himself was born of a slave woman. When, therefore, the mother of the infant had come to the palace to console her stepson, he meanwhile sent one of his nobles, the son of Evrenes, by name Alin, his chief usher at that time, into the house of the aforementioned, and he strangled the child. On the following day, he also put that same Alin to death, and he gave the mother of the child, even against her will, in marriage to his father's slave, who was called Isaac. He wished also to give his other stepmother, the daughter of George, the Despot of Serbia, a woman most devoted to the Christian piety, in marriage to some other slave; but fearing lest her father should incite the war of the Hungarians against him, while his own rule was not yet consolidated, but was still in the course of establishment, he was unable to do what he had purposed. For the Despot, having heard of the death of his son-in-law Murat and that Mehemet had girded himself with the rule, immediately sent envoys to console him and to comfort him for having been orphaned; and to renew the treaties and sworn agreements which he had had with his father, and to secure them by oaths; and furthermore to request his daughter and take her back to his own house; all of which Mehemet performed, yet not with the intention of wishing to live peacefully and kindly and to rule, but as one redeeming the time. For when he receives it, he will commit acts of injustice and lawlessness. These and other things he did, having put on the sheep's skin, a wolf even before his birth. Having therefore received the envoys in a friendly manner, and having given and received sworn treaties, he dismissed them in peace, having also sent his stepmother back to her father with great glory and honor, and having bestowed upon her very many benefits, and assigned to her lands from the borders of Serbia, for her sustenance and every kind of care.
Likewise, the miserable and unfortunate Romans living in Constantinople at that time, together with the Despot Constantine, having themselves learned of the change of rule, sent ambassadors for the sake of consolation and to salute the chair of the principate. Who to whom? The lambs to the wolf, the sparrows to the serpent, those gasping for breath to death. But he, the Antichrist before the Antichrist, the ravager of the flock of my Christ, the enemy of the cross and of those who believe in him who was fixed upon it, having assumed the mask of a friend, as a disciple of Satan who transformed himself into a serpent, accepts the embassy, and writes new covenants, and swears by the God of the false prophet, and by the prophet synonymous with himself, and by his foul books, and by the angels and archangels, that he will observe peace and remain
in love and harmony with the city and the Despot Constantine, throughout his life, together with all the surrounding regions and cities subject to the same dominion. And the goodwill and disposition which his father possessed toward the Emperor John, who had reigned before him, and toward the Despot Constantine now, he would maintain in that same frame of mind to live and die. And beyond these fair promises, he also granted annually to the Roman Empire three hundred thousand aspers from the revenues of the regions watered by the Strymon. The wretched men asked for these funds for their sustenance, as well as for other expenses of the aforementioned Orchan 21, a descendant of Othman. And having done well according to their desire, they departed expressing their love, and they themselves were glad; likewise those of Wallachia and those of Bulgaria. And those who inhabit the islands, the Mitylenians, Chians, Rhodians, and those from Galata, the Genoese—all coming from every side 22 with gifts—worshipped the one who was truly incarnate as a demon, and having received his assurances as they wished, they departed.
Everything, therefore, as that evil man himself reasoned, he had arranged well; and having falsely demonstrated a state of peace to all Christians, and having secured a three-year truce with the regent of Hungary, Jango 23, he himself went on a military campaign against the Caraman 24, under the pretense that he himself was a sincere friend of the Christians, and that the Christians held a guileless friendship toward him, though they were of different nations and of a foreign religion; while the Caraman, being a Muslim and a worshipper of the rites of Muhammad, always and at all times did not cease to foment wars and disturbances at every opportunity. Wishing—or rather, he desired, and as he desired, so it came to be. For Mehemet had heard that the Caraman, upon hearing of the death of Morat, had rushed from his own borders and had seized three fortresses 25 and a considerable amount of land; yet these fortresses and that land were not possessed by Morat from his ancestors, but had been taken by the Caraman some years earlier from the
ruler, just as the story previously related has shown. The son of the raptor, having therefore found a reasonable pretext against the one who had formerly been wronged and who was for that reason investigating his own affairs, marched against him with an army. Having crossed the strait with the armies of the West, and having waited at Prusa for the armies of the East, he departed from there and arrived at Cotyaeum; from there he went into Phrygia Salutaris, to that place called by the Turks Carasaris, near the borders of Caraman. Then the Caraman, having heard of the arrival of Mehemet, sent envoys from among his own magnates, requesting forgiveness for the transgressions committed and saying that he was prepared to restore the fortresses which had been taken away. To these, for the sake of the pretext to be spoken, the tyrant yielded. For the foolish and senseless assembly of the Romans had devised a reckless plan, sending envoys to him to announce that Constantine was emperor; for he was not yet crowned, nor was he even likely to be crowned on account of the aforementioned reasons, yet they called him Emperor of the Romans. They therefore first announced the messages of the embassy to the Mesazontes, as was their custom, saying that the Emperor of the Romans did not accept the customary quantity of three hundred thousand aspers (26). For, they said, Orchan, who is himself also a son of Othman, just as is your leader Mehemet, is a man of mature age, and every day very many people flock to him, hailing him as lord and leader. But since he does not have wherewithal to be generous to them and to honor them with gifts, he asks the Emperor, who, being short of money, cannot satisfy the petitioner. "We therefore ask one of two things: either double the pension for us, or allow us to set Orchan free. For it is not our duty to feed the descendants of Othman; rather, they should be fed from the public funds. It is enough for us that he is detained, and that we prevent him from escaping the city." Halil Bassa listened to these and many other things (for he was always a friend of the Romans for two reasons: the one, that he was gentle and mild in disposition, and the second, that he was a bribe-taker; and if anyone discoursed with him while carrying gold in his hands and holding it up like a mirror, he could, without fear of offense, blurt out any harsh words whatsoever). Having, then, heard the words which the envoys brought from the Emperor and the Senate to the Prince Mehemet, he spoke thus to the apocrisiarii: "O foolish and senseless Romans, I have long known the cunning plots of your minds; abandon what you are holding [i.e., Orchan]. The departed prince was gentle and was a true friend to all, and a man of good conscience; but our current prince Mehemet is not what you suppose. For if his hands, whose audacity, ferocity, and impulsiveness are well known to me...
that God still overlooks your schemes and distortions. A Foolish men! The oath-bound treaty we made with you just the day before yesterday is barely finished; and if it were permitted to say so, the script written on the tablets is not yet dry. Now, therefore, because you have crossed into Anatolia and are staying in Phrygia, do you wish to make us afraid by displaying, as is your custom, manufactured scarecrows? We are not children, lacking in knowledge or strength; if you can do anything, do it. If you wish to declare Orchan prince in Thrace, declare it. If you are planning to bring the Hungarians to this side of the Danube, let them cross. If you also intend to invade our lands and try to reclaim what you lost many years ago, that is also permitted. Yet I would have you know: none of these things will turn out according to your wishes; on the contrary, even what you think you possess will be taken from you. Finally, I will report all these things to my lord, and whatever shall seem good to him, that shall be done.
Having heard these things, Mehemet was inflamed with anger and hung in uncertainty; he was therefore brought to terms of peace with the Caraman, whom he had decided to crush with all his might. But, moved by these arguments, he thought to himself thus: "While," he said, "I am warring in Anatolia, the Emperor of the Romans will incite the other Christian nations against me, and will set Orchan free; and with the aid of these nations, he will become master of the East, and will cede the lands of the West to the Romans." Revolving these and similar thoughts in his mind, he admits the legates of the Caraman with a serene and gentle face: he speaks threatening words to them at appropriate times; at other times he addresses them gently and kindly, until he had secured the peace by oath, and bade them farewell with an embrace. But to the Emperor’s legates he answered these words: "We shall shortly be at Adrianople; when we have arrived there, set forth to us all things that are necessary for the Emperor and the city; whatever you may ask, I am prepared to provide." Having used these and other flattering speeches, he dismissed them. Mehemet, therefore, crossing the strait in a few days, arrived at Adrianople; and immediately he sent one of his servants into the region situated on the banks of the Strymon, who was to forbid the revenues granted to the Emperor from being paid to him; and he expelled the administrators and stewards of those revenues, who had received a pension for only one year. Having accomplished this, he embarked upon another undertaking, very harmful and ruinous to the Romans. As winter approached, he ordered edicts to be promulgated throughout every province of the West and East, and commanded that a thousand master builders, along with laborers in proportion to the number of craftsmen, and lime-burners, be assembled in every place, according to the size of the population; and, to say everything in a word, all things...
necessary for the completion of the work and the gathering of materials might be ready at the approach of spring, for the building of a castle at the sacred mouth above Constantinople. When the Romans heard this bitter report—those in Constantinople, those in all of Asia and Thrace, and the Christians dwelling in the islands—they were consumed with anguish and sorrow of heart. They had no converse or speech among themselves other than: "Now the end of the city has approached; now are the tokens of the ruin of our race; now are the days of the Antichrist. What shall we become, or what shall we do? Let our life be taken from us, O Lord, and let not the eyes of thy servants see the destruction of the city, nor let thine enemies say, 'Master, where are the saints who protect it?'" This cry was not only shouted with wailing and weeping by those in the city, but by the Christians dwelling scattered through Anatolia, the islands, and in the West, who sent forth the same words mixed with tears and lamentations.
Mehemets, now that spring had begun, sent everywhere to gather craftsmen and laborers. But the Emperor sent ambassadors to Adrianople—not to ask for what he desired, nor to seek to receive double the revenue—but the ambassadors spoke to him in this manner: "It is now the hundredth year, or even more, since Adrianople was taken from us by your great-grandfather Morat, son of Orchan; and from that time, no one of the race of princes descending from him has ever conceived of placing a hut, let alone a tower, in the vestibule of the city after the treaties were established. For although the cause of war might arise and both sides would join battle, they afterwards descended to conditions of peace, and once concord was reconciled, things were restored to a tranquil state. For your grandfather, Mehemetes, wishing to build a fortress from the foundations on the eastern shore of the strait, long and much, as a son is wont to do with a father, besought the Emperor Manuel and tried to persuade him until he should obtain this from him. He finally yielded to him and permitted him to build the castle on the eastern shore, since for many years before, all of Anatolia had been possessed by his ancestors. But you, with whom we behave peacefully and as is fitting, are seen to wish, without a doubt, to interdict the navigation of the Euxine Sea, to ward off the Franks from it, to starve and consume the city with hunger, and to cut off the revenues which are received in it from the taxes on merchandise. Cease from this plan, we beseech you; and we shall keep a faithful and integral friendship with you, such as we had with your excellent father, the ruler. Furthermore, if you command us, we are prepared to pay tribute."
To this, Mehemetes replied: "I am not seizing anything that belongs to the city, which possesses nothing outside the ditches nor has any dominion. For if I wished to build a fortress at the sacred mouth, no law forbids me from doing so. For all things are under my authority, and the fortresses situated to the east of the mouth, even within them, Turks dwell—
and those in the West that are uninhabited are mine; for the Romaioi do not have the safety to dwell in them. Or do you not know in what straits and dire distress my father was placed, when the Emperor was allied with the Hungarians? Those men, having come by land, crossed the Hellespont by sea bringing along the Frankish triremes; and having blocked the strait of Kallipolis, they would not grant my father passage. But he, having ascended as far as the place near the sacred mouth, and at the small fortress which his father had built, crossed over with his scouts, God consenting. For the Emperor's triremes were watching there to prevent the crossing; but I was sitting in Adrianople, being a child, awaiting the arrival of the Hungarians. The Hungarians were plundering the regions around Varna, and the Emperor was rejoicing, and the race of the Muslims was distressed, and the Cavurides were rejoicing. Then my father, having crossed over after many dangers, swore to build another fortress on the western shore, opposite that which is situated toward the East. He did not have time to do it, but I intent to do this through the help of God. Why do you hinder me? Is it not permitted for me to do what I wish in my own territory? Go away, tell the Emperor: "The present ruler is not like those who preceded him; what they could not accomplish, he can do promptly and easily; and what they did not wish, he desires and wills." And whoever comes hereafter on behalf of this matter shall be flayed alive.
When the envoys heard the answer of the tyrant, breathing wrath and fury, they returned to the city and reported everything to the Emperor. Then all the citizens of the city, seized with anxiety and fear, spoke to each other saying: "This is he who is about to enter the city and devastate it, and will bring all under the yoke, and shall trample the sacred things under foot. He will level the noble and distinguished temples to the ground; and the relics of god-bearing men and of martyrs deposited in them, he will scatter and destroy across the squares and the crossroads." "Woe to us! What shall we do? Where shall we flee?" These and other things the wretches, weeping, lamented concerning their own lives, sending forth words broken by cries and wailing. But Mehemet, as spring had just begun and the month of March had already passed, lime had already been made ready, in very many kilns at Cata-
phygia, which were turned out daily; and from Nicomedia and Heraclea of the Pontus, beams were brought, and from Anatolia, stones. In accordance with the command, all those in authority, those in the provinces of Anatolia and the West, arrived, bringing with them those who had been pressed into service. Then the governor also departed from Adrianople and arrived at the place where he intended to set the foundation of the fortress. And having arrived at a slope below Sosthenion, called from of old Phonea, he determined to lay the foundation there in a triangular shape, which was also carried out. He ordered the name of the fortress to be called Paschesen B (32), which, when Hellenized, signifies 'head-cutter,' having opposite to it the fortress which his grandfather had built. He distributed the construction thus: to Halil Pasha he gave one of the corners lying by the sea, to build one tower of immense size, and as solid as an acropolis; to Zaganos, another in the other corner lying on the land, also a large one; to Saritsia another in the third corner; these three towers were to serve as bulwarks and acropolises, built at their own expense. The wall and the other construction of the fortress the governor himself took upon himself. And it was possible to see the crowds streaming from all parts of the earth, together with the *Cadisi*, that is to say the judges, since the tyrant had ordained the death penalty for those who refused. And having divided the building by the cubit for each craftsman—the craftsmen were about one thousand, and with each craftsman two assistants near him outside the wall, and inside, as many again, both craftsmen and assistants. Those who were carrying stones, lime, and baked bricks were beyond number. And even the nobles at times worked as assistants, offering stones and lime, having observed the cruelty of the tyrant. The materials, both from the opposite shore and for the entirety of Byzantium, were taken from the ruins of the once great monuments that lay there; from which they also transported some columns from the ruins of the church of the Taxiarch Michael (33). Some of those in the city, moved by zeal, went out to hinder the Turks, but they were all captured and died by the sword.
The Emperor, therefore, seeing that the tyrant's designs were reaching their conclusion, turned to another course.
And so, having sent envoys, he sought to obtain from him garrisons to protect the Romans in the villages near the city, so that the Turks, passing through, might not damage their crops, since harvest-time was already near. He even sent him various gifts, and daily provisions for food and drink, compelled by necessity and force, honoring the fierce dragon as if it were a necessity.
But Mehemed sent some of his own servants, with orders to look diligently and keep watch, that they should in no wise hinder those Turks who were driven or sent into the fields to pasture mules, horses, or other beasts of burden that were being used in the construction of the castle, so that they might suffer no injury from them; rather, they were to let them graze freely. If, however, the Romans in their indignation attempted to resist, then they too were ordered to join with the Turks and together resist the Romans.
At that same time, the son of Spendiar, the son-in-law of Morat—married to the sister of Mehemed, whom the narrative has previously mentioned—obeying the public decree of the prince, set out from Adramyttion with his followers, coming to offer his own labor to the prince in the construction of the castle. When he had approached near to the tower which is called Epibata, he began to make his own men—the retinue he was leading—proceed on foot; and they drove their horses, unbridled, and the other beasts of burden that were carrying their baggage and packs, into the crops of the Romans. There, the grain, other vegetables, and legumes were devastated and destroyed. A certain Roman, seeing the damage being done to his carefully cultivated and plowed fields, ran up and drove the horses from the field. One of the Turkish grooms struck the Roman. Other relatives of the man who had been struck ran up, and then another, and likewise, from the opposite side, the Turks. A clash ensued, and some fell on both sides, Roman and Turkish.
The next day, Kagiabeg—for such was his name—approached the prince. After saluting him according to custom, he recounted all that had occurred at Epibata. The prince, scorning to learn the matter more accurately from anyone else or to investigate it further, suddenly ordered Kagiabeg to depart in haste, surrounded by his own cohort, and to cut the inhabitants of that village into pieces with the sword, an order which was then carried out. For the soldiers suddenly rushed upon the reapers who had gone out in the morning to harvest, and slaughtered about forty of them. This was the origin of the war which followed, and of the destruction of the Roman people.
Upon learning of this, the Emperor ordered the gates of the city to be closed, and all the Turks he happened to find within the city he bound and placed in prison, releasing them again after three days had passed. For what else could he do? Among those who were captured in the city were eunuch boys from the palace of the prince.
A, who, having been brought before the emperor, said: "If you release us, O king, before the sun inclines toward the west, we will be grateful to you; but if it is after sunset, and we are not found before the prince, know that being released after that will not be pleasant for us, but rather deadly. Therefore, show us mercy and release us at this hour; if not, command that our heads be cut off; for it is better to die by your hands than by the destroyer of the common world." Having heard these things, the emperor was moved in his resolve and released them at that hour. And having sent envoys to the tyrant, he said: "Since you have preferred the matters of war, and I am unable to persuade you to follow either oaths or flatteries, do what you will. For I take refuge in God, and if it is His will to give this city into your hands, who is able to gainsay it? But if He again implants peace in your heart, I will gladly accept that as well. However, for the present, you are released from the treaties and oaths by which you bound yourself; I shall henceforth keep the gates of the city closed, and I will defend those within as best I can; you, in the meantime, rule as a greater power, until the just judge renders the righteous verdict for both me and you." Having heard these things, the barbarian, not even troubling himself to think of any excuse or apology, immediately ordered that the proclamation of war be made. The emperor, foreseeing the future, had six months prior kept the fortresses in good repair, and had brought the villagers near the city inside; and they brought inside the harvested wheat and the winnowed grain. C The prince Mehemet meanwhile completed the fortress in all respects, with a wall and towers built to a thickness of thirty spans, and with a corresponding height. And in the tower that Halil Pasha had built, he placed bronze cannons which discharged stones weighing over six hundred pounds. He placed Pheruz Aga [(36)], his most faithful servant, in charge of the guard of the fortress; and he commanded him that ships, triremes, biremes, vessels, and boats, whatever might sail from the Hellespont to the Pontus, or from the Pontus to the Hellespont, of whatever lordship or dominion they might be, whether Genoese, Venetian, Constantinopolitan, Trapezuntine, Amysine, Sinopian, or even, he said, if they belong to my own subjects, they are to be prohibited from sailing past unless they first, having lowered their sails, pay the duty to the navigator, by which toll they may pass; and whichever ship does not obey, let it be sunk, shattered by a cannon shot. Having ordered these and other things, the arrogant tyrant, having also given him four hundred youths for the guard of the small fort, went himself to Adrianople, having completed the whole matter in four months, already of the
second year of his reign, from the creation of the world 6960 (of Christ 1452).
CHAPTER XXXV
Mehemetes revolves designs for the occupation of Constantinople. A caster of bombards casts a great bronze cannon for Mehemetes. A Venetian ship sailing the Bosphorus is sunk, its captain and passengers captured and cruelly put to death by Mehemetes' order. The power of the bombards is tested at Adrianople. Mehemetes calls Halil Bassa to him by night and discusses with him plans for the subjugation of Constantinople. Halil, thinking he has been delivered from great danger, departs from Mehemetes, joyful.
Summer having now passed and the autumn season beginning, Mehemetes, residing at home, allowed no rest to his eyelids, but by night and by day he had the care of the city, how he might take it, how he might become its master. While he was still in the small fort and busy building, there came out of the city a certain craftsman, a Hungarian by birth, an artisan of the highest caliber, who made cannons for stone-throwing. This man had long before come to Constantinople and, having signaled his craft to the ministers of the emperor, they reported it to the emperor. But the emperor, having assigned him a daily allowance not worthy of his knowledge, nor even that meager and trifling sum, they did not pay the craftsman. Wherefore, despairing of his livelihood, he left the city and on a certain day ran to the Barbarian. And he, receiving him gladly and treating him honorably with food and clothing, gave him a salary as great as, had the emperor given him a fourth part of it, he would never have fled from Constantinople. Being asked by the ruler, therefore, if he could create a foundry to cast a cannon carrying a stone of enormous size, insofar as regards the strength and thickness of the city wall, he replied: "I am able, if you wish, to construct a foundry of the size of the stone shown to me. For I know the walls of the city accurately; not only those, but even the walls of Babylon, I could reduce to dust with stones discharged by my cannon. Everything that belongs to my art and work I will accomplish duly. But as for the range of the shot, I neither know nor assert it." Hearing this, the ruler said, "Construct the foundry for me, and I myself will see to the discharge of the stone." They began to gather bronze. The craftsman then fashioned the model of the engine. In three months, therefore, a certain monster, terrible and extraordinary, was constructed and cast.
At that time, as a certain Venetian captain named Ricius was sailing with a large ship from the sacred mouth toward the fort of Bascesen, and not [furling its sails, the men of the fort shot an enormous stone, and the ship sank...]
having lowered the sails, they hurled an enormous stone from the castle, which shattered the ship; and as it sank into the depths, the captain, with thirty others, boarded a small boat and escaped to the shore. But the Turks apprehended them, and having bound their hands and necks in chains, passing them through as if in a single line, conducted them to the prince, who was then residing at Didymoteichon. He ordered all of them to be beheaded; and the captain to be put to death by a stake driven through his anus, and their bodies to be left unburied—which I myself saw a few days later, while I was staying there. After departing from Didymoteichon in the month of January, he went to Adrianople, and having prepared all sorts of martial equipment, he wished to test the cannon which that artisan had cast. And having skillfully placed it before the great gate of the courtyard of the palace—which had been built by him in that same year—and having carefully inserted the stone and measured the powder, he intended to discharge it on the following day; and it was made known throughout all of Adrianople so that they might have in mind the roar and the thunderous, heaven-shaking crash, lest any, hearing it suddenly and unexpectedly, should remain speechless, and pregnant women should miscarry their embryos. In the morning, therefore, he applied fire to the powder, and the spirit being heated, and the stone having been struck, it was released from the cannon with a heavy, air-borne noise that filled the air with smoke and mist. The roar reached as far as a hundred stadia in length; and the stone fell a mile away from the place whence it was discharged. And where it fell, there occurred a pit about one fathom deep. Such is the power of the mixture of powders that hurls the stone. The prince, therefore, having both by night and by day every care and preoccupation, whether lying down or rising, and whether inside or outside his court, [was considering] by what war and by what engine he would take Constantinople. Often, when evening came, with only two companions, sometimes riding on horseback, at other times on foot, wandering through the whole of Adrianople in the guise of a soldier, he would listen to the things that were said about him. For if any of the common people grasped in his mind that it was the prince, and wished to salute him with acclamations as is the custom, he himself would immediately inflict a deadly wound without delay, neither sparing nor pitying; but just as someone feels a sense of pleasure in crushing a flea, so he too, deserving of death himself, took delight in killing [others] with his own hand. On one of the nights, about the second watch, he sent some of the palace guards to bring Halil Pasha to him. They arrived at his house and, having explained the message to his eunuchs, they entered the bedroom and announced how the prince was calling for him. He, becoming trembling, and having renounced himself, and having embraced his wife and children, went away, carrying with him a gold dish full of [index: entries preserved] Ismael Bullialdi notes. Return to Constantinople safely, on the ship of that best of men, Antonio Rizzo, who later suffered martyrdom for the faith of Christ.
thinking that this was his own, he embraced his wife and children and departed, taking with him a golden dish full of gold coins. For he was always tormented inwardly by fear on account of the reason I have previously explained. Entering the prince’s bedchamber, he saw him sitting and dressed; and having bowed down and placed the dish before him, he was questioned by the prince with these words: "What does this mean, Lala?"—as if one were to say in our common tongue, *tata*, that is to say, tutor. He replied, "My lord, it is the custom for the satraps and the nobles, whenever the prince summons any of them at an untimely hour, not to approach him empty-handed. Indeed, I have brought nothing from my own wealth in approaching you, but rather I offer you your own gifts from your own stores." The prince replied: "I am in no need of your things; I will give you more than you possess; one thing I ask of you: that you permit me to take possession of Constantinople." At these words Halil, who had always protected the Romans, and whom they used as a right hand, filling that hand with gifts—so much so that he was called by all *Cavur Ortachi*, that is, fellow and helper of the infidels—was terrified. Then Halil, replying to the prince, said: "My lord, God, who has subjected the greatest part of the Roman dominion to your empire, will also deliver the city to you. For as it seems to me, with the help of God and the forces in which you excel gathered together, it will not escape your hands. I and all your servants will exert our efforts for you, not only with money, but even by shedding our blood profusely; be certain and secure in this purpose of ours." These words pacified that savage and cruel man for a time; he said to Halil, "Do you see this bolster? I have spent the whole night passing it from one side of the bed to the other, lying down and keeping vigil, and sleep has not come to my eyes. I warn you, therefore, do not let silver or gold corrupt you or turn you from your purpose. Let us fight the Romans with a firm and constant mind; trusting in the decree of God and the prayers of the Prophet, we shall take the city." Having used these and similar flattering words, he dismissed him—he whose spirit, mindful of itself and conscious of many things, was agitated, and whose blood was kindled—having sent him away in peace. He plotted and contrived everything against the city, and spent all those nights without sleep. He even sketched the location and circumference of the city on paper, and shared it with those who knew the state of the ramparts and walls of the city. He weighed the plans of where and how the engines were to be moved, the mantlets to be constructed, the siege-towers to be advanced, and where the mines were to be dug so as to reach the moat, and where finally the ladders were to be brought up to the wall; and, to put it briefly, he took care that all the apparatus, pondered and sketched by night, should be manufactured and brought to completion in the morning.
CHAPTER XXXVI
A 1057 But let us return to the city of Constantinople, and let us consider what the Constantinopolitans were pondering in their minds, and what care and anxiety they showed so that they might preserve [the city], snatched from the hands of Nebuchadnezzar [the sultan]. The emperor had already sent [envoys] to Rome beforehand, asking for aid, and that they might reach an agreement on the concord and union that had taken place in Florence; and that the pope’s name should be mentioned in the Great Church; and that the Patriarch Gregory D (40) would return to his throne. He had also called for some of the pope’s [men] to arrive, in order to pacify the implacable hatred of the schism. The pope had sent the Cardinal of Poland, Isidore, formerly the Archbishop of Russia—a man prudent and sober, and learned in orthodox dogmas, a Roman by race, and himself a venerable father who had been at the council in Florence, as the narrative previous has shown. And when he went to the island of Chios with a very large Genoese ship, he spent enough days there until the merchants of the ship could do their business, and sell the necessary items, and obtain what they sought, waiting also for another ship that was intended to sail to Caffa. The cardinal 41 thus, having with him up to fifty Italians, hired also a great many other Latins from Chios. And when the ship they were expecting finally appeared, they left Chios and sailed toward Constantinople, arriving there in the month of November of the year 6961 [1452]. The emperor received him graciously and honored him as was fitting, and they came to the discussions of the union; and finding the emperor inclined toward this, as well as some of the Church [officials], the greater part of the 42 priestly and monastic order—abbots, archimandrites, nuns—[objected]. What do I say, "the greater part"? For the nuns moved me to say and write that none of them all, and that even the emperor himself, had leaned toward it only feignedly. Nevertheless, those appearing [to agree] according to the opinion of the union—priests and deacons of the clergy, along with the emperor and the senate—met in the Great Church so that they might celebrate the divine liturgy to God with common concord, and offer up prayers with a sincere mind. Then the schismatic party went to the monastery of the Pantocrator, to the cell of Gennadius—formerly called George Scholarius—and said to him, "What shall we do?" He, keeping himself enclosed, took paper and, having written his opinion, made known his advice through the writing. The things written therefore declared thus: "Wretched Romans, into what have you been led astray, and why have you distanced yourself from the hope of God, and put your hope in the power of the Franks C ..."
for by them you have lost the very city and the true religion, which will soon be overthrown in it. Woe! Be merciful to me, O Lord. I call you to witness before me that I am innocent of such a fault and offense, and that I am pure. Pay attention, miserable citizens, to what is being done: while you are increasing the miseries of the servitude which hangs over your necks, you have denied the faith received from your fathers and ancestors, and have professed impiety. Woe to you when you are judged." A Having written these and many other things, and having nailed them to the door of his cell, he shut himself inside, and the paper was read. Then the nuns, who were considered pure and who lived in God with orthodoxy—in accordance with their own judgment and that of their teacher Gennadius, together with the superiors, spiritual men, and the rest of the priests and laypeople—cried out an anathema; and they anathematized the decree of the synod, and those who had accepted it, those who were accepting it, and those who were going to accept it.
The common and marketplace rabble, having gone out from the courtyard of the monastery into the wine shops, holding in their hands the cups full of undiluted wine, were anathematizing the Unionists, drinking to the intercession of the image of the Mother of God, and begging her to become the protectress and helper of the city—just as once she had fought against Chosroes, and the Chagan, and against the Arabs, so too now against Mehmet. "For," they said, "we have no need of the help of the Latins, nor of the union; far from us be the worship of the Azymites."
But the Christians who had assembled in the Great Church, having offered earnest prayer to God and having listened to the words of the cardinal, accepted the decree of union. They also agreed unanimously that once the danger from the Turks had passed and tranquility had returned, some select, distinguished, and upright men should examine the decree, so that if there were anything that did not perfectly reflect the truth, they might correct and amend it. In that agreement, therefore, they consented that a common liturgy should be celebrated in the Great Church, performed by Italians and Greeks, and that Pope Nicholas should be commemorated in the sacred diptychs, as well as the exiled patriarch Gregory. These sacred mysteries were completed in the month of December, on the 12th day, in the year of the world 6961 (A.D. 1452). There were also many who did not accept the offering of the antidoron, as if it were a defiled sacrifice performed in the unionist liturgy. But the cardinal, searching every heart and every intent of the Greeks, was not unaware of the intrigues.
Many, indeed, abstained from the sacred gifts offered, because they considered that liturgy, celebrated for the sake of reconciling concord, to be an impure and abominable sacrifice. Meanwhile, the cardinal explored and scrutinized the minds and hearts and the purpose of the Greeks, whose fraud and deceit did not escape him. Yet, since he was of that same race, he strove to ensure that aid was brought to the city; he acted more slowly and remissly, however, and the events that subsequently followed provided a legitimate excuse for the Pope, and many ascribed their downfall to the will of God, who directs all things to a useful end.
But the populace, savage and hostile to what is good, the germ and root of arrogance, the branch of vain glory, the flower of pride, the dregs of the Greek race—which, though contemptible itself, holds other nations in disdain—regarded all these actions as if they had never taken place. Those, therefore, who took the side of the Unionists, conversing with the schismatics, used these words: "Leave it alone, and let us see if God removes this enemy from our midst—this huge dragon who stands in battle array against us and boasts that he will devour this city utterly. If God destroys him, it will then be clear and manifest to you whether we have returned to concord and friendship with those who use unleavened bread."
When the wretches boasted in this way, it did not enter their minds that the oath, so often repeated by them for the sake of establishing peace and concord among the Christian Churches—the Council held at Lyons in the days of the first Palaiologos, the Council held at Florence in the days of the last of the Palaiologan emperors, and now, in this divine and holy mystery—would, in consequence of the indissoluble excommunication added in the name of the Holy Trinity, lead to their memory and that of the city being blotted out from among men.
O wretches, why do you busy yourselves with vain thoughts in your hearts? Behold, your priests and priestesses, your monks, your sextons, both men and women, who would not partake of the immaculate body and blood from the hands of the Greek priests—who administer the divine things according to the ecclesiastical tradition of the East—claiming that they are defiled and not Christian, shunning the blessing of the priests, and calling the temples altars of the gentiles: tomorrow they shall fall into the hands of the Barbarians to be defiled and polluted in both soul and body.
For I saw with my own eyes a nun, instructed and learned in the divine Scriptures, not only feeding on meat and clothed in barbarian dress, but also offering sacrifice to the false prophet, and shamelessly confessing her impiety, having cast off all shame and modesty. But why have I allowed myself to leap over an interval of five months? The day that follows will bring with it this calamity to be recounted with tears. The Emperor, suspecting that he would be besieged by the tyrant at the beginning of spring, sent some of the nobles of his court to the islands and other Christian provinces to purchase grain and all kinds of legumes, and whatever food was necessary, expecting the arrival of the tyrant in the spring. There were, therefore, four very large ships sent to the island of Chios, for the purpose of bringing back grain, wine, oil, dried figs, chickpeas, barley, and other legumes.
and they were awaiting another cargo ship from the Peloponnese. And thus, when there were five of them altogether, with great and brave crews—I mean also very many, and with no small amount of full armor—they prepared to sail to Constantinople. All the islands, therefore, were in distress and anxiety concerning the city. And some surmised that it would be stormed and captured by the Barbarians; others, however, supposed that just as his father and grandfather, in their own times, having desired to take it, appeared to have labored in vain, so too would this man follow the same path.
CHAPTER XXXVII
*Mehmed orders that great bronze cannon, or bombard, to be transported near Constantinople. The Turks occupy cities situated on the Euxine Sea, and towns adjacent to the Propontis, except for Selymbria. The Greeks keep themselves enclosed within the walls of Constantinople and suffer from discord over the reconciled union of the Churches. Gennadius adds fuel to the discord. Ducas reproaches the Greeks for their unsound mind and persistence in schism. Mehmed gathers his forces. He encircles the city with a siege, and the Greeks show themselves more and more alienated from the union of the Churches.*
The month of January having passed, and as the beginning of February arrived, the prince ordered the furnace to be transported to Constantinople, and having yoked thirty wagons, sixty very strong oxen—I mean oxen drawn from oxen—dragged it from behind. And on both sides of the furnace there walked two hundred men, so that, lest it should stumble on the road, by pulling it this way and that, they might keep it in equilibrium. Fifty carpenters preceded the wagons, and two hundred laborers, to build wooden bridges to level out the unevenness of the road. And so February and March passed away, by which time it had been hauled to a certain place five miles distant from the city. For Karaca Bey had previously been sent with a force to the fortresses of the Pontus, namely Mesembria, Achelous, Byzus, and the rest, and had brought them over to himself. C Similarly, he took by war the towers of Saint Stephen lying toward Selymbria, slaughtering all those who were within; the remaining towers, however, submitted, as did their crews. All who yielded to the conqueror were saved, but those who resisted were beheaded. Selymbria alone resisted stoutly. Therefore, having brought the equipment to the place where they were ordered, and with a command to Karaca Bey to guard it, he arrived with his forces and began to make forays into the regions around the city, and to prevent the Romans from coming out through the gates of the city. For during the entire winter, troops of Mysians and Paphlagonians had had their winter quarters stationed around the city under three standards, so that they might suppress the Romans' eruptions against the Turks and prevent them from making sorties from the city. The Romans, indeed, could not go out beyond the gates, being surrounded by such great enemy forces; nevertheless, they made forays by sea with biremes and triremes, and carried off plunder from the maritime villages of the Turks even as far as Cyzicus; and they also took captives.
this is the first page of the chain)
of many, some of whom were slain, while others were brought to Constantinople and sold. By the time this period of light skirmishes had passed and the days of the fast began to be numbered, the dissension in the Church did not cease; rather, one could see a strange discord among those entrusted with listening to the reasonings of men. When the Christians came to confess their faults, they were questioned by these men as to whether they had communicated with those who were cut off from the Church, or if they had chanced to hear a liturgy from a Unionist priest. These things were considered a severe canon (48) and a heavy penance. Yet after having performed the penance according to custom, he who was deemed worthy by participation in the Body and Blood of the Lord was forbidden, under a heavy penalty, to approach and receive them from the Unionist priests. For they said that these were not priests, nor were the offerings perfect. For if they were called to a funeral of the dead, or to a memorial of one who had died, and a Unionist priest appeared there, they would immediately strip off their phelonia (49) and flee as if from fire. The Great Church was also considered by them a den of demons and a Greek gentile temple. Where were the candles? Where was the oil for lighting the lamps? Everything was in darkness, and no one was there to dispel it. The holy sanctuary appeared desolate, foreshadowing the desolation that was soon to befall it due to the sins and iniquities of those who lived within it. Gennadius also, while in seclusion, continued to teach, imposing curses upon those who embraced peace and reconciliation.
After these things, I happened upon a noblewoman who had been taken captive, and she told me how, when she was seized by the pains of childbirth on the Holy and Great Wednesday of that year, she had called for her spiritual father, named Jacob, and made her confession. He urged her to receive Holy Communion. When she asked the old man if there were any hindrance to her receiving it from the hands of the priest who was officiating in the chapel within her own house (for that priest had, on the 12th of December, merely been present with the Unionists in the Great Church, but had not actually communicated with them; for he had not been reckoned among those concelebrating at the altar from the beginning, but had happened to be outside with others Ismael Bullialdus' notes.
church where heretics had been present, and had not communicated, since he had not been chosen into the number of those ministering at the altar from the beginning of the liturgy; but he had stood outside the chancels with others who had arrived later, and who had worn nothing other than their sacred vestments). The pneumatic said to her: "It is permitted to you; God will forgive you. Go, communicate, casting away all darkness. For he is a priest and a minister; communicate without doubt."
But she, fearing the aged man’s decree because it was unobstructed, for he was on the side of the schismatics, calls to herself one Neophyte by name, and reveals to him the dissolution of her pneumatic’s command; for this Neophyte himself was enjoying boldness of speech, and was acting as a spiritual guide in the houses of the nobility and of the great ones. But he forbade her, saying: "It is unforgivable. For if you take communion from his hands, you have eaten bread and drunk wine." O the extent of thy long-suffering, Christ King! O dark and blind one! If the priest had been a Latin, O you who are blinded by darkness, your folly might have been excused by some reason, however absurd; namely, that he had recited prayers to God in the Latin tongue, and that the bread was not leavened, and that warm water was not used, and other such absurd accusations, which an orthodox person would never utter with his mouth, nor would he murmur even in the slightest against divine mysteries performed in this manner; for anyone who dared such things would deserve to be stoned. What? Or how can you gainsay divine mysteries celebrated in your own tongue? What can you oppose to those prayers which are in common use for you with the other priests of the East? You cannot allege anything else, O vain Pharisee, except that you are pure and intact, and separated from the rest of Christians—I will add, and excommunicated.
That noble woman, wavering in spirit between these contrary commands, was blocked by her own reasoning, and on that day did not partake; and through the night she remained uncommunicated. For if death had followed, that soul would have been sealed with the loss of the Spirit on account of Neophyte, and the evil spirit that dwelt within him. But let us return to the waves of our narrative, and let us look upon the raging sea, with the pilot cast out, seeking to swallow the ark of Noah and drag it into the deep, and let us contemplate the clean birds, as if they were unclean, being cast out to be torn apart by the claws of the unpolluted.
For the tyrant, beginning in the month of March, sent messengers and heralds into all the provinces, ordering each man assigned to the army to come to fight against the city. All, therefore, who were receiving pay under registered names arrived; and to these were added an infinite number of those who followed the camp of their own accord. For all who heard that the city was to be besieged, to the very boys who, on account of their youth...
could hardly walk, as well as the old men burdened by years, hurried along. The citizens of Constantinople, meanwhile, supplicated God that the tyrant, whose arrival by chariot had been announced, might not assault the city during Holy Week. Therefore, on Friday of the week of Renewal (53)—that is, the Friday after Pascha—Nabuchodonosor came to the gates of Jerusalem, and having pitched his tents in front of the Charsi gate, behind the hill. And all his force, from the Wood Gate (55), which lies near the palace, as far as the Golden Gate (56) which faces south; and further, from the Wood Gate as far as the Cosmidium (57), and from the south to a width as great as the vineyards, already laid waste by Caracza, could occupy, all his forces pitched their camps. Therefore, on the sixth day of April, the Friday after Pascha.
Notes by Ismaël Boulliau
(53) The week of Renewal, or restoration, is that which follows the day of Pascha: of which Codinus Curopalates makes mention in c. 14 of his book *De officiis aulae Constantinopolitanae*. It is also called the "new" week, on account of the catechumens renewed by baptism, who had been baptized at Pascha. The Latin commentary by Balsamon on the Apostolic Canons, canon 69, of which the Greek text does not survive, has it thus: "The week of Renewal is considered as the great day of the Lord itself." In that year the golden number or cycle of the moon was 10, the cycle of the sun 6, the letter G. Pascha was April 1, a Friday; the week of Renewal was April 6; Pentecost was May 20; the Sunday of All Saints was May 27. According to Ducas, therefore, the siege of Constantinople began on the 6th of April. According, however, to Leonard of Chios, and those who followed him, Bizarus, it began on the 5th of April. Phranzes asserts that it began to be besieged on the 1st of April, lib. 2, c. 8. The Turkish histories report the assault on the 17th of Rebiul-euel, which was the 28th of March.
(55) The Wood Gate is that which is nearest to the western angle of the city. It was once called the Blachernian, because it was near the temple of the Blachernae. See Gyllius, lib. 1, ch. 20; Leunclavius, *Pandectae Hist. Turc.* 200, who calls it Xylokercon. But I am persuaded that they were different, and that this Xylokercon is the same one that Ducas calls the Kercoporta, which had been kept closed for a long time. That we may believe and assert this, our authority is Cantacuzenus, lib. 3, c. 9. He also speaks secretly with his friends who were staying in Constantinople, acting as to how they might deliver the city to him. They promised that they would break through the gate which is called Xylokercon, which had been closed for many years by a wall, and would bring him into the city.
(56) The Golden Gate was still closed. It was formerly called the Selymbrian gate, as Leunclavius notes in the cited place. Beyond it, outside the walls, a fountain still exists, near which a temple of the Blessed Mary Theotokos had been built. The labors of Hercules, adorning the Golden Gate, are seen sculpted in marble. But when I viewed them with Apno, they were coated with the whiteness of lime, as was the whole circuit of the walls: so that the elegance of the sculpture escaped the eyes.
(57) "As far as the Cosmidium." Zonaras, *Annal.* tom. III, in the life of Romanus Lecapenus: from which it is clear that it was situated outside the city, toward the shore of the Ceratine gulf. And so also in the *Annals*: "And the horsemen, with the infantry that preceded them, occupied the Cosmidium": having found little resistance from the Romans about the bridge there and the so-called Perforated stone. And the ships, and the vessels, and the *dromones* anchored there. And those who were within the walls saw their upright tents. And in the following chapter, Ducas sufficiently shows that the Cosmidium was situated outside the city, at the shore of the Ceratine gulf. That place, therefore, was situated at the extreme shore of the Ceratine gulf, near the bridge of St. Mamas: and it can be no other than that which is called today Atbazari: to which is near the mosque called IVP, in which the pontiff of the college of doctors and jurists, called the Mufti, after the new emperor has obtained the empire, with certain prayers added, girds him with the scimitar.
Mahomet girded the city with a siege. From the day that the reconciliation of concord was made in the Great Church, the Constantinopolitans shunned it as if it were a synagogue of the Jews; nor was there in it either offering, or burnt-offering, or incense. If any of the priests happened to celebrate the divine liturgy on some solemn day, those who were praying would stand there until the time of the offering of the sacred gifts; and then all would go out, the women as well as the men, the monks as well as the nuns. What need is there to say more? They considered that temple to be a shrine and an altar of the gentiles, and the sacrifice to be performed just as if it were to Apollo. For this reason, Isaiah, as if out of the mouth of God, says: "Behold, I will proceed to remove this people, and I will remove them with a removal; and I will destroy the wisdom of his wise men, and I will bring to nothing the understanding of his prudent men. Woe to those who take deep counsel, and not by the Lord. Those who take counsel in secret, and their works shall be in darkness, and they shall say, 'Who has seen us? And who shall know us, or what we do?' Therefore thus says the Lord: Woe, rebellious children, you have taken counsel, but not by me, and confirmed your agreements, but not by my Spirit, to add sin to sin." B Meanwhile, Gennadius did not cease to teach and write every day against the Unionists, and, striving to prove them heretics, he aimed his arguments and syllogisms against the most wise and blessed Thomas Aquinas and his writings, as well as against Lord Demetrios Cydones. He had as his companion in the work and adherent from the senate the first Mesazon, who was also the Grand Duke; whose rash impudence against the Latins—or rather against the city itself—burst forth to such a degree that, when the Romans saw the countless army of the Turks (or rather, when they saw them against the city), he said that it was better to see a Turk’s turban reigning in the midst of the city than a Latin tiara. For the people of the city, having despaired, used to say: "Would that the city had been given into the hands of the Latins, who call upon Christ and his mother the Theotokos, and that we had not been cast into the hands of the impious!" The Mesazon preached the contrary of this, as we have related. But Isaiah addressed him, just as he did Hezekiah: "Hear the word of the Lord Sabaoth; behold the days are coming, and they shall take everything that is in your house. And as many things as your fathers have gathered..."
up to this day, they shall go to Babylon, and nothing shall be left; and from your children who shall come out of you, whom you shall beget, they shall take, and they shall make them eunuchs in the house of the king of the Babylonians."
CHAPTER XXXVIII
Constantine and the Galatians attend to the defense of the city, and the Venetians as well. Joannes Justinianus arrives at Constantinople with soldiers and is honored by the emperor. From the beginning of the siege the besieged make sallies against the enemy. The Galatians wish to be on good terms with Mehemet, yet they favor the Byzantines and bring them aid. Mehemet’s fleet approaches near Constantinople. Five ships laden with provisions enter the harbor of Constantinople, though the Turks try in vain to stop them; for this reason Mehemet subjects his Contostaulo, Palda, to insults and blows. Mehemet transports ships and biremes by land from the Bosphorus into the Golden Horn. Mehemet attacks Constantinople by land and shatters the walls with artillery. A remedy is applied to the artillery so that they might not break. An envoy of Joannes Huniades, misled by false opinion, gave pernicious council against the besieged regarding Mehemet’s bombardment. The walls of the city at the gate of St. Romanus are destroyed. The besieged resist strenuously, but Constantine is struck; and so that he might bring Mehemet to peace and the lifting of the siege, he offers a tribute, which Mehemet refuses. Justinianus attempts with poor success to set fire to the Turkish biremes in the Golden Horn. The Turks sink a ship of the Galatians. Mehemet constructs a bridge in the Golden Horn.
But the Emperor Constantine was intent on defending the city, as much as his strength allowed, together with the Genoese inhabitants of Galata. For they also held a fixed conviction in their minds from which it was not easy to move them: that if the city were captured, their own fortress would also be devastated. For this reason they had previously written letters to Genoa, asking that aid and supplies be sent to them. To these the Genoese replied that one ship, which would carry five hundred soldiers to protect the fortress of Galata, would set out for them. The imperial and Venetian inhabitants of the city also detained the Venetian merchant galleys engaged in commerce that had returned from the Maeotic marsh, the Tanais river, and Trapezunt, and did not permit them to return to Venice, so that, if fate should so allow, they might be of help and use to the city. C Joannes Longus, of the Justiniani family, had arrived from Genoa transported in two large ships; these were equipped with many excellent siege engines and other apparatus of war, as well as soldiers distinguished by the vigor of their age and nobility. Joannes himself was a man clever in arraying battle lines and most experienced and skilled in joining combat. The emperor received him kindly and paid the wages of his soldiers; furthermore, he honored him with favors and the rank of Protostrator of the armies. He therefore took upon himself the burden of defending and fighting for that part of the city’s walls adjacent to the palace; for they had noticed the tyrant planting his stone-throwing artillery there, and all his other combat阵 against the walls. Moreover, the emperor even granted him the island of Lemnos by chrysobull, should Mehemet be repulsed and forced to turn back empty-handed, out of those things he hopes to gain from the city. From then on the Latins fought heroically with Joannes, sallying out from the city gates and taking their stand at the outer fortification and in the moat; and the Romans, often leaping even outside the moat, were engaging the Turks, sometimes driving them back, at other times...
dragging captive Turks with them; and with these they joined hand-to-hand combat. This, however, was of very little advantage to the Romans; for, truth be told, a single Roman stood against twenty Turks. What advantage could they reap by engaging in close-quarters combat with the Turks by way of sorties from the gates? Therefore, the counsel was given that the Romans should hold stations along the fortifications, some fighting with javelins, others with arrows; others, using iron canisters, were discharging leaden balls against the enemy. These, five or ten at a time, being the size of Pontic nuts, were emitted all at once by means of igniting powder, and they possessed the power of piercing and penetrating; so that if one were to strike a man clad in iron, it would pierce through his shield and body, and leap into another who was in the way, and from him into yet another, until the force of the powder cooled. By this impact, it was possible for two or three men to be killed at once. The Turks eventually learned this, and they themselves began to use the same, and even more advanced, devices.
Two-thirds of the month of April were passed in a few skirmishes and sudden battles, while the tyrant, having contracted new forces, was augmenting his army. To this army, a countless multitude of soldiers flowed in, both those who had been summoned for service and those who had come of their own accord; those who observed it estimated them to exceed four hundred thousand men. Even before the tyrant came, while he was still at Adrianople, the Genoese of Galata had sent envoys, announcing their unstained friendship toward him and renewing the previously written treaties. He replied that he was their friend and that he would not allow himself to be parted from the affection which he held for them, provided only that they were not found to be assisting the City—which they themselves had promised not to do. Yet, as the outcome proved, one party was deluded and mocked by the other. For the Galatans, knowing how the City had been besieged and encircled in vain in previous times by his ancestors, who had departed with their mission unaccomplished, were persuaded that the same end awaited this prince. Thus, being benevolent and friendly to the Constantinopolitans, they sent auxiliary cohorts from their own towns; and because Mehemed’s friendship appeared to them highly suspect and feigned, they bore aid to the City secretly, as befit them. The tyrant, for his part, was saying to himself: "I shall let the serpent sleep until I have slain the dragon; and then, with one light blow struck to its head, I shall trample it, dizzied." Which, indeed, also happened afterward. At that time, his ships were gathered, arriving by sea, with triremes, biremes, and small boats, up to three hundred in number. The harbor of the City was, therefore, closed by the chain from the part of the gate of the City which is called the [Gate of the] Fair, toward the side of Galata, and the ships were positioned inside in a cluster... D
guarding the harbor and the chain. Now the ships, five in number, one of which was the Emperor’s, carrying a cargo of grain from the Peloponnese, and the other four being hired from the Genoese by the Emperor, had stayed in the harbor of Chios until the entire month of March for some needs of their own. When April arrived, and they wished to weigh anchor, the north wind stood in their way. Consequently, both the citizens and the ships’ crews were in great distress. When the north wind finally subsided and the south wind began to blow, they left the harbor of Chios; and while it blew lightly on the first day, on the second it strengthened, and the ships were violently driven by it. So the people of the city stood waiting for this pleasant arrival, even though it brought them no profit. When the ships appeared, the tyrant, like a wild dragon, immediately rushed against his own triremes and other vessels, saying and ordering them that one of two things must happen: either they must capture the ships or prevent them from entering the harbor. Then the vessels went out and stood waiting for the arrival of the ships, outside the harbor of the Golden Gate. As the ships came along the level path, wishing to pass by the acropolis of Megademetrius to enter the Golden Horn, the vessels blocked the way. For the sea at that hour was calm, the wind not blowing. And it was a strange sight to behold; for the sea, having been covered with the three hundred sails of the Turks and the five massive ships, the sea stretched out like dry land; and because of the missiles, they could not even lower their oars into the waters. But those on the ships, like winged eagles from above, sent down the missiles of the crossbows like lightning bolts, and they shattered the rigging, and no small slaughter of the Turks occurred. But the tyrant, driven by excessive arrogance while riding his horse in the sea, imagined that he could cut through the sea and ride his horse right up to the ships; so great was the fury in his heart, and the armed guard with him. Then, a wind blowing and the sails swelling, the ships cut through their path into the harbor and sailed, while the other vessels remained. For if the fleet of the barbarian had been in front of them at that time, those five ships could have sunk the three hundred. The tyrant, not knowing the science of the sea, only screamed. C His Great Contostaulus did not wish to listen, for he was ordering things unreasonably. Then, angered, the tyrant ordered the fleet to depart to the Double Columns, and for the Great Contostaulus to be brought before him. Having been brought, and thrown to the ground, and stretched out by four [men], he himself, the ruler, struck him with his own hands, giving a hundred blows with a golden rod, the head of which was of pure gold, weighing pounds.
This was five hundred [66]. He himself had prepared it to play with it as a sample. Now the man was of the race of the Bulgarian Elki, and was named Palda, the son of one of the Bulgarian princes [67]. He had been enslaved before the time, had renounced his ancestral worship, and was a servant of Mehemet’s father. He was the same one who had come to Lesbos four years before and had taken a boundless number of captives. He was not a good friend to the pirates, as he would snatch their spoils. And when they saw him being despised and beaten with rods by the tyrant, one of the Azapes took up a stone and, striking him on the head, gouged out one of his eyes. When the ships arrived in the port, the people of the city lowered the chain and gave them entry. Then the tyrant, seeing the large ships—there being eight of them—and the small ones, more than twenty, and the imperial triremes, and the Venetian triremes, and many other small vessels, he understood that it was not possible to take the port, and he devised a noble and brave stratagem. He ordered the thickets behind Galata to be cleared, from the part facing the east, below the Double Column [69], to the other part of Galata situated toward the shore of the Golden Horn, opposite Cosmidion. And having made the road as level as they could, he placed the biremes on rollers [70], and setting up the sails, he ordered them to be dragged by land from the strait of the Holy Mouth [71], and to bring the ships into the Golden Horn; which was done. The boats were moved, and in each one a bowman sat, and another sat at the steering oars; another held the yardarm and shook the sail, another struck a drum, and another played a trumpet, singing a sea-song. And sailing with the wind, the thickets and the torrents were traversed by land, until they reached the water, [where] they D [NOTE: The above text continues from the anchor while incorporating the provided fragments including the Greek/Latin narrative content.]
until they reached the water, [where] they brought eighty of these, being biremes, and left the remainder there. Who has ever seen such a thing? Or who has heard of it? Xerxes bridged the sea, and such a great army passed over it as if it were dry land. But this new Macedonian, and as I think, the last tyrant of his lineage, turned the land into a sea, and drove ships over the crests of the mountains as if they were waves.
