Yet he surpassed Xerxes: for the latter, having crossed the Hellespont, returned having donned the shame of the Athenians. But this man, having crossed the dry land as if it were water, destroyed the Romans, and took the truly golden Athens, the ornament of the world, the queen of cities.
These things were done by sea; and by land, having brought that enormous melting-furnace opposite the wall, he set it near the gate of St. Romanus. And the technician took note; for he had two smaller ones fashioned by the side [of the great one], capable of holding stones of roughly seventy pounds, naturally constructed for the purpose. And whenever he wished to discharge the great one, he would mark the spot, first shooting the small one; and then he would aim at the maximum. And having struck the first blow, those within the city, having heard the report, became struck dumb, and they cried out, "Lord, have mercy." At that time, according to custom, the icon of the all-immaculate Theotokos was found in the palace during the week of New Sunday [Diakainesimos]; and ever since then, they frequently held litanies in the monastery of the Chora, and the icon remained there until the conquest. And when he wished to discharge... [The great cannon of the Hodegetria's arrival: the icon of the most holy Theotokos Hodegetria, on her first appearance, stays in the palace until the great Sunday of Pascha. The Emperor meets this icon as it comes to the gate of the palace; and on the second day, he escorts it as it departs to the high places outside. And having made a memory of the emperors there, the emperor returns.] D
Then was fulfilled that which was spoken by God through Jeremiah, saying: "To what purpose bringest thou me incense from Saba, and cinnamon from a land far off? Your whole burnt offerings are not acceptable, and your sacrifices have not pleased me." For this reason, the Lord says these things: "Behold, I am giving weakness upon this people; and fathers and sons together shall be weak in it; the neighbor and his friend shall perish." The Lord says these things: "Behold, a people comes from the North, and a great nation; and many kings shall be roused from the ends of the earth; they shall seize bow and javelin. It is impudent, and will not show mercy. Its voice is like the surging sea; they shall stand in battle order upon horses and chariots, as fire against thee, daughter of Zion."
Now the sophist of that wickedness, the craftsman, knew a method to prevent the casting from rupturing. For we know that cast vessels, once discharged, if they were not immediately covered and protected by thick woolen felts, would shatter like glass; and even with such care applied, after two or three explosions, the air penetrating the pores of the metal would cause the same result. But what art did he use to prevent it? After the stone had been hurled, the bronze cannon, heating up from the heat of the saltpeter and sulphur, was immediately drenched with oil, whereby the pores being obstructed warded off the injury of the penetrating air; and by the warmth of the oil, the force of the cold was blunted: and thus that machine was sufficient to endure the explosions, until it brought about the destruction of the city. It remained still entire for the tyrant’s use, whenever it pleased him. After a part of the wall was struck and shaken, he was aiming the stone to be discharged again at that same spot; but when Janko’s apocrisiarius [envoy], who was then present, received the intended shot with a laugh, and said to him who was aiming: "If you wish to make the walls fall to the ground with no difficulty, move the equipment to another part of the wall, at a distance of four or five or six fathoms from the first point of impact, and then, leveling it with the first shot, fire another shot. When the two sides have been struck carefully, then fire a third, so that the three shots may be found in the shape of a triangle, and then you will see such a wall falling to the ground."
The plan was pleasing, and thus the craftsman did, and thus it resulted. But from what, having been moved, the Hungarian gave this plan to the tyrant in this way, I shall tell. In that year, the king of Hungary had been designated Emperor of the Romans, and had received the crown from Pope Nicholas. Janko also, who had administered affairs in the name of the curator [regent], having been discharged, the king himself, as emperor, took on the administration of the entire kingdom.
Notes by Ismael Bullialdus
(76) "The king of Hungary." The situation is thus: In the year 1453, on the 10th of February, Ladislaus the Posthumous, son of Albert, king of Hungary, came to Buda; and by Joannes Hunyadi de Corvino, who had been regent of Hungary after the defeat at Varna, and had administered the Hungarian commonwealth, the fortresses as well as the administration of the kingdom were then turned over to him as he assumed power. But because the bad faith of the Turks always rendered them suspect, Corvino undertook to defend the lower parts of Hungary. And having spent many days in the royal court, and with all councils communicated with him, he was honorably dismissed by Ladislaus. But of a peace entered into between Mehmed and Corvino, or of the written instrument of that peace, or a messenger sent to Mehmed, Hungarian history makes no mention. Indeed, when Ladislaus took up the administration of the kingdom, Corvino immediately girded himself against the Turks, with Joannes Capistranus as his exhorter.
And, having been crowned by Pope Nicholas and having girded himself with his authority, Iancu was ejected from the viceregal power, and the king and sovereign took upon himself all the care of the government. Having, however, oaths of affection with Mehemet determined for a period of three years, and with one and a half years already fulfilled, he sent word to Mehemet, saying: "I have surrendered the kingdom to my lord, and from this hour I am not the one to defend what I had promised; take the documents you gave, and return ours, and behave as you wish toward the king of Hungary." This was the cause of the arrival.
Regarding the counsel, which, being a Christian, he ought not to have given, I write what I heard. It is said that after the third defeat (77), which the narrative has already related, while Iancu was fleeing—and not as he wished, or as was becoming, having reached his own territory—he happened to encounter one of the spiritual men, and as he was recounting the events of the defeat and was distressed at how fortune had abandoned the affairs of the Romans and looked with favorable eyes upon the impious, the old man replied: "Know, son, unless total destruction comes upon the Romans, fortune will not smile upon the Christians; for it is necessary for the city to be destroyed by the Turks, and thus the misfortunes of the Christians will have an end." Therefore, having this ominous prophecy in his ears, the envoy of Iancu desired the city to be conquered more quickly, and for this reason, he taught the counsel of how the wall should, and was destined to, fall easily.
When two walls had fallen, having one tower in the middle, and the tower at the gate of Saint Romanus (78) also lay on the ground, those within and those without were beholding one another. And Joannes Justinianus was fighting bravely with all those under his command, and with those of the palace, having a not insignificant body of armed men from Galata, for they themselves were demonstrating friendship. And they would go out and remain in the camp of the army fearlessly, and they gave the necessary supplies abundantly to the tyrant, and they brought oil for the use of the siege engine, and anything else the Turks appeared to be asking for. But they were secretly aiding the Romans, and by crossing over at night, they were fighting for them the whole day; and on the following night, exchanging places, others in the city, and they themselves, were spending their time in the houses and the camp so as to evade the Turks. The Venetians also were fighting against the Turks, mingled with the Romans, at the Imperial Gate (79) as far as the Cynegus. And the Grand Duke, with five hundred armed men, was patrolling the city, heartening the soldiers everywhere, and inspecting the watches, and searching for those who had been left behind—and this he did every single day. For he did not assemble the war
of the most holy Constantine through so many and such great Scythian, Persian, and Arabic wars, that it had ever happened that even a single stone weighing one pound was dislodged from the walls. Seeing, therefore, such a ruin of the walls rising before his eyes, and perceiving that he was being pressed by an immense army and fleet, and that a level path into the city lay open to the enemy, he was cast down with such despair of spirit that he sent envoys to the tyrant to implore him that, upon payment of an annual tribute of whatever amount he pleased, and even with the city's resources and riches surrendered to a greater ruler, and with other conditions imposed, he might lift the siege and, having moved his camps from the city, embrace peace. To the envoys the tyrant replied in this manner: "I cannot in any way withdraw from the siege: either I shall take the city, or the city shall take me, whether I be alive or dead. If, however, you wish to depart from it of your own accord, and not be forced, I grant the Peloponnese to you; I will give other provinces to your brothers, and thus we shall be joined and united in mutual friendship. But if you do not peacefully yield me entrance, and I enter by means of battle, I will strike down all your magnates with the sword, and I will leave the remaining crowd to be plundered by my soldiers, since the city will be empty enough for me." The emperor could never bring his mind to listen to or obey these terms; for it was not possible to hand over the city, taken from the Romans, to the Turks. For if he had committed this crime, what path could they take, to what place could they depart, and the avenger—awaiting the hour [(80)] observed by the soothsayers—true. But the emperor, seeing the walls [(81)] fallen, and a bad sign against the city, and judging the fall to be against himself. For it had not happened during the times of the most holy Constantine in so many wars—Scythian, Persian, Arabic—that even one stone weighing a single pound had fallen. But then, seeing so much, and such an uncountable army, and a heavy fleet, and a wide path, he despaired, he lost hope, and having sent envoys [(82)] he begged the tyrant that, for whatever amount of tribute he wished each year, and even beyond his power, and other demands, only to depart from there, and to grant and embrace peace. But the tyrant said: "It is not possible for me to depart. Either I take the city, or the city takes me either alive or dead. If you wish to depart from it, I give you the Peloponnese with peace; and to your brothers I will give other provinces, and we shall be friends. But if you do not grant me the entrance peacefully, and I enter through battle, I will strike all your magnates with the sword, and I will grant all the remaining people to be disciplined by every one of my soldiers who wishes, and the empty city is enough for me." The emperor having heard these things [(83)], and not casting them into his mind in the slightest—
For it was not possible for the city to be surrendered to the Turks from the hands of the Romans. For if this were to happen, what path, or what place, or what city did they have to emigrate to, where they would not be spat upon by Christians, and insulted, and treated with contempt by the Romans? Not only Christians, but even the Turks and Hebrews themselves had cause to despise them.
At that time, Justinian the Long (84) planned to approach the biremes by night and set them on fire. And having prepared one of the triremes, and having placed upon it the most proven of the Italians, and all sorts of mechanical devices, they stood waiting for the hour. But the Genoese of Galata, having learned of what was being done, reported it to the Turks. The latter, having spent that night without sleep, and having drawn up their equipment ready, awaited the Latins. But the Latins, not knowing of the betrayal by those of Galata to the impious ones, around midnight weighed anchor, and the trireme was approaching the ships in silence. The Turks, however, who had been awake the whole night, having ignited the fuse of their engine—for they had been vigilant all night—discharged the stone against the trireme. It struck it with a great noise, and having shattered it, sent it down to the bottom with its passengers. This threw the Latins into no small fear and anxiety, and John into no small despair; for all those who were drowned from his ship were well-equipped young men, and excellent warriors, more than one hundred and fifty in number. And the Turks, elated by their success, and having raised a great cry with yelling—all of them, both those on the ships and those in the tents—sent up such a noise into the heavens that that region of the earth seemed to be shaken. And because of the fear, those of the city and those of Galata all cried out.
When day had broken, and they were fighting back joyfully and courageously, exulting in the unexpected destruction of the trireme, they fitted another stone, and that one of huge size, to the mouth of the gun. And, as it happened, a ship was anchored near the gate of Galata, carrying a commercial cargo of all kinds of goods and intending to sail to Italy—it was indeed the ship and cargo of the merchants of Galata. The Turks, having released the stone, struck the hull of the ship, and it was shattered and immediately sent to the bottom. This gift was the repayment of the "pure friendship" which the Turks showed to the Galatians. For they went to the magnates that very day, shouting, "As we are friends, and are showing the fruits of friendship, we have signaled the arrival of the trireme; for if you had not been listening for its arrival with us, those many labors of the eighty biremes hauled across the land and brought into the harbor would have been in vain."

for you would have been ash and dust at the hands of the Romans. You, however, by paying this compensation, have caused us such great loss." The intermediaries replied: "Not knowing that the ship was yours, but rather trusting that it belonged to our enemies, we have done this. B Have courage, therefore, and persevere in expecting us to take the city; for truly it is already present, and the time is near, and then every loss and everything else owed to you shall be given." With these soothing words they departed, not knowing, the wretches, that they themselves, and their city, just like that of Constantine, would soon meet the same fate. Meanwhile, the tyrant constructed a wooden bridge [(85)] from the shore of Galata toward the Cynegion. The construction was as follows: having gathered by order upwards of a thousand wine-casks, and having bound them with ropes across a width such that two such casks placed lengthwise would take up, he formed one row, and then another row similar to the first; having then joined and fastened the two rows together, and having nailed beams from both sides, he laid down planks. The bridge had become so wide that five foot soldiers could easily walk across it abreast. C Having thus finished everything, as seemed good to him, he sent a herald within, saying to the Emperor: "Know that the preparations for war are now completed, and it is time from now on to carry out what has long been intended by us. We leave the outcome of our undertaking to God, on whose will it depends. What say you? Do you desire to abandon the city and depart wherever you wish, together with your lords and their possessions, leaving the common people to be unharmed by us and by you? Or is it your resolve to resist and fight, and thus perish together with your life and your possessions, you and those with you, while the people, taken captive by the Turks, are scattered throughout every land?" The Emperor replied with the Senate: "If you desire, as your ancestors also lived, to live in peace with us, then thanks be to God. For they regarded my forebears as fathers, and honored them as such, and this city as their own homeland. For even in times of need, all who entered into it were saved, and no one...

### Chapter XXXIX.
Mehemetes urges Constantine in vain to surrender, and therefore prepares to storm the city. Justinian fortifies a broken part of the wall. In May, the Turks attack the city fiercely and vehemently, and on the next day until the ninth hour of the day. On the day of May, after sunset, the fighting was more fierce. Mehemetes encourages his men. Justinian, injured in the hand by a lead bullet, ceased from fighting; the besieged are struck with fear at this event. The Turks finally climb onto the walls, throw down the defenders, and as affairs become desperate, the Greeks flee, and the Turks burst into the city. Constantine is killed. The Turks slaughter those they meet everywhere, and plunder temples, monasteries, and houses. The Greeks flee into the church of Saint Sophia, believing in their false opinion that they would be safe therein. The Turks invade them and carry them all off as captives. The church is defiled and plundered. The Grand Duke is captured and by the order of Mehemetes is kept at home. Justinian calls his men back from the battle. Some ships and not a few of the Galatians flee. The others are called back from flight by Zaganos. The Galatians surrender themselves to Mehemetes. All the Greeks and others who survived alive in the captured city were transferred either to the ships or the camps of the Turks.
The Turks being duly instructed in all things for storming the city, as seemed good to Mehemetes, he sent a herald to say such things to the Emperor: "I inform you that all things for the assault are now ready, and the time has arrived to finally accomplish that which I have long since decided. We trust in the outcome of our enterprise to God, upon whose nod it depends. What do you answer us who are urging you to surrender? Does it please you to depart from the city, and to go wherever it pleases you, with your court nobles, their belongings, and treasures? Is it under this condition that neither of us shall inflict harm upon the people? Or is it your resolve to resist and fight? Therefore, do you choose to lose your life and your riches, and likewise to betray your people to be led away captive by the Turks through all regions?" The Emperor replied in the presence of the Senate: "If you wish to have peace with us, imitating your ancestors, we give thanks to God for that. They, indeed, revered my ancestors as fathers, honored and observed them; and this city, in which...
all those entering amidst the crisis were saved, and no one standing against them lived long. Restitute also the fortresses and land unjustly seized from us, as is just. And cut off also the tributes (87) as much as we are able to give you per year, and depart in peace. For what do you know if, daring to profit, you may be profited as a noble man? But as for giving you the city, it is neither in my power nor that of any others who dwell therein. For it is the common resolve of all of us to die of our own free will, and we shall not spare our own lives.
Hearing these things, the tyrant, despairing of the peaceful surrender of the city, resolved that proclamations be made throughout the entire army, and he declared the day of battle, swearing that he required no other gain except the buildings and the walls of the city; but all other treasure and captivity were to be your gains. Then they all applauded. And when evening came, having sent heralds round the camp, he ordered that great lights and fires be lit in every tent; and when the lights were kindled, he ordered everyone with noise and shouting to sound their unholy cry (88), which signifies their impiety. And it was a strange wonder to see and hear; for the lights, overflowing on land and sea, shone brighter than the sun, illuminating the entire city, Galata, all the ships, and the vessels beyond Scutari; and the entire surface of the water glittered so intensely that one might say it was like a thunderbolt. And would that it had been a thunderbolt, not only lighting up, but also burning and consuming the fleets and camps of the tyrant from heaven! The Romans, thinking the camp was burning with fire, went forth as far as the ruin of the wall to investigate; but seeing their dances and hearing the joyous shouts that were made, they foresaw what was coming, and with contrite hearts said to God, "Lord, spare us from Your just threat, and deliver us from the hands of our adversaries." The townspeople, too, merely seeing such a sight and hearing the cry, drew breath like the half-dead, unable to draw in air or exhale. John, however, having struggled throughout that night, and having ordered all the twigs that could be found in the city to be gathered and placed in the ruins, having constructed another trench inside to protect the walls that had been damaged. But the Romans, seeing their entrance and exit exposed, and being unable to go out of the gate and resist the Turks in the outer fortress because they were unprotected by the fallen walls. There were some of the elders who knew of a postern gate, from many
years securely blocked up, towards the lower part of the palace; and having informed the emperor, by his order it was opened. And they went out from it, protected by the sound walls, and fought against the Turks in the outer enclosure. The name of that secret gate was once called the Kerkoporta (89).
The tyrant began to join total war on Sunday; and truly, when evening came, he gave no rest to the Romans that night; for that Sunday was the feast of All Saints, the twenty-seventh day of May. As the day dawned, he joined battle until the ninth hour. After the ninth hour, he divided the army from the palace as far as the Golden Gate. And he placed eighty ships from the Xyloporta as far as the Plateia (90); the other ships, which were stationed at the two columns, made a circuit around from the Beautiful Gate (91), traversing the Megademetrion (92), the acropolis, and the small gate which is at the monastery of the Hodegetria (93). Having descended to the Great Palace, and having crossed the harbor, they encircled the area as far as the Vlanga (94). Each one of them carried a ladder equal in height to the walls, and every other sort of equipment for war. So, when the sun had set, the trumpet sounded, and the tyrant himself, on horseback, at the second hour of the night, with his most trusted youth fighting bravely and fiercely, surrounded by ten thousand of his own slaves, and mounted on a horse, fought at close quarters in the part of the wall that had fallen down. Behind him and on his flanks were over one hundred thousand brave cavalrymen. And in the lower parts, as far as the harbor of the Golden Gate, were another hundred thousand and more; and from the place where the commander stood unto the palace, the extremities held another fifty thousand; and on the ships and the bridge an infinite multitude. The besieged, too, had divided their stations for defense. The emperor and John Justinian were fighting at the ruined part of the wall, on the outer embankment, holding it with three thousand Latins and Romans; the Great D Duke was at the palace with about five hundred. And the walls facing the sea, and the bulwarks from the Wooden Gate as far as the Beautiful Gate, were guarded by archers and bowmen numbering over five hundred.
this is the first page of the chain)
of the Beautiful Gate, making the entire circuit up to the Golden Gate; in each bastion was an archer, or a crossbowman, or a stone-thrower. Thus they passed the whole night without sleep, not having slumbered in the least. The Turks, however, at the instigation of their leader, were eager to approach the walls, bringing ladders beyond number that had been prepared in advance. The tyrant, therefore, behind the line of battle, brandishing an iron rod, drove the archers toward the walls, at times coaxing them with words, at times threatening them, while those in the city fought back bravely with all their might. John stood gallantly with his men, and the emperor himself was there, armed and fighting along with the whole array.
When, however, the successes of fortune were about to shift into the hands of the Turks, God removed from the midst of the Roman camp their general, a giant, strong and a warrior of a man. For he was struck by a leaden bullet in the hand, behind the arm, while it was still dark, and it pierced through his iron chlamys, which had been fashioned like the armor of Achilles, and he could not remain steady because of the wound. He said to the emperor, "Stand firm and courageously; I shall go to the ship, and there, after receiving treatment, I shall return quickly." For at that hour it was destined that what had been spoken by Jeremiah to the Jews should be fulfilled: "Thus shall you say to Zedekiah: Thus says the Lord God of Israel: ‘Behold, I will turn back the weapons of war that are in your hands, with which you are fighting against the king of Babylon and the Chaldeans who have surrounded you outside the wall in a siege; and I will bring them into the center of this city. And I myself will fight against you with an outstretched hand, with a high arm, with anger, and with fury, and with great indignation. And I will strike the inhabitants of this city, both man and beast, with a great death, and they shall die. I will not spare them, and I will not pity them.’" The emperor, seeing John depart, became fearful, and those with him also—though they continued to fight with all their might.
The Turks, having approached the walls little by little, protected by shields, placed their ladders; however, they achieved nothing, for the defenders, throwing stones from above, drove them back, so that they stood there obstructed. All the Romans, together with the emperor, were drawn up against the enemies, and the whole force was there, and the goal was not to allow the Turks to gain entry through the fallen sections of the walls; but God, having willed it, brought them in through another way. For having seen the gate—which we have already mentioned—standing open, about fifty men among the renowned servants of the tyrant rushed in, and having ascended the tops of the walls, breathing fire and killing those they encountered, they struck down the skirmishers. And it was a sight full of horror to behold. For of the Romans and Latins who were holding back the Turks who were moving the ladders to the walls, some were cut down, others, with eyes closed, threw themselves from the walls, and having their limbs crushed, were finally deprived of life by a bitter fate. Thereafter, the Turks, having easily applied their ladders to the walls, climbed up like eagles.
Meanwhile, the Roman soldiers fighting along with the Emperor were unaware of what was happening; for the entry of the Turks had occurred at a considerable distance, and furthermore, their entire focus was on those opposing them. For twenty battle-hardened Turks were fighting against each single Roman, and the Roman was not as capable a combatant as the average Turk. Toward those, therefore, were their purpose and concern directed. Then, suddenly, they see missiles descending from above, striking them down. Looking up, they glimpse the Turks; seeing them, they turned inward to flee. Unable to enter through the gate called Charisius, being crushed by the crowd, those who were stronger and more robust trampled upon the bodies of the weak and forced their way in. Then the tyrant’s army, having caught sight of the Romans’ flight, raised a cry and rushed in together, trampling and slaughtering the wretches. Arriving at the gate, they could not enter; for it had been blocked up by the bodies of those who had fallen or were breathing their last. So, the majority entered through the breaches in the walls and cut down those they encountered. The Emperor, therefore, having given himself up for lost, stood holding his sword and shield and let out a wail worthy of commiseration: "Is there no Christian here to take my head from me?" For he had been left utterly alone. Then one of the Turks struck a blow to his face, and when he had received this, he offered his bare head and other cheek to another Turk. Finally, run through by a lethal wound, as another attacked him from behind, he fell to the ground; for they did not know that he was the Emperor, but, having killed him as they would a common soldier, they left him.
When the Turks had entered, no more than three of their own had been lost in the entry. It was the first hour of the day, with the sun not yet fully risen above the earth. Having entered and dispersed from the Charisius Gate as far as the palace, they slaughtered those they met, and the fugitives likewise. They thus slaughtered up to two thousand fighting men. And indeed, the Turks had been fearful, for they were always calculating that there would be at least fifty thousand combatants inside the city. In this engagement, they slaughtered two thousand. For if they had known that the entire armed force did not exceed eight thousand, they would not have killed anyone; for this race is so addicted to greed that even if a murderer of their own father fell into their hands, they would release him for gold; how much more so someone who had done them no prior injury? For after the war, I conversed with many, and they told me, "Struck by terror and dread of those who had fought in the vanguard, we slaughtered whoever we first encountered; but if we had known of such a lack of men existing in the city, we would have sold everyone like sheep." Meanwhile, the tyrant’s *Azapides* (95), who
rushed, some into the palace, others toward the monastery of the great Forerunner, St. John the Baptist, which was called Petra, and into the monastery of the district, in which the icon of my blameless Mother of God was also found at that time. O tongue, and lips, that must utter what happened to that icon because of your sins! As the apostates struggled to rush elsewhere, one of the impious stretched out an axe, aided by his vile hands, and divided it into four pieces, and casting lots, each took his own share, and having seized the precious vessels of the monastery, they departed. Entering the house of the Protostrator, they opened the treasures that had been stored up from days of old, waking the noble ladies from their beds—for it was the twenty-ninth of May—and the morning sleep was sweet in the eyes of the young men and women, for they were sleeping without a care, trusting as they had the day before and the day before that. Then a great troop of the impious went along the road leading to the Great Church, and one could see the trick of fortune on both sides. For as it was morning, with the day still at twilight, some of the Romans, during the incursion of the Turks and the flight of the citizens, arrived fleeing to reach their houses and provide for their children and wife. Passing through the parts of the Taurus and crossing the column of the Cross, being covered in blood, they were asked by the women what had happened. When they heard that detestable cry, "Enemies are inside the walls of the city, slaughtering the Romans," they did not at first believe it, but rather they even insulted and disparaged the one who brought the ill-omened news; but when they saw another behind him, and another after him, all covered in blood, they realized that the cup of the Lord's wrath had been brought to their lips. All the women, therefore, and men, monks, and nuns, ran to the Great Church, carrying their infants in their arms, both men and women, leaving their houses to whoever wished to enter them. And one could see that street crowded and full of people. And why did everyone take refuge in the Great Church? For they had been hearing for many years from certain false prophets how it is destined that the Turks will…
city must be surrendered to the yoke of the Turks; and that they, bursting into it by force, would slaughter the Romans and advance as far as the pillar of Great Constantine. And when they arrived there, an angel would descend from heaven, who, bearing a sword, would deliver the kingdom, along with the sword, to a certain unknown man found at that time standing at the pillar—a man very unkempt and impoverished—and would say to him: "Take this sword, and avenge the people of the Lord." Then the Turks would turn in flight, and the Romans would pursue them, striking them down, and would drive them out not only from the city and from the regions of the West, but also from Anatolia itself, as far as the place called Monodendrion, situated on the borders of Persia. Possessing these as matters destined to happen, some were running and urging others to run. This was the expectation of the Romans, which they had been studying for many years past, as the event now brought to pass: for they supposed that if we leave behind the pillar of the Cross, we shall escape the coming wrath. And this was the flight into the Great Church. So it happened that in one hour that immense temple was full of men and women, both below and above, and in the porticoes, and in every place an innumerable crowd. Having shut the doors, they stood there, hoping for salvation from them. O miserable Romans, O wretched ones! The temple which you were calling, yesterday and the day before, a den and an altar of heretics, and into which not one of you would enter for fear of being defiled, because those who embraced the union of the Church performed the sacred rites within—now, because of the wrath that has come upon you, you rush into it as into a saving refuge. But not even when the just wrath of God had come, did it stir your bowels toward peace. For even in such a crisis, if an angel were to descend from heaven, asking you: "If you accept the union and the peaceful state of the Church, shall I drive the enemies from the city?" would you not have refused? And even if you had agreed, would not the agreement have been a lie? Those who, a few days before, were saying, "It is better to fall into the hands of the Turks than the Franks," know this. When the Turks were plundering, slaughtering, and taking captives, they reached the church before the first hour had fully passed; and finding the doors closed, they tore them down with axes without delay. Having entered, swords drawn, and seeing the numberless multitude, each one began to bind his own captive. For there was no one there to offer resistance, nor was anyone doing anything other than offering himself as a sheep. Who will recount the calamity there? Who will relate the lamentations and cries of the infants, the tears of the mothers, and the wailings of the fathers that occurred then? The random Turk would search out the most delicate [woman], or grab hold of a nun; another, becoming more powerful, would snatch away and bind [her].
The cause of the seizing and dragging was the plaiting of hair, the exposure of chests and breasts, the stretching out of arms. Then the maidservant was bound with her mistress; the master with his bought slave; the archimandrite with his gatekeeper; tender youths with maidens—maidens whom the sun had scarcely looked upon, maidens whom their father had barely seen, and who, if they had attempted to repel the raper by force, were driven on with clubs. For the despoiler wished to lead his prey to a safe place, and having deposited it in security, to return a second and third time to plunder. The rapers, those avengers of God, were emboldened, and it was possible to see all men in one hour bound, the men with ropes, and the women with their own head cloths. And one could see endless ropes of people coming out from the temple, and from the inner sanctuaries of the temple, like herds and flocks of sheep, weeping, lamenting, and there was no one to pity them. But the things of the temple—what am I to say? Or what shall I speak? "My tongue has cleaved to my throat." I am unable to draw breath, my mouth having been sealed. Suddenly those dogs cut down the holy icons, taking away the ornaments, the chains, the lampstands, the coverings of the holy table. They broke some of the light-bearing vessels, and took others. They gathered together in one moment all the precious and holy vessels of the sacred treasury—gold and silver, and those made of other precious materials—leaving the temple deserted and bare, having left nothing at all behind.
Then, even in the new Sion, the things spoken by God through Amos the prophet were fulfilled. For thus says the Lord God Almighty: "I will take vengeance upon the altars of Bethel, and it shall be dug up; I will break the horns of the altar, and they shall fall to the ground; and I will smite the vaulted house upon the winter house. And the ivory houses shall perish, and many other houses shall be utterly destroyed," says the Lord. "I have rejected your feasts, and I will not take pleasure in your festive assemblies. For if you offer me your whole burnt offerings and sacrifices, I will not look upon them. Remove from me the sound of your songs, and I will not hear the psalm of your instruments." And the Lord said to me, "The end has come upon my people Israel; I will not again pass by them anymore, and the ceilings of the temple shall howl in that day," says the Lord. "Hear this now, you who oppress the poor in the morning, and lordship over the needy of the earth. You who say, 'When will the month be over, that we may sell? And when will the Sabbaths arrive, that we may open our treasures,' for the purpose of making the measure small, and increasing the amount, and making an unjust scale, so as to obtain the poor for silver, and the needy in exchange for sandals?" "In that day," says the Lord, "the sun shall set at noon, and darkness shall settle upon the earth in a day of light. And I will turn your feasts into mourning, and all your songs into lamentation and wailing." For it happened on that fearful day of the capture
of the city that the memory of the holy martyr Theodosia 99 was to be celebrated with a festival. A great multitude therefore gathered; for from the evening many, both men and women, had kept vigil at the shrine of the saint. But when day broke, the majority, and the women along with their husbands, going out for worship and carrying candles and incense, adorned and dressed as they were, suddenly fell into the snares of the Turks. For how could they have foreseen the sudden wrath that had spread over such a breadth of the city? Only those who knew its dimensions could understand. This threat, which we have mentioned, had broken out and was burning from the Gate of Charisius, and from [the gate of] Saint Romanus, and from the parts of the palace. The fleet, however, and the resistance at the harbor did not give the Turks an opportunity to place ladders against the walls. The Romans were stronger than the Turks, attacking them with stones and missiles until the third hour of the day; until, having arrived and having brought back a portion of those who had been pillaging inside the city since the morning, and seeing the Romans fighting those outside, and having let out a shout with all their might, they ran up onto the walls. The Romans, seeing the Turks inside the city and letting out a cry of lamentation, "Woe is me," fell headlong from the wall. For neither strength nor power remained to the Romans there. Then even those in the ships, seeing the Turks inside, understood that the city had been taken, and quickly placing their ladders, they climbed inside and, having smashed the gates, they all entered within. The Grand Duke, seeing the Turks come to the place where he was stationed—for he was overlooking the Imperial Gate—departed to his own house with a few men; for the rest had been scattered. And some were captured before they could reach their houses; others, finding their own houses empty of children, wife, and goods—and they themselves, before they could groan or weep, had their hands bound behind their backs. Others, returning to their houses and finding their wife and children already being led away, were bound and tied up together with their most beloved ones and their spouse. As for the old men who were in the house, those who were unable to leave because of sickness or old age, they slaughtered them all, men and women, without mercy, and cast out the newborn infants into the streets. The Grand Duke, having found his daughters, and his sons, and his wife—for she was sick—shut up in the tower and keeping the Turks from entering, was himself captured along with those who were following him; and the tyrant sent some soldiers to guard both him and his entire house. He gave much money to the Turks who had come and surrounded his house, so that it seemed he had bought them off by an oath.
Ismaelis Bullialdi notæ.
(99) The temple of this saint, in that part which is today called Casan Bassa, located beyond the Ceratian Gulf, adjacent to Galata, was later converted into a mosque. But how could they cross the gulf when the Turks were filling all the shores?
The Turks, having all entered the city, began to plunder and seize everything everywhere, even the muleteers and cooks. As for John Justiniani—whom I have already mentioned as having gone to his ship to have his wound dressed—while he was at the harbor, some of his men came running and told him that the Turks had entered the city and the Emperor had been slain. Upon hearing this most bitter and stinging news, he ordered the heralds to recall his shield-bearers and shipmates with trumpets. The other ships likewise began to prepare for departure, as most of them had lost their captains, who had been taken prisoner. And there was a piteous spectacle to be seen on the shore of the harbor: men, women, nuns, and monks crying out lamentably, beating their breasts, and begging those on the ships to take them in. But this was not possible, for it had been decreed that they should drink the cup full of the Lord’s wrath. Indeed, even if the sailors had wanted to take them on board, they could not; for even if the tyrant’s vessels had not been occupied with the plunder and sacking of the city, not even one vessel could have been spared; but the Turks, having left their ships, were all inside, and the Latins, having found an opportunity, were departing from the harbor. The C tyrant gnashed his teeth, but he was unable to do anything further, and he endured it against his will. The inhabitants of Galata, seeing this incurable disaster, ran to the strand with their wives and children, surveying the small boats. And wherever they chanced upon a skiff entering, they would scramble into the ships, abandoning both their goods and their houses. Many who were pressed by the violence even cast their treasures into the deep sea, and sustained other terrible losses. One of the tyrant’s ministers, who was held in high favor at that time by Mehmed because he had encouraged and praised the tyrant’s plan to undertake the assault, ran to the parts of Galata—Zaganos was his name— D crying out: "Do not flee!" He swore by the tyrant’s head, saying, "Do not fear, for you are friends of the leader, and you shall have your city unmolested by any man, and the treaties you had with the Emperor shall be ratified with us under even better conditions; put aside any other thought, lest you provoke the leader to anger." Having said these things, Zaganos prevented the Franks of Galata from departing. Nevertheless, those who were able to flee did flee. Then the rest, having consulted, took the keys of the citadel along with their podestà and went to do homage to the tyrant. Having bowed and surrendered the keys, he received them with great joy, and dismissed them after addressing them with gracious words and a gentle expression. Only five of the great ships spread their sails, for the others were not able to leave, since their captains had been taken prisoner and they had been left behind. Thus the ships that fled saved themselves by leaving their captains behind as captives. Having sailed out of the harbor and...
as a north wind blew, their sails full, they sailed away with sighs and lamentations, weeping for the calamity of the city; the Venetian merchant galleys did the same. The Turkish sailors from the ships, having found all the common people outside the city, gathered all the men and women together wherever they were and led them onto the ships. The remaining people of the city were rounded up outside into the tents of the camp.
CAPUT XL.
Mehemetes enters the city, and comes to the temple of St. Sophia, and commands the Imam to recite his prayers there. He speaks to the Grand Duke who has been summoned to him. The head of Constantine is fixed upon a column in the Augustaeum. Another account concerning the Grand Duke Orchanes. Mehemetes consoles the Grand Duke and describes the names of the illustrious men. He visits the wife of the Grand Duke and addresses her gently. Mehemetes commands the youngest of the Grand Duke's sons to come to a banquet; when the Grand Duke refuses to send his son, Mehemetes orders him to be put to death. The Grand Duke encourages his sons to undergo death with a calm and brave spirit, and he himself is finally beheaded. All the nobles are ransomed by Mehemetes, and killed.
All that has been related thus far was accomplished from the first hour of the day until the eighth hour. Then the tyrant, having put aside all suspicion and fear, entered within the city with his viziers and other satraps, having before and behind him his own slaves breathing fire, all of them archers superior to Apollo, young Heracleidae, each one ready to engage ten men. Having descended to the Great Church and dismounted from his horse, he entered and stood there speechless, looking hither and thither in wonder and astonishment. But when he noticed a certain Turk breaking one of the marbles, he asked why he was destroying the floor. He replied, "For the sake of the faith." He, stretching out his hand, struck the Turk with his sword, saying this too: "The treasures and the captives are enough for you; the buildings of the city, however, belong to me." For the tyrant had repented of the agreement that had been made, seeing the treasury being drained and the limitless number of captives. Having dragged the Turk out of the doors, they threw him out half-dead. He himself then, having ordered one of his impure priests, summoned him to ascend the ambo, and he proclaimed his profane prayer. The son of iniquity, the forerunner of Antichrist, having climbed upon the holy table, performed his prayer. Alas for the calamity! Woe to the dreadful monster! Woe is me, to what pass have our affairs come! Alas! Alas! What have we seen! A Turk trampling the holy altar with his feet, and standing upon the relics of the apostles and martyrs deposited therein. Let the sun shudder. Where now is the Lamb of God, and where is the Son and Word of the Father, who is sacrificed and eaten upon that altar and yet is never consumed? In truth, we were deemed as bastard and adulterate. The nations have treated our religion and ceremonies with contempt because of our sins. The temple which was built and consecrated in the name of the Wisdom of God the Word, and called the temple of the Holy Trinity,
and New Sion, has today been renamed and become a temple of the Barbarians and the house of Mohamed. Righteous is your judgment, O Lord. The tyrant then went out from the temple and ordered the Grand Duke to be brought before him, and he was once again presented. Having come and bowed, he said to the tyrant, "You have done well not to surrender the city. B Look how much loss there has been, how much ruin, how much captivity." But the Duke replied, "My lord, we did not have the authority to surrender the city to you, nor did the Emperor himself; especially since some of your own people were encouraging the Emperor with words, writing to him: 'Do not fear, for he will not prevail against us.'" The tyrant suspected this was on account of Halil Pasha, for he was already nursing a grudge against him. Then, upon hearing the name of the Emperor, he asked if the Emperor had run away with the ships. The Duke replied that he did not know, for he himself was at the Royal Gate at the time when the Turks encountered the Emperor as they entered the city through the Charsi Gate. Then, two young men were pulled out from the midst of the camp, and one of them said to the tyrant, "My lord, I killed him. For as I was being forced to enter and plunder along with those who were with me in the rear, I left him there dead." The other claimed that he had been the first to inflict a wound. The tyrant then sent both of them immediately and ordered them to bring his head. They ran quickly, found it, cut off the head, and presented it to the ruler. The tyrant said to the Grand Duke, "Tell me the truth: is this really the head of your Emperor?" Then, having examined it, he said, "It is his, my lord." Others also saw it and recognized it. Then they fastened it to the pillar of the Augusteion and it remained there until evening. After this, he had the skin flayed and stuffed with straw, and he sent it everywhere as a trophy of victory to show to the leader of the Persians, and to the Arabs, and to the other Turks.
Others, however, say that the Duke was found together with Orchan in the tower of the Frankish castle, and that they surrendered there, seeing that it was no longer possible to resist the Turks. There were many noble lords there with the Duke, and Orchan asked a certain monk for his vestments; having put them on, he gave his own to the monk, and through a certain arrow-slit, he threw himself down to the ground outside the city walls. But those from the ships took him, bound him, and cast him inside with the rest of the captives. Those who had surrendered in the tower were also taken on board that ship.
Then one of the Roman captives, having negotiated his own freedom, said to the naval commander, "If you will free me today, I can deliver Orchan and the Grand Duke to you." When the naval commander heard this, he swore to set him free. Then, pointing out Orchan, who was dark-clad, and having confirmed that it was truly him, he cut off his head. He brought the Grand Duke alive—along with the head of Orchan—to the ruler, who was then at Cosmidion. He thanked the naval commander and, having bestowed many gifts upon him, released him. He ordered the Grand Duke to sit down, comforted him, and directed that his children and wife be sought out by a trumpeter throughout the camp and fleet and brought to him. The prince distributed a thousand aspers to each of them and finally, having encouraged the Grand Duke to have hope, with a long and humane speech he eased his grief, saying: "I wish to entrust this vast city to your faith to be governed and cared for, and I shall honor you with higher honors than those you held in the time of the emperor; do not be downcast." Having expressed his thanks and kissed his hand, the Grand Duke went to his house. B Having learned from him the names of the nobles and of the distinguished officials of the palace and court, he wrote down all their names. And having gathered them all from the fleet and the camps, he ransomed them by giving a thousand aspers to the Turks for each one. When morning came, after the passage of that first and gloomy day in which the total destruction of our race occurred, the tyrant entered the city and came to the houses of the Grand Duke; the latter went out to meet him, bowed to him, and he entered. His wife was ill and bedridden. Then that wolf in sheep’s clothing approached her bed and, greeting her, said: "Greetings, O mother, do not grieve for what has happened. Let the will of the Lord be done. I have more than what you have lost to give you; only be well." His children came and bowed to him, and after they thanked him, he left, going around the city. For the whole city was deserted; neither a human, nor a beast, nor a bird was heard crying out or making a sound inside; only some of those who were unable to seize anything—because of their own weakness—were searching the houses. For many were killed by one another in this cause, while they grabbed spoils from each other, which fell to the stronger and more robust, with the weaker ones being overcome by lethal wounds. On the second day, the thirtieth of May, they entered again and collected the remains of the booty. Then the tyrant, having traversed most of the city, held a banquet and made merry near the parts of the palace; and indeed, having been baptized by the wine and having become intoxicated, he ordered his chief eunuch—and giving the command he said, "Go…
“Go to the house of the great Duke, and say to him, ‘The commander orders that you send your younger son to the banquet.’” For the youth was fair of face, being fourteen years of age. Having heard this, the father of the child was struck dead [with shock], and his countenance was changed, and he said to the chief eunuch, “It is not in our custom to hand over my child with my own hands to be defiled by him; it would be better for me that you send an executioner to take my head from me.” The chief eunuch advised him to give the child, so that he might not inflame the tyrant to anger. But he, not being persuaded, said, “If it is intended for you to take him and depart, take him and depart. But that I should give him to you by my own will, this shall never happen.” Then the chief eunuch, having turned back, told the commander all the things spoken by the great Duke, and how he was not willing to give the child. Then the tyrant, having become enraged, said to the chief eunuch, “Take the executioner with you, and turning back, bring the child to me.” And let the executioner bring the Duke, and his sons. Then having come, and having learned the message, the Duke embraced his children and his wife, and went with the executioner, he himself and his son, and his son-in-law, Cantacuzene. The chief eunuch took the child with him. C Having entered then, and having shown the child to the commander—the others remaining at the gate of the palace—he ordered the executioner to cut off their heads with a sword. Then, having taken them a little below the palace, the executioner told them the sentence. But his son, having heard of the slaughter, wept. But his father, having stood nobly, strengthened the young men, supporting them and saying: “My children, you saw yesterday, in one moment of time, all our things become as nothing. Our inexhaustible wealth, the marvelous glory which we had in this great city, and through it in all the earth where Christians dwell. But now, at this hour, nothing else remained for us except this present life. And this shall not be for us unending; for late or soon, we shall die. And how? Being deprived of the goods which we possessed, of the glory, of the honor, of the authority, being insulted by all, held in contempt, and oppressed by hardships, until death comes upon us, having taken us hence in disgrace. Where is our Emperor? Was he not killed yesterday? Where is my fellow father-in-law, and your father, the Great Domestic? Where is Palaiologos, and the Protostrator with his two sons? Were they not slaughtered yesterday in the war? Would that we had died with them! But even this hour is sufficient; we shall not sin any more. For who knows the weapons of the devil, if by delaying death, we might be wounded by his poisonous arrows? Now the arena is prepared, in the name of Him who was crucified for
us and who died and rose again, let us also die, that we may enjoy His good things together with Him." Having said this and having strengthened the young men, they became eager to die. And he said to the executioner, "Do what you have been ordered, beginning with the young men." And the executioner obeyed and cut off the heads of the young men, while the Grand Duke stood by and said, "I thank Thee, O Lord," and "Just art Thou, O Lord." Then he said to the executioner, "Brother, grant me a short delay to step inside and pray," for there was a small shrine there. He granted it, and the duke went in and prayed. Then, coming out from the door of the shrine—for the bodies of his children were still twitching there—and again sending forth a doxology to God, he had his head cut off. The executioner, having taken the heads, went to the banquet and showed them to the bloodthirsty beast; he left the bodies there naked and unburied. Likewise, he slaughtered all the nobles and palace officials and dignitaries whom he had ransomed, having sent the executioner to them. He selected the beautiful virgins and handsome boys from their wives and children and set them aside for himself, and handed them over to the chief eunuch to be looked after by him. The rest of the throng of slaves he gave to others to look after until he should be washed clean at the Babylon of Hadrian—I mean Adrianople. And it was possible to see the entire city in the tents of the camp, while the city itself lay deserted, lifeless, prostrate, naked, silent, stripped of its form and beauty.

### CHAPTER XLI. On the captured city, and the destruction of the Christian empire in the East.
O city, city, head of all cities! O city, city, center of the four quarters of the world! O city, city, boast of Christians and ruin of Barbarians! O city, city, another paradise planted toward the west, containing within it all kinds of plants, abounding in spiritual fruits! Where is your beauty, O paradise? Where is the flow of the spirit's graces that used to irrigate body and soul? Where are the bodies of the apostles of my Lord, deposited long ago in that ever-flourishing paradise, surrounding the purple robe, the spear, the sponge, and the reed—things which, while we venerated them, made us imagine Him who was lifted up on the cross? Where are the relics of the saints, where are the martyrs? Where are the ashes of the great Constantine and the other emperors? The streets, the porticoes, the crossroads, the fields, the fences of the vineyards, were once scattered everywhere with the relics of the saints, noble and chaste bodies of ascetics and nuns, but oh, what a loss! They have been laid low. "They have set, O Lord, the dead bodies of Thy servants to be food for the birds of the sky, the flesh of Thy saints for the wild beasts of the earth around the new Sion, and there was no one to bury them." [Ps. LXXVIII, 2, 3.] O temple! O earthly heaven! O celestial altar! O divine and sacred shrines! O beauty of the churches! O sacred books and divine utterances! O laws old and new! O tablets inscribed by the finger of God! O Gospels proclaimed by the mouth of God! O theology of men clad in angelic bodies! O doctrines of men inspired by the divine Spirit, institutions of heroes and demigods! O republic, O people, O army, once exceedingly glorious,
but now vanished like a ship engulfed at sea while sailing! O dwellings and palaces of every kind, and sacred walls! Today I summon everything together, and as if they were living beings, I lament with them, taking Jeremiah as the leader of this pitiable tragedy. "How does the city sit solitary, that was full of people? She has become as a widow that was great among the nations! She that was princess among the provinces is become a tributary." Weeping, she has wept in the night, and her tears are upon her cheeks, and there is none to comfort her among all her lovers. All who loved her have dealt treacherously with her, they have become her enemies. Asia has been moved from her humiliation, and from the multitude of her bondage. She has sat among the nations, she has found no rest. All her persecutors have overtaken her in the midst of straits. The ways of the city mourn, because none come to the solemn feast; all her gates are desolate; her priests sigh, her virgins are afflicted, and she is bitter within herself. The oppressors have become her head, and her enemies are at ease, because the Lord has humbled her for the multitude of her transgressions. Her little ones have gone into captivity before the oppressor. And all her beauty has departed from the daughter of Zion. Her princes have become as rams not finding pasture, and they have gone without strength before the pursuer. The enemies saw her, and laughed at her Sabbaths. Jerusalem has sinned, therefore she is removed. The oppressor has stretched out his hand upon all her pleasant things, for she saw nations entering into her sanctuary, concerning whom thou didst command that they should not enter into thy Church. All her people sigh, seeking bread; they have given their pleasant things for meat to relieve the soul. "See, O Lord, and consider." All you who pass by the way, attend and see if there be any sorrow like unto my sorrow! He has sent fire from on high into my bones, and has brought it down against me. He has spread a net for my feet, he has turned me back. He has made me desolate and faint all the day. The Lord has taken away all my mighty men from the midst of me; he has called a set time against me to dash my young men in pieces. The Lord has trodden the winepress for the virgin daughter of Judah; for these things I weep. My sons have become desolate, because the enemy has prevailed. The Lord is just, for I have rebelled against his commandment. Hear, I pray you, all people, and behold my sorrow! My virgins and my young men have gone into my captivity. I called for my lovers, but they deceived me. My priests and my elders expired in the city. Hear, I pray, that I sigh. The Lord was as an enemy, and he has pulled down as a hedge his tabernacle, he has destroyed his feast. He has caused to be forgotten
the feast and the Sabbath in the city, and in his fierce anger he has provoked the king and the priest. The Lord has cast off his altar; he has spurned his sanctuary. He has broken down in his hand the wall of her foundations. He has given forth a sound of war in the house of the Lord, like that of the psalmody chanted by the Levites on feast days. A Look, O Lord, and observe, to whom have you shown this? Infants clinging to the breast have been slaughtered. Shall they kill the priest and prophet in the sanctuary of the Lord? Child and old man lie on the ground in the lands of their exile. My virgins and my young men have gone into captivity, the Lord has finished his wrath. He has poured out the fury of his anger, and has kindled a fire in the city, and it has devoured its foundations. Remember, O Lord, what has happened to us; look and see our reproach. Our inheritance has been turned over to strangers, our houses to aliens. We have become orphans, as those not having a father; our mothers are as widows. We have been pursued, we have labored, we have had no rest. Our fathers sinned and are no more, and we have borne their iniquities. Slaves have ruled over us, and there is no one to deliver us from their hand. Our skin has withered like an oven-blackened thing, it has shriveled from the face of the famine. Chosen men have ground at the mill, and young men have been hanged on wood. Elders have fallen from the gate, and the chosen have ceased from their psalms. The joy of our heart has been destroyed, our dancing has been turned into mourning; the crown of our head has fallen. Woe to us, because we have sinned in this. Our heart has become painful, for this our eyes have darkened over the new Zion, because it has been laid waste; foxes have walked through it. But you, O Lord, dwell forever, your throne is from generation to generation. Why do you forget us to the end, and forsake us for a length of days? Turn us, O Lord, to you, and we shall return, and let our days be renewed as before, because you have utterly rejected us; your anger has been kindled against us exceedingly.
These are the lamentations and wailing of Jeremiah, which he brought forth because of the conquest and destruction of the ancient Jerusalem; yet, it seems likely to me that the Spirit also suggested them to the prophet because of the new disaster. For what tongue is so eloquent and fluent that it could tell of the calamity with which the city has been afflicted? Who can relate the miseries of the captivity and the bitterness of the transplantation by which it has been tossed about? The inhabitants were not carried away from Jerusalem to Babylon or to the Assyrians, but from Constantinople to Syria, to Egypt, to Armenia, to the Persians, to Arabia, to Africa, to Italy, scattered about in Asia Minor, and in the remaining provinces. And how, indeed? The husband in Paphlagonia, the wife in Egypt, and the children in other regions, everywhere torn apart, being changed from language to language, and from piety to impious—
and from divine books to absurd writings. Shudder, O sun, and do thou, O earth, groan at the total abandonment that has occurred in our generation by the just Judge, God, because of our sins. We are not worthy to lift our eyes to heaven, but only looking down, and placing our faces to the ground, we cry: Righteous art thou, O Lord, and just is thy judgment. We have sinned, we have acted lawlessly, we have acted more unrighteously than all the nations. And all the things which thou hast brought upon us, thou hast brought in true and just judgment. Nevertheless, spare us, O Lord, we beseech thee.

### CHAPTER XLII.
The extent of the plunder the Turks carried off from the captured city. Mehemet enters Galata, and destroys part of its walls. He transforms Saint Sophia into a mosque. He returns to Adrianople. The wife of the Great Duke dies. Christian princes congratulate Mehemet on his victory. He imposes tribute on the Serbs and orders George the despot to depart from Serbia. The Hungarians ravage the provinces of the Turks. Mehemet besieges Smederevo in vain. Mehemet departs for Adrianople enriched with plunder: he builds a palace in Constantinople. A prophecy concerning the Palaeologi.
Three days after the capture, he gave the order for the fleet to sail, so that each might return to its own province and city, bearing a cargo so heavy that they almost sank. And what was the cargo? Expensive clothing, vessels of silver, gold, bronze, and tin; books beyond number; captives—both priests and laypeople, nuns and monks. Every ship was full of heavy plunder. In the tents of the camp, too, there were countless captives and every kind of plunder resembling what was previously mentioned. And it was possible to see in the midst of the Barbarians one man wearing a priestly sakkos [(8)], and another bound by an epitrachelion [(9)] of gold, leading dogs on leashes, using as blankets embroidered lambs of gold thread! Others were sitting at banquets, eating from the sacred plates before them along with various fruits, and drinking undiluted wine from the sacred chalices. As for all the books, which exceeded number, having loaded them onto wagons, they scattered and dispersed them everywhere in the East and West. For one coin, ten books were sold—Aristotelian, Platonic, theological, and every other kind of book. They would rip off the gold and silver from the Gospels that were adorned beyond measure, and then some they would sell, and some they would throw away. They delivered all the icons to the fire; and with the flame that had been kindled, they cooked meat and ate it.
Then, after the fifth day, he entered Galata, and having ordered a census to be taken of all those dwelling therein, he found many houses locked. For the Latins, having boarded their ships, had fled. Therefore, he decreed that their houses be opened, and that a census be made of all their wealth, that if they returned within the term of three months, they might receive their properties; but if they should not return...
they would belong to the Sovereign. Then he ordered the whole army to dismantle the surrounding villages and to cast down to the ground the walls of Galata, and to release them, which was also done. Having therefore dismantled the walls that abutted the mainland, they left those that faced the harbor. He further commanded the lime-burners, for the whole month of August, to have lime ready to rebuild the walls of the city that had collapsed. He himself, having registered five thousand families from the provinces of the East and West, commanded them to be in the city by the month of September, on pain of capital punishment; and he appointed as prefect one of his servants named Suleiman. And having consecrated the great temple as an altar of his own God and of Mahomet, leaving the others deserted and abandoned, he himself, as victor, set out for Adrianople, drawing behind him an infinite multitude of captives, a number beyond counting. He left the city, therefore, on the eighteenth day of the month of June, taking all the noble women and their daughters in carriages and on horses. Now the wife of the Great Duke had died on the journey, near a village called Mesene, and they buried her there; she was a woman renowned for her almsgiving and compassion for the poor, modest and temperate, free from all passions of the soul. When Mahomet had come into Adrianople with a most magnificent triumphal procession, one could see all the surrounding and remote Christian princes and leaders flocking from all sides to pay him homage. Anyone could conjecture the sentiment of their hearts and the expression on their faces; for, unwilling and constrained, and anxious to avert the same calamity, they flattered him with gifts and did him homage. The tyrant, therefore, proud and insolent, elated in spirit by the overthrow of the city, sat upon his throne, while the Christian leaders stood trembling, awaiting what he might show himself to be towards them in the future. He signified first to the envoy of Serbia that he should impose upon their treasury the annual tribute of twelve thousand coins to be paid to the Turks; and that the despots of the Peloponnese should bring a gift of ten thousand coins and come to do him homage each year. To the prince of the island of Chios, he ordered an annual sum of six thousand coins to be paid as tribute. He ordered the Mitylenian likewise to pay three thousand coins annually; and the Trebizondians, and all those who dwell in the Euxine sea, to come every year, paying the taxes and bringing gifts to do him homage. In the first year, therefore, in the month of August, those from the despot of Serbia arrived, and…
After the city was first captured, in the month of August, envoys came from the despot of Serbia, who paid the tributes due and distributed generous alms to the captives in Adrianople. For by the mandate of the despot George, an hundred young women and old, once ransomed, were restored to liberty. Furthermore, the illustrious captives, and those who traced their lineage to the palace, having set out for Serbia, received from him and his wife the queen the money by which they might redeem themselves, under the name of alms. A Autumn then set in, and with it the year 6962 from the foundation of the world, and Mehmed having passed the following winter at home, was agitating in his mind to invade the despot upon the coming of spring, and to annex the whole of Serbia to his own empire. The despot, indeed, after the capture of the city, had been expecting this bitter news and this unjust treatment from the greedy tyrant every day. For the despot was a practical old man, and one who had suffered much from the injustices of the tyrant, as we have often said. What, then, was the source of this injustice? [The tyrant] sent a message saying: "The land which you rule [(14)] is not yours, nor is it [yours] by paternal right, namely Serbia; but it belongs to Lazar, the son of Stephen, and therefore it pertains to me. Withdraw, therefore, quickly from its borders. I am able to grant you a portion of the land of your father Vuk, and the city of Sofia. If not, I am coming against you." Having sent these things through one of his most trusted servants, he ordered him to be found before him in twenty-five days, in order to learn the reply; and if [the despot] did not [reply], he threatened to cut off the servant’s head and cast his body to the beasts for food.
The tyrant's envoy, having come into Serbia and finding the despot passing time beyond the Ister, was detained by the princes of Serbia, who claimed that the despot was coming today, and would arrive tomorrow. By these means they busied themselves with their small towns, and heaped everything needful into storehouses. The envoy, therefore, seeing that he was being deceived, and fearing the penalty of the time limit—for he had passed the thirty days—was afraid. The tyrant, then, filled with anger, went out from Adrianople with his whole army and occupied Philippopolis. But the servant, having come and reported the flight of the despot into Hungary, and [how] the princes had detained him, and would not release him—for the tyrant intended to execute him—nevertheless, the servant had sent before the deadline to the ruler, declaring his own delay, and the preparations of the Serbs, and the tyrant, incited by anger, moved and came to Philippopolis. Meanwhile, the herald whom he had sent met him and reported that the despot had fled into Hungary:
Notes of Ismaël Bullialdus
(14) *The land which you rule.* I do not know what right Mehmed claimed to have in Serbia: he did not trace his maternal lineage from the Vuković line; for Mehmed was not born of Maria, the daughter of George, but of a slave woman: see what we have said above at chapter 30. From this we can gather how harmful and pestilential it is to have too close an alliance with the race of the Turks; who boasted that a right was acquired for themselves through such a contracted marriage. Those affinities and treaties were to be shunned, especially by Christians: who were drawn by them to certain destruction. Yet it is permissible and useful and convenient to enter into peace and alliance with them, and to trade with them, such as exists with other Christians. It is also right to oppose them against the unjust invasion of a usurper: and no one who is a student of equity can justly reproach a king or a republic who, being unequal in fighting, prepares aid for himself from that source against a more powerful invading enemy. He sins who by attacking drives his adversary to seek refuge in such protectors and helpers: and [he] prepares the way for them to occupy our provinces. For whatever perishes for one Christian prince, perishes for all.
And [the tyrant] exposed to himself the ambushes and deceits of the nobles who had estranged him. Indeed, the tyrant would have condemned him to death, had he not earlier, before the appointed day, informed him by letters regarding the causes of such a long delay, the military preparations of the Serbs, and the flight of the despot. The Hungarians, having crossed the river and already ravaged and plundered the fields surrounding Trnovo, and having joined battle with the Turkish army and won a victory, had crossed the river again, heavy with spoils.
Having moved his camp from Philippopolis, the tyrant approached Sophia, and leaving there his entire army with the Mesazontes and his whole senate, and having taken with him twenty thousand infantry, he broke into Serbia; he did not encounter anyone who would fight against him: for the despot and his nobles with their entire families had long since crossed over; after he had placed garrisons in the citadels, he had ordered the entire population to take refuge within them, and exhorted them to be of good heart and not surrender to the enemy, promising that he would soon arrive with a powerful army. But the tyrant proceeded as far as Smederevo, which fortress, situated on the bank of the river and providing a convenient crossing into Hungary, he greedily desired to capture: and, having attempted it in vain, he withdrew from it. Then, having besieged—but not taken—a certain sufficiently firm and strong castle, the town subject to it, which was less firm, within whose walls the peasants from the surrounding villages and fields were protecting themselves, came into his power by surrender, upon conditions pledged and ratified by oath: then, having violated the oath, he led away as captives all who were in the town.
Having returned to Sophia, and having moved his camp from there, he returned to Adrianople laden with booty; which he shared with his nobles and those who had rendered him service. A portion of the captives, which he kept for himself, four thousand men and women, he led away as new colonists to the villages near Constantinople. Setting out from Adrianople, he went to Constantinople, whose walls, which he had ordered to be repaired while he was at Philippopolis, he found upon his arrival to have been completed. After he came into the city, having measured a space of eight stadia or more in its center, he ordered the area to be enclosed with walls, and palaces to be built within it. He covered the domes and roofs of the constructed buildings with leaden sheets, which he took from deserted monasteries. Fullers had occupied the monastery of Pantokrator, and shoemakers were sewing shoes in the middle of the temple. Turkish monks (Turcocalogeri) had their seats in the monastery of the Manganon; in the rest, the Turks were lodging with their wives and children.
These things, which were done after the capture of the city, it is not permitted for me to write. For it is surely not fitting for me to weave a history of the victories and the prosperous deeds of the tyrant, the destroyer of our race and our mortal enemy: but what is [...]
fitting, I will here relate. When I was still a young man, I understood from certain excellent old men that the tyranny of the Othmans and the empire of the Palaiologoi would fall together, because Othman and Michael Palaiologos had seized tyranny and empire at the same time. Indeed, Michael took up the rods of rule a little before, and immediately afterward, while Andronikos, the son of Michael, was reigning, Othman began to rule. While Michael was still alive, Othman was only known for brigandage and plundering. Therefore, the order of nature demanded that the ruin and conquest of the emperors and the city should come first, and the ruin and overthrow of the Othmans should follow. Michael had formerly inquired of soothsayers and augurs whether he would have an heir in the empire after he had succumbed to fate; for he was burdened by the conscience of the crime by which he had nefariously seized the empire, after blinding the legitimate heir. Therefore, the oracle uttered a voice...
As you know, most ingenious Timothy, since we were holding our discussion in the school’s portico, the most reverend Epiphanius, the Arabian merchant, stood by us, having recently arrived from Arabia, and after he greeted us, we also welcomed him gladly and kindly. We said to him: "You have arrived, friend, and you find us at our fine studies." He replied to us very graciously: "And what special thing," I said, "have you brought to us philosophers?" The merchant said: "If there is anything else I do not know, I am ready to recount, especially what I have seen abroad, which makes us foreigners wonder and marvel." "How is it?" I said.
