And he said to me: "Tell one of your students to take down the astrolabe, and know the horoscope degree, noting also the movement of the stars and the clear confirmation of the centers, because of the new story and strange undertaking." I immediately ordered my Sophronios to take down the astrolabe; and while he was taking it down and inquiring minutely about the hour, the merchant opened his mouth and told us that in the desert of Ethribon (4) a certain man appeared from the tribe called the Korrasianoi, of the lineage of Ishmael, and his name was Mohammed; and he says that he himself is a prophet. He appeared in the month of Pharmouthi, which in Roman [style] is April, of the year [1174] from the beginning of the era of Philip. He introduces new utterances and a changed doctrine, and promises to those who accept his teaching victories in wars, dominion over enemies, and the delights of paradise. I, having pondered these things, and having been struck with fear at the prosperity of the man, and how he uses favorable fortune, and is strengthened in manliness, I made it my goal to entrust these things to you, the philosopher, so that through your given wisdom you might find knowledge regarding this very man. Having inquired of these things from the man, I immediately became thoughtful; and after dismissing, as you know, that school at that time, and sending the man on his way, I carefully examined the matter suggested by the astrolabe...
And, having seen the fearful and formidable threats directed against our race, we look forward to its liberty and restoration as if in a dream. And, with a most fervent spirit, we hope that the things foretold by wise and prudent men—that God, who punishes and again heals those who entreat Him, will grant an outcome to the things that have happened since the terror inflicted upon us by the tyrant—will come to pass. But let us return to the history.
CHAPTER XLIII
The tyrant, in the second year from that in which he became lord of Constantinople, the year 6963 from the creation of the world (1455 A.D.), while he was sojourning at Adrianople, was visited by the brothers, the knights of the military Order of Jerusalem, who paid him homage with very many gifts, and requested that sworn treaties be entered into, so that they might conduct commerce in the parts of Caria and Lycia, which border on their own domain; and that, in turn, the Turks might be allowed to cross over safely and securely into Rhodes, so that they might procure necessities for themselves in the island itself and its dependencies, and behave peacefully and as friends toward one another. The tyrant demanded a tribute from them; the legates replied that they possessed no instructions regarding this matter. The ministers warned them with these words: "Unless you are willing to pay tribute, peace and friendship with the prince will not be established; for from now on he shall be lord of all the islands that lie in the Aegean Sea. Just as the Chians, the Lesbians, the Lemnians, and the Imbrians, and the other islands, have obeyed, so you too must do. C If, however, you refuse to obey, a grave war will arise from this, and the great prince will devastate and topple your island and the surrounding ones." The envoys answered: "Let some one of the prince's servants come with us, and let him speak about this to the Grand Master; and if it is acceptable to him, let a tribute be paid, and anything else that might contribute to the advantage of the island. For we have no power to give an answer to these things." The plan pleased him, and he sent one of his celebrated servants with them, having dismissed them as was fitting. When they had arrived in Rhodes, and the Grand Master had heard well what the prince had prompted, he answered the servant, saying: "This island is not mine; I am subject to the Pope, just as you are to your lord. The Pope therefore forbids me to pay tribute to anyone, not only to your prince, who is of another nation, and alien and differing from our faith, but also to any of the kings of our own race and religion. I say therefore thus..."
note: Ismaelis Bullialdi notæ. (19) “They come also from Rhodes...” Jacobus Bosius, lib. vii, Histor. militia Hierosolymit., agrees entirely with Ducas, and that the Grand Master responded with a bold and brave spirit, and refused to pay a tax to Mehemet altogether.
if he desires to be a friend, and every year sends me ambassadors at my own expense to greet his neighbor and great ruler, behold, it is good; but if not, let him do what he can." He dismissed the subordinate then with these mocking words.
When the tyrant heard these words, and, filled with anger, having become thoroughly enraged, he proclaimed a fierce war, and granted leave to anyone who wished to depart, to take captives, and to ravage and destroy as much as he could. Then the Turks inhabiting the province of Caria, boarding biremes and other vessels up to the number of thirty, crossed over to the mainland and, landing like pirates on one part of the island, took forty souls captive, and in the island of Cos they did the same.
When spring arrived, he prepared a great fleet: twenty-five triremes, fifty biremes, and one hundred or more moneres, so that the whole fleet amounted to one hundred and eighty ships. In the month of June, they set out from Callipolis and arrived in Mitylene, commanded by an admiral, Hamza, whom Mehemet had once appointed—having previously held the office of cupbearer to his father—as governor of the whole Chersonese and commander of the fleet. The prince of Lesbos received him honorably, and designated me to provide the services and courtesies that were appropriate. For the admiral did not enter the harbor, but turning his prow toward the opposite shore—where there is a harbor capable of sheltering a fleet—he moored there, so that the city might not be disturbed in any way, as the prudent and experienced man, Hamza, deemed it necessary to do. Accordingly, being sent by the prince of Lesbos to greet him, I cultivated his goodwill with many gifts and other things customarily provided, and I joined him in fraternal friendship with the prince.
The gifts offered were as follows: silk garments and woven wools, six thousand silver coins, twenty cattle, fifty sheep, over eight hundred measures of wine, two modii of leavened bread, one modius of soft bread, over a thousand pounds of cheese, and countless vegetables besides. Gifts were also given to his councilors, in proportion. And having spent two days in that place—which is called Agiasmaten—he spread his sails and went to Chios. He followed the same course that he had in Lesbos, mooring his fleet against the mainland opposite the island; and the Chians, having no honor for him in his station there, did not emulate the generosity which the ruler of Lesbos had shown them. For the Chians had but recently been slighted and harshly treated by the tyrant on account of a matter of forty thousand coins, which Franciscus Draperius, one of the leading men of Galata, had claimed as the price of alum that had been sold and demanded to be paid to him. This Franciscus had come with the fleet and with Hamza; and the tyrant had given orders to Hamza that if the debt was not paid to that Franciscus, he should attack Chios itself and raze it as much as he could. On the following day, the fleet set sail from the opposite shore and, having dropped anchor, stood near the church of the martyr Isidore. The Chians sent some men to greet him, and he gave them the tyrant’s orders; and having read them, they replied that "The debt we..."
owe to Francis we neither acknowledge nor pay; let him do as he pleases." Then Hamzas, having landed the Turks and made a partial raid into the surrounding villages, caused damage to the vineyards and gardens, for there was nothing else he could do in the city. For the multitude of men was outside the city, while the interior was host to weaponry, as well as to hot-tempered Italians, ready for slaughter. The city was surrounded by double ditches extending to a great width and a depth of over three fathoms. The harbor itself was guarded by more than twenty ships from Genoa, all full of men and weapons. Then, when Hamzas saw that he could achieve nothing, he sent word to the leaders to have one or two of them come to have a talk with Francis on one of the triremes, having given them protections. Two of them, trusting him, went off—one of the elders named Cyricus Justinias, and the other a young man.
As they were proceeding on their way to the fleet, they were troubled and pressed by their own reasoning, saying to themselves: "If the Turk, having repented the promises he gave us, should wish to seize us while we are on the triremes, who will be there to oppose him or to say that he acted wickedly?" None of the Turks, but rather they will consider the deed a display of manly spirit and a clever maneuver. Amid these deliberations, the fleet was already close. The closer they approached the fleet, the more fear took root in their souls. They turned the reins back and compelled their horses to run in the opposite direction. A multitude of Turks, therefore, having been found in the vineyards and gardens, leaped out and blocked their passage. Having caught them—the Franks who were following them not preventing it in any way, but on the contrary pelting them with missiles—they drove them back, and presented the two lords to the captain. Having taken them on board the trireme and raised the anchors and hoisted the sails, he sailed toward Rhodes.
When they arrived and viewed the city from afar, and saw the harbor full of large ships, all drawn up for battle, and the city of immense size, and realized the preparations were double those at Chios, they split the sea toward the island of Kos. Having disembarked there, and finding the general town deserted, they plundered what was found, and having encountered a portion of old men and women, they asked them about the citizens. They said they had moved to another town, which is called Rachia D (20), as it was most fortified. Therefore, having taken them, the fleet crossed over to Rachia; having disembarked, they pitched their tents, and on the following day, having sought out the town and [having received] oaths that they would not be taken prisoner—the one who carried out the discourse was Francis—the people of the castle, the Frerii, through...
their skirmishes, drove them away without even giving a reply. Then Hamza, with those under him, having attacked the small town through breastworks, ladders, and siege engines, and by every other method, for twenty-two days, and having gained nothing, withdrew, having left behind many Turks, some slaughtered by the town and others by a stomach ailment. On the way, Hamza having spoken in words with Cyricus and having come to an agreement, both parties agreed to dispatch two of the nobles of Chios to the governor in Adrianople, one of whom was to be Cyricus, so that they might report the entire conduct to him, and they would remain steadfast in what was decreed by him. Having arrived in Chios, he released them to their homes. And they, as might be expected, honored both him and those with him.
But Fortune, looking askance with harsh eyes at the Chians, what snares she weaves! The Turks, having exited from the triremes and become drunk, began to cause riots, to insult, and to commit other shameful acts. One Turk, having approached a certain church, began to throw tiles from the roof down and to break them. An Italian, having seen the Turk boldly breaking the tiles, strikes the Turk; other Turks ran up to his aid. Seeing this, the Christians, both Latins and Romans, all set upon the Turks, beating some with swords and others with clubs. The Turks, having been turned to flight, ran quickly to the bireme. For that bireme belonged to Hamza. Now Hamza had forbidden anyone to leave the triremes, threatening him who went out with the gallows; but those fleeing from the bireme, some into the sea, others into the bireme. The Christians ran behind them, beating them until they reached the bireme. And indeed all the Christians and Turks, having pressed upon one side of the bireme, caused the keel to turn upward and the roof deck to be immersed in the waters, and the Turks thrust the ship into the deep: all were drowned and perished—the guilty and the innocent—among whom was the head servant of Hamza, very dear to him and placed in charge of the management of his whole household. C Hamza was deeply grieved at this event, as were the nobles of the island. Nevertheless, the good sense of the man and the zeal of the nobles assuaged his anger; they gave him the price of the bireme, and of the servant, and of the things that had perished, doubled, and having made peace, they sent him away in peace.
When the fleet had reached Mitylene, the governor summoned him, and he entered the harbor. Having been sent by the governor, and having prepared a sumptuous dinner, I myself went aboard the trireme, and we dined together. In the morning, having left the harbor, he sailed toward Gallipoli—having been away for two whole months—and from Gallipoli, he arrived at Adrianople. The tyrant, having become angry at the ill-success of the voyage, both insulted and disparaged him, saying, "If I did not know the love [which he bore towards me, I would have flayed the skin from your flesh," thus speaking he drove him away
After a few days, having learned from others what had happened in the bireme, and about the death by drowning, and how the Chians had raised a hand against the Turks and slaughtered them, he summoned Hamza and asked in anger, saying: "Where is the bireme which was sunk by the Chians, O Hamza?" And he replied, "It was swallowed and overwhelmed by the deep," he said. The tyrant asked, "Was it while sailing?" Hamza answered, "No, master, but while it was standing in the harbor." "By whom?" said the prince. "By the Latins," said Hamza. "For the Turks, even though I did not wish it, went out, and having become heated with wine, they began to tear down the doors and roofs of the churches, and when the Latins saw them they restrained them, but they attacked them all the more. The base rabble, then, having pursued them in a disorderly fashion and entering the bireme, and leaning to one side of the ship, the sea poured inside, and being unable by reason of their drunkenness to balance it, it sank, and drowned them all completely." Then the tyrant said to Hamza, "And why did you not tell me of this occurrence?" He replied, C "I did not wish to burden you with grief, for the loss was measured against me; the ship was mine, the slaves who were drowned were mine, and everything in the ship was mine. What did I have to report to you, master? A number of Turks were drowned, and all were guilty of death and perished justly." Then Hamza ceased his defense, and the tyrant proclaimed implacable war against Chios. The aforementioned Franciscus, who was standing before the tribunal of the tyrant, was asked by the same: "Where are the forty thousand gold pieces, O Franciscus?" For he was owing this amount to the tyrant. He replied, "Go, be free from the debt from this moment. For I am such that I will demand double the amount from the Chians to cover what is mine, and the price of the blood of the Turks." Franciscus, having kissed the hand of the tyrant and received a written release, departed. Hamza was expelled from Gallipoli and sent to Attalia in Pamphylia to govern there. Against Chios, however, he proclaimed enmity and implacable war.
In this same year, on the 30th of June, the prince of the island of Lesbos, Dorinus Gateluzus, died. And on the first of August, I was sent by the new prince, his son Dominicus Gateluzus, to Adrianople, to pay the annual taxes which were given, three thousand gold pieces for the island of Lesbos, and two thousand three hundred and twenty-five for the island of Lemnos. For it was near [this island that the island was given by the tyrant to the prince of Lesbos, to provide annually ...]
the prescribed tribute; and to the governor of Ainos he gave the island of Imbros, that he too might provide for the same island one thousand two hundred gold coins. Having arrived therefore according to custom, I did obeisance to the governor, kissed his hand, and sat before him until he had eaten his midday meal, after which I paid my respects and departed. On the following day, having received the gold pieces, I came and surrendered them into the hands of the viziers. When they had received the tribute, they asked me, saying: "How is the prince of Mitylene? Is he in good health?" I replied, "He is in good health and sends his greetings to you." They continued, "We are asking about the elder, the lord of the whole island." I replied again, "He passed away forty days ago. He who now rules is his son, who was proclaimed prince six years ago. For as the father was bedridden and lying infirm, he voluntarily ceded the principality to his son, who indeed came to the city once and twice to do obeisance to the Great Prince and to offer him congratulations." They said, "Dismiss what you say. Today it happens that he cannot be called Prince of Lesbos unless he has approached the most high Prince and received the principality from him. Go, therefore, and take care to bring him here. If he does not obey, he knows what will happen." Therefore, having returned to Mitylene, I brought the Prince of Lesbos with several prominent Latin and Roman men. Placing our hope in God, we set sail from the island and, having crossed the Chersonese, we arrived at Adrianople. But the prince kept changing his residence on account of the sweeping plague; for the contagion of this pestilential disease was so ruinous to the Chersonese and the whole of Thrace that unburied corpses were lying in the crossroads. When we discovered that the prince was staying in Philippopolis, we hastened there; but after we arrived, we learned that he had departed two days earlier on account of the violence of the raging disease and had moved toward the parts of Sofia. Leaving Philippopolis, therefore, and having crossed the steep and rugged mountains, on the third day we arrived at a certain Bulgarian village called Izlati. C There the camp with the tyrant was situated. Having arrived and appeared before the high officials, the Pasha Mahmoud and the Pasha Seit Achmet, with the many gifts, on the following day we appeared before the Prince. And after the Prince of Mitylene had kissed the hand of the tyrant, we departed. On the next day, a message came through the high officials to our prince from the tyrant, to the effect that he desired the island of Thasos as a gift, and he requested that it be donated by him. The Prince of Lesbos, having nothing with which to contradict or speak, bestowed the island. On the following day, another message came, that he wished to have the tribute, which he received annually, doubled. The Mitylenean, taking this painfully, replied: "He can take all of Lesbos too, if he wishes to have it: but what he asks of me is far beyond my strength and resources; nevertheless, I ask you, lords, to assist me in this matter." The *mesazones*, regarding this matter with the tyrant...
added another thousand gold pieces, and no more; for whereas he had been receiving three thousand gold pieces annually, it became four thousand. Then they clothed him in a gold-woven garment, and us in silk, and having drawn up written oaths, we departed, and after thirteen days we arrived at the island of Lesbos, all of us praising God, who had delivered us from the hands of the avenging demon.
The tyrant, as we have mentioned, having fitted out a small fleet, ten triremes and ten other biremes—while we were still in Philippopolis—gave command of it to a young and handsome Genoese, whom he had also appointed governor of Gallipolis and *grand conostaulus* of the fleet; and having departed from the Hellespont, he sailed against Chios. When he had come to the Troad, and as he began to unfurl his sails from the Troad, behold, a heavy storm and a great sound of winds. As a heavy wind blew, churning the sea, and the violence compelled the passengers to direct their course elsewhere with their ships, five of the twenty were sunk, and two went aground on the shores and were wrecked. But the Genoese *conostaulus*'s navigator, skilled in such squalls and agitations of the sea (for he was a Latin, a Spaniard by birth), by turning the stern and skillfully and gently cutting the troughs of the waves with the rudders, sailed upon the open sea. Having passed Chios from the west, and having traversed the Cyclades islands that entire day, and the weather having quieted during the night, they presented themselves in the morning at the eastern side of Chios; and having recognized it to be that island, they sent up hymns of thanksgiving to God and to their prophet Mohammed. O the abyss of the judgments of God! In such a swell and violent disturbance of the sea, how was the ship not submerged? But because of our sins, the disciple of the tyrant was saved. For it was the only trireme, the one separated from the Genoese's course. The remaining ones, having been saved, found refuge in the harbor of Mitylene. They questioned the inhabitants about their leader, and when they learned that he had not been seen in those parts, they remained in distress. Then, as evening was already falling, a sail appeared from the side of Chios, like a bireme sailing. This was the Mitylenean bireme sent by the brother of the ruler to Chios, to learn whether any piratical ships of the Catalans had arrived from the west, so that they might give notice to their neighbors, the Turks, to be on their guard. For from the beginning this was the charge of the Lesbians, in their ignoble slavery: to avoid being late in giving report of the arrival of pirates, so that if any damage should occur to the Turks, the Lesbians themselves would be obliged to make restitution to the Turks for what was lost. Ismaelis Bullialdi notæ.
A ...and the limits of his authority [extended] from the mouth of the river Pergamon [(24)] as far as the city of Assos, which is now called Machramion. After the bireme entered the port, another sail was seen from afar, and from the breadth of the canvas and the variety of its colors, those watching conjectured that the commander of the fleet was approaching, and they were filled with joy. He finally arrived in the port and, having disembarked onto land, he rested from the great tossing and swelling of the sea beneath tents erected by his servants. Sir [that is, lord] Nicolaus Gateluzus, the brother of the prince of Lesbos, having made a great banquet to receive him, descended from the fortress to the tent and, after sitting for a little while, returned. Then the disciple of the wicked Alastor [the devil], being angered, fabricated a scheme against him, saying: "The bireme which I have pursued up to this point belongs to me, both it and everything that is in it" (there was, in fact, inside it one of the women from the leading families of Chios, the most noble, having with her much finery of gold and silver). "If, therefore, you are friends of my master, surrender it to me; if not, at this very hour I shall write of these things to the Great Amiras." They replied: "We do not know of what you speak; for the bireme was sent by us on other necessary business of ours to Chios. The noble lady, moreover, of whom you speak, has been here for a long time." She was indeed the mother-in-law of the prince [(25)], and when he was about to depart, he had called her to stay with his lady and her daughter; and in truth this is how it really stands. But the commander, having heard these things and not believing them, wrote to the Amiras what he wished; and having departed from there for Phocaea, he came to what is called the New [City], and sent a message to the magistrates and the podestà of the region to come out and meet with him. They, however, had come out even before the message arrived, and met him. Then the commander showed them and read the orders of the tyrant, for it was written that if they did not willingly surrender the little town, they would all be utterly taken captive and the city razed to the ground. C The people of the city, without a word or reply, betraying the land, let them inside. They seized the goods and property of the Genoese merchants who were trading there, and threw the merchants themselves into the triremes. After they had listed all the townspeople, they carried off about a hundred boys and girls, and having installed one of the Turks as guardian of the little town and having spent fifteen days there, the triremes departed on the fifteenth day of the month of November of the year [1455]. When the triremes arrived at Callipolis and the commander learned that the prince was staying in Constantinople, he himself rode on horseback, and taking the captives along with the boys, he departed. The prince, having seen the merchants and learned that they were Genoese, [ordered them to come]. But the prince of Lesbos, having set out for Mitylene, and having been informed by his brother of what had happened: that...
Ismaelis Bullialdi notæ.
(24) Of the river Pergamon. This river so called, formerly the Caicus; which flows past Pergamon, the homeland of Galen; it received its name from that city in these later centuries.
(25) For she was the mother-in-law of the prince. She was, therefore, the wife of Paris Justiniani of Chios. See below at the following chapter. Final note.
he ordered to be sold, and this was done. The prince of Lesbos, having come to Mytilene and learned from his own brother what had occurred, and how the [Genoese] commander was seeking his mother-in-law, as she was one of the noble ladies there on Chios, and the rest, sent me to make a defense concerning this matter. Having arrived in Constantinople and spoken before the viziers together with the Genoese commander, and having stated on oath the whole truth—while the Genoese swore to the whole lie—he was acquitted, and I was condemned. The prince therefore ordered me to choose one of two things: either to pay ten thousand gold coins, or for a battle to be fought. I, resisting such a great injustice, he himself, by an order of which some were unaware, sent one of his servants and seized the so-called "Old Phocaea," which belonged to the prince of Lesbos, on the 24th day of December of the year 6964 [1455]. Then, when the tyrant learned of the capture of Phocaea, he released me and put an end to the lawsuit. Having departed from Constantinople on the 24th of January, he went down to Aenos and took it; and having taken boys and girls, he turned back to Adrianople. The prince of Aenos was staying at that time on the island of Samothrace.
CHAPTER XLV
The Chians, attacked by war, buy peace from Mehmed with a great sum. The Lemnians summon the Turks, and their prince, Nicholas, is cast out of the island. Mehmed besieges Belgrade in vain. Pope Callistus sends triremes to bring resources to the islanders, Catalans occupy the islands, and the Prince of Lesbos comes under suspicion by Mehmed, as if he had summoned the Westerners. Envoys from the Comneni and Usun Hassan come to Mehmed. The Castle of the Seven Towers, commonly called [Yedikule], is built at Constantinople. Mehmed’s expedition into the Morea. The Bezestan is built in Constantinople. He crosses into Asia. Mehmed's words to a certain curious acquaintance of his, the Prince of Sinope, and he transports into Europe the Trebizondian emperor [who had been] despoiled of his possessions. He demands tribute from the Wallachian, who refuses to give it; he impales those sent to him. He defeats the Turks entering his territory under the leadership of Hamza, and impales the living captives on stakes as well. Mehmed moves against him with an unsuccessful outcome. He demands Lesbos from Prince Nicholas, who had strangled his brother Dominic. Mehmed crosses to Lesbos, compels [them] to surrender, departs, and imposes the burden of besieging Mitylene upon the vizier Mahumet.
Summer was now beginning when the tyrant ordered a great fleet to be prepared against Chios. The Chians, having learned of this, sent envoys, and after much struggle they agreed to give—on account of the bireme and the Turks who had perished with it—thirty thousand gold coins, and an annual tribute of ten thousand. Having thus made peace, they went away. But the Lemnians, having ill-will against their leader Nicholas, secretly sent some of their lords to ask the tyrant for one of his servants to govern the island. He, having heard the proposal eagerly, informed the eunuch Ismael, who was at that time governor of Gallipoli (for he had expelled the Genoese and was overseeing the province of Caria). This Ismael was brought in as *constabularius* and governor in the Chersonese. He therefore ordered him to go to Lemnos with triremes and to hand over the island to the servant Hamza, to govern and administer as is right. While these things were being done, the prince of Lesbos, having sent one of his biremes and a ship with a hundred men or more, having as commanders a certain John Fontana and Spineta Columbotus, entrusted them [with instructions] that if they saw the Lemnians had repented of what they had done, they should look upon them kindly, and through gentle words and agreements, [bring] the island back to him.
If not, they were to take his brother A Nicholas and return. He was dwelling in the old fortress. But they did not act in this way; instead, they emerged in arms and fought. The Lemnians, however, having sallied forth on horseback, some five hundred in number, routed them—cutting some down and pursuing others into the sea, where they drowned. They captured forty men by hand. The rest, who had remained in the bireme and ship, took Nicholas and sailed back to Lesbos. Three days later, Ismael also arrived in Lemnos, bringing Hamza, the new governor. Upon learning what had happened, he praised the Lemnians. Taking the Lesbians as prisoners, he returned to Gallipoli in the month of May of the year [1456]. B Having informed the tyrant of the events in Lemnos, it kindled his wrath against Lesbos and its ruler. Being presently turned toward Belgrade with a huge army and vast siege equipment, he undertook the expedition with the intention of taking it. After the city was encircled by a blockade, the wall demolished by stone-throwing engines, and sixty vessels intercepted in their navigation of the river, the assault reached such a point that the Turks entered and began to plunder. Then the aforementioned Jancus (as my account has already mentioned), having crossed the river—for he had arrived that very day—entered, pursued them, and, striking and cutting some down, drove them out of the city. Having gone forth from the gate himself with a great force of soldiers, he captured all the war materiel. And having slaughtered many of the Turks, and even wounded the tyrant himself in the thigh, he finally returned into the city and set fire to the Turkish ships. The tyrant, having suffered humiliation and a repulse, returned to Adrianople, threatening to campaign against Belgrade in the new year. These events took place in the month of July of that same year. In the month of August, I was sent to pay the annual tribute that the prince of Lesbos owes. D Having paid it, I asked for those whom the Lemnians had handed over as faithless, but he did not wish to give them up; rather, he ordered that their heads be cut off, for they were imprisoned in Adrianople. As they were being led to the place of execution, the tyrant, moved by regret, ordered that they be sold, and they were sold for one thousand gold coins. In the year 6965 [1457], eleven triremes arrived from Rome, having as their commander the patriarch of Aquileia, sent by Pope Callistus to provide aid to the islands adjacent to the Turks, such as Rhodes, Chios, Lesbos, Lemnos, Imbros, Samothrace, and Thasos.
They arrived at Rhodes, which was under the Pope and had refused to pay tribute to the Turks. Setting sail from Rhodes, they arrived in Chios, requesting that they not pay tribute to the Turks, but rather choose to fight; but they did not consent. Likewise, the inhabitants of Lesbos did the same. And then, from Lesbos, having gathered the Pope’s ships, along with those of the Catalans and other pirate ships—numbering up to forty—they departed for Lemnos, and after taking that island, they arrived in Samothrace (28), and having taken it as well, they came to Thasos. And having placed guards on the islands and secured them well, they returned to Rhodes.
Then the tyrant, learning of what had happened, wrote the entire case to the governor of Lesbos and, having stirred up a fierce war against him, prepared a heavy fleet and sent it in the month of August to Lesbos, having as its commander Ishmael. And when he had arrived at Methymna, and had attempted many methods and mechanical operations through stone-throwing engines and scaling ladders and mining, he gained nothing; on the contrary, he lost many of his own men, and thus returned unsuccessful.
In the year six thousand—he sends to the despots of the Peloponnese a servant with a fearful command, arguing: "How is it that you willingly promised to pay me as tribute ten thousand coins per year, but now I see you despising me and neglecting the treaties? Choose, therefore, the better of two options: either pay what is owed, and there will be friendship between us, or quickly depart, leaving the territory to my dominion." For they were in arrears for three years of payment.
In this same year, envoys were sent by the Comani (29), from the one who was lord over the parts of Armenia and neighbor to the Colchians, Uzun Hasan (30), who was demanding from him certain matters of contempt, saying that he owed him tribute for sixty years, to be given every year with a thousand horse-caparisons for his horses, and a thousand harnesses, and a thousand head-dresses, which his grandfather had ordered to be paid annually to the grandfather of that one. And he replied: "Go in peace, and in the coming year I will bring these things with me and I will pay the debt."
That winter, the tyrant began to build at the edge of the city, at the place called the Golden Gate (31), a small fortress which John the elder, the emperor, had wished to build, but Baiazid, the tyrant’s great-grandfather, had forbidden him. But when spring had already begun, having assembled his forces, he moved into the Peloponnese, and Corinth was received by him through surrender without the crisis of war. Being made informed of those things which were being done, the despots—the one, Thomas, namely, headed for Italy with his wife and children; the other, Demetrios, submitted himself to the tyrant of his own will and paid him homage. Thus, with the whole of the Peloponnese subdued and governors imposed upon it, he returned to Adrianople, taking Demetrios with his whole house and the other palace officials along with him.
He massacred the chieftains of the Albanians, leaving no other stronghold intact except Monemvasia, and that against his will and reluctantly. As for the naval expedition, he sent about one hundred and eighty biremes and triremes into the Aegean Sea and among the Cyclades islands against the enemy; having achieved nothing, he transported two thousand families and as many boys from the Peloponnese. These youths were enrolled as military recruits, and for the families, a part of the city of Constantinople was granted as a dwelling place.
He spent the winter partly in Adrianople and partly in Constantinople, where he had a vessel of enormous size constructed. In the city he also built a theatre, which is called the clothing market, and in Persian, *Bezestan* [(53)]. In the following year, he prepared a fleet of about two hundred triremes and biremes, and ten ships. As the year turned, having crossed the straits, he came to Prusa in Bithynia, with no one knowing or sensing his plan, and I shall relate something miraculous regarding this. His doctor of law, who was also judge of judges at that time, relying on the familiarity he had with the prince and the respect shown to him by the prince, when he was alone with him, audaciously inquired: "My lord, where do you command this army, prepared by land and sea, to be moved?" The tyrant looked at him with somewhat of a scowl and said: "Heus, you, learn this from me: if I knew that one single hair of my beard was conscious of my secret, I would pull it out and burn it in the fire." So dissimulating and irascible was he by nature. The fame of this expedition terrified not only the Wallachians who inhabit Lycostomium [(54)], but also the Caphatini, the Trapezuntines, and the Sinopians, as well as the islands of the Aegean Sea, Rhodes and its surrounding small islands. Even Chios and Lesbos, although they were tributary, dreaded his inconstant and fickle spirit.
Departing from Bithynia, the prince reached Ancyra in Galatia, where, after he had pitched his camp, the son of the prince of Sinope was sent to him by his father with very many gifts; he approached in a servile habit and manner, showing reverence. Having been received humanely and kindly by the prince, he listened to whatever matters were to be conveyed to his father, with the intention of fulfilling the messenger's duty himself before his parent. These were of this kind: "You shall announce to your father that I greatly desire that he hand over Sinope to me; if he should depart of his own accord, and not compelled by force, I will grant him the prefecture of Philippopolis as a gift. But if he refuses to obey, I will arrive shortly." Meanwhile, the fleet arrived at Sinope by the Pontic sea. The son of Ishmael, the prince of Sinope, having also traveled to his father, reported all the words of the tyrant. Moreover, the report that the fleet had arrived at Sinope [caused fear].
The ruler, having departed from Bithynia, came to Ancyra of Galatia, and having pitched his tents there, the ruler of Sinope sent his son with a great many gifts, and having met him, he did obeisance in a servile manner. He received him gladly, and announced to him what was to be made known to his own father, and through him—as a messenger of the things to be said—he declared everything, saying: "Announce to your father that I desire Sinope; and if he should freely yield it, I for my part will graciously return to him the province of Philippopolis; but if not, I am coming quickly." The fleet arrived at Sinope by way of the Pontic sea. The son of Ismael, the ruler of Sinope, went to his father and announced to him all the things spoken by the tyrant.
But the tyrant, having learned that the ascent of the fleet had taken place at Sinope, was himself journeying thither by land. And Ismael, being at a loss, went out of Sinope, and having met him, did obeisance in a servile manner. The tyrant received him pleasantly, commanding all his treasures to be taken, and horses, and mules, and camels, and whatever else he possessed in his treasuries, and that no one should touch anything belonging to him. Having then set Sinope in good order, and having appointed one of his own slaves as ruler, he himself proceeded further into the interior of Armenia. C The aforementioned ruler, Uzun Hasan, was spending his time in the mountainous borders of Persia with his men, not having the strength to confront the tyrant face to face. Having crossed Armenia, and having passed the river Phasis, he captured some territories, while others he bypassed, not being able to conquer them; and having ascended the Caucasian mountains with much toil and lack of necessities, he descended into Colchis. And truly, having arrived at Trebizond, he sent to the Emperor of Trebizond to choose the better of two options: either to hand over the empire to the tyrant without any loss of any of his existing treasures—silver, gold, copper, and any other kind of property, of male and female slaves, and every other movable possession—or, along with the empire, to lose these things as well, and his life besides. Having heard these things, the emperor went out with his whole household and did obeisance. For the fleet had departed from Sinope for Trebizond many days before, but it was accomplishing nothing by fighting every day, until the tyrant arrived by land. When the emperor went out with his wife and children, he did obeisance. This was David Komnenos, the son of Alexios Komnenos, and broth-
er of John Komnenos, the former emperor, whom he sent to Constantinople together with the triremes, with his whole family and others [Koryroi?], his uncles and cousins, and with the nobles and aristocrats of the palace; each of them carrying his personal property, apart from his immovable assets. He himself, having governed the affairs of Trebizond well, returned after having completed a full year in that exile. In the year 6930 [1422], he sent an envoy to the Vaivode of Walachia (38) notifying him to come quickly to pay homage, being accompanied by 40 children and the annual tribute prescribed, which was ten thousand gold pieces. He replied that while he was ready to pay the gold, he could not provide the children; and as for his own coming to pay homage, this was even more impossible.
Having heard this, the tyrant became enraged, and having dispatched one of his prominent men accompanied by one of his secretaries, he said: "Bring the tribute to me, and I will consider the rest." They arrived and declared the contents of the message to the Walachian, who first placed them on stakes—a death inhumane, painful, and disgraceful; then, having crossed over with his army, he fell upon parts of Dystra (39), and having taken a large rabble of people in Walachia and having brought them across, he meted out the same death of the stake to all of them, ending their lives. And one of the leading commanders of the tyrant from those borders, wishing to show some prowess, passed into Walachia with ten thousand Turks. The Walachian engaged them in battle; those whom he killed in the conflict he slew, and those whom he had captured alive he condemned—all of them, as well as their commander Hamza—to the cruel death of the stake.
When the tyrant learned this, he was filled with dizziness and confusion, and having gathered power from everywhere exceeding 150 thousand, in the spring he set out from Adrianopolis and arrived at the Danube. Having pitched his tents there, he waited until his entire force was gathered into one body. The Walachian, for his part, moved everyone under his command into gorges and wooded places, and having left the plains deserted, and having driven all manner of animals into the inner borders toward the Alans and Huns (40), he himself spent the days in the thick forests and in secure places with the army under him. C The tyrant, having crossed the Danube and traversed a distance of seven days, found neither man nor animal, nor any food or drink. Upon finally arriving at a grassy and well-situated place, he saw stakes planted by the myriads, heavy with dead bodies instead of fruits; and in their midst, the aforementioned Hamza wearing the purple and scarlet robes he had worn, being pierced upon the stake. Seeing this threat, the tyrant was struck with horror, and on that very night in which he had pitched his camp, he kept himself confined within, having dug trenches around it. At the crack of dawn, the Walachian led his troops, drawn up in battle array, and having chanced upon the right wing of the camp, he suddenly broke into it; and until daybreak arrived, he caused a great slaughter of the Turks, with countless numbers being slain. The Turks, trembling in the darkness and unable to recognize the enemy, wounded one another. When it was light, the Walachians retreated into their own camp and remained there. The tyrant then broke camp, retreated in disgrace, crossed the Danube, and returned to Adrianopolis. In the year [of Christ 1462], having equipped a fleet of sixty triremes and seven ships, in the month of September he set sail for the island of Lesbos; but he approached by land, having taken his forces with him. He approached the island from Nicosia…
his tents, he raised fortifications and lay in an entrenchment of ditches. The Vlach, having waited for dawn and having drawn up those under him well, descended while it was still dark, and having chanced upon the right side of the trench, he entered suddenly, and until morning he slaughtered more than can be numbered. Many of the Turks killed one another until the day shone forth. When morning had come, the Vlachs went into their sheepfolds to sleep, but the tyrant, having risen ashamed, crossed the Danube and came to Adrianople. In the first year, having made ready a fleet of sixty triremes and biremes and seven ships, he came down to the island of Lesbos in the month of September, and he himself came by land along with an army. Having arrived, therefore, he demanded the island (41) from the ruler, Nicholas Gateluzo, who was the brother of Dominic (42), who had ruled before, whom the aforementioned Nicholas had deposed from the lordship and strangled. He himself had been established as ruler of Lesbos for four years in his lordship. Now Nicholas had securely prepared Mytilene with war-making equipment, a multitude of weapons, and the digging of ditches and casting up of earthworks, and he sat in the middle with a great number of combatants, more than five thousand, and a rabble of people along with women and children, more than twenty thousand. The tyrant having crossed from Hagiasmation and requested the city along with the island, Nicholas answered: "It is not possible to surrender the city and the island, unless first they themselves shall have been killed by the law of war." Then the tyrant, having crossed the strait again, left his own vizier, Mahmut, to besiege Mytilene. And indeed, having placed stone-throwing engines directly opposite, and throwing stones at the one part of the city called Melanoudion, he razed it to the ground; similarly also from other sides the fortifications and the towers. Being aware, then, those inside...
DUKE MICHAEL DUKE’S NEPHEW BYZANTINE HISTORY A.D. 1341–1462

### CHAPTER ONE.
A brief account of the generations from Adam to the Nativity of Christ. Enumeration of the years elapsed from Christ to the beginning of the reign of Constantine. From Constantine to Justinian, from Justinian to Constantine and Irene. From these to Alexius Comnenus. Thereafter, a brief enumeration of the Emperors of Constantinople until the capture of the city by the Latins.
Numbers of the years from the first man to our generation.
From Adam, the first man, to Noah, in whose age the flood occurred, ten generations took place. The first is Adam himself, created by God. After 200 years, the second is that of Seth, born to Adam. After Seth, 205 years, the third is that of Enos, from Seth. After Enos, 117 years, the fourth is that of Cainan, from Enos. After Cainan, 170 years, the fifth is that of Maleleel, from Cainan. After Maleleel, 165 years, the sixth is that of Jared, from Maleleel. After Jared, 162 years, the seventh is that of Enoch, from Jared. After Enoch, 165 years, the eighth is that of Mathusala, from Enoch. After Mathusala, 167 years, the ninth is that of Lamech, from Mathusala. After Lamech, 188 years, the tenth is that of Noah. Noah was 600 years old when the great flood took place upon the earth. So that the years counted from Adam to the flood are 2,242. Likewise, from the flood to Abraham, ten generations passed, totaling 1,121 years. Abraham was 75 years old when he migrated to the land of Canaan from Mesopotamia, and having lived there for 25 years he begat Isaac; and Isaac begat two sons,
Notes of Ismael Bullialdus.
(1) At the beginning of this work, the author’s intention was to present a synopsis of the years elapsed from the origin and creation of the world according to the calculation of the Eastern Church, which counts 5,508 complete years from the beginning of the world to the first year of the common Christian era, starting from the September preceding the Kalends of January of the first year. None of those who are somewhat versed in chronology are unaware that the Greeks begin their year from that term of the Kalends of September: so that Christ is said to have been born in the year 5509, whether in the autumn or at the beginning of winter, when the Theotokos gave birth to Him. All also know that the Seventy—the interpreters of the Old Testament, so named and believed—calculated more years from the world’s beginning to Abraham in their version than are found in the Hebrew text. It is difficult to ascertain the reason why this happened. To be sure, the Hebrew text shows only 1,655 years from Adam to the flood, while in the meantime the LXX interpreters count 2,242. In the words of this chapter, the text is correct: even if from the numbers of the generations explained, 2,249 are gathered. From the flood to Abraham, the Hebrew text counts 292 years, but the interpreters count 1,178; this author of ours counts 1,121. There is no space here to speak of this disagreement in calculation; nor is it our intent to investigate and scrutinize whether the Hebrew text, which they used, differed from that which is circulated and approved by all. Or whether those men, who were subjecting sacred history to the eyes and judgment of the Gentiles—especially the Egyptians and Greeks—were moved by some reasoning to intercalate several years from the creation of the world to the flood, and thence to Abraham, in order to decline the importunate objections of the nations who were blinded by idolatry.
Isaac. Now Isaac begat two sons, Esau and Jacob. Then Jacob, when he had lived one hundred and thirty years, went down into Egypt together with his twelve sons and his grandchildren, who were seventy-five in number. Abraham dwelt with his seed in the land of Canaan for a space of four hundred and thirty-three years, and having multiplied, they were reckoned as twelve tribes; and the multitude of the descendants of the twelve sons of Jacob was numbered at six thousand thousands. And these are their names: Ruben, Simeon, Levi, Juda, Issachar, Zabulon, Nephthalim, Gad, Aser, Dan, Joseph, and Benjamin. Moses and Aaron derived their lineage from Levi; the latter first served in the priesthood, while Moses applied himself to the administration of the state. In the eightieth year of his life, he trod the Erythraean Sea and brought the people out of Egypt. This Moses flourished in the times of Inachus, who first reigned among the Greeks; thus the Jews are more ancient than the Greeks. Having spent forty years in the desert, and having been ruled by Joshua, son of Nave, for twenty-five years, and by the Judges for four hundred and fifty-four years until the kingdom of Saul, who was the first king established among them—in whose first year of his reign the great David was born. So that from Abraham to David there are gathered fourteen generations, comprising one thousand and twenty-four years. And from David to the deportation to Babylon there are likewise fourteen generations, covering six hundred and nine years; and from the deportation to Babylon to Christ there are counted fourteen generations, covering five hundred and four years. In total, following the sequence of years, we have calculated from the first Adam to Christ five thousand five hundred years. And from the Incarnation to the great Constantine there are two hundred and eighteen years. From the Incarnation. And in the time of the great Constantine, he went away into the church of the Holy Apostles, wherein also his holy sarcophagus is laid. In the eleventh year took place the dedication of the Great Church, and the procession went out from the Holy Resurrection together with the patriarch and the emperor, with the people. And from the day of its burning until the dedication, five years, eleven months, and ten days passed; for in the two hundred and eighteenth year from the creation of the world, in the fifteenth indiction, on the twenty-third day of the month of February, at the first hour of the day, Justinian began to restore the Great Church.
in the third year of his reign. The Latins also were driven from the city (12), and Michael Palaeologus entered as emperor, having set out from the parts of the East. Up to this emperor, the following provinces were subject to the Roman Empire and paid tribute: Asia Minor, Paphlagonia, Mysia (which is also Bithynia), Greater Phrygia, Phrygia Capatiana, Caria, and a part of Cilicia. But the Turks, who were inhabitants of Lycaonia, ruled the regions beyond, namely Lycaonia, Cappadocia, Galatia, Pamphylia, Armenia, Helenopontus, Pisidia, Lycia, Coele-Syria, and others. Michael reigned for 24 years. After Michael, his son Andronicus (13) Palaeologus [reigned] for 43 years. In the ... year of his reign, the metropolis of Asia, Ephesus, and the province of Caria were captured by Mantachia; and Lydia as far as Smyrna [was taken] by Atin; and Magnesia as far as Pergamum, and all the province of Magedon (14) by Sarchan, in the year 6768, on the 25th of July. Two years had passed since Michael had become master of the imperial thrones.
The Caraman Alisurius held the greater part of inland Phrygia, and even the regions up to Philadelphia, and all the nearest places from Antioch on the Maeander. Another, named Sarganes, [held] the regions thence as far as Smyrna and the inner coastal areas of Ionia; for, having reached the parts around Magnesia, Priene, and Ephesus, a satrap named Sasan took them away. Those [lands] from Aeolis as far as the Mysia which is by the Hellespont [were held by] the one called Calames and his son Carases; the regions around Olympus and whatever else of Bithynia lies nearby [were held by] another named Aiman. The lands from the river Sangarius as far as Paphlagonia were divided among the sons of Amurius. Cheter and Amur...
Notes of Ismael Bullialdus
Andronicus the senior, so-called, died at the age of 73, having reigned for 13 years. Andronicus was succeeded by his grandson, John Palaiologos [(17)], who was still young and being educated by Lord John Cantacuzenus. During his reign... the Turks [(18)] began to cross the Hellespont. From Asia, Umur, grandson of Atin, a leader of the Turks who held Smyrna, Ephesus, and the surrounding regions, set out; and from Prusa, Orchan, grandson of the aforementioned Othman, set out. Crossing in a piratical fashion, they ravaged the whole Chersonese, and as there was no one to resist or rise against them, they raided without fear as far as Didymoteichon [(19)], and toward the imperial city as far as Selymbria [(20)], intending to bring the whole of Thrace under their hand. B In the reign of the aforementioned John, while he was still a boy, the island of Chios was captured by the Genoese, and the remaining islands of the Cyclades were taken by the Franks who had arrived from Navarre [(21)].
He made the Great Domestic John Cantacuzenus—who had also become emperor—superior to the Panhypersebastos. He made him master of all, both of the nephews of the grandfather and emperor—who were his own cousins—and of all the others, and of the Panhypersebastos [and] of the vestiary. Thus, this man was there the Great—that is to say, Domestic—after the Caesar.
Notes of Ismael Bullialdus
[(17)] After Andronicus, John Palaiologos... Andronicus the younger left his son, whom he had begotten by Anna—of our Alemanna, Cantacuzenus, and Savoy, and others Pannonian—as heir to the empire. John was born to Andronicus after the death of the grandfather Andronicus in the year of the world 6840, Christ 1332, on June 18, as Gregoras noted, lib. 11, cap. 3. But Andronicus the younger died in the year of the world 6849, Christ 1341, so that John was still very much a child, in his ninth year when he obtained the empire: which even Cantacuzenus records, lib. II, cap. 2. Wherefore the father, dying, gave this John Cantacuzenus as tutor by will to administer the affairs of the empire, the author of the history already often cited, a man indeed praised by Gregoras and our own; he was suspected by Phranzes of desiring the kingdom and accused of wishing to transfer the empire to his own children. Phranzes must be read, lib. 1, cap. 3 and 15. Andronicus the younger esteemed that Cantacuzenus so much that in his will, which he drew up in the year of Christ while suffering from a serious illness, with his grandfather Andronicus having been passed over—who was still alive and not yet a monk—and even his own mother Xena, he gave him as tutor to his posthumous son, if he were to be born of his wife Anna, then pregnant. Nor must we omit what is reported by Codinus the Curopalata concerning the benevolence and love of Andronicus toward John Cantacuzenus, *De offic. palat.* He made the Great Domestic John Cantacuzenus, who later reigned, equal to the highest Panhypersebastos. And after a few lines, he narrates that after the death of Andronicus the senior, Cantacuzenus was increased by this younger [emperor]: "He exalted him above the others, the nephews of his grandfather the emperor, and his own uncles, and all the others, [placing him] above the highest Panhypersebastos and [the rank of] vestiary in the order of dignity, and by this sanction the Great Domestic was second after the Caesar."
[(18)] "In his year... the Turks began." This is the first irruption of the Turks into Europe under the auspices of the Oghuzians or Ottomans, during the reign of Orchane or Urchane: for Turks had previously crossed into Europe, summoned by the Catalans who were waging war on Andronicus the senior and his son Michael, as Gregoras narrates in *Hist. Rom.*, lib. VIII, and after him Laonicus, lib. 1. Turks also crossed a little after the year, as Laonicus testifies in the same place, lib. 1. The same author also mentions this expedition of the Turks into Europe in the place cited, but when Orchane was already dead, and his son Suleiman was reigning. However, the narrative of the Turks brought forward by Leunclavius in *Hist. Musulmanicæ*, lib. V, and Phranzes, lib. 1, chapters 26 and 27, to which better faith must be given, agrees with our own. But that crossing is noted, because then the Turks first fixed their seats in Europe, Callipolis having been occupied in the year 758 according to Turkish Annals, of Christ 1357. Matthew Villani in *Hist. Florent.*, lib. vi, c. 29, says the crossing of the Turks happened in the year 1356.
[(19)] "As far as Didymoteichon." A town of Thrace which the Hebrus washes. Nicetas Choniates mentions it in two places: "Rain falling suddenly and with force in the places above Didymoteichon, which the river Hebrus, overflowing its banks, washed, widened the waters." To the Turks, Dimotuc.
[(20)] "Selymbria." A city of Thrace: it takes its name from Selys; for *Bria* is said by the Thracians to mean a city.
[(21)] "From Navarre having arrived Franks." These are those from Navarre, whom he elsewhere calls Catalans, who inhabit Tarraconensian Spain. That expedition of the Genoese is noted by Augustine Nebiensis, Uberto Folieta, and Peter Bizarus in the year of Christ 1346, in which, under the leadership of Simone Vignosio, the Genoese added Chios, Smyrna, and both Phocæas to their dominion. John Villani testifies to the same, *Hist. Florent.*, lib. XII, cap. 463, "In the year 1346, they did similar to the island of Chios in the Archipelago of Romania, and they took it, and they are its lords, and they took it from the Greeks, where the Mastic is born, which is of great profit and revenue." I do not see, however, why he brings the Navarrese into this place, unless it is because in those times Peter IV, king of Aragon, had married Maria, daughter of Philip III, king of Navarre, in that year.
And the whole of the Peloponnese, except for Lacedaemon and Monemvasia, and the Phocaeas in Ionia, were taken by the Genoese.
5 CHAPTER III
*The death of Orchan, the Osman. His son Murad succeeds to the empire and makes war upon the Serbian Despot Lazarus, and is killed by a young Serbian. After his slaughter the Turks begin the battle, slaughter the Serbs, and inflict a great defeat. Lazarus is alive [in the Greek text, this is an error and is corrected in the sequel] and many of the Serbian nobles are captured and put to death in the tents of Murad. The empire of Ildrim Bajazet is deferred to the younger of Murad’s sons by the viziers. Bajazet blinds his elder brother, having overcome him by fraud.*
In the same passing year, the aforementioned Orchan, prince of the Turks, died, leaving his dominion and principality to his son Murad, who, having become master of the cities of Thrace, extended the limits of his empire and occupied Adrianople, and the whole of Thessaly, except for Thessalonica. Having thus, indeed, brought almost the whole land of the Romans under his hand, he also arrived at the Triballi [the Serbs], and having utterly destroyed many of their towns and villages, and having taken their inhabitants captive, he sent them across the straits through the ferry at the Chersonese to Asia, which lies opposite Europe. Seeing this, Lazarus, who at that time ruled Serbia, son of Stephen the King of Serbia, having gathered together all the power under his command, grappled with the tyrant, and in that battle there fell very many from both forces. Then there occurred a new and unaccountable feat of skill. A certain young Serbian nobleman, brave and...
bold, as he later proved, broke away from the ranks of the Christians and, as if he were a deserter, fell into the middle of the Turkish battle line. The Turks at once seized him, and he, calling the commander by name, said, "I wish to see him, and to whisper certain words into his ear so that he may be victorious in this war; for the sake of this, I have come as a deserter," he said, and they pointed out the commander. Amurath signaled with his hand for the man to come toward him, and the youth, having rushed forward and arrived nearby, dealt a fatal wound to the heart of the tyrant with a small dagger, and he himself was chopped limb from limb by Amurath’s spearmen and bodyguards. Then the Turks, seeing this new and entirely unexpected catastrophe, and unable to endure the evil that had so suddenly fallen before their eyes, devised a plan that was very clever and sophisticated: having erected a tent in the middle of the battle line, they placed the half-dead Amurath inside it; and they themselves, as if they had not sustained any danger from the many, while avoiding the great number of casualties, retreated inside their ranks like rabid dogs. The Serbs, however, being ignorant of the success which that good young man had achieved on their behalf, and of the damage the commander had sustained from the Turks, but rather having despaired—thinking that that good general had perished without the expected fruit—fought back against the Turks with cowardly hearts until the battle at last came to an end. Lazarus was therefore captured, and with him most of his magnates. They were led into the tent where Amurath was already breathing his last, and there, alongside Lazarus, all those under his command were slaughtered in total, and both he and Amurath met their end. The right wing had not yet perceived anything of what was happening, nor had the left; for these things had been done in the rear guard. The leader of the right wing was Sabutzes, the firstborn of Amurath’s sons, while the leader of the left was the second, Bajazet, a man fierce and more energetic than any other. Those whom the council of Amurath's most eminent men—whom they call "viziers" in their language—summoned, they informed of what had occurred and revealed their father’s corpse. He, without even a sign of lamentation or weeping appearing on his cheeks, summoned his brother Sabutzes, as if by their father’s order, so that they might deliberate on more serious matters. Sabutzes, being ignorant of the drama, came willingly to his father, and, against his will, was seized by his brother and blinded. Then Bajazet was proclaimed leader of the Turks, a man of fierce intellect and quick in the works of war, a hater of Christians such as no one of his age had been, and a most zealous observer of the religion of the Arabs, adhering to the impious precepts of Mohammed and observing them with the greatest strictness. He spent sleepless nights, devising strategies and weaving traps against the rational sheep of Christ.
Notes of Ismaël Bullialdus
The historians differ among themselves regarding the elevation of Bajazet to the empire. Ducas asserts that Sabutzes was blinded; Laonicus and Phrantzes maintain he was strangled. Leunclavius (book V) writes that he died by the same manner of death, and that Bajazet-Ilderim, whom we call Iitrin—a name they interpret as falsely—was the firstborn; and that his brother Jacupes Zelebis was the younger. Laonicus reports that Suleiman was the firstborn and Bajazet the younger. Phrantzes calls him a Mussulman, the Turks call him Jacupes, and Laonicus and the Greeks call him Suleiman, whom Ducas names Sabutzes.

### CHAPTER 4.
After he had assumed the hegemony, following the slaughter of Moralis and Lazari which we have set forth, he first compelled the Serbs to pay tribute, and having received hostages, he laid down these conditions: that the son of that Lazari, Stephanos (whom Serbia had elected as *Crales* after that disaster), should serve in the army wherever Bajazet might be, and that he should also campaign with him; and that he should give his own sister, Maria, the daughter of Lazari—who was still a tender and blooming virgin—to him in marriage; and that significant talents of silver from the mines of Serbia should be paid to him. By these laws, and with the fidelity of the Serbs pledged and bound to the Turks, Bajazet gathered the entire Thracian and Thessalian cavalry. He set out on a march toward the East into provinces situated beyond the sea, and having crossed the strait which lies between Callipolis and Lampsacus, with huge forces of Turks and Romans whom he had conquered, he hastened toward Cotyaeum, the metropolis of Phrygia. He captured both the city and Carmianus, the ruler of Phrygia. Having established matters there, Bajazet sent Carmianus away to Prusa, but not long afterward he fled to the Persians. Thereafter, Bajazet traveled through the whole of Phrygia; proceeding from Laodicea to Ephesus, he gained control of Ionia. He seized Iesaes, the offspring of Aten, who was the ruler of Ionia, and exiled him to Nicaea in Bithynia, and there he passed the remainder of his life. Having then transported all his forces across the Maeander river, he took the whole of Caria and Lycia without any martial tumult, as their ruler, Eliez, fled to the Persians. From there he led his army back into Lydia, and through the very high mountain Tmolus he came to Sardis, the metropolis of Lydia. Then, as he was tending toward Magnesia, situated at Sipylus, he encountered...
Achetir, the chief of Lydia and the Aeolian cities, the descendant of Sarchan, who surrendered himself. Having granted him a measure of honor—since Achetir was his brother-in-law—he sent him to Prusa. Shortly thereafter, he had him killed by poison. Bayezid then set his course toward Philadelphia [(33)]; for this city, being outstanding in size and populous, had maintained its independence for nearly a hundred years, while the whole world was held in subjection by the Turks; like a star shining in the zenith amidst cloudy skies, this city appeared. Having besieged it ... and being unable [to resist] because of the lack of provisions, they surrendered. Having taken all the forces of the East and established chiefs and leaders in the provinces according to his own will, he set out for the western regions. And indeed, having crossed the strait, since the fortress of Callipolis had long since been ruined and utterly destroyed by the Catalans and the Turks themselves, he built a new one from the foundations, and constructed it as a base for keeping triremes, and a massive tower, standing over the harbor, to counter hostile attacks.

### CHAPTER 5.
The beginnings of discord between John Cantacuzenus and the empress Anna and the nobles of her court. Cantacuzenus left the city; his adversaries attack him by treachery; he is warned by friends, who are for that reason thrown into prison by Alexius Apocaucus; they kill Apocaucus, and on account of this almost all are put to death. Michael Ducas, the author's paternal grandfather.
C [(34)] While these things were happening, Emperor John, having passed through his boyish and youthful life, and having finished his majority and manhood, was preparing himself, with all the lethargy [imputable] to that time, for his advanced age; for he was young, and employed as his tutor the aforementioned Lord John Cantacuzenus, a man prudent and most fierce in military matters, and, if one might say so, a fragrant blossom among noblemen. For being such, even Andronicus, who had reigned before him, esteemed him in all things as a brother and his son—the empire and the son under Andronicus and John being driven about and tossed like ships in storms—until finally they perished. Whoever desires a broader knowledge of these things should approach the history of Cantacuzenus and Gregoras. We have already stated that that Cantacuzenus, on account of the splendor of his lineage and the eminent and distinguished virtues by which he was renowned both at home and in war, was praised by Gregoras and our author, but accused by Phranza of affected tyranny and perfidy against John. Cantacuzenus purges himself in the history he wrote of these charges brought against him, and removes from himself, as much as he can, every suspicion. Whatever the case, he wished the imperial crown to be placed upon himself and his wife twice. He designated Matthew, his eldest son, a despot, and ordered him to put on the purple boots; he proclaimed Manuel, his younger son, despot of Sparta: so that he seems to have wished to pave the way to usurp and retain the empire for himself and his kin. But the infirm and fleeting nature of the forces with which he was provided, the disturbance of the affairs of the empire, which were daily worn down and falling into ruin, and the imminent dangers from the Turks, persuaded him to abandon the undertaking.
In this plight, the evil and cruel fortune of the Romans sowed discord and sparked envy. For men are wont to envy those more who are advancing in virtue; hence, at that time, when the Emperor John was still a young man, Cantacuzenus desired to become his father-in-law [(35)] by bestowing upon him his daughter Helena. But the rest of the senators, out of jealousy, approached the mother of the emperor, saying that she should seek a wife for the emperor of the Romans from Germany, according to a long-standing custom, and not from among his own subjects, so that we might obtain aid and assistance from that nation in a time of need. When the Empress Anna, who was also a German, consented to this—for it was very dear to her heart to dye the purple of the emperor and her child with the same blood—Cantacuzenus was neglected and set aside. Having shaken off the burden of tutelage and administration, he left Constantinople and withdrew to Macedonia. Those who were nursing their envy found an opportunity, fabricated a charge of high treason against him, and reported the whole invention as a proven fact to the empress and mother of the emperor, as they advised her that the matter should be carefully examined. "Let your Majesty," they said, "order the Domestic to gather all the Macedonian troops immediately and bring them to Byzantium." For they intended either that, if he complied with the decree, they would have the man they were hunting as a puppet, or, if he resisted the command, they would clearly proclaim his guilt and appoint someone else to manage affairs. Cantacuzenus’s kinsmen and friends secretly informed him of the scheme by letter and warned him that, if he wished to enjoy the light and flee the darkness, he must not show defiance to these commands.
Before he left Byzantium, he had gone to the palace to bid farewell to the empress, and although she urged him to betroth his daughter to the young Emperor John, he delayed doing so until his return from the West. Our historian Ducas disagrees with Cantacuzenus, who narrates that he had sought to make the emperor his son-in-law; Ducas says that Cantacuzenus, impatient at the rejection and perceiving that he was being targeted by the envy of the nobles, abandoned Constantinople.
[(36)] Anna was, as it is said, of the Germans; which perhaps is because she knew the Counts of Savoy were subjects of the Empire, or because she believed her to be from that same region, and that Anna, wife of Andronicus the Elder, was of the stock of the Dukes of Brunswick. But Cantacuzenus asserts that she was of the Counts of Savoy. This is confirmed by Lambert Vander-Burch in his genealogical history of the Dukes and Princes of Savoy, though he calls her Joanna: he writes thus: "Joanna, wife of the Byzantine Emperor Andronicus Palaeologus, daughter of Amedeus V, Count of Savoy, and of Joanna of Brabant." Gregoras, in the penultimate chapter of his eighth book, states that she was called Anna, having changed her name.
If you wish to see the sun and yet avoid the darkness, grant the primacy to obedience; for they have written: "If you are obedient, you will have light before death." Learning of this, Cantacuzenus, despising the decree, openly resisted. Those in the city, however, appointed another prefect in his place, Alexius Apocauchus, a man base and unmanly, yet versatile in knavery and cunning in his depravity, whom the empress also raised to the office and dignity of Grand Duke. Upon learning who had revealed to Cantacuzenus the plot and the sequence of the intrigues against him, he arrested all his kinsmen and friends, over two hundred men, heroes and scions of the Pelopidians and Aeacidae, and shut them in the prison of the Great Palace. Just as one might keep sparrows trapped within a net, he held them there, fearing lest they might stir up some new disruption, prevail over the guards, and seize the palace, aided by the zeal and effort of their relatives and friends.
For the greater part of the citizens, when they saw him ruling, decided to lock the prisoners in by lowering them from above with ropes, so that they might use the cells at night, and during the day be allowed a moderate respite in the space remaining between them. Having appointed Apocauchus as the *parakoimomenos* and ruler of Byzantium, they commanded him to wage war from wherever it seemed best to him. For this *parakoimomenos*, hailing from Bithynia, an obscure man born of base stock, had first worked for low wages as a scribe for those who collected public taxes, being base and cowardly. Fortune, however, favored him, and he was promoted to the highest dignities of the palace, so that he was made Grand Duke. He devised a new prison within the palaces of Constantine the Great. For there stood a large house called the Justinian, the roof of which had been destroyed by the passage of time; having blocked off every entrance, he intended to divide the interior into many small cells on each side, and to enclose the prisoners.
For the people—both because the greater part of the city, as much the senatorial class as the rabble, revered Cantacuzenus as most magnificent and most charitable to all—he concocted an evil scheme: to allow them to congregate and converse freely amongst themselves during the day within the prison walls, but at night to lock them away in groups of two or three in certain small cells for safekeeping. The intention was put into action: planks and timber were prepared, and carpenters were summoned. When the prisoners understood what was being done, they said among themselves: "This is nothing other than our manifest destruction. For this nocturnal separation from one another portends either choking in the night or being sunk into the depths of the sea." Saying this, they fell into despondency.
Meanwhile, Apocaucus came to show the carpenters the plan and order they were to follow in constructing those chambers, accompanied by no cavalier, but only one slave, who, as was his custom, followed on foot. Having entered within the prison gate, as soon as he was seen by those held captive there as a common plague and one who waylaid all their lives, one of them, a man of noble birth from the Raoul family, seizing a plank intended for the threshold that had been hewn to shape, struck Apocaucus on the head in place of a sword. He fell from his horse to the ground, just as another Satan falls from heaven. But the slave grappled with Raoul, and both stood as if in a duel. While they struggled together, another of the prisoners snatched an axe from the hands of the carpenter and decapitated the man fallen on the ground, and fastening his head upon a stake, fixed it to a part of the rampart.
Such a deed left the Byzantines not a little astonished—the Empress herself and the entire army; thus, all indiscriminately rushed in a crowd and entered the palace, not, however, without fighting and slaughter, but having made a path for themselves with much force. They massacred everyone except six who escaped by hiding in the underground vault of the church of the New Monastery; they slaughtered very many even in the middle of the temple, nor did the majesty and reverence of the sanctuary or altar avail anything to spare anyone. C Among those, indeed, who were snatched from such great peril was my paternal grandfather, MICHAEL DUCAS. Having donned the mantles or cowls of the monks of that monastery, they fled from Constantinople, and having crossed to the opposite continent of Asia, they scattered into the eastern regions—one to Bithynia, another elsewhere—and my grandfather sought Asia, and approached Jesaeus, the son of Atenis, and recounted to him what had happened to him. Being, indeed, a man of learning, and full of other wisdom and not unskilled in the medical art...
Notes of Ismael Bullialdus
(40) From the Raoul lineage. Whence that Raoul derived his lineage is not known to me; Gregoras, book VI, makes mention of someone of the same name in two places, who took as his wife Theodora, left behind by Muzalon, the granddaughter of Emperor Michael [VIII] through his sister Eulogia. Below he reports that Constantine Porphyrogenitus took as his wife a daughter of Raoul. Phranzes, book III, ch. 23 and 25, makes mention of Georgius Raoul, a man of distinguished nobility of lineage, but whether he was descended from the same family is not known to me.
(41) From the paternal grandfather. By this passage, the author of this history indicates that he derived his paternal origin from the ancient family of the Ducas; from which sprung some emperors: Constantine Ducas, Michael, Alexius called Murzuphlus, and a fourth, John nicknamed Vatatzes: if, however, he was born of that same family; whom we have learned from Georgius the logothete was a native of Didymoteicho.
full of all other wisdom, and not unskilled in the medical art, tracing his descent from those ancient Ducas and shining in that lineage like a golden link in a chain.
