The tyrant received him honorably, and provided that all things necessary and provisions of all kinds should be supplied to him, and having heaped benefits upon him, granted him Ephesus for his dwelling: these seats, though alien, were as pleasing and dear to him as his homeland; and he honored and respected the barbarian and foreigner no otherwise than as one established by divine providence, considering the wickedness of the Romans, and foreseeing that before long all the territories of Thrace, and as far as the Danube, would fall into the hands of the Turks, and that they would appear as emperors in a short time, just as they had also recently done in Phrygia and Asia and the regions beyond, God allowing it because of the sins of the Romans who were governing then, and of our own forefathers.
CHAPTER VI
Cantacuzenus dons the purple buskins, is hailed as emperor, flees to the Kral of Serbia, and strikes a treaty with him. [(42)]
Joannes Cantacuzenus, therefore, who has been mentioned often in the preceding parts, having learned of the unjust slaughter that had occurred against his kinsmen and friends, and with a not inconsiderable number of them having arrived at him from the city—men who were his close relations and kin to those who had been murdered, and even more related by affinity, wearing mourning garments, they stood before Cantacuzenus weeping and wailing, and crying out against him, saying: "For your sake we are killed all the day long, and we are losing our own; the flower of the Romans has withered and perished; the empire is being wielded in the hands of a woman, like a shuttle spinning and working the purple, and the authority is in a suckling infant, who can barely use his mind and tongue amid toys and babble; the power is in the hands of marketplace men and base fellows. Trust our words, and take up the leadership, and gird your sword upon your thigh, and bend your bow, and speed on, and reign for the sake of truth, and meekness, and justice." Then Cantacuzenus, reflecting upon the uprisings— D
[(42)] Since these things which Ducas narrates seem to have happened after the death of Apocaucus, rather than before, namely in the year 6850 (of Christ 1342), at which time the emperor John Palaeologus was 10 years old; to which beardless age those words "the authority is in a suckling infant" etc., apply; for after the death of Apocaucus, not long after, John Cantacuzenus entered Constantinople in the year 6855 (of Christ 1347), at which time Palaeologus was almost 15 years old, and could no longer be called a suckling and babbling infant.
[(43)] Then Cantacuzenus put on the imperial ornaments of his friends, silk buskins of scarlet or purple color, which were the insignia used by the emperors of Constantinople. Zonaras, in volume iii, mentioning a certain Basilinus, a rower of the imperial trireme of Michael, son of Theodora, says: "He gave him (that is, the emperor Michael) red buskins and commanded him to be called emperor." He puts on the red buskin, and is hailed as Roman emperor by all the Orientals: since he was not blessed with male offspring of his own, he had commanded this buskin to be worn by her, so that both she and the one who would be joined to her might be the successor to the empire. He gave him the purple-colored buskins, and commanded him to put them on, and proclaimed him emperor.
And those of the city, having learned of the defection of Cantacuzenus, and that he had put on the imperial insignia, and was being proclaimed by all who dwelt in the Thracian parts as far as Selymbria itself as emperor, were pained in their soul. And having become full of cowardice and fear, they were held in a state of agitation, each one discussing with his neighbor what indeed would be the outcome, and what fate, which tends toward evils, had spun for the Romans.

### CHAPTER 7.
Homur, the son of Atines, having crossed the Hellespont, came into Europe; he put in at Callipolis and set out for Didymoteichon, where the wife of Cantacuzenus had remained. The Turks devastate Thrace. Smyrna, having been captured by the knights of the Jerusalemite militia, is vainly attempted to be recovered by Homur, and he falls in the siege.
One of the sons of Atines, the Turkish prince, named Homur, the leader of the small towns in Smyrna and of Smyrna itself, which he had received by succession from his father Atines, being himself bold and stout-hearted; having come upon the harbors that Ionia embraces as they curve into bays, and having found woods full of trees suitable for the construction of transport ships and long triremes, he constructed them as he wished for his piratical biremes and triremes. And embarking upon them, he ravaged the cities and islands in the vicinity, Mitylene with the whole island of Lesbos, Chios, Samos, Naxos, and all the islands in the vicinity. But having learned of the civil discord of the Romans, and how John Cantacuzenus was a man of noble birth and a descendant of the heroes of old, manly, most warlike in military matters, and prudent in all good habits, he formed an evil plan. For, having equipped a fleet of more than forty ships, he departed the harbor and arrived at Callipolis unbidden; and having departed from there by land, he reached Didymoteichon. For it happened that the wife of Cantacuzenus was staying there with her whole household. For when he was departing to Serbia, having collected all the gold and silver in the house and all other wealth, and his children and wife, he had brought them from Adrianople to Didymoteichon, and having made every other necessary provision for the small town, he then arrived at the Queen. But Homur, not having found the man he desired, was distressed and vexed; for he longed to see him, and to converse and give oaths, and to receive from him, that they would be brothers and allies for the duration of their lives. But the wife of Cantacuzenus, having welcomed him and received him graciously with all abundant provisions and all manner of good things, kept him for three months awaiting Cantacuzenus, having with him up to five hundred Turkish horsemen, and as many foot soldiers who had been carried by his triremes; while the rest of the fleet having gathered together, and having embarked upon the larger vessels, were ravaging the entire coastline from it.
Notes of Ismaël Boulliau
He left the city of Divolopotamum in Thrace to fate. Urosh, his only son, succeeded him, who lost the empire through sloth, and experienced the curses and imprecations of his grandfather, cast upon his son and his descendants. Above we noted that Lazar, son of Vukašin, had taken away from Urosh a part of the paternal empire. Mauro Orbini in the *History of the Kingdom of the Slavs*. See also chapter 30, below.
all the way from Callipolis to Selymbria, as if they were allies of Cantacuzenus, but in truth they were tracing the land of Thrace. He himself, having run by land with his men as far as Rhaedestus, and after plundering and devastating everything he met, turned back to Didymoteichon. Now, seeing that the arrival of Cantacuzenus was slow, and wishing to return—for he had heard that the friars of Rhodes (46) had arrived at the harbor of Smyrna with a constructed fleet and had begun to build a fortress there, in the name of Saint Peter, for the sake of the salvation of runaway captives—he disposed himself well toward peace and friendship. Cantacuzena, having entertained him with very many gifts, sent him away; he departed taking many captives with him, and the Romans dwelling in Thrace and in all the parts of the West tasted these first fruits of their error. For the Bithynians and the Phrygians and those inhabiting all the provinces of the East had already been ruined by the time that had passed, and they had been destroyed by the Turks. When Umur returned to Smyrna and saw the little town already filled with the friars, and full of warlike and resourceful men, completely finished and needing no other construction, he was pained in his soul and deliberated persistently with himself, deciding either to capture the fortress or to lose his life. Having begun to fight and contend, and to examine and invent engines of war, he did not cease night or day stirring up battles by means of skirmishes, mining, mining-tunnels, and all other types of siege-works. C Now, in such contests and struggles, behaving like another Lyaeus, he fought and found a way to cross the moat of the little town with his men, and to set scaling ladders against the walls; and like a mad dog, he rushed to be the first to climb up and himself alone take the trophy of victory. But Providence on high, which governs and moves all things well, seeing his beast-like and serpentine ferocity, while he was already in the middle of ascending the rungs of the ladder, and had pushed back his helmet slightly from his face to see how much of the battlement was still missing, an archer from the upper battlement wounded him with a bolt, which pierced through the middle of his eyebrows. Struck, Umur fell headlong from on high.
*Notes of Ismael Bullialdus.* Bosius, who wrote in Italian the history of the religion and military of Saint John of Jerusalem, says that Smyrna was captured by the confederates in the year of Christ 1344, but he makes no mention of the castle built. Indeed, this time-marker rightly agrees with those things that are narrated by Cantacuzenus; for at the beginning of this civil war, Umur came to Didymoteichon. Cantacuzenus agrees with Bosius in Book III, chapter 68, and relates that Smyrna was captured by the Rhodian knights and others joined in the war-covenant. Four triremes, and twenty Latin [vessels] prepared by the Rhodians and some others, sailed to Smyrna, and captured the fortress at the harbor, and burned not a few Persian ships. And Umur, being present and defending himself, was unable to overcome the Latin force. Our Ducas and Cantacuzenus are clearly at odds with each other: for if the things which Cantacuzenus narrates are true, namely that after Smyrna had been occupied by the Latins, Umur attempted in vain to storm it, and then crossed the Hellespontine strait again to bring help to Cantacuzenus, then he could not have fallen in the attack on Smyrna, as our author narrates. Furthermore, those who are called the "Friars of Rhodes" are religious men and soldiers of the Order of Saint John of Jerusalem, who are today commonly called the Knights of Malta.
and the canopy hits him right between the eyebrows, and he falls headlong from above, and in this violent manner he breathed his last. The soldiers having seized him, after he had fallen inside [having fallen into the trench, many Turks having fallen], they carried him dead into the small fortress of Smyrna, which was situated on the summit of the mountain—a fort that had once been the acropolis of the ancient and ruined Smyrna, having been rebuilt not many years earlier by John Doukas, the emperor of the Romans. Now Atin, the chieftain of the Turks and father of Umur, had taken and held it from the Romans in the days of Andronikos the Elder. Such was the end that Umur met.

### CHAPTER VIII.
Cantacuzenus returns to Thrace. Empress Anna seeks and obtains aid from Orchan. The Turks plunder the provinces of the empire and carry off captives.
Now Cantacuzenus, having made a pact with the Krale and established a truce—with the castles, cities, and provinces of the unfortunate empire of the Romans being handed over to barbarian chieftains, the Triballi and the Serbs, in place of Roman masters—began to overrun, pillage, and destroy all the cities of Thrace as far as Selymbria. But those who kept themselves within the walls of the city, reflecting on what had been done by Umur during the winter of the previous year, and considering that Cantacuzenus had summoned him and was the cause of Umur’s arrival—ignorant of the fact that he had come of his own accord, or that an evil fortune for the Romans, spinning the threads in reverse, had prompted his coming and the trampling of the blooming fields of the Roman land—devised a wicked plan, and invoked upon their own heads a god-sent anger and wrath. They urge the Lady Anna, the mother of the Emperor John, who was still a youth, to send envoys to the chieftain of Bithynia, Phrygia, and also Paphlagonia—the one whom the narrative has already signaled, Orchan—to ask for aid and assistance in order to suppress Cantacuzenus, a rebel against the empire. Thus, Anna promises that she will give him a large quantity of gold, and grants to the Turks the freedom to sell and trade, wherever they pleased, any Romans they might capture who adhered to the faction of Cantacuzenus. To those who did not wish to sell their own captives, she gives the free ability to cross over and lead them through Scutari, and to take them wherever they wished. Having heard these things, Orchan—for he had long hungered for such a feast—leaping up boldly, and with great pleasure and joy, accepts the proposals and sends the envoys away exultant and rejoicing; the wretches did not know whom they were summoning to bring them aid, nor what kind of lion…

Orchan, therefore, having sent ten thousand soldiers, who crossed the strait of the city, were received with joy by the citizens. And having trampled the city walls and the streets within, and having been entertained by the empress and the Romæi, they set out against Cantacuzenus. But Cantacuzenus, having secured the fortresses (48) and having well provided for food and all other necessities, also went out with the Romæan and Serbian armies that were with him. And having engaged in battle both a first and a second time, the Turks were unable to gain anything from his forces. For the man was most warlike in all things, possessing strength and skill in warfare as no one else of that time did. As many of the Turks as they captured in battle, they put to the sword; but as many of the Romæi as they took, they stripped of their garments and sent them home naked. But the Turks, having abandoned the fighting, ran off to plunder the villages. And now they were dragging long columns of captives bound in chains, and were leading off to Constantinople men, women, suckling infants, adolescents, priests, and monks like sheep, and were driving them along the public road like Scythians or Abasgi (49) for the purpose of being sold. And the bitterest part was that if a redeemer did not happen to appear immediately, the Romæi were beaten by the barbarians in the very sight of their fellow Romæi—oh, the inhuman crime! And the intention of the one striking was such that, moved by pity, someone might redeem them. But those who were not redeemed were immediately transported across the strait to Prusa, and were sent further away to be sold among the Turks. And it was a pitiable sight to behold: everywhere lamentations, everywhere wailings, everywhere tears in the sight of the Romæi, and there was no one to show mercy, neither Greek nor Barbarian. Then Cantacuzenus, having turned his mind to what had happened, and not enduring the unseemly deed which those of the city had lawlessly committed against the Romæi without,

Thinking upon the crime so unworthy and nefariously committed by the citizens of Constantinople against other Romæi, and not being able to bear it, [the rest follows].
he chooses a pernicious counsel, God, as it seems, hardening his heart, by which the Romæi might perish utterly. Having sent ambassadors to Orchan, he asks for help from him, as having suffered injustice from the Romæi, and as having been in charge of the administration of the empire of the deceased emperor Andronikos, from which he was driven by envy: he complains also that his own kinsmen were slaughtered, and that he himself was made a fugitive. If, therefore, he is willing to bring help and offer a hand of support, he promises to give him his daughter in marriage, along with many treasures by way of dowry, and to hold him as a son, and to obey his every wish. Then Orchan, having heard the ambassadors speaking beyond expectation of nuptial arrangements and promising infinite treasures—gaping just as an ox, thirsting in the burning heat of summer, in a pool full of very cool water, drinking without being satiated by the streams—was thus also inclined towards the barbarian incontinence. For this race is uncontrollable and frenzied, more unrestrained than all nations, and insatiable in debauchery. It is so inflamed, that it does not cease to copulate shamelessly and intemperately, both according to nature and contrary to nature, with females, with males, and with irrational beasts; and this shameless and inhuman race, if it possesses a Greek or Italian or some other foreign woman, either captive or a runaway, embraces her as some Venus or Semele, but abhors its own fellow-genous female citizens like a bear or a hyena.
The aforementioned leader Orchan, therefore, having heard of the union for the marriage of the girl—for she was beautiful in appearance and not unpleasing to the sight—and of the magnitude of the dowry, and the pre-nuptial gifts sent by Kantakouzenos, yielded readily. Having treated the ambassadors with gifts, he sent them back, having given and received oaths that from this time forward he would be the son-in-law of Kantakouzenos, and would stand ready, as a son to a father, for every aid and assistance; on the sole condition that he send for the bride-to-be, along with the dowry, quickly before the spring. For it happened that this wicked betrothal took place in the month of January of that year. And along with these, about five thousand Turks were sent to Kantakouzenos, men most warlike and quick to anger, and spoilers of the Romæi, such that one might liken them to sharp-toothed dogs, or Charons.
Having therefore received them, Kantakouzenos, according to his usual hospitality, with very many gifts and promises, burdened them with duties, and prepared his expedition against Byzantium, dragging behind himself the troop of the Turks, and others as many or even more—Serbs and Romæi—whoever were then inhabiting Thrace. And already, with the dowry and splendid pomp and much magnificence, his daughter having been sent to Orchan, he himself was girding for war, and from Selymbria to Constantinople...

Thrace then had Serbs and Romans equal at that time. And indeed, having prepared the dowry, and having sent his daughter to Orkhan with every honor, and pomp, and glory, and with great brilliance, he himself occupied himself with war. And so, having begun from Selymbria to plunder and burn all the villages and cities up to the city itself, he sent the unfortunate Romans, some as captives to Serbia, where they were enslaved by the Serbs, others he sent across the strait to Prusa and the remaining cities as prisoners of war. And it was a pitiable sight to behold. Who were the captors? Romans. Who were the captives? Romans. Who were the ones striking with the sword? Romans. Who were the ones being struck? Romans. Whose were the dead bodies? Romans’. Who were the ones who had put them to death? Romans. O bitter calamity!
Coming then with his army, as we have said, even to the gates of Constantine, B Cantacuzenus, having destroyed many of the Romans and taken very many as prisoners of war, and having reduced everything around to desolation and ruin, sought the city, saying, "I have not come, O men, intending to do injury to anyone, or having done so, but as one having suffered injury and being wronged. I am the guardian of the Roman empire by commission of the departed emperor Andronicus. This youth, the heir of the empire, is my emperor and my son by designation; for thus his father committed him to me before God. What sin have I committed if I wished to take him as a son-in-law? Do you not know that his father always cherished and loved me as a genuine brother, and entrusted the care of the empire to me just as to himself, and shared it with me? I am certainly noble, illustrious, and famous, and the most supreme among those who claim to be wealthy, and the bravest of those who handle arms and war. Why, being men of the lowest sort and defiled by the stain of barbarians, are you contemptuous and disdainful of me? For this reason I have approached, O citizens, not to inflict loss upon anyone, but rather to give to each his own according to equity and justice. Indeed, to those who have sinned, I grant pardon, and for those who have suffered loss, I will make compensation from my own treasures, and I will introduce a peaceful state into the Roman republic. But if I should avenge your crimes, as God commands? Open to me therefore the gates—I swear by the Lord Christ and His all-pure mother—I will appear not as an enemy, but as a friend."
But the inhabitants of the city gave no answer at all, spurning the words of Cantacuzenus; nay, even men from the dregs of the populace threw contumelious words at him from the ramparts and tore him apart with reproaches, and burdened his spouse and his daughter Helena, who in a short lapse of time was to be established as their lady and empress, with insults as if she were a harlot. Then Cantacuzenus understood that he could not recover the city by admonition or by verbal castigation; but he turned to other arts, and made trial of war, and finally, by the aid of friends and relatives who had remained in the city, he entered it, to see whom all flocked, and followed with auspicious acclamations, and hailed him as emperor.
CHAPTER X
Cantacuzenus is received into the palace. He approaches Anna, who sat with an intrepid spirit and fearless countenance, and pays her homage. He renders her placated toward him, composes the tumult, and soothes the populace. Celebration of the nuptials of John Palaeologus and Cantacuzenus's daughter Helena. Cantacuzenus is crowned. The Turks, while laying waste to the Chersonese under the leadership of Suleiman, son of Orchan, are afflicted with a great slaughter by the despot Matthew Cantacuzenus.
Empress Anna, who remained shut up within the palace with her son and a few soldiers, would by no means yield, but cried out and did not cease saying that she had been wronged. Cantacuzenus’s soldiers wished to leap in and enter, intending to overturn everything above and below, but Cantacuzenus restrained them. The soldiers, remembering the idle chatter and the insults of the commoners, which they had to hold back in his presence, were angry against them. But he, by persuasive words, calmed the crowd. Then those in the palace, seeing that they were in danger of dying, surrendered themselves. Having entered the palace, he went as far as the innermost chambers and found the lady sitting with her son, not having been moved in the least, nor having been unsettled by the anger which she had borne against Cantacuzenus; rather, she sat trembling not at all, nor fearing anything whatsoever.
But Cantacuzenus, with his head uncovered [(55)], approached and kissed the hand of the youth; then, as was customary, having paid homage to the mother and lady of the youth, he hailed them as emperors of the Romans. Seeing his supreme goodness and lack of malice toward his enemies, the entire army then praised and glorified him. He sent away his guests, the Turks, as was fitting, with many gifts, granting thanks to the prince and his own son-in-law, Orchan; he also favored the citizens with feasts and many honors. By soothing the lady with sweet words and by thoughtful actions, he persuaded her to be agreeable to taking his own daughter, Helena, as a daughter-in-law for her son, the emperor John, whom she had borne from the aforementioned Andronicus Palaeologus, as the account has previously indicated. Therefore, the marriage is prepared, and the church of our blessed Lady, the Theotokos, in Blachernae is adorned for the celebration of the sacred rites of the coronation. [(56)]
[(55)] *With his head uncovered.* This also has its own unique and particular character; and if he should see any small tuft, or dust, or anything else upon the garment of the emperor, or the *skiadion*, or whatever head covering he might be wearing, he extends his hand, removes it, or cleans it without being asked.
OF THE SOLEMNITY OF THE IMPERIAL CORONATION
The solemn rite is performed, and signs of public joy and acclamations are heard, with which the people wished many years to the most pious John Palaiologos, the most powerful emperor of the Romans, and to the most religious Augusta, Helena. At the same time, John Cantacuzenus, the father-in-law of the emperor, is crowned with his spouse and proclaimed emperor, and his son Matthew is designated Despot. In this celebrated banquet, one could see a ring of emperors and empresses, lords and ladies, like the banquet of the twelve gods recorded of old; for Emperor John was flourishing in the flower of youth, and the Empress Helena had not yet passed her thirteenth year; but having become pregnant, she bore the emperor a firstborn son, whom they named Andronikos. But he, having reached virile age, began to defile himself with crimes and to act youthfully, not devoted to the handling of arms, but to stupration and whoredoms, which galled the spirits of many and stirred up a bitter and noxious smoke from their hearts. But Cantacuzenus did not grant sleep to his eyelids, nor slumber to his temples; but as the Turks had previously scouted and come to know the passages of Thrace, and their entries and exits, they did not cease from crossing the strait, some from Sestos to Abydos, others from Lampsakos in very small boats, and they were plundering the Chersonese. Cantacuzenus, indeed, was kept continually vigilant in defending the fortresses and camps situated on the Thracian borders.
Notes of Ismael Bullialdus.
The custom of praying for many years for the emperors in festivities in the Constantinopolitan court, as is to be seen in many places in Codinus Curopalates, they said in one word, "Long live the emperor." And this custom still endures today in the Church of Constantinople; so that while the patriarch is celebrating the holy liturgy, one of the officials of the Church from time to time, but at intervals, cries out, "Many years, master." These words are now used by the Greeks as thanksgiving, when they offer words of grace for the office or duty received, for they say, "Many years to the emperor," or "Many years, master."
As for the fact that *he wrote in chapter 4, book iv, that he was crowned a second time that year, and that he wanted his wife also to be crowned*: he had already been crowned at Adrianople; wherefore he wished to have the crown placed upon him again, he himself provides this reason: He had already been crowned at Adrianople by Lazarus, the patriarch of Jerusalem; and that anointing with holy chrism was sufficient among those who were well-disposed. But so that no occasion for calumny might be left to those who spoke evil and were hostile to him, on the grounds that he had not received the crown at Byzantium according to the ancient custom of the emperors, the solemn coronation was repeated and performed a second time. This rite was deemed necessary to a certain extent for the management of affairs in that empire by imperial authority. For since Constantine, who fell in the storming of Constantinople, was not crowned, he is not considered an emperor by our author; for he calls John Palaiologos, son of Manuel, the last of the Palaiologan line, and calls Constantine, his brother, only a Despot. After the death of John, when he himself administered the affairs of the empire at Constantinople, Michael, the first of the Palaiologoi, assumed the crown so that the affairs of the empire might be administered and conducted under his authority and auspices; meanwhile, since the legitimate heir was not being crowned, because he was inept for conducting business on account of his childish age, and by that solemn ceremony it seemed that not only the insignia of the empire, but also legitimate power had been handed over; and it could also have been granted for a time, since Patriarch Arsenios, who crowned Michael, did not grant the empire to him in perpetuity. *But (as Gregoras says, book iv) he did not grant the imperial authority to him in perpetuity, but only so that he might administer the empire for the time being, as circumstances demanded, until the legitimate heir and successor reached age; then he would willingly yield it to him alone, along with the imperial thrones and all the imperial symbols.* It is evident from Cantacuzenus himself, book III, cap. 56, that to oppose Cantacuzenus with the authority of John Palaiologos, the Empress Anna and the Constantinopolitan senate saw to it that he was crowned, so that affairs might be conducted under his auspices and legitimate authority. But when the succession to the empire is certain, as soon as the predecessor dies, the right and title of the heir and the insignia of royal majesty pass to him; nor is there need for that anointing or coronation for him to act as king, to possess the sum of affairs, and for everything to be conducted under his auspices and in his name.
Ducas reverses the location of the places. For the Turks, crossing from Asia into Europe, were carried over; for Abydos lies adjacent to the shore of Asia, and Sestos to Europe.
He was deeply grieved by John, who was living in luxury and drunkenness, and one day, having rebuked him to his face, he left the city with two triremes and arrived in Italy (62). Emperor Cantacuzenus, being left alone to rule the empire, resisted the encroaching enemy—both Turks and Serbs—to the best of his ability. The Turks, consequently, would frequently pounce upon and ravage the Chersonese. Emperor John spent two years in Italy and Germany. Having collected many treasures from the Italians and Germans as a charitable contribution, he returned to the city to protect it. He came to the island of Tenedos, which at that time was inhabited and subject to the Romans, and he was anxious about how he would be received by his father-in-law, the Emperor. At that time, a certain Genoese nobleman, who had set sail from Genoa with two triremes, was heading for the Hellespont. Since the Roman state was shattered and its affairs had reached a point of complete ruin, he too moved out from Genoa, intending to seize a portion of the fortresses of the Chersonese and to rule them, just as others held Chios and other places—the Genoese and the Venetians. By chance he encountered the Emperor while passing by, and, after they had held discussions with one another, the Emperor revealed his intent to him and found the man to be compliant and ready to provide help in any way possible. He bound him with oaths that he would lay down his own life for his sake, and, God assisting, would deliver the city from the hands of Cantacuzenus, and would establish him alone as Emperor of the Romans, both inside and outside the city. This man was named Franciscus Gateluzus. The Emperor replied, "If this happens with God's assistance, and you help me in reclaiming my empire, I will take you as my son-in-law and give you my sister Maria in marriage." Having both agreed to these promises, they sailed through the Hellespont as was necessary. Sailing up opposite the city during the night, they arrived at the small gate known as the Hodegetria (63). A strong wind was blowing— as he sailed into Byzantium, with no one aware of it, during the night, at the harbor situated at Heptaskalon.
Francis, however, devised a stratagem. He had many oil jars in his triremes. For when departing from Italy, he had loaded the triremes partly with oil, which he had later sold and distributed, but he carried back empty amphorae. He therefore ordered the rowers to carry one amphora each, two by two, along the wall of the city and smash them, from which a loud noise would erupt; and thus they did not cease from creating a clamor and shouting until the guards, having been awakened and alerted by the noise, stood up and asked the cause of such a clamor and din. The crews of the triremes replied, "We are merchantmen, carrying much oil, part of which we intend to sell in the Pontic Sea, and part in the Queen of Cities itself; and while we were sailing, look, one of our ships was damaged. Be willing, therefore, to be of assistance to us, and we shall share the remaining cargo with you as with brothers, provided that you keep us ourselves unharmed and safe; for the sea was growing rough, and the waves were rising with briny foam." Then those who were guards inside the doors opened them, and about twenty came out; but those who were armed and lying in wait, numbering about five hundred, broke out from the triremes and entered, and slaughtered the guards they found in the tower. Leaving the triremes empty, about two thousand armed men entered the city with all their weaponry and battle array. The Emperor, having entered, and having immediately sent some of his own men to the residences of the Palaiologoi and his paternal friends, announced his arrival, and everyone came running; for it was night. Francis, having gone up into one of the towers and having fortified it with shield-bearers and captains, brought the Emperor up, surrounding him with Latin and Roman heavy infantry. The same man ran along the wall with a great many guards, shouting with a loud voice, "Long live the Emperor John Palaiologos for many years!" And it began to grow light, and the populace, having heard the shout, ran to the Hippodrome. When it was first light, both those from the palace and the greatest number of the people were flocking together in crowds. But the Emperor Kantakouzenos, having promptly entered the monastery of the Peribleptos, cuts his hair and puts on the black robe, and informs the Emperor, his son-in-law, that the entrance to the palace is open to him. And the Emperor, having descended from the fortification, walked along the road leading to the palace, accompanied by all the Italians and their leader Francis, and by the whole multitude of the city, as many of the nobility as were following the common people. Then also the Augusta, having gone out to meet the Emperor with his son Andronikos, who was still an infant, they embraced one another and, rejoicing, entered the palace. The Emperor Kantakouzenos, having abandoned both glory, and the empire, and worldly pleasures, requested from the Emperor permission to leave the city and to go to the Holy Mountain to live as a monk in one of the monasteries; which he also did, and having spent a significant amount of time well, he rested in peace. At that time also Orchan was near Ismael s Bullialdi notæ.
died, leaving the principality to his son Morat.

### CHAPTER 12.
The eldest son of the Emperor John, Andronicus, and Cuntuzes, the second-born son of Morat, conspire against their parents, and plot to seize the tyranny. When this was revealed, Morat deprived his own son of his sight, and signified to John that, if he wished to have peace with him, he should also blind Andronicus; John, complying with him, deprived his son and also his grandson [born from him] of their sight, and cast them into prison. Andronicus, having been liberated by the Genoese, invaded the empire and cast his father and brothers into prison; but they freed themselves from the prison, and John was restored to the imperial throne. Manuel was designated as his successor. The nuptials of the Catallusii and of Maria Palaeologina.
The Emperor John, when he was over twenty-five years of age and had reached manhood, begot two sons after Andronicus, Manuel and Theodore. Andronicus indeed surpassed all his contemporaries in bodily strength, and excelled many in stature and beauty. Morat also had sons: the aforementioned Sabutzius, and Kuntuzes, and Bajazet. Now Kuntuzes was of the same age as Andronicus, and because they associated and took pleasure together from time to time, a rumor was bruited about that both of them had conspired and planned a rebellion, whereby each might remove his own father from the midst—Kuntuzes removing Morat, and Andronicus removing John his father—and that henceforth there would be a fraternal friendship and a treaty between them, so that the one would receive the empire and the other the principality.
When these things were reported to Morat, after a diligent and accurate examination of the matter, and having discovered that the conversations they had had between themselves were true, he ordered his son Kuntuzes’s eyes to be gouged out; he dispatched a letter to the Emperor John, declaring that his son had been blinded by his order and explaining the cause of the deed. He also accused Andronicus, the other participant in the conspiracy, and threatened that, unless John punished him with a similar penalty, he would wage a war of extermination against him. Then the Emperor John, whether conscious of the weakness from which he suffered and fearing to provoke Morat as an enemy against himself, or burdened by gross ignorance, complied. For he was for the most part dull and stupid, and handled no business; but he was entirely occupied with catching beautiful and comely women, so as to entice and ensnare any one of them in any way he could. As for other matters, he let them be rolled along by fortune, and was not solicitous about their outcome—about where they might finally lead—but was indifferent to successful or unfortunate results.
Therefore, he blinded Andronicus; and not only him, but also his son John, who was a mere infant and could scarcely lisp; and in his place he crowned his second son, Manuel, as Emperor of the Romans. The third son, Theodore, he established as Despot of Lacedaemonia. He shut up the blind Andronicus, along with his child John and his wife, in the Tower of Anemas (65); for two years, while in...
Ismael Bullialdi’s note
(65) Concerning the blinding of Cuntuzes and Andronicus see Laonicus, book 1, who calls him Sauzen, not Cuntuzes, and says he was the eldest of Morat’s sons. The Emperor John, when he blinded him, had hot vinegar poured into the eyes of Andronicus. Phranzes, book 1, chapter 16, calls this son of Morat Mosen Zelebin, and says he was beheaded by order of his father. Leunclavius makes no mention of their blinding.
(66) In his *Pandectae Historiae Turcicae* he teaches that he learned from Zygomalas that those towers at Constantinople, which Leonard of Chios in his *Narration of the Conquest of Constantinople* calls Aveniades, are truly called by the name of the Towers of Anemas, and that they are those which were seen situated at the Pentapyrgos fortress, at the eastern angle of the city, near the church of the Blachernae.
Once they were shut in, having received help from the Latins of Galata, they escaped from the tower, and the Genoese, having received this man, began to fight against the citizens, holding Andronikos as a mask. And after they had fought for many days, father against son and son against father (this being characteristic of the inhumanity of the Romans and their hatred toward God), and because of the violation of the most terrible oaths made at that time, Andronikos enters the city and is proclaimed Emperor of the Romans. He keeps his father and his brothers, Manuel and Theodore, locked up in the tower, which he himself had held as a Tartarus—just as Zeus once held his father Cronus and his brothers Pluto and Poseidon inside—and he himself laid claim to the empire. So, having been in the tower for two years, they also escaped through the agency of a certain evil spirit; his name was Angelos, but his byname was Diabolos; and blending the name with the byname, he was called Diabolangelos. He, therefore, casting them out of the tower, whether by the art of an angel or a demon, transported them by boat across the water to Scutari. But the Emperor Andronikos, having learned of the flight of his father and his brothers, did not wish for the misfortunes of the Romans to continue indefinitely, nor did he himself wish to be the cause of these evils; but he calls his father and brothers back, gives them sworn assurances, brings them into the city, raises his father to the imperial throne, and falls at his feet, and asks for forgiveness for his transgressions, and he releases him. For Andronikos had one of his eyes wide open, but John, his son, was squint-eyed in both and looked askance. Then the Emperor, having been moved and having been greatly grieved by what had happened, sent him with his child and his wife to live in Selymbria, having granted him this city, along with Daonion, Heraclea, Rhaedestos, and Panidos. (68)
And the emperor crowns Manuel with ribbons and proclaims him emperor of the Romans. And he gives his own sister to Francesco Gattilusio—whom the narrative previously pointed out as a good and most faithful friend—as his wife, and the island of Lesbos as a dowry. And having celebrated the marriage, they departed thence and settled in Mitylene, and down to the present day they have not ceased to possess that island by succession from their lineage. Since, however, the narrative, in drawing us back from Bayezid to his grandfather Orxan on account of the accusations made against Cantacuzenus, has halted, come, let us begin again with the same momentum and proceed toward the affairs of Bayezid, or rather, toward the misfortunes of the Romans; and let us see where the history strives to arrive.
CHAPTER XIII
Bayezid demands tribute from the emperor, and requests that one of his sons come to serve him in the military. He invades the Cyclades Islands. John fortifies Constantinople; he tears down the fortifications built by his own order at the command of Bayezid, and finally dies. Manuel, who was serving in the military with Bayezid and living in his court, having heard of his father’s death, secretly arrives in Constantinople. Bayezid, taking this ill, imposes heavy and harsh conditions upon him, occupies Thessalonica, vexes Constantinople, and prevents food from being brought into it. The Hungarians and the greatest part of the Western princes move against Bayezid, and at Nicopolis they are struck by the Turks and defeated.
After Bayezid had effaced all the principalities of Asia—which were many—and had acted as monarch of Bithynia, Phrygia, I speak also of Mysia and Caria, he then set his mind and eyes against the City. And at first, having sent envoys to the emperor, he demanded that tribute be paid, and that in the expedition one of his sons be sent with one hundred soldiers. The emperor, being destitute of help from any of the kings, or the aristocrats, or the commoners, complied with Bayezid; and more than once Manuel went with a cohort of one hundred armed men.
[Notes of Ismael Bullialdus]: This statue was placed without doubt by the Perinthians; when Byzantium was captured by Severus, which, compelled by famine, surrendered to him, its walls, baths, and public buildings were destroyed, and it was reduced to the form of a village, and all private jurisdiction was attributed to the Perinthians, as Dion Nicaeus relates in his Life of Severus. He made it liable to tribute, and collected its goods well into the public treasury, and granted it and its lands freely to the Perinthians. In that inscription these words, "The senate and the people of the Neocori," signify the corporation, or college of priests, or aeditui. The Latins also used this term, as we read in Gruter’s book of inscriptions, p. 1102: VETTIO AGORIO PONTIFICI, VESTE PONTIFIC., Soli Quindecimviro, Auguri, TACROBOLIATO, CURIALI, NEOCORO, HIEROPHANTE, PATRI SACRORUM. Zosimus, who is subsequent to the time this monument was erected, testifies in his book that in his time the name of Perinthus was dropped and it was called Heraclea. Stephanus de Urbibus testifies to the same.

to this he finally yielded; and for the first time, and then a second time, the Emperor Manuel, with one hundred 72 armored soldiers, was sent by his father, the Emperor John, to serve under Bajazet, as he was marching toward Pamphylia against the Turks. Abranezes as commander (81), and he plundered all of Laconia and Achaia. To the cities lying along the Euxine Sea he sends Turachanes (82), and by emptiness he laid them waste; and, to speak simply, everything was vanished and became uninhabited. The city had no one 83 to harvest or to thresh, but it was constricted by the magnitude of the famine and was breathing its last. For the tyrant did not fight it with war—neither hurling against it, nor wall-scaling, nor skirmishes, nor any other engines of war did he introduce—but only by having more than ten thousand men sitting in a circle far off, and watching the exits so that nothing could enter or leave it. There was, therefore, a stiff famine inside the city of grain, wine, oil, and other kinds; and for the need of bread and every other equipment that kitchen boys provide, there being a lack of wood, they tore down the magnificent houses and burned their beams. The Emperor Manuel, being at a loss and seeing no help anywhere, writes to the Pope, to the King of France, and to the despot of Hungary, notifying them of the blockade and the constriction of the city; and that if help and aid did not arrive quickly, it would be surrendered into the hands of the enemies of the Christian faith. The leaders of the West, therefore, moved by these words (84), and having armed themselves for the counter-battle against the enemies of the Cross, came into Hungary as spring was beginning. Both the one from Flanders, and most of the English, and the magnates of France, and not a few of the Italians; and, indeed, at the call of the King, they pitched their tents along the banks of the Danube, having with them the despot of Hungary, Sigismund, who also was and was called King of the Romans. And so, having crossed over to the other side at Nicopolis, and having been well-prepared, they armed themselves against Bajazet. But Bajazet, having learned some days before of the gathering of the peoples from the West, and having himself gathered all his army—both from the East and the West, and those who were guarding the city—drove right at them; and having passed by Philippopolis, and the very tall mountains, and on to the plains that... withdrew, and waited there. On the following day, the Christians, having drawn up their battle line, proceeded into the sight of the Turkish army; and having formed a testudo, they broke through the middle of the enemy’s phalanx at the first onset, and they fought most strenuously; and as long as they had not penetrated to the last line of the enemy, they cut down all who resisted. And they performed their duties so strenuously in a dense mass that they rendered the work of the Turkish slingers and archers useless. When at last the Flemish cohorts noticed that the battle was succeeding against the Turks, and that the latter were yielding to flight, they themselves also charged in a dispersed run with broken ranks against the rear and penetrated into the middle of the Turkish battle lines, and they filled the muddy pools of the plain with the gore of the slain; and moving back, they rushed into those same ranks. Then finally the satellites of the prince Bajazet—who are called the "Porta," being as it were the door of the palace of the court, all of them purchased for money, and more than ten thousand of them pressed into service from various Christian nations—hiding in ambush, with one onset and a shout, launched an attack upon the Franks and the Hungarians, and having surrounded them on all sides with joined hands, they partly cut them down with the sword, and partly turned them to flight. But the men of Flanders, having turned and seen the rout of the Hungarians, and the Turks shouting and sending cries into the air and running behind them, were suddenly set upon by others with a tumultuous noise and the sound of trumpets, who rushed into the ranks of the Franks, and some they pursued, others they threw down under their horses, and the rest who resisted they slaughtered; and having pursued the remainder as far as the Danube, most of them threw themselves into the river and were drowned. They therefore captured alive the great noble, the Duke of Flanders (85). C
Ismael Bullialdus’s notes.
(85) The Duke of Flanders. This is John, Duke of Nevers, son of Philip the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, and nephew of John, King of the Gauls. Furthermore, all the historians of that age attribute the blame for so great a disaster to our men, who, unaware of the method and art of Turkish fighting, rushed with a reckless attack to their own ruin and that of the others. The year of this battle, however, is reported differently by various authors. The Turkish annals, which Leunclavius follows, claim that this slaughter of the Christians was committed by the Muslims in the year of the Hegira 794, which began on November 29, 1391. Calvisius followed the Turkish chronology in his first edition: but he wrongly writes that the year of the Hegira 794 began in November 1391; perhaps it is a typographic error: indeed, in the later edition, he moved it to the year 1392. But as to why the Turks should have written that this battle was fought in the year of the Hegira 794, I shall offer a reason, which seems to me quite probable. From Bonfinius, *Hungarian History*, decade 3, book 11, it is evident that Sigismund, the king of Hungary, after the Wallachian and Turkish army had been cut down and routed, besieged and captured the minor Nicopolis in the year of Christ 1392; this disaster suffered by his own men is what the Turks expunge from their annals; in the year 1392, when their army was cut down, they assign the battle of Nicopolis, notable for the slaughter of the Christians and for their own ruin: thus they confuse two battles, and transfer one prosperous to themselves in 1392, so as to obliterate the memory of the disastrous one. Froissart contradicts this in the cited place, who says that it happened in the year 1396, on Monday or the second day of the week, before the feast of St. Michael, which was September 25. Since in that year the Dominical letters were, A, Bonfinius, in the cited decade/book, says it happened on the Calends of October, 1396. In Brașov or Corona, in Transylvania, it is written thus on the walls of the church: In the year 1396, Sigismund fought unhappily at Nicopolis against Bajazet in September; thus in the volume of the authors of *Hungarian History*. Maurus Orbinus agrees with this in *History of the Slavs*. Buntingus and Ubo Emmius write that it happened in the year 1396. But Phranzes, whom we have had only in Latin until now, refers that slaughter to the year of the world 6900, that is, to the year of Christ 1392, and it agrees with the Turkish Annals. Where it should also be noted that Phranzes places that disaster in Nicopolis, so sorrowful to the Christians, after Manuel’s departure to Italy, as well as Ducas; it is evident from the *Venetian History* that in 1395, Manuel left Constantinople and arrived in Venice: because if his departure followed the disaster at Nicopolis, the year of the battle of Nicopolis preceded the year 1395. How these may be reconciled, I do not see: but I think we ought to trust our own authors more, who observed the times more accurately and, in this place, better than the Turks.
and Bergonia, and other Frenchmen, and high-ranking barons, whom, having sent [them] to Prusa, he shut up and later sold for a large sum of money, having received a guarantee from the lord of Mitylene, and the son of the aforementioned Francis Gateluzi.

### CHAPTER 14.
Bajazet demands that Constantinople be surrendered to him; and having ousted Manuel, he establishes John as emperor. Manuel, consulting for the safety of the city and the people, departs from Constantinople to the Peloponnese; from here he proceeds to Italy, and having traveled through the kingdoms and provinces of the West, he returns to the Peloponnese.
Consequently, having grown arrogant in such good fortune and having become exceedingly puffed up, he sends emissaries to Emperor Manuel, demanding the city. He, however, gave no answer at all. But most of the people of the city, being pressed by famine, were being distressed and were inclined to surrender the city. But, reminding themselves of what had been perpetrated in Asia by the Turks, the destruction of cities, the desolation of holy temples, and the temptations and slanders at every hour to abjure their piety, they turned their minds backward, saying: "Let us not grow weary; let us place our hopes in God, let us endure for a little while. And who knows if perhaps God, overlooking our sins, will have mercy on us, as He once did the Ninevites, and save us from this beast?" And the tyrant, as much as he saw the citizens resisting and not yielding to his will, by so much did he grow savage and angry against the city. And what happened? The recently mentioned Andronicus, the brother of Emperor Manuel, had died in Selymbria, and the youth John, his son, having reached manhood and holding his father's place, was sought by Bajazet for Selymbria. But he would not endure it, speaking [of it] and recounting the injustice he and his father had suffered from his grandfather.
Notes of Ismael Bullialdus
[86] "Having received a guarantee from the lord of Mitylene." Froissart writes similarly about the surety given by the Prince of Mitylene; but in matters of the geography of the Eastern regions he shows himself to be quite ignorant and unskilled. At this point, however, it will not be at all irrelevant to note a matter pertaining to the history of that battle of Nicopolis. Among the princes of France who took part in it, Philip of Artois, a prince of royal lineage, Count of Eu, and Constable of France, is counted: he was captured together with John, Duke of Nevers. Regarding the day and place of his death, where he succumbed to fate, I observe that our historians and the monuments that exist at Constantinople differ among themselves. The most famous brothers Sammarthanus, in the *Genealogy of the House of France*, lib. xxx, declare that Philip of Artois died on the ... of June at Prusa, commonly Bursa; and that his body was transported to France and buried in the choir of the monastery or abbey of St. Laurent of the Eu, commonly of Eu. But while we were in Constantinople in the year 1647, during the months of February, March, and April, in one of the chapels of the monastery of St. Francis in Galata, adjoining the peristyle or cloister, we saw the marble tomb of that prince, on which reads the following epitaph carved in Gothic characters: "The tomb of the magnificent lord Philip of Artois, Count of Eu and Constable of France, who died at Micalici on the ... day of June ... in his flesh: may his soul rest in peace." In this epitaph, a cross placed in the middle divides it into two parts. On the flank are the ancestral arms of France, such as at that time consisted of an indefinite number of lilies, with the addition of the peculiar trifid label of the Artois family in the forefront of the shield. Micalici or Michalizi is a city and region, distant no more than ten miles from Lake Lopadium, and a city of the same name; which today the Greeks call Lupadi, and the Turks Ulubal. Burusa is also two days' journey away. Laonicus, lib. IV, makes mention of the region of Michalizi, and Leunclavius, *Histor. Musulm.*, libb. XII and XIII, and in the *Pandectae*, cap. 86. What that "g" signifies in that epitaph, I have not yet been able to ascertain.
and sought to rely upon them for the empire. He, having wronged them, gave the empire to his second son, and gave my father this small town, as you see; and if you were to take this too, I have been treated with extreme injustice. Then Bajazet, having found another opportunity, turned aside. For he had long been considering in his mind by what artifices he might invade Constantinople; and so he did not omit the pretext of the name of John, who was the nephew of Manuel through his brother, and he ordered Manuel to depart from the city, and that John be brought in as the natural heir to the empire, and he would grant peace and a quiet state to the citizens. Then the Emperor Manuel, seeing the people tossed about by dissensions, and one part rising up and clamoring, while the other took great courage and cried out that John should be brought in and the scandals removed; and the Emperor Manuel, being thoughtful and full of learning, seeing the common people whispering and complaining that he would not yield the chair to the successor, but intended to rule tyrannically and had no care for the welfare of the public, deliberated a plan that was most wise and very sagacious. He sends word to John, who was then camping outside Constantinople with ten thousand Turks, and gives him oaths, and receives from him the promise that he would be brought inside the city and would deliver to him the empire of the Romans, while he, Manuel, would depart with the triremes that were to be found, and go wherever God might will. Persuaded, therefore, by his promises and oaths, he enters; and the Emperor, having received him kindly and handed over the palace to him, and having made a public address before all the nobles and the people, embarking on the triremes with his wife and children, left the city, having handed over the empire to John. But what was the objective of Bajazet, and what was that of the Emperor Manuel? For Bajazet imagined that he would have the city in the power of John; for he had sought this before and he himself had agreed to it, and Bajazet had promised on oath to give the Peloponnese in exchange for the city, and that for the future he would have a peaceful state. But the Emperor, being most Christian and initiated in divine things, and full of wisdom, seeing all his subjects suffering under indigence (for a modius of wheat was selling for more than twenty gold pieces, and wine likewise, and a scarcity of other necessary foods); and the common people, out of necessity, tending toward disbelief and the betrayal of their country; and he himself confessing each hour and day to God, saying: "Far be it from me, Christ the King, nor let it be heard among the distant nations of the Christians, that in the days of Manuel the Emperor the city was surrendered, and the holy and precious vessels within it given to the impious and to the enemies of Christ." Having found, therefore, that John was at that time conspiring with the tyrant to make him emperor; and the tyrant managing the affair as if it were on his behalf, Manuel said, "Save him who saves, and do not concern yourself about the empire." Having come to the coastal regions of the Peloponnese, he left his lady there with his children. For he had John as a babe, and the Theotokos.
Theodore. Having sent back the triremes, he boarded one of the great ships and sailed to Venice, to Milan, Genoa, Florence, Ferrara, and having traveled through all of Italy, he journeyed from Provence to Germany, or Francia. And all the kings, dukes, and counts honored him and rewarded him with gifts as if he were a demigod. Having traveled through all of Francia and crossed the borders of the Alemanni, he came again to Venice. The Venetians, having acted as proper hosts and sent him away with very many gifts, he returned to Methone with their triremes. And having met with the empress and the children, he sat awaiting the misfortunes of the city, or rather, the misfortunes of the Roman nation.
The emperor John, having entered into the city and been crowned emperor, first introduced, according to the agreement of Bajazet, a Turkish judge, who would himself adjudicate the disputes that arose between the Romans and the Turks according to the Arabic law. And all the lands that the Romans held as far as Selymbria, Selymbria itself also became Bajazet's, and John was reigning only within the city. Now Bajazet, sitting in Prusa and seeing the high-crowned trees of good fortune teeming with fruit, and every day wantonly enjoying himself with the various warblings of birds—for there was nothing lacking in the kinds of tongues that was beautiful, whether in the body of an animal, or metal, or some other thing in the world given by God for the sweetness of the sight—so that it would not be and be found in his treasuries. Therefore, selecting the purest of bodies, and those of handsome appearance, both male and female, they stood by, young and tender boys, and maidens shining more than the sun. Of whom? Romans, Serbs, C Vlachs, Albanians, Hungarians, Saxons, Bulgarians...

### CHAPTER XV.
John obtains his rule precariously from Bajazet, and admits a Cadin, that is, a Muslim judge, within the walls of the city. To Bajazet, immersed in pleasures, come ambassadors from Temyr Chan, who depart insulted by Bajazet; he himself then moves against Armenia. He demands Constantine's surrender from John, but the Constantinopolitans refuse to make surrender. Temyr invades Syria, storms cities, and rages inhumanely against the inhabitants. He plunders and ravages Damascus and Aleppo.
After Emperor John entered the city and assumed the imperial diadem, fulfilling before all else the condition laid down by Bajazet, he established a Turkish judge in the city, who would discern the litigations and controversies arising between Greeks and Turks, and settle them according to Arabic law. Furthermore, all the towns situated as far as Selymbria, and Selymbria itself, fell into the dominion of Bajazet, with John reigning only within the city walls. Meanwhile, Bajazet in Prusa, as if enjoying the fruits of good fortune hanging from that tree and taking up the daily growth amidst the singing of birds, and given over daily to luxury and delights, was occupied securely with various kinds of lust. For in his treasuries he had collected whatever beautiful and graceful thing all nations could send, both animals preeminent in bodily form, and metals and other things which God produced in the nature of things as pleasing to the eyes. Chosen boys and girls stood by, intact in form and body, and tender in flourishing age, virgins also...
and Latins—each one singing in his own vernacular language, and they not consulting together. But he, sitting and indulging in licentiousness, did not cease from committing acts of lust, behaving lewdly with both males and females. These were the wages of our transgressions, a just training by God. But do You, O Lord, render unto them also according to their works; overlook our iniquities, O Master, and do not allow us to be crushed as reeds of hemp, but look upon us with Your merciful eye.
While he was thus indulging in excess, behold, on one of the days, a message came that envoys had arrived from Persia seeking to see the ruler. "From whom?" he asked. They replied, "From Temür Khan, Sultan of Persia and Babylon." He commanded that a place be given to them for rest. After a few days, he summoned them and sought to hear the business of their embassy. They, having entered and standing before him, said, "The Great Khan Temür, through us his servants, gives thee notice, saying that it is not permitted for thee to seize the things of others, and by that means to become a great leader. Be content with those things which God has permitted thee to take from the infidels. But the provinces which thou hast snatched like a robber from the rest of the princes, restore them at once, turning back, so that it may go well with thee before God, and thou mayest have the gratitude and praise of the rest of the princes. But if not, I, with God's help, shall be their avenger."
Having said these and many other things, Bayezid ordered their beards to be shaven off with a razor and them to be sent away in disgrace, saying to them, "Go, announce to your lord: let him come quickly, for I am waiting for him. Let him be separated from his lawful wife if he does not come." After having spoken these and other trifling insults to them, he sent them away in disgrace.
He, however, not neglecting this, but with all his army marched toward the higher regions of Armenia; for in the preceding time he had taken the great Sebastia of Cappadocia. And in this campaign, having crossed the borders of Greater Armenia and entered the land of the Turco-Persians, he took one of the cities called Arsyngas. Having then turned back, he came to Prusa; and having departed from Prusa and crossed the strait, he came to Adrianople and sent word to the Emperor John, saying: "I, even if I drove the Emperor Manuel from the city, did not do this for your sake, but for my own. If you wish to be our friend, depart from your present position, and I will give you whatever province you desire; if not, God and His great prophet are my witnesses that I will spare no one, but will utterly destroy all." C Bajazet sent these and other messages filled with rage, but they entrusted their hopes to God. For they had been practicing for a long time taking little for sustenance. They answered, saying: "Go, announce to your master that we, being in weakness and great oppression, have nowhere to take refuge except in God, who helps the weak and casts down the powerful; and do whatever you meditate." In those days, messages arrived from Amasia, saying that Temyr Chan was campaigning against Syria. Bajazet, having crossed the strait and staying in Prusa, sent everywhere to gather forces from all parts of both East and West. Meanwhile, Temyr Chan traversed Armenia, first conquering Arsyngas by the law of war, and slaughtered all the colonists who had been brought there by Bajazet. Then he came to Sebastia, which was a large city, and pitched a camp; and seeking to take the city, and when those within did not surrender, he dug around it, set it upon beams and planks from the foundations, without anyone within knowing what was happening to them. For the diggers had begun the excavation from a mile or more away from the city. The city was built of sun-dried brick. Then he sent word again to those inside, saying: "If you wish to be saved, surrender the city." But they, not being persuaded, but having poured forth boundless insults, he cast fire D [on the beams upon which the city was set, and it fell from its foundations, and entering...]
they began to strike down the citizens without mercy and to plunder and despoil them. Furthermore, Temyr Chan ordered all the chief men of the city to be gathered into one place, and directed that pits be dug like vast sepulchers, and that they be bound with a bond which none of the tyrants of past times had ever devised. For they bent their necks, and having thrust them between their legs, until the neck of that wretched and unfortunate man, whoever he might be, was brought down to the anus, and his shanks alongside his knees were pinned from both ears. And the man, like a hedgehog, orb-shaped, was hurled into the sepulcher; and though ten or even more were in one grave, they did not cover them with earth; but having fastened them with boards, they piled earth over the boards, so that having been stifled not quickly or easily, they might be deprived of life. Such a torture did the Scythian devise. When, therefore, he had destroyed it utterly, he came into the regions of Phoenicia, and as far as Damascus itself, and burns and plunders everything, and takes away incalculable wealth and a great multitude of captives. And having devastated Damascus, he crosses over to Aleppo, and destroyed it also, and transferred many masters of the arts to Persia, and having frightened the Arabs, he journeyed back to Samarkand, the capital of Persia. But Bajazet, hearing the things that had come to pass at Arsyngan, in the city of Sebastia, in Syria, and in Damascus, and at Aleppo, did not cease from making census-takings both in his own lands and in Asia, gathering a new army and increasing it beyond measure. The poor citizens, with the emperor, lifting their hands to God and shedding most copious tears, supplicated, saying: "O God and Lord of mercy, have mercy upon us, your useless servants; and give to him who threatens us, this our house, and the holy things that are in it, some other concern, some other care, another thought, so that, having been delivered from his tyranny, we may glorify you, Father and Son and Holy Spirit, the one God, unto the ages. Amen."
CHAPTER XVI
Temyr moves toward the Tanais. Bajazet gathers an army, and encounters Temyr, who has encamped at Ancyra. A comet shines. A battle is started by the Temyrians against the forces of Bajazet: Bajazet is deserted by a great part of his troops. He is defeated. Taken, he is led before Temyr, who was playing at Zatrichium—that is, chess. Temyr consoles Bajazet and behaves humanely toward him, though strictly keeps him in custody. The forces of Temyr spread throughout the whole of Asia Minor. Mehemetes attempts to free his father, but in vain. Chociapherulzes, the prince of the eunuchs, captured together with his master Bajazet, is put to death by Temyr's command.
Temyr Chan, as spring began, moving from Persia toward the regions of the Tanais, and having gathered a collection of Tauroscythians, Zychians, and Ishmaelites,
and having razed the small towns in the Bosporus, he crossed into the parts of Armenia; and having passed through Cappadocia with a large army, and having taken up not a few of the Armenians, he arrived at the parts of Galatia, having an army equal in multitude to that of Xerxes of old. Bayezid, for his part, having gathered every army, both Thracian and Eastern, and another newly conscripted army, and having with him Stephen the son of Lazarus, the Serb, together with many guards, also went out to meet Temyr. But when he too approached the regions of Galatia, he learned that Temyr was encamped at the city of Ancyra. Having approached nearby, and having fixed his tents in the middle of the plain near Ancyra, he had a river flowing by, and potable water for the need of the army, the horses, and the entire host. Temyr, however, was dwelling on arid ground. But what happens? Bayezid orders a proclamation to be made in the midst of the camp: that the following day everyone should go out on a hunt. B He went out, therefore, with his entire army, hunting and chasing deer for three days. But Temyr, rising from the place where he was, came and encamped on the banks of the river where Bayezid had previously sat. Water, therefore, being scarce—since the sun was also making its journey in Leo—Temyr was no longer concerned about obtaining water. But Bayezid, boasting and haughtily showing his disdain for the engagement with Temyr, as if he were considering it a secondary matter, busied himself with the hunt; and this was the beginning of his misfortune. For having gone out, and with the sun at its meridian, the soldiers were failing in life under the heat, and they sought water and there was none, and they fainted and died. Five thousand men therefore died in that hardship. After three days, when he turned back to the place where he had been lying, he found Temyr having arrived there first, and the water was not under his own control, but the location of the place kept it at a distance, and they could not [get to it] easily. By necessity, therefore, they knew that on the next day they would necessarily have to join battle. In the year that was already waning, while the sun was traversing the twelfth house of Gemini, in the western region, a sign appeared in the heavens, a messenger of evils: this was a comet of great...
Notes of Ismaël Boulliau
(5) The Tauroscythians are those who dwell between the Borysthenes and the Tanais, and inhabit the Tauric Chersonese. The Zychian people are those by the Euxine Sea, otherwise called Sindi. Pliny, Book VI, ch. 7: "By the Cimmerian [region] dwell the Maeotici, Vali, Serbi, Archi, Zingi, Pessii." These Zyngi are, according to Pliny, the Zinchi, located on the peninsula of Corocondama. The Sindi and Zinchi are the same; in Eustathius on this verse: "Behind the Sauromatae follow the Sindi, who by some are called Zinchi." The region of the Zinchi is called in the Royal Library, book 118, in the formulas of subscriptions and inscriptions of the epistles of the Patriarch of Constantinople: and it is held among the Metropolitas to whom the Patriarch writes. Constantine Porphyrogenitus, in [his work] *On the Administration of the Empire*, left this noted about Zinchia: that in the part of Zinchia toward the place of Papagia, which faces the side of Panagia, where the Zinchi reside, there are nine springs giving forth a foul scent, the water of which, if drunk, brings ulcers and pustules to the lips.
(6) Emperor Leo’s *Tactics*, Book I, ch. 2, has this title: *On the arrangement of the "aplekta"*. To "aplekton" and "fossaton" are the same, and denote a camp, and the verb "aplekeuein" signifies to pitch a camp in the same place. By apocope of the "a," Ducas wrote "plekeuon," a figure so familiar to the Greeks even now that one word is scarcely pronounced whole by them, nor can traces of the ancient Greek idiom be discerned.
(7) Ancyra is a city of Galatia.
and clear, revealing an erect mane in the likeness of a flaming fire; and above four cubits, not unlike a spear, it cast beams from west to east; and when the sun had submerged below the horizon, it illuminated all the borders of the earth with its own rays, nor did it allow the other stars to emit their light, nor the air to be darkened by the shadow of night: because its light surpassed the splendor of others, and it stretched out flaming toward the vertex of the heavens as long as it stood above the horizon. This portent was seen by the Indians, Chaldeans, Egyptians, Phrygians, Persians, the inhabitants of Asia Minor, the Thracians, Huns, Dalmatians, Italians, Spaniards, and Germans, and whatever other nations dwell upon the shores of the Ocean: and this reddish and shining portent, most terrible of all, which is called a Lampadias, endured until the autumnal equinox, when the sun began to pass through the sign of Libra.
But let us return again to the matter, and consider how God, by a new and miraculous prodigy, submerged one Pharaoh into the deep sea by means of another Pharaoh, and how the people of God obtained a respite and cessation from their many labors; yet they neither saw nor understood it. The Scythian, therefore, having issued a proclamation throughout the camp in the evening, so that all might be present at the following light, mounted on horseback and armed, arose at the deep of dawn and drew up into battle-order the commanders of the cohorts and the chiliarchs. C Upon the right wing he placed his eldest son as leader; upon the left, the grandson whom he had by him: for Temyr had already exceeded sixty years. He himself, however, led the rear of the battle-line; and then he encouraged his men with these words: "O my multitude, invincible army, nature of adamant, wall of brass, insuperable generation, you have heard what our ancestors performed gloriously from the beginning, not among the eastern nations—for the East is our fatherland—but in Europe and in Africa, and, to speak in a word, throughout the whole world. You know accurately the expedition undertaken by Xerxes and Artaxerxes against the Greeks, I say the Greeks, the demigod heroes; for these semibarbarian Turks can no more be compared with them than a locust can be compared with a lion. Nor do I recall these things to your memory to rouse your boldness, for the prey can no longer escape from our hands; but let no place of flight be given to this bugbear. And that it may be taken alive and intact, and that we may carry it off into the Persian land as a spectacle for our children, let us teach it not to adjure us hereafter by our wives. I wish, therefore, that this great body of troops which we see might be surrounded,

And let the right side be led in a circular manner, and likewise the left; and fortify the whole plain, and let the enemy be found in the center, as if he were the fixed point of a compass. Then the two horns, one from the right and the other from the left, began to circle the territory, since it was still early morning. Bajazet, as the sun was rising, having drawn up his own legions and having sounded the war-trumpet, stood awaiting the starting signal from the Scythians. But they carried out their orders without voice or shouting or any ordinary sound, laboring like tireless ants. Therefore Bajazet began to chatter and insult his own high officials, and to demote and beat the B *Tziavousidas*, as if they were not opposing the war properly. But one of the leading men from the *bandon* of Atin, having heard that his lord Atin was standing face-to-face with his brother in the battle line of Temyris, let go of all the reins, and having seized the *bandon*, fled with five hundred hoplites to the enemy. Those of Sarchan and those of Mantachia and Carmian did the same, seeing their leaders shouting and making signs, and they all fled to them and went toward the adversaries. Bajazet, like the jackdaw, was gradually stripped bare. C The host of the Scythians was circling around, and it became a sphere as it had just been [suggested]. Seeing this, Stephen, the son of Lazar and brother-in-law of Bajazet, still being with him with five thousand Serbian spear-bearers, and not bearing the defeat, advanced with martial spirit against the Scythians, having set all the spears facing forward toward the Scythians. The Scythians, seeing the audacity full of spirit, opened a gate and gave them a way out. The Scythians shot their arrows from behind at the soldiers in the hindquarters of their horses; for they could not harm the riders, as they were fenced in by black iron. The Serbians, turning back again, and opening the gate again, the Scythians gave them passage; yet, from both sides, not a few fell. Stephen approached Bajazet and spoke sufficient words into his ear, but he did not make him amenable to fleeing; for already many dogs had encircled him, and fat bulls were pressing around him. Stephen, therefore, observing the things that were happening and foreseeing what would come to be a little later, secretly took his own men and the firstborn son of Bajazet, the one called Musulman, and striking again into the middle of the adversaries, and with great force thinning them out, and throwing down many, he himself...
