Stephen was fleeing along the road leading to Prusa, and Musulman with him. But the Scyths, sparing none of the Turks who were in flight, cut them all down without mercy, until Bajazet (15) ascended a certain hill in the middle of the plain because of the severe congestion, having with him ten thousand slaves bought for money, whom they call Janissaries; all the rest had dispersed in a rout. The Scyths, pursuing the Turks, when they saw Bajazet in the midst of the ranks already struggling like a sea-bass, after a cry went out that no one should kill anyone, stripped them and let them go. For this is a law (14) transmitted from ancestors to descendants, remaining uncorrupted not only among Romans, but also among Persians, Triballi, and Scyths, because they profess the same religion: to plunder their goods, but not to enslave their bodies, nor to kill anyone outside the battle array. Then the slaves of Bajazet, like lions, turned upon the Scyths. But the Scyths, because of their excessive ordering, stood against the Turks; for what could ten do against a hundred Scyths? Nevertheless, they were all slaughtered, and the misfortunes of Bajazet had reached such a point that the Scyths approached him and said: "Dismount from your horse, O Bajazet, and come hither; Temur Khan calls you." [regarding] Genitzeros, when he writes that they deserted Bajazet at the very last: and that they did not surrender until, with no hope of safety remaining, they saw that Bajazet was soon to be captured. Concerning what our author adduces, Leunclav. lib. vi relates the purpose of Temyr, and reports his words to Bajazet: "At what time," he says, "I was departing from my own regions, about to undertake this expedition, I swore and promised to God that, if I were to emerge victor from the ensuing battle, I would kill no one from that time forward." But when Ducas says that the Romans used the same custom, it must be understood as being towards Romans; just as the Musulmans use it towards Musulmans. The Turks refer this defeat and captivity of Bajazet to the year of the Hegira 803, ending three days later, which was the year of Christ 1401, August 7, feria 2; for the year began August 11, feria 5; a comet seen in the spring preceding this epoch of time confirms this, which Juvenalis Ursinius testifies shone in the year 1401, and in the Chronology of Buntingus, as we have already said, which for the rest, and also for the vulgar characters of the year, is more certain. The hottest time of the year, when the Sun was traversing the dodecatemorion of Leo, also agrees. Ursinius, however, relates that the battle was begun in the year 1402; Phranzes wishes it to have happened in that year on July 28, as is gathered from lib. i, chapters 21 and 22. In that year he writes he was born on August 30, while Constantinople was being besieged; but it is certain that the siege of the city had been resolved long before Temyr had defeated Bajazet in war; wherefore the July in which Phranzes relates these princes fought in line of battle will be the year 6910, of Christ 1402, which is also confirmed by his words, in which he confesses, chapter 24, that he will write thenceforth regarding the glorious deeds and worthy of memory that happened from the year 6910: whence that year 6909 is excluded. It has not been concealed that the mark or character of time, which Leunclavius refers from the history of Hanivaldana, agrees with July of the year of the world [Christ 1402]; for he says it was fought at Ancyra on feria 6, which is called Zuma-Juma, that is, the day of the temple, by the Turks: and from there the day of July was feria 6 in the year of the Hegira ending, and after three days beginning the year 805, August 1, feria 3. Paulus Iovius in Annal. Genuens. lib. v, Ubertus Folleta lib. 13, Petrus Bizarus also lib. ix of the History of Genoa, [and] Augustin. Justinian. in the Genoese Annals write that the battle was fought in the year 1402. That Damascus was captured and devastated by Temyr in the year 1400, Augustinus Justin. testifies, the destruction of which city, according to our Ducas, preceded the battle at Ancyra by one year. When he had heard that Bajazet had fallen into his power, he ordered a tent to be erected, under which he sat with his son playing at zatrikion, which game the Persians call *shatranj*, but the Latins *scaccum* [chess]. By this playful diversion, he wished to show that he was not so anxious about the capture of Bajazet, and that he had held [the] prey before his nets in his countless forces; yet, what the reality was, he hid. For although he had drawn up his battle line with forces twice as large, he was nevertheless exceedingly anxious and angry within himself, until he perceived that matters had turned out happily for him; then he began to act with cunning and wile, and to measure the gifts of fortune by his own bravery. Finally, they bring up Bajazet, and place him standing at the vestibule of the tent, and with a loud voice they pursued Chan Temyren with auspicious acclamations, and among them the name of Bajazet was heard most often: "Behold, the prince of the Turks stands fettered before you." But Temyr, intent on the game of chess, did not leap up at the voices of those acclaiming him; therefore, those present acclaimed again with a more insistent voice, and repeated the name of Bajazet once more. Temyr, having then been defeated in the game of chess by his son, gave him the name in Persian *Siachruch* [Shah Rukh]—which is called by the Italians *Scacco zocco*—and he called his son by that name from then on. Having then gazed and seen the line of troops and Bajazet in the midst like a criminal, he asked them, saying: "Is this the one who, a little while ago, was threatening that he would separate our wives if we did not join battle?" To which Bajazet, having received the reply, said: "I am he; for it does not befit you to hold the conquered in such arrogance and to despise them; but learn, you who are also a prince, to impose limits and measure on your rule." Then Temyr, perceiving the immoderately inflamed bile within him, because he had remained fasting from morning until evening and, parched by the most bitter heat and dust, was scorched and dried up; and as he stood upright, Temyr ordered him to sit before him, and he soothed him with a gentle and mild speech, and consoled him. He then commanded three tents...

that is to say, magnificent pavilions, to be pitched, saying to him: "Go, take your rest, and do not expect me to do unto you what you have done unto others. Then, Bajazet having entered the tents which Temyr had gifted him, Temyr commanded a trench to be dug around the tents, and ordered a thousand Persian soldiers to keep guard in a circle about the tents, and outside the trench five thousand picked men from his own household guards, changing them every day and night.
For eight days he remained in that same plain where the battle took place. And in these days the Persian army dispersed from Galatia into Phrygia, Bithynia, Paphlagonia, Lesser Asia, Caria, Lycia, and Pamphylia, so that in every province and city all the army of Temyr, and Temyr himself, seemed to be present; thus, in those eight days, that multitude overflowed and flooded [everything]. Temyr, having plundered immense wealth and many captives from Ancyra, and burning and consuming all those he met, came to Cotyaeum, the metropolis of Phrygia, bringing with him also Bajazet, well enclosed in the manner we have already described. However, something happened in Ancyra that is worthy of memory.
While Bajazet was still engaged in the war, four of his sons were with him in the army: first Musulman, the second Esses, the third Mehemet, and the fourth Moses; but at home he kept two others who were still infants, Mustapha and Orchan. Now, in the year that the battle was fought, the father had assigned the province of Galatia, to be governed by his third son, Mehemet. When he saw that his father was about to fall into the hands of the Scythians—as it seemed in a short time—he himself also fled with those under his command, and he wandered through the mountains as a fugitive, awaiting the outcome of events. CHAPTER XVII
Temyr visits and captures several cities of Asia, devastating everything with fires and looting. He seizes the treasures of Bayezid kept at Prusa or Bursa. He captures Smyrna; the princes of the Phocaeans send envoys to render him appeased and win him over with gifts. He traverses Caria, and thereafter directs his journey to Salutaria, and there Bayezid dies. Temyr returns to Persia in the year he finished the expedition.
Departing from Cotyaeum, Temyr, overturning everything, enslaving all, seizing every treasure to be found with numerous tortures and punishments—burning, hanging, showing men buried alive, and performing every other torment—came to Prusa; and opening the treasuries, he emptied out the heirlooms won by the Romans: gold, silver, precious stones, and pearls measured by the choinix like grains of wheat. He found there also his wives and concubines, and with them the daughter of Lazarus. And having taken all that belonged to Prusa, Nicaea, Nicomedia, and the surrounding cities—the inexhaustible treasuries—he arrived in lower Phrygia; and having plundered all the small towns and cities, he came into Asia. And having crossed Adramyttium and Assos, he came to A B [Notes of Ismael Bullialdus:]
grew up again. For the remainder, in exceeding great numbers, trampled upon the bodies of the fallen Scythians, and placing ladders, they ascended, and some reached the battlements of the walls, while others entered the path that leads to Hades and death. Nor did any survivor turn away from trampling upon the bodies of their own fathers or children, nor did they make any distinction between theirs and others; but each was intent only upon this one thing, how he might be the first to ascend and place the scepter on the tower. Then, having ascended from all sides and having pursued the friars into the inner part, they were concerned only for their own safety in flight, and bringing the triremes near the acropolis, they boarded in confusion and disorder, having the Bailie himself and the rest of the friars along with them. But all the Christians who had come there for protection from the outside, along with their wives and children—some in the sea, some clutching the rudders of the triremes, others the oars, others the lines of the prow and the anchors—cried out to the passengers: "Have mercy on us, for we are Christians, and do not abandon us here." But they, striking with cudgels at the hands reaching out, and spreading their sails, sailed away, leaving them half-dead. The Scythians, having taken the acropolis and having collected the captives into one place—for they were, with their wives and children, over a thousand—brought them before Temyr, and he ordered all their heads to be severed with the sword. And having built a single tower, putting in one stone and one head, joining them together, so that the faces might stand in sequence; and in the other order, where there was stone, there was a head upon it; and where there was a head, there was a stone upon it, with all the faces visible on the outer surface. And it was possible to see a strange monster and an inhuman contrivance.
The Phocaeans sent legates before he arrived in the regions of Ionia, and they did him homage with very many gifts; and he received them and made peace with them. For one of them belonged to the Genoese, which was also called the New, and the other was subject to the governor of Mitylene, which was also called the Old. Temyr, having come to Smyrna and warring against it, sent his grandson to explore the Phocaeas; and when the governor of Lesbos learned of this, he boarded a trireme and came to the Phocaeas. And going out of the city and playing the host as was proper to the grandson of Temyr, they ate and drank and gave themselves to joy together, and he then sent him away with many gifts. The kin of Temyr bestowed upon him a scepter as a sign of affection, and having embraced one another, the one by trireme and the other having mounted a horse, they parted from one another. And having arrived and finding that Smyrna had been razed to its very foundations, he made his journey toward Ephesus, and having gathered his army from all sides. D
For a command had been issued by him from Ancyra: “Wherever the grandees and satraps with those under them may happen to be, let all be found at Ephesus.” For indeed he was journeying back from Ephesus toward his native lands; there he pitched his tents and spent thirty days, and after gathering all the surrounding fortresses of the city, and cities, and villages, and after collecting—through many tortures and burnings—all the gold and silver and every other precious material and costly clothing left behind by their ancestors, he departed. And he came to the metropolis of Caria, Miletus [Mylasa], B where such a fierce winter set in, with cold and frost, that the very nature of four-footed animals, as well as the birds of the air and the water creatures, were frozen stiff, their nature having been turned into ice. But when the army of Temyr migrated from one city to another, he left the place from which he was departing so desolate and full of the horror of solitude, that not even a dog’s bark could be heard anywhere, nor the twittering of a tame bird, nor the wailing of a child; but just as a fisherman draws a net from the sea onto the shore, pulling in whatever it has caught—whether a small fish or a large one, and even the vilest little fish and tiny crab—so did they likewise plunder the whole of Asia and depart. From Miletus they went to Upper Phrygia Cappatiana, doing the same things. From Laodicea they arrived at Phrygia Salutaris C (which the Turks in their own language call Karasar); there also the much-afflicted Iltirim Bajazet died. Many affirm, then, that he deprived himself of life with poison. For Temyr indeed wished him to live and to bring him into Persia, and to show the Persians what a beast he had captured, and to put him on display and lead him in triumph, and after that, to cause him to be relieved through great affliction. But since he was breathing his last, he signifies to Temyr [saying]: “I am now exchanging this life for death; but you, look upon me dead with a joyful and cheerful face, and give my body to be buried in the tomb built by me.” And having heard these words, the Scythian was softened in his resolve; and having sent him off by slaves who were undertakers as if he were...
one of a hundred whom he liberated, he brought him to Prusa, and they buried him in the tomb which he himself had built. Temyr, having departed from there, arrived at Lycaonia, and from there to Caesarea, then to Lesser and Greater Armenia. Having spent one year outside of Persia, he returned as a victor and a triumpher after that time, bearing booty and spoils such as no tyrant of the Persians ever had. But let us return again to the later leaders of the Othmans, and let us see in what way the prosperities of the sovereignty passed over to them. For the Emperor Manuel, having heard of the defeat of the Turks, and the sudden change of Bajazit B —how he had fallen as lightning from heaven—immediately returned to Byzantium. And his nephew yields the helm of the empire, and he himself is sent to the island of Lemnos. And Manuel is hailed as sole emperor by the palace and the people. But Mousulman, having crossed over into the West, entered within the city and falls at the feet of the emperor, and beseeches him, saying, “I will be to you as a son, and you shall be my father; and from now on there shall be no tares of discord sown in our midst, nor will there be any offenses; only appoint me governor of Thrace, and of such other land as I possessed through my fathers.” He handed over to him as hostages one of his under-age brothers, and one of his sisters, called Phatmacatun; promising to give to the emperor Thessalonica, and the places by the Strymon as far as Zetunium, and the Peloponnese; and the lands surrounding the city from Panium as far as the Sacred Mouth, and from the Sacred Mouth as far as Varna, all the coastal fortresses situated on the Euxine Sea.
CHAPTER XVIII
Emperor Manuel returns to Byzantium, and relegates his nephew, born of his brother, to Lemnos. He enters into a treaty and friendship with Musulman, the son of Bajazit. The state of affairs in Asia after the departure of Temyr Chan. Ese, or Isa, the son of Bajazit, being attacked in war by his brother Mehemet, is captured by Temyr as leader and strangled with a noose. Cineites the Smyrniote becomes known, expels the sons of Atinis from Ionia, and follows the party of Musulman. The sons of Atinis, with the help of Mantachius, storm Ephesus. Homur, the son of Atinis, contracts an affinity with Cineites, and dies shortly after. An expedition of the Musulmans against Cineites. The petty kings of Asia conspire against Musulman, but are dissociated from each other by mutual suspicions.
Emperor Manuel, when he had heard of the defeat of the Turks and the sudden change of fortune of Bajazit, who had fallen like a lightning bolt from heaven, returned to Byzantium instantly, and received the helm of the empire to be governed from his nephew, whom he relegated to Lemnos. Manuel, therefore, is greeted as emperor alone by the palatine officials and the populace. But Musulman, having crossed the strait, betook himself to the western regions, and having entered Constantinople, fell at the feet of the emperor and addressed this suppliant speech to him: “I will be a son to you, and you will be a father to me; and from this time forth no tares of discord shall be disseminated between us, nor shall any offenses come between us; only constitute me prefect of Thrace and of other regions, as many as my ancestors possessed.” He also handed over hostages from his under-age brothers, one, and one sister called Phatma-catun; and he promised that he would restore to the emperor Thessalonica, and the towns situated as far as Zetunium by the Strymon, and the Peloponnese, and also the towns near the city from Panium as far as the Sacred Mouth, and from hence as far as Varna, all the coastal fortresses placed upon the shores of the Euxine Sea.
Once peace had been established, the Emperor sent him to Adrianople and dispatched Demetrius Leontarius, 37 a man prudent and quick in military matters, to receive Thessalonica. When he had taken it and notified the Emperor, he brought Emperor John inside and proclaimed him emperor of all Thessaly. Likewise, the Emperor sent famous Romans to all the cities and small towns, and they recovered them, having driven out the Turks; and in the Thracian regions there was peace of every kind and undisturbed tranquility. But in the East, there was great turmoil and a sudden change of rulers in the provinces. Therefore, with the onset of spring, after that severe winter and tempest had passed, a powerful famine and plague arose in all the provinces which the feet of the Scythians had trodden, along with civil wars. Thus, the Carmanian 38, having received permission from Temyr, returned to his ancestral domain and recovered it; likewise, Sarchan recovered his ancestral principality of Lydia. Orchan and the two sons of Atin, Homur and Esses, all occupied Ionia for themselves. Elias, the son of Mantachia, also gained possession of Caria and Lydia. As for the sons of Bajazet who had been left in the East, one of them, Mehemetes, 39 remained in Ancyra in Galatia, since he had no inheritance or province; his younger brother Moses, being still a child, lived with him. Esses, the other one, wandered hither and thither, possessing no authority or empire, and Mustaphas was in the same condition. Wherefore Mehemetes ordered one of the magnates who accompanied his father, named Temirtes, who was then present in those regions, to march against Esse from Ancyra; and having engaged him in battle, Temirtes emerged victorious and cut off his head. Thus Mehemetes was magnified in Galatia. Meanwhile, in the part toward Ionia 40 that belonged to Atin, there arose a man named Cineites, the son of the one called Karasupasi, a man brave and experienced in military affairs.
Ismaelis Bullialdi notes
37 Demetrius Leontarius. Pro Leontarius, in the common idiom: Phranzes mentions this Demetrius, bk. I, ch. 39.
38 The Carmanian who was called Alysar. In his *History of the Muslims*, he relates that Temyr restored the provinces of which Bajazet had been despoiled to the princes: he is called here the Carmanian Alysar, but in Laonicus, bk. ii, he is called Caramanus Alosurius. See Leunclavius in *Pandectae Historiae Turcicae*, no. 56.
39 Son of Bajazet, namely Mehemetes. Leunclavius, bk. x, xi, narrates this slaughter of the brothers. In bk. ix, he explains the deeds of Mehemetes against Isam-beg; he says that Temirtas stood on the side of Eses or Isa, and was killed by the soldiers of Mehemetes, and that Isa, after he fled, was never seen again. But our author affirms that Temirtes, who is the same as Temirtas, fought for Mehemetes. Laonicus, bk. iv, writes that Jesus or Isa fought a war against the Muslim and, being captured in battle, suffered death: Phranzes, bk. i, ch. 50, agrees with this. But what Leunclavius says at the beginning of bk. x is most true: that Laonicus's narrative is confused and mutilated, from which even sharper minds can scarcely extricate themselves. The *Annales* of Becanus and the *Historia Verantiana*, by the testimony of the same Leunclavius, and while rejecting them, relate that Isa was killed by Musa.
40 The mention of Cineites is very frequent in this history of ours. Laonicus, bks. iv and v, speaks of him and calls him Zounaiten or Cineites. Leunclavius mentions him first in bk. x, where he composed the history of Dusme, or the pseudo-Mustaphas, and names him Tzoneiten. Ducas everywhere has what we have rendered as Cineites, so that the first syllable is pronounced with an Italian sound. This Cineites is called by Leunclavius Ismyroglius, that is, son of the prince of Smyrna: but Ducas reveals him to have been the son of Kara-Supasi, that is, of the black Subassi, and that he drove the sons of Adinis or Atimis, who were the Ismyroglii and princes of Smyrna, out of Ionia. We shall observe here in passing that in narrating the affairs of the interregnum, our Ducas differs much from Laonicus and Leunclavius.
and skilled in the art of war; his father, while Bayezid held supreme power, had governed Smyrna, and because his rule had been long-enduring, the Smyrniotes revered him as their general toparch and prefect. At this time, he undertook a war against the sons of Atin, for they dwelt in Ephesus. Cineis, having gathered the Smyrniotes and about five hundred men from the surrounding villages, descended and plundered those in the field of Ephesus. In a short time, having gathered more than five hundred others, he arrived at the city of the Ephesians itself. Having laid siege to the town, in a few days the son of Atin abandoned it and fled, and Cineis became master of the principality. Nevertheless, he constantly wrote to Musulman, who was in Thrace, saying, "I endure these toils for your sake; it is not for myself that I have taken hold of the principality of Atin, but for you. Send me help, therefore, so that I may oppose your enemies to the end as long as they persist." Placing his trust in these words, Musulman sent much treasure from Gallipoli to Smyrna once, twice, and many times over, with which he met the daily expenses of the war until he drove out the heirs of Atin.
In the beginning of spring, in the second year after that terrible incursion of the Scythians, one of the sons of Atin, who was also called Homur—the other having died—returned to his uncle, Mantachias Eliezpegus, the prince of Caria, and as a suppliant, falling at his feet, he begged for help. Mantachias received him very kindly, assented to his request, and, having gathered his entire army, went to Ephesus in the company of Homur, bringing with him about six thousand men. But they who were in the city, with Karasupasis, the father of Cineis, numbered only three thousand, because Cineis was at that time staying in Smyrna. The Ephesians, however, did not submit then but, resisting courageously, cast fire into the city. The flame, having been kindled through the four quarters, devoured the houses, and those things which had been left behind by the Scythians, the fire consumed like hay. And the whole city was ash and dust in two days. The Ephesians, seeing such great ruin, surrendered. Karasupasis retreated into the citadel and endured the siege until the autumn, expecting help from his son, Cineis. But he was unable to leave Smyrna and go to Ephesus, because the scarcity of soldiers forbade it. Finally, therefore, having thrown open the gates, he surrendered the citadel, which fell into the hands of Mantachias; he took him and the others who were in the town, and led them off in chains to his own principality. He settled the son of Atin, Homur, in his paternal principality, and Karasupasis...
Ismaelis Bullialdi notae.
(41) *Homur*—this was the brother of Ese or Isa, and both were grandsons of that Homur from whom Smyrna was snatched by the Knights of the Order of Jerusalem, as was narrated above, chapter 7. They are called sons of Atin because they traced their lineage from Atin, the leader of the Turks; by the name of sons, nephews and descendants are also included.
(42) *Eliezpegus*—that is, the Eli-beg of the descendants of Mantachias.
in a small town, having bound and thrown him into a tower, along with those who were with him; Mammalos is the name of the small town. But what, then, is Cineites doing? Setting out from Smyrna with one bireme, he sailed along the coast of Caria and arrived at Mammalos, where he secretly sent word to those who were imprisoned that he had come to steal them away. They, having made a banquet for their guards, and having poured out unmixed wine until they were sated and had put them to sleep as if they were dead, exited the tower themselves; and having lowered themselves via ropes from the wall, they boarded the bireme, and sailing away, came to Smyrna. Thus there was great joy at such a theft.
At the beginning of winter, Cineites marched against Ephesus and shut Homur inside the small town, giving the whole city up to his soldiers to plunder. And apart from the people, who were not enslaved, everything that they had possessed after the incursion of the Scythians, they looted, and many of the citizens were slaughtered, and the destroyer committed myriad other horrible deeds. Then, having come to terms with Homur, and having given his daughter to him as a wife, and having confirmed the truth with oaths, he exited the castle; and they embraced one another as father and son, and he renounced his obedience to the Musulman with an oath, and was proclaimed general of Atinis. C Accompanied by him, he traversed the entire principality and drew to his own side all the cities toward the Maeander and those toward the north—Philadelphia, Sardis, Nymphaeum, as far as the Hermus river. And having placed in them men most faithful to himself, and having entrusted the entire government and administration of them to his own kinsmen and friends, he himself stayed in Ephesus with his future son-in-law. One day, however, in the morning, a rumor spread among the citizens that the leader had died. After sunrise, therefore, they carried his body out to the small town which is called Pyrgion, situated at the foothills of Mount Tmolus; and there they buried him near his ancestors. Cineites, having been raised in power and considering the principality as his paternal inheritance, was called supreme duke of Asia. For this reason, since the Musulman could not bear his great insolence, he resolved to cross over into Bithynia. And having crossed the strait and entered Prusa, all the Prusans welcomed him gladly, and with as much joy as they were ready [to die] for him. Then, with spring having begun, he prepared an army.
against Cineites; but he, accompanied by only a few horsemen, flew to Iconium, the metropolis of Lycaonia, and addressed Caraman. From there he came to Cotyaeum, and after having held the same conversation with Carmianus, he drew both of them with their troops to Ephesus. The speech which he made to the princes was as follows: "You know accurately what great damages Bajazites inflicted upon you and your parents: some he slaughtered, others he stifled with a rope, and he himself became monarch after driving you out. Since, however, that pestilence has been removed from our midst by the just judgment of God, let not the offspring of the asp devour us, but let us rather crush his head as quickly and nimbly as possible, while he is not yet vigorous and strong, and let us lead a secure life hereafter."
When the princes heard his words and considered them useful to themselves, they traveled in chariots; Caraman brought thirty-three thousand soldiers, Carmianus ten thousand, and Cineites five thousand, and they encamped at Ephesus. Musulmanus himself also came from Prusa to Lopadium, and after counting his whole army at twenty-five thousand men, and moving from Lopadium, he came to Pergamum, in the plain of Maenomenus [47], and from the plain to Smyrna. Having learned of the meeting of Caraman and Carmianus, he was perplexed and troubled. Departing from Smyrna toward Ephesus, he came and pitched his tents at a place called Mesaulium [48]. And there, fearing the adversaries, he crowded his tents together, dug a trench, raised mounds, and sat himself in the middle with his army. His adversaries were holding camp at Ephesus, and were not even half a day’s journey—that is, a distance of six hours—apart from one another. But neither did he dare, hindered by cowardice, to provoke or attack them, nor did they [dare to attack him] because they were unequal in strength.
When therefore both sides declined to fight, and the business of war was not burning, one of the secret and intimate friends of Cineites approached him and said, "Caraman and Carmianus have agreed together and wish to hand you over this night into the hands of Musulmanus; they, having made a peaceful settlement, will return fearlessly to their own lands; they are to accomplish the whole matter this night." When Cineites heard this, as evening fell, he lit torches and lamps in his tents, and having selected swift horses, he went up to the citadel to his brother Bajazites—for he was the guard of [the citadel]—and after he [informed him] accurately of the state of his affairs,
and instructed him to guard the city diligently until morning, he himself, with the rest of his servants, went to Musulman. And in the middle of the night, when the soldiers of Caraman and Carmian came to the tents of Cineites, they found no one. But Cineites, when morning had already come, having put a noose around his neck, came before Musulman, weeping and saying, "Lord, I have sinned, I am worthy of death. I have myself placed the noose upon my own neck. Do with me as you wish; I am rightfully subject to every punishment." Musulman, softened by these words and moved to pity for him, clothed him in a shining garment and asked, "Where are those commanders now and where is their army stationed?" He replied, "In Ephesus; and if you wish to entrust the army to me, I will go to them and bring them to you in chains." But Musulman, fearing that some treachery might be lurking behind these pretenses, did not wish to pursue them. But when the sun had risen, he himself mounted his horse and proceeded with all his army toward Ephesus, having Cineites with him. B Caraman and Carmian, as we have said, having come around midnight to the tents of Cineites and finding him not there, perceived the ambush; and a great noise and confusion arose in the camp. Some were searching for their horses, others for their saddles and blankets, others for camels and mules, to load them with their baggage and gear, and others for their wagons. And when the sun rose, and all was properly arranged for departure, the commanders, with the cavalry and infantry, stood on a high place, so that the mules and camels, which they were driving before them with all their baggage, might cross the passes of the Meander; but they themselves stood in line of battle for so long as they saw that the heavy burdens had passed through those defiles. Finally, they themselves, maintaining their ranks, entered those passes, and when those who were closing the rear guard had already entered them, Musulman sent his infantry across the bridge which is near Mount Galesius and entered Ephesus at the fourth hour of the day, with the sun entering the sign of Libra. But Cineites tried in vain many things by which he might induce this prince to pursue them, but he could in no way be persuaded. For besides the fact that he was very easy-going and was touched by the miseries of others, he feared the tricks and devices of Cineites. And Musulman was as upright and simple as Cineites was wicked and crafty. Thus, having pitched his camp in the territory of Ephesus, he spent four months there, indulging his spirit and seeking pleasures, passing his time in luxury and delights; for he was more addicted to wine than others and prone to lust, as far as Musulman was, so good and very simple, as Cineites was wicked and crafty. Having therefore pitched his tents D (51)
Notes of Ismael Bullialdus
(50) To Mount Galesius. This mountain is near Ephesus, and undoubtedly took its name from the city [near it], of which Stephanus mentions in his work on cities: Galesium is a city subject to Ephesus. Parthenius [mentions it] in his funeral oration for Auxithemis. Abraham Ortelius mistakenly opines concerning that mountain, when he makes it near Constantinople, and cites Gregoras to support his opinion.
(51) Having pitched his tents. Leunclavius notes that this was the tutelary spirit of Soleiman or Musulman, so that he would indulge in shameful practices, sometimes for four-month periods, in drinking bouts: which sloth and negligence at length brought utter ruin upon him.

### Chapter XIX.
Moses (52) defects from his brother Mehemet and withdraws into Wallachia; he invades and defeats his brother Musulman. While Musulman seeks to save himself by flight, he is killed by young men in a certain town; Moses burns the town and its inhabitants, moves against Serbia, and then attacks Constantinople in vain. Emperor Manuel summons and stirs up Mehemet against Moses. Mehemet, defeated twice, retreats to Byzantium; finally, he defeats Moses; the latter is killed while fleeing, and his body is carried to Prusa to be buried.
Now Moses, whom we mentioned earlier, while dwelling with his brother Mehemet in Ancyra of Galatia, fled and came to Sinope, to the ruler of the Turkoman, Spentiares (53). Having been kindly received by him, Moses asked that he might be able to cross over to the opposite mainland, Wallachia, with his help and assistance, which he obtained from him quite easily, and he crossed into Wallachia. Then he betook himself to the Voivode Miltzes (54), to whom he made known by certain proofs who he was, and whence and how he had come thither. Wherefore the Voivode granted him freedom to travel securely through all of Wallachia, and the power to act as he pleased. But when the governors of the West, who were guarding the parts of the Danube, learned of the entry of Moses into Wallachia, they wrote and informed B Musulman of what had happened, and that if he did not hasten to cross into the regions of Thrace, Moses would possess the West, and he himself, while lingering in Asia, would arrive at it. Musulman, having given heed to these words, came quickly from Ephesus to Lampsacus, bringing with him also Cineitēs, having appointed another governor in his place in Ephesus and in the whole province. Now at Lampsacus, he was building a very large tower in his own name, on the shore opposite to Gallipoli. The duumvir was Salagruzo de Negro (55), a Genoese of the nobility, who, having built it as was fitting, and Musulman having seen it, he bestowed upon him very many riches. And having crossed to Gallipoli, and sitting in drinking bouts and carefree, indulging and committing excesses, he did not concern himself about Moses. Moses, meanwhile, did not cease writing to the grandees and setting out for them all things useful, should he become master of the principality; and he was not only concerned with these things, but also, having gathered Turks from the regions of the Ister (Danube), he was proclaimed by them prince of all Thrace, Thessaly, and Illyricum. Musulman, [sending] Cineitēs toward the parts of Bulgaria, in the regions of the Ochrids (56). [...] to Justinian, Most Blessed Archbishop of First Justiniana, Achrida, and all of Bulgaria in the Holy Spirit, beloved brother of our mediocrity.
He appointed a governor and sent him off; he himself made his journey to Adrianople, and upon entering the city, everyone proclaimed him a benefactor and provider of all good things. And in truth it was so; for wherever Musulman went, whether in a city or in a village, to spend thirty days there, both the wealthy and the poor, and even those begging for lack of food, all became self-sufficient. Then Musulman, having gathered an army from Adrianople, sent it against Moses, while he himself spent his days in drinking. Moses, having joined battle and appearing the stronger, pursued the army of Musulman almost as far as Sofia, and the rumor went everywhere that Moses was about to become the ruler of the West. And indeed, Musulman, having become aware of the imminent entrance of Moses into Adrianople—for all the multitude was flocking to him, and not a few of the notables—finally recovering somewhat from the fatigue of his drunkenness, desired to go to Constantinople. Having begun the journey with a few companions, they themselves soon abandoned him and fled, riding off to Moses. Musulman, while traveling, met with some people in a certain village (57), and the villagers saw him, and from the form of his horse, his clothing, and his appearance, recognized that he was the ruler, and ran to see him. Five young archers, carrying bows and arrows, arrived first; Musulman, feeling disturbed, let fly an arrow at them, and one of them, struck, fell headlong. He then fired a second and laid another low; then the three who remained, for these five were brothers born of the same father and blood, with one accord turned their weapons against Musulman, threw him from his horse, and once he had fallen, cut off his head. The citizens of Adrianople admitted Moses, whom a long train of attendants accompanied, into the city, honored him with all the refinement they could, and he was proclaimed ruler of the West. Upon learning of the death of his brother Musulman, he mourned him and sent soldiers and the chief of his satraps, who brought his body to Adrianople; later they bore it with great pomp to Prusa and laid it in the monument that he himself had built. He even conducted a diligent inquiry into those who... Ismaelis Bullialdi note: Laonicus, in his Chronicle, makes mention of Achrida. Lib. I calls the city of Macedonia "Ochridem." The Acts of Pope Leo IX against Michael Cerularius and Leo, bishop of Achrida, also clearly show it to be a city: in them exists a letter to: "The universal patriarch of New Rome, and Leo, archbishop of Achrida, metropolis of the Bulgarians, to our beloved brother in the Holy Spirit, John, bishop of Cannensis." Cantacuzenus also calls it so, lib. II, cap. 20, so that all doubt is removed, and it is established that Achrida is a city. (57) Beccani’s Annals and the Verantian History relate that the death of Musulman happened in almost the same way. Hanivaldana disagrees with them. Leunclavius, lib. X, ascribes the year of the death of Musulman to the year of the Hegira 815, which began on May 6, the 3rd feria, in the year of Christ 1410. Laonicus...
having made an accurate search for the murderers of Musulman, and having found all three, sent them to the village where he had been killed; and having gathered all the villagers, and bound each one together with wives and children, and having secured each one in their huts, he set them on fire. And children and parents, and kinsmen, and the huts, and the whole village were reduced to ashes and became dust. Such a punishment did that inhuman man inflict upon humans, showing the first fruits and specimen of the evils which he was destined to commit in his days. Having therefore gathered the magnates of Thrace and Macedonia and the other provinces—for they were all gathered for his veneration—he spoke to them in an address, saying: "O men and friends of my father—for I do not call you slaves—you know accurately the threat which the part of Asia sustained from Temyr, and more than that, that my father was handed over into his hands like a sparrow. Yet none other than Constantinople and its emperor summoned the Scythians and Persians, and called the rest of the nations into our fatherland. But since my brother, who ruled the parts of Thrace and the remaining land which our father ruled, not only did not show the veneration and piety owed to his fatherland, but rather, if one must say it, became a *giaour*, that is, an infidel: for this reason God, having turned away from him, delivered into my hand the sword of the prophet, to cut in two the infidel, and to exalt and raise up the faithful. For this reason, then, it is not fitting that the land of Constantine should hold so much, nor Macedonian cities, and especially Thessalonica, which my father acquired through many labors, and transformed the altars of idols into sacred precincts of God and the prophet; but even the mother of cities herself, and the murderer of my father, if it is pleasing to God, I shall, applying myself earnestly to the work, submit to my empire, and the temples which stand in that city, consecrated to God and his prophet, I shall constitute as houses of prayer." At these words, all applauded with auspicious acclamations, and received his words no differently than those of God. Having therefore gathered a sufficient army, he first invaded Servia D (for the lord [Stephanus, son of Lazari...])
had abandoned it, struck by the arrival of so great an enemy, and whose very name he feared), and making an excursion into very many towns and open fields, he led away as captives handsome youths, beautiful in body and face; the rest he slaughtered with the sword. And having captured and harvested three small towns by war—and while harvesting, he spread a table upon the corpses of the Christians and held a splendid and famous banquet with his chief men and nobles. Departing from Servia, he returned to Adrianople, and after resting for a short time, he prepared siege engines for the conquest of Constantinople. Having sent an army—not small—into Thessaly, he besieged Thessalonica, and having occupied all the regions except for Zetunion, and having placed his camps by the Strymon, he himself advanced toward Constantinople, and found all the towns deserted, for the Emperor Manuel had transferred the inhabitants into the city; he handed everything over to fire. And he himself, having pitched his tents, was confident in his mind that he would become master of it, but in action and with the remaining force, he was standing at a distance. Yet, every day, he did not cease from fighting, and being fought, and slaying, and being slain by the citizens. For the citizens would sally forth and engage the Turks; and for one Roman, three Turks would fall. This did not please the Emperor, for he held the Romans, for the most part, because of their scarcity, as dear and commendable as the pupil of the eye. He would say, "What profit does it bring me if I lose ten Roman soldiers out of a hundred? Or what injury does it cause to Moses if a hundred out of a thousand Turks perish?" Yet the boldness of the Romans did not cease from sallying forth and engaging the Turks. Therefore, in the fighting, the Turks captured one of the illustrious men, the pincernas of the former Emperor John and of the Emperor Manuel's son, whom they beheaded. When the Romans learned of the slaughter, they sallied forth. And after much fighting and shouting, they carried his body inside the city, but the Turks brought his head to Moses. Then Nicolaus Notarius, the father of the deceased and an interpreter for the Emperor lord Manuel—who was very rich—immediately redeemed the severed head with many hundreds of coins and buried it together with the body. For that youth, there was great mourning among the Romans, and for his father and his brother Loukas, who during the days of the last Emperor John Palaiologos served in the office of grand logothete, and who finally, in the total destruction of the city, was himself beheaded along with his children. But let us now return to the series of the narrative. For the Emperor Manuel, when he saw the savage and inhuman spirit of the tyrant, and the war of extermination...
Notes of Ismael Bullialdus
[notes regarding Laonicus Chalcocondyles, lib. IV; Phranzes, lib. I, cap. 30; and the deeds of the sons of Bayezid, stating that after being defeated once or twice, Mehmed finally attained victory over Moses in the third battle].
Since he bears implacable hatred against the Christians, he advises Mahomet, his brother, who was still residing at Prusa, to come to Scutarium, from where he would transport him by imperial galleys to Constantinople; and having gone out from Constantinople with the help of God and the Emperor, he would engage in battle with the tyrant. And if fortune should incline toward the tyrant, the city will always be ready to receive him; but if the opposite should occur—which is what we ardently desire—[he says], "You will take possession of the leadership, and you will be as dear to me as a son." Mahomet, having heard these words and having become eager, marched with all his forces to Scutarium with great readiness. The Emperor, having learned that he had arrived at the opposite shore, crossed over with the galleys he had prepared, and having met with Mahomet and exchanged solemn oaths, he brought Mahomet with him to Constantinople. And having celebrated a great festival in his honor upon his entry for three days, on the fourth day Mehmed went out from the city with his entire army and a small band of Roman soldiers; and having joined battle with Moses, he was defeated, and once defeated, he fled back into the city. But the Emperor, having comforted him with persuasive words and having replaced the military equipment he had lost, took care again that he should go out a second time to engage with Moses. Now Moses, having come out from the borders of Constantinople and having with him the entire western army, was preparing against Mehmed and the city. And Mehmed went out a second time and was again defeated, and again he fled into the city, and again the Emperor received him. Then Mehmed, having become despondent and reflecting that the turning of fortune is as fickle as a sling, said to the Emperor: "You, holy father, who weigh the moments of events and oversee the shifting of the scales, do not permit me, as you observe fortune casting my affairs up and down, to be betrayed or to have the enemy handed over to me by her. But I say this: everything that has been written on the foreheads of each one of us by the finger of God will inevitably come to pass. Order me, therefore, to begin the road leading toward Adrianople with my own forces; and pray for me only as a father for a son, as I am indeed, and let us leave future events to the providence of God." Then the Emperor, having heard his words, and having embraced and kissed him, and having prepared a sumptuous dinner, they rejoiced together with gladness. When morning had finally come, Mehmed went out from the city and divided his army into two parts: one part he sent toward the regions of the Euxine, and the other he led toward the road bearing to Adrianople. Then Moses, again hearing of this and learning how he had divided his forces into two sections, pursued the parts that were heading toward the sea. And indeed, the two armies came into conflict, and those of Moses, having been defeated, gathered themselves to Mehmed. He received them with joy. But Moses, seeing what had happened, and [seeing] the... Ismaelis Bullialdi nota.
(61) Everything written on the foreheads: According to the belief of the Muslim religion, which asserts inevitable predestination, and claims that nothing is done by the free will of man.
Moses, struck by this turn of events and the inconstancy of fortune, fled, and having entered a swamp without realizing it, he was pursued by one of the satraps who was serving in Mahomet's army; turning around, Moses killed him. But the satrap’s servant, who was a knight, having caught up, cut off Moses's right arm from the shoulder, throwing it into the swamp; and having entered with but one arm, and having swooned from the loss of blood, he fell from his horse. The satrap's servant having come to the ruler, reported both the death of his master and the wounding of Moses; having come to the swamp, they found him dead, and his body was brought before Mahomet. He, seeing and mourning him according to the inhuman custom of their people, sent his corpse to be buried in Prusa, near his forefathers. Mahomet, having returned to Adrianople and sitting on his paternal throne, was visited daily by the leading generals and magnates of the West, who came to pay him homage. In those days, while Moses was occupied and distressed after his brother Mahomet, Cineites secretly fled from the Thracian regions, and having crossed the Hellespont, he came into Asia; and having gathered an army from Smyrna and Thyræa, he occupied Ephesus; and the Muslim whom he had placed in charge of its guard, he beheaded, and he soon became master of all Asia before Mahomet had arrived in Thrace.
CHAPTER XX
. Manuel sends envoys to Mahomet; other princes also send legates, whom Mahomet greets kindly, and embraces peace with all. Manuel gives to his son, John, as wife the daughter of the great Duke of Russia, who dies of the plague, and one of the sons of Bajazet, and he is baptized. The second and third marriages of John. Manuel's departure for the Peloponnese.
When therefore the Emperor Manuel received the message that Mahomet held the supreme power, he sent chosen magnates from his principal nobility as envoys to him, and requested, according to the covenant entered into while he was acting in Constantinople, the things that were comprehended in the negotiated pacts. Mahomet received them graciously; and having confirmed the pacts with an oath, he restored all the fortresses situated on the Euxine Sea, as well as the towns and camps of Thessaly and those adjacent to the Propontis. Having finally treated them with honor and heaped them with many gifts, he dismissed them in peace, having given this answer: "Go and report to my father, the Emperor of the Romans, that, by the help of the divine power and with my father and emperor providing aid, I have recovered the paternal kingdom. From now on, I am and will continue to be a subject to him, as a son to a father. For I am not ungrateful, nor shall I be found unthankful. Let him command whatever he wishes, and I shall execute his orders as promptly as possible with the greatest pleasure." Likewise, the envoys from the Serbs and the Wallachians, and the Bulgarians, and the Duke of Ioannina, and that of...
despota of Sparta and prince of Achaia, and having addressed them all kindly, and having invited them to sit at table with him, and having honored them all with gifts, he sent them away in peace, saying to them: "Announce to your lords, that I grant peace to all, and I receive peace. Whoever destroys peace through guile, may the God of peace be against him." Since the affairs of the Emperor Manuel were in a secure state and subject to no attack, he determined to arrange a marriage for his son John. And having sent to the king of Russia [(64)], he obtained his daughter, a young girl, as a bride. And having betrothed her, and having changed her name to Anna, he did not wish to crown her as empress at that time; for the girl was in her eleventh year. But when three years had passed, and a plague epidemic had overtaken the city, and a great multitude of people had died from the buboes, the Empress Anna also passed away, leaving great mourning for the citizens.
The son of Bayezid, who had been given as a hostage by the Mussulman to the Emperor Manuel, was one of two: the first, along with his sister Phatma, had been released and was being raised in Bursa; but the other was smitten [(65)] with a love for Greek learning, still being with the Emperor’s son, John. And going to school, he was initiated into letters and was being taught. So much, then, was he inflamed by the love of learning and by his studies with John, that he even approached the Emperor Manuel, asking to be baptized according to the Christian rite. And he confessed to the Emperor every day that he was a Christian and did not accept the dogmas of Muhammad. But the Emperor did not wish to listen, so that no occasion for scandal might arise.
Then, during those days when the plague was consuming and destroying bodies, without respecting or sparing any age, it reached also the young son of Bayezid. He informs Emperor John, saying: "O Emperor of the Romans, my master and father, I am now meeting my summons, and though I do not wish it, I am leaving everything and departing to the tribunals that are in the life to come. I truly confess that I am a Christian; yet you do not grant me the earnest of the faith and the seal of the Spirit. Know, therefore, that if I die unbaptized, I shall bring an accusation against you before the tribunal of the incorruptible God." Then the Emperor, moved by these words, sent someone to baptize him, and he himself became his sponsor; and on the following day he died. D The Emperor buried him with all honor in the monastery of the Prodromos, in the Studion, in a marble sarcophagus near the church inside the gates.
Ismael Bullialdus’s notes.
(64) Concerning the marriage [of John], Phranzes writes a few things in book 1, chapter 38. He writes that the death of that Anna from Rhosia, or Russia, occurred in the year 6925, [the year of] Christ 1417, and that she was consumed by the plague.
(65) "But the other was smitten." That the youngest of the sons of Bayezid was a Christian is testified by Laonicus in book IV, who calls him Jesus, and by Phranzes in book I, chapter 30, and he relates that his name was Jusuph, or Joseph.
After an interval of about three years, the emperor wished to take another bride for John, his firstborn son, and also for Theodore, the younger. Therefore, he sent legates to Italy 66 and obtained the daughter of Theodore, the Marquess of Montferrat, for his son John, and the daughter of Count Malatesta for Theodore. When they had returned to the city, the father, the emperor, celebrated their weddings according to the laws and rites of marriage, and designated them crowned with the diadems of the Emperors of the Romans. He also celebrated the wedding of Theodore and the daughter of Count Malatesta, and proclaimed him Prince of Lacedaemon by bestowing upon him the ornaments and symbols of that office. But the Emperor John was not fond of his spouse; for although the girl was very well-proportioned in body, having a comely neck, flaxen hair, and tresses gleaming like radiant gold flowing down to her ankles, wide shoulders, arms, chest, and hands of excellent proportion, fingers imitating the luster and splendor of crystal, and a body of erect, even above-average, stature, she yet possessed a most beautiful face, nose, eyes, and eyebrows—such that, to use a common proverb, she seemed like Lent in front and Easter behind. B Seeing her thus, the Emperor John did not cohabit with her, nor did he ever share a bed with her. For this reason, she remained alone in one of the bedchambers of the palace. The emperor then wished to send her back to Italy to her father’s house, but he was restrained by the love that he bore for the Emperor Manuel. When, therefore, the empress fully understood the stubborn and obstinate disposition of his mind 67, she contemplated taking herself out of their midst; and this she did, having sent to the Genoese of Galata and made known her departure. One day she went out of the city into one of the pleasant gardens for the sake of relaxation, accompanied by her fellow-countrywomen, and with a few youths whom she had brought with her from her father's house. Then, towards evening, having prepared a bireme, the leading citizens of Galata went aboard, approached the shore, received the empress with honor and reverence, and transported her across to Pera, where everyone, as though she were their mistress and empress, went out to meet her and venerated her with every service due to her. The citizens of the city, however, did not perceive any of these things that were happening when evening had already fallen; but on the following morning, the matter became known throughout the entire palace, which everyone took poorly 68. And not bearing the contempt which they had suffered at the hands of those of Galata, they prepared to make a raid and destroy their suburbs. But the Emperor Manuel prevented it, and the Emperor John, as for the event itself, treated it with a moderate manner, though with a displeasing countenance.
Notes of Ismael Bullialdus
66 The second marriage of the emperor was celebrated according to Phranzes in the year of Christ 1419, January 19, so that a period of two years at most intervened between the death of Anna of Russia and these second nuptials: by no means three years according to the calculation of Ducas, who calls this second wife of John "Sophia" and describes her, shining with extraordinary and absolute beauty, ironically; he compares her front parts to Lent, the rear to Easter, by a proverb not too honest. Hence one may conclude that she was of a thin and not blooming face and deformed. Laonicus, book IV, not far from the end, relates that she was of honest morals indeed, but of an unpleasing and deformed face. In the last book, Phranzes testifies that she fled in the year of Christ 1426, in the month of August. 67 The emperor, however, [shows] the unchangeable nature of his mind. 68 The Emperor Manuel prevented it. Phranzes and Ducas disagree in assigning the time,
and they also endured being considered despised and rejected by the townspeople of Galata; indeed, arms were already being taken up by them to invade and utterly overthrow their suburbs, had not the Emperor Manuel restrained their attack. However, John was delighted at these things which had been done. There was present a very large Genoese merchant ship, which was soon to depart for Italy. Therefore, a North wind having risen, the empress boarded it, being worthily equipped; and with sails spread, she sailed for Italy. She returned, having gained nothing else but the fact that she was not anointed with the crown, though she said even this: "This is enough for me as a testimony that I was and am the Empress of the Romans; I care not for the ten-thousand-talent treasures." A Having arrived at the borders of the territory of Ferrara, those who were preeminent in that principality, having learned [of her arrival], went out with her brother the marquis to meet her, and escorted her as far as the palaces of her ancestral home. She, having gone to one of the monasteries, chose it for her residence there, and having dedicated herself to God, she fulfilled the remainder of her life.
The Emperor John B (69) having sent to Alexios Comnenus, the emperor of Trebizond, betrothed his daughter Maria as his wife, who was beautiful in both figure and character. And having brought her from Trebizond, they brought her down to Constantinople. And the Patriarch Joseph joined them through the customary sacred rites, and she was proclaimed Lady of the Romans. The emperor also, having departed from Constantinople (70) with many triremes, went down to the Peloponnese. And having subjugated the Prince of Achaia, and having taken as subjects others of the descendants of those who originated from Navarre, he returned to Constantinople, leaving behind his son Theodore as Despot of all the Peloponnese. And having returned also to Gallipoli, he encountered Mahomet, and demonstrated such faith in the emperor, that even in the trireme from Sarmatia, the daughter of the ruler of the Sarmatians.
Notes of Ismaël Boulliau
regarding the time in which Sophia fled to Italy. Ducas records that this happened while Manuel was still alive: on the other hand, Phranzes asserts that Manuel had already died; for Manuel yielded to fate, as Phranzes reports in the last chapter of the second book, in the year of the world 6933 [Christ 1425], on the 21st day of July. Sophia, however, fled in the year 6934, in the month of August, clearly after the death of Manuel. We will also note here other points of time indicated by Phranzes regarding the death of Manuel and the beginning of the reign of John. The death of Manuel occurred on the aforesaid 21st of July. Then in the first chapter of the second book, he narrates that in the month of August the sum of affairs had devolved upon the Emperor John. This indeed does not seem likely to me, that John, already being crowned emperor a year after the death of his father Manuel, attained the sum of power. I think, therefore, that Phranzes, or whoever transcribed him, erred, either by writing August in place of September, or if he began to administer the affairs of the empire in the month of August, then for the year 6934 we should read 6933.
(69) ...[concerning] chapter 1, he writes that Maria of Trebizond arrived at Constantinople on August 29, in the year 6935 [Christ 1427], and that in the same year 1427, in the month of September, the solemnities of the nuptials were celebrated. But Laonicus, disturbing the order of events, narrates that after the daughter of the Marquis of Montferrat had fled, John took another wife, the daughter of the King of Sarmatia of the Sarmatians—that is, of Russia or Muscovy; which is contradicted by two witnesses, Ducas and Phranzes, who assert that the third wife of John was the daughter of the Emperor of Trebizond. Our author has thus far followed the history of the three wives of John by way of a digression. He returns next to the series of the narrative, and explains the expedition of Manuel to the Peloponnese: which the emperor here undertook in the year following the arrival of Anna from Russia, as Phranzes testifies, namely in the year of the world 6923 [Christ 1415], in the month of March, on the 23rd day of which he arrived safely at the port of Cenchreae. In the following year, 6924, he returned to Constantinople. Laonicus makes mention of that expedition, book IV, and of the Hexamilion, which Phranzes also testifies was rebuilt by him. Pope Martin V later granted plenary indulgences to those who were willing to go to defend the Hexamilion. However, since mention has been made here of the naval base and port of Cenchreae, we shall advise the reader that Leunclavius, in book XIV of his *Historia Musulmanica* and in the *Pandects of Turkish History*, chapter 120, is neither consistent with himself nor has he attained the truth at all. He is not consistent with himself, because in the book he places Geremen on the Isthmus of Corinth near Corinth; but in the chapter of the *Pandects*, in Laconia or Tzaconia. Which is impossible, for the same city to be situated in two places. He has attained the truth in part, when he said that Geremen is situated on the Isthmus of Corinth near Corinth; but it is not Corinth, but Cenchreae in the Saronic gulf, where once the shipyards of the Corinthians were.
Having entered into the imperial city and dined with the Emperor, the Emperor, having treated him and those with him with many gifts and honors, departed. And the triremes sailed with the Emperor with the greatest joy, completing the return journey. And all the people of Constantinople, with the patriarch and the senate, went out to meet him, and with acclamations and hymns led him into the palace; and the matters of the return were thus brought to completion.
57 CHAPTER XXI
Mahomet crosses into Asia. He brings Cüneyd into order (71), whose insolence was at its peak. The Great Master of Rhodes restores the fortress of Smyrna, but is forbidden by Mahomet. Smyrna is surrendered to Mahomet by the wife of Cüneyd. The Great Master is permitted to build a fort on the borders of Caria and Lycia. Cüneyd obtains pardon. The Turks attack Naxos in a naval war, but are defeated in battle by the Venetian fleet. The Venetians attack the tower of Lampsacus in vain. Cüneyd is made prefect of Nicopolis on the Danube. A new religious sect instituted by a Turkish monk in Ionia is embraced by many, against whom Mahomet sent the son of Susman and then Hali Beg; these, having acted unsuccessfully, perished in the enterprise. Finally, they were oppressed and destroyed by Bajazet, the son of Mahomet, the Bassa, and they were killed while professing voluntary poverty.
At Mahomet, with things in the western provinces duly established and disturbances everywhere settled, crossed into the eastern parts. He came to Prusa, and having repaired the buildings which Caraman had burned, he set out from there on an expedition into Asia. For Caraman, at that time when Mahomet had gone to Constantinople and was waging war against Musa, had departed from Iconium with an army and descended upon Prusa, which he plundered. Moreover, he dug up the bones of Bajazet, the father of Mahomet, from the tomb and delivered them to the fire. For this same Bajazet had once ordered the father of the aforementioned Caraman to be beheaded at Iconium. Having descended into Asia, Mahomet found that Cüneyd had grown powerful and was leaping beyond set bounds. Having arrived at Pergamum in Asia, he notified Cüneyd to yield the places which he occupied there and to depart from the province. But Cüneyd, regarding him not at all, fortified his castles and sat waiting for his approach. Mahomet, having come to Cyma (72), and having demanded the fortress—for it was held by Cüneyd—besieged and captured it. And he put to death his soldiers by the sword, but set the local inhabitants free. Departing from there, he came to the plain of Menomen, in which there was a fortified stronghold called by the name of the Archangel, which the Turks renamed Kagiacik (73); having captured it with great force and skirmishing, he came to Nymphaeum (74); D and having taken Nymphaeum by war, [index: entries preserved]
he went to Smyrna. Having fortified Smyrna as was fitting and placed a great number of soldiers, and having prepared a great supply of arms and men, and other necessary provisions, Cineites himself went to Ephesus, leaving his mother, and his brother Bajazites, and his children shut up in Smyrna. But his son-in-law and slave, Audulas by name, being found at Nymphaeum by the men of Mahomet—for he was the guardian of the fortress—they captured him to bring him before Bajazites, the Vizier, that is to say the Mesazon, of Mahomet; for he was in great power and license, a second leader as it were; for he was a slave of Mahomet, but because of his exceeding servitude he had made him prince of his house. This aforementioned Bajazites, while Mahomet was still in Thrace, wrote to Cineites: "If you wish to be lord of Ionia and not to have any trouble from us, give me your daughter in legal marriage, and I shall be your son-in-law, and you shall be my father-in-law, and thenceforth you shall live secure and untroubled in your principality." But Cineites, wishing to display his arrogance and pride before the messenger (75), with the slave Audulas present who belonged to him, said to him: "Whose slave are you?" He replied, "Yours, my lord." And Cineites, "And of what race?" Audulas replied, "An Albanian." "Of what religion?" Audulas replied, "Formerly I was a Giaour, but now I am a Mussulman." Cineites then said to his grandees: "This day, in the presence of you all, I give my daughter as a lawful wife to my slave Audulas; and I make him free and my son-in-law from this day, and one of my kinsmen." And all who were sitting in council having acclaimed Cineites, he opened his mouth and said these words to the messenger: "Report to your master Bajazites that we have taken as a son-in-law from the Albanians one such as he is, a slave bought with money such as he is, younger than he is, and wiser than he is." The messenger, having understood the words, revealed the whole gist to his master, and from that time he nursed an implacable rage against Cineites. Finding an opportunity, when he needed to, he seized Audulas at Nymphaeum and cut off his testicles, making him a eunuch. But let us return again to the thread of the history. For Mahomet, having come to Smyrna and besieged it, found there the Grand Master of Rhodes with three triremes, rebuilding the fortress that had been destroyed by Temyre, even against the will of Cineites. Then the rulers of the surrounding islands, having learned of the arrival of Mahomet at Smyrna, all ran to meet him on account of two causes; [since]...
because of the goodness and gentleness and the exceeding power of Mahomet, and because of the craftiness and piracy of Cineites. Therefore, the rulers of the Phocaeans, some by land and others by sea; the ruler of Carmian in upper Phrygia, the ruler of Mantachia in Caria, the ruler of Mitylene with triremes, the ruler of Chios also himself by trireme, and the great Master of Rhodes who was [already] there, all went to pay homage to him and to assist in the overthrow of the tyrant; and he greeted them all amiably as brothers. Having spent ten days attacking Smyrna, with all the islanders bringing naval aid as they were able against those besieged, on the tenth day the mother of Cineites, along with his wife and children, came out and prostrated themselves before Mahomet, begging forgiveness for their sins. Consequently, they surrendered Smyrna; and taking it, he demolished its walls as far as the ground in many places, and tearing down the ramparts and its towers in part, he allowed the inhabitants to dwell [there] without fortifications. B Now the great Master (76) was building a very large tower at the mouth of the harbor, and had raised it to more than half its height. But Mahomet, having commanded the Turks by night, demolished it from its foundations. In the morning, seeing what had happened, the Master was pained and went to the ruler, and having spoken many words, and having represented how the fortress had been built in the days of his predecessor at the expense of the Rhodians—and that if he did not grant permission for it to be rebuilt, there would be strife between his dominion and the most blessed Pope, and a great force would come from the western parts and would destroy and lay waste a great part of his dominion—Mahomet, hearing his words with an equal mind, answered nothing harshly. For the memory of the things which they had suffered, when the Scythians were acting severely and harshly against them, was still fresh in the minds of the Turks. "I, indeed, father," he said, "desired to be generous and munificent to all the Christians of the world; for it is the hallmark of a government to benefit the good and to punish the wicked, and also to see to the utility of one's subjects. For having come into these regions, there were no Muslims who stood before me who spurred on my mind and intellect, but [many] saying: 'Even if Temyr did nothing useful in Asia, but only destroyed and left in ruins the small town at Smyrna, he set up a great monument to Ionia; for the Ionians who were in the condition of slavery, all fleeing into that citadel, would escape to freedom; and those traveling by land and by sea, sailing in pirate skiffs, all luck-"
lessly were taken into the yoke of slavery, and they acted with hostility toward one another, both on sea and on land—the Rhodian knights and the Turks. On account of this, the impious Temur was well-regarded. "Do you wish, then, that I should conduct myself more impiously than that tyrant? My soul recoils from this. Nevertheless, so that your desire may be satisfied, and the pleas of the Turks may not prove vain, I grant you a place, as large as you wish, in the borders of Caria and Lycia; betake yourself there, and build a small city wherever you wish." Then the Grand Master, having heard these words, said to Mahomet: "O ruler, grant me a part of the lands under your power, and do not send me away into foreign provinces." The ruler replied: "I give you from my own, for I have bestowed the province upon Mantachia; let this not be a concern to you." Having requested an imperial order, and having received it, he departed. Likewise, the people of Chios, the Lesbians, and the Phocaeans all had their requests gladly received, and, having fulfilled their wishes, the ruler sent them away in peace.
The mother of Cineites, making humble supplications, did not cease until she had obtained a hearing and freed her son from the death penalty. He also came and prostrated himself before Mahomet, giving him oaths that he would no longer act in disorder, but would live faithfully for all the time of his life, and that he would hold and call those descended from the Ottomans lords and masters. He gave the province to the son of Alexander Susmanus (77), whom he also converted to his own impiety; and having ordered Cineites to follow him into Thrace, having set the affairs of the East in good order, he returned to the West. And having come to Callipolis, he prepared a fleet against the Duke of Naxos (78) and the rest of the Cyclades islands that were under his hand, accusing him of not having come to greet Mahomet, just as he had not done formerly at Smyrna. The fleet therefore having departed from Callipolis, having as admiral Tzialispegis with thirty triremes and biremes together, went to the island of Andros, and to Paros, and to Mylon (79); and having gathered many of the islanders, and having caused very great damage, he returned. The Venetians, having learned what had happened, did not tolerate it. For the Duke had long since...
Notes of Ismael Bullialdus
(77) That Susmanus was the Duke of lower Mysia, having been captured alive by Bajazet and thrust into prison. In order to save his life, his son, of the same name, became a Muslim, which is written by Leunclavius in book 5. Laonicus also makes mention of Susman in book 1. Cantacuzenus also mentions Sisman in book 1, chapter 2; who was the son of Michael, King of the Mysians, who fled first to the Turks and then to Constantinople. Alexander, the Mysian king who had succeeded Michael, sought him back.
(78) Regarding the Duke of Naxos. Leunclavius has nothing in that war and battle. Laonicus, book 4, not far from the end, in his customary confused and intricate manner, narrates that, and asserts that the leader of the Venetian fleet was Petrus Lauredanus. He disagrees with Ducas in what he wrote about the Venetians; that they received Lampsacus by surrender and, having imposed a garrison, sailed home. Ducas writes that they attempted it in vain and sailed to Constantinople. Phranzes, book 1, chapter 31, discourses in very few words about that war, and notes that the leader of the Venetian fleet was Petrus Lauredanus.
(79) In Paros and Mylon. According to modern pronunciation, he wrote Mylon, though the ancients said Melum, the Latins Melos.
And when spring arrived, they also prepared ten triremes, and they were watching the Adriatic Gulf (80), Euboea, Crete, and the Cyclades islands. When seven triremes arrived at Tenedos, they desired to reveal themselves to the enemy, and having entered the Hellespont, they sailed as far as Lampsacus. Now, the Turkish fleet, being extremely well-equipped, was stationed in the port of Callipolis. In the meantime, they spotted a small sail which had set out from the port of Constantinople, and the Venetian fleet commanders, thinking it was Turkish, sent one of their triremes to attack that ship. When the Turks saw what was happening, and surmising that the one being pursued was one of their own, another trireme went out from among them, wishing to defend it. B It was, in fact, a Lesbian vessel sailing down from Constantinople. When the Venetians saw the Turkish triremes coming out in a chain, they charged against them, sounded the war trumpet, and engaged in battle. In the first assault, they struck the trireme of the admiral, called Giali Beg, and, rushing upon it, they slaughtered everyone indiscriminately with the sword and hacked Giali Beg himself into pieces. Then, one by one, they boarded the others and captured them all, pitilessly hacking the Turks to pieces in the sight of their wives and children, who were standing on the shore at Callipolis, which is one mile distant from the place where the battle occurred. When the day was already inclining toward evening, the Venetians sounded the retreat and with sails unfurled led the twenty-seven Turkish triremes along with their own to the island of Tenedos. Having entered the harbor, and having carefully weighed and examined everything, they collected all the Turks separately and slaughtered them. C Regarding the Christians, they conducted a different inquiry: for those who were being held captive and in chains on the triremes, their lives were spared; but those who, having received pay or being led by some other reward, had voluntarily hired out their services, were all hanged on the island of Tenedos. Then one could see all around the circuit of the island gallows arranged like vines, and the corpses hanging from them like bunches of grapes. When the Venetian triremes arrived in Crete, they dispersed the captive Christian oarsmen, some throughout that island, some in Euboea, and some were transported to Venice. After winter had passed and spring was beginning, the Venetian fleet sailed again from Venice and entered the Hellespont, and attempted to take the tower which Musulman had erected at Lampsacus. The Venetians attacked and battered it with their triremes, since they were unable to disembark on the shore. For Chamzas, brother of Bajazit the Mesazontes, was present there with an army of ten thousand men and more, keeping watch for the approach of the Venetians. When they saw that their efforts were fruitless, they abandoned the attempt, sailed for Constantinople, and left the tower semi-demolished and shattered: they had struck off its roof from the top to the bottom and riddled it through like a sieve. Then Chamzas, seeing the triremes leaving, he himself [… the Turks]
(80) The Adriatic Gulf. Improperly called the Adriatic; the Adriatic Sea takes its name from the city of Hadria, not from Adrian. It should be noted furthermore that here the Ionian Sea is understood by the Adriatic Gulf, which flows between Sicily and the Peloponnese; and even today it is still called by sailors *il Golfo*.
having ordered him, he razed it to the foundations, saying: "It is not fitting to gain disgrace without profit."
