And Mehmed, having crossed over to Callipolis, gave Cineites a lordship in the region of Nicopolis, near the Danube River, having charged him to guard the frontiers well and to fight on behalf of the Muslims.
At that time there arose one of the Turks, a private and rustic man in the regions of the mountain which lies at the mouth of the Ionian Gulf, commonly called Stylarium, situated opposite Chios toward the east. He taught the Turks voluntary poverty and stated that everything, except for wives, was to be common—provisions, clothing, teams of oxen, and farmland. "I use your house as my own," he said, "and you use my house as your own, save for the female portion." And having deceived all the rustics with this doctrine, he craftily dealt for the friendship of the Christians as well. For he set forth a doctrine: "Whoever of the Turks says that the Christians are not god-fearing, this man is impious." And all those who were subjects of his opinion, meeting any of the Christians, would show them hospitality and honor them as an angel of God. He himself, meanwhile, did not cease daily sending apostles from Chios to the governors and those inscribed among the clergy of the Church, announcing to them his opinion, and that there is no other way for anyone at all to be saved except through concord in the faith of the Christians.
It chanced at that time that an anchorite, a Cretan elder, was living on that island in the monastery called Turlote. And that false abbot, having sent two of his apostles, who were dressed in a single tunic, with heads shaved and uncovered, feet without sandals, and a small cap—and having saluted the elder and announcing, "I, too, am your fellow-ascetic, and to the same God whom you serve, I too bring my worship; and by night I am with you, crossing the sea with silent foot." The true abbot, being deceived by that false abbot, began himself to speak absurd things concerning him, saying: "While I was staying on the island of Samos, he was my fellow-ascetic; and now, crossing over day by day, he associates with me; and we converse together," and he was spouting other such monstrosities of fables before me, who write these things.
Notes of Ismael Bullialdus.
(81) "In those days," he pursues the history of the new sect in Leunclavius, lib. XI, and in *Annal. Turc.* The name of Bedreddin Simavna is unknown to our author, just as the Cretan monk is also unknown to Leunclavius. With great and singular prudence Sultan Mehmed opposed this nascent sect, which would have excited seditions and tumults, such as later occurred under Soliman in the year 1526, having been incited in Asia Minor, as Leunclavius says, lib. XVIII.
(82) "Commonly called Stylarium." Italian sailors in their nautical charts denote the name of that place as Capo Stylari, and assert that it is 40 miles distant from Smyrna, 20 miles from Old Phocaea (*Foia Vecchia*), and 10 miles from the Holy Panagia of Chios. Dominicus Marius Niger, in *Comment. Asiae Primo*, discoursing upon the Chersonesus of Chalcitis, writes as follows: In (this should have been said of Mimas) what the moderns call Cape Stilari. In ancient times, as Strabo relates in Book XIV, it was called this; and on that promontory there were stone-quarries for millstones, which ancient appellation corresponds to the modern Turkish: for it is called today Kara-borru, or commonly pronounced Kara-bornu, that is, "Black Nose" or "Black Promontory." Leunclavius, in the cited Book XII, is mistaken, for he thinks that Caraboru, or Karaburun, is a town of Lycia, and that the Turkish name is derived from there. Caraburun, where that sect had grown, is situated in the territory of Aidin, which Adin or Atin had ruled, part of which was Ionia; that Cape of Kara-borun or Kara-bornu is very high, and lies on the right to those entering the gulf, adjacent to which is Smyrna.
Basmani, then, the son of the one mentioned above, who had been appointed by Mahomet to govern the province, levied an army and marched against that false abbot, but it was not in his power to overcome the mountain passes of Stylarium. The inhabitants of Stylarium, gathering together—more than six thousand of them—stood in the difficult, nearly impassable terrain and slaughtered the entire army along with the leader Basmani himself. Then all the crowd that followed Percligia Mustapha—for this was the name of the false abbot—placed their hopes in this impostor, extolling his name above the prophets; subsequently, a decree was issued by them not to cover the head with the cap they call a *zarkula*, but rather to lead a life wearing only a single garment, remaining bareheaded, and to associate more with Christians than with Turks. After these events, Mahomet ordered the governor of Lydia, Hali Beg, to march with all the forces of Lydia and Ionia against the Stylarians. The Stylarians again guarded the narrow entrances and mountain passes, and when the greater part of the enemy forces had entered the defiles, they were almost all slaughtered by the rustics, so that Halibeg escaped to Magnesia with barely a few men.
When Mahomet heard of this accepted defeat, he sent his son Morates, who was yet an adolescent, only twelve years old, and joined as his attendant Bajazites Mesazon. They gathered all the forces of Thrace, Bithynia, Phrygia, Lydia, and Ionia, and with great force broke through those narrow roads that were so difficult to approach. They killed everyone they encountered without discrimination—old men and infants, men and women, and to speak truly, they raged savagely against every age—until they arrived at the mountain which these *monochitones* (that is, those wearing one garment) had undertaken to guard. They fought there most fiercely, with countless numbers of those fighting for Morates falling, until the surrender of them all, along with their false abbot, ensued. They seized and bound them and led them all to Ephesus, where, although they subjected that impostor to various tortures, they found him nevertheless intrepid and constant and stubborn in his opinion. Therefore, they placed him on a camel, stretched out in the form of a cross, with his hands expanded and nailed to planks, and led him in triumph through the middle of the city as if it were a spectacle of triumph. His disciples also, who would not deny the errors of their teacher, they slaughtered all in his sight, saying nothing else but "Tete sultan eris," which is to say, "Lord abbot, hasten." And then they would gladly accept death. For the glory of many of his students prevailed for a time, as [Notes of Ismaelis Bullialdi follow: Since Leunclavius, in the Turkish histories he published, does not mention the expeditions undertaken by Alexander Susman and Hali-bego against the author of the new sect and his followers—mentioning only the last, of which Morales, son of Mehemat, and Bajazites Mesazon were the leaders—for the Turks willingly admit they have been conquered, and they do not acknowledge having been broken in battle until now except once or twice: namely in the Temyrian war and in the naval battle at the gulf of Naupactus, commonly called Lepanto, where they were overcome by Christian princes allied with the Venetian republic: whom furthermore Ducas calls Bercligia Mustapha, and Leunclavius calls Baruglusem Mustapham. By which title they show veneration to men preeminent in holiness and gravity. "Dede" signifies grandfather in Turkish. I once heard a certain Dervish called by them Sidik Dede, that is, "intimately faithful grandfather," which was done by them out of honor; for he was the second after the leader of the Dervishes.]
Among his disciples, a belief prevailed that he was not dead, but continued to survive among the living; and a certain ascetic, whom I spoke to after these events had transpired, was caught up in such a delusion. For when I asked him what he thought of the man, he answered me that he had not died, but had crossed over to the island of Samos, where he had formerly had his residence. But I, scorning the fellow’s ravings and placing no faith in them, could not bear to listen to him any longer. Once these matters were settled, Bajazet, leading the youth Morat along with him, traveled through Asia and Lydia and delivered all the Turcocalogeres (that is, Turkish monks) whom he encountered living in voluntary poverty to a bitter death. Having crossed Phrygia and traversed the straits, he reached Adrianople, and presented his son Morat to his father Mahomet as a victor crowned with trophies. Then Mahomet bestowed upon him the government of Amasia and the regions towards Cappadocia, for he was still young; and he appointed one of his great men and officials, a person called Georgitz-beg, to manage affairs for him.
CHAPTER XXII
The aforementioned Grand Master [(85)] in that year fully equipped a fleet with three biremes and a portion of his ships, and brought on board all the necessary materials, such as lime, cornerstones, timber, planks, and whatever else was useful for building a fortress. Coming to the borders of the province of Caria, at a certain promontory, he planted the fortress in the name of the prince of the apostles, Peter, calling it Petronium. Once he had well laid the foundation and begun to build the walls, Mantachias Eliez-beg also came with a great force, intending to obstruct the undertaking; but he accomplished nothing. Having therefore successfully completed the fortress and fitted it with lofty towers, and having installed a garrison of brethren within, the Grand Master returned to Rhodes. As he departed, he left behind laws and customs for the guards of the fortress—to always be sober and vigilant, and to take every care for the fugitive captives, to receive them and save them in the fortress, and for them to be registered as freedmen of Saint Peter [(86)]; which name is preserved even to this present day.
Notes of Ismael Bullialdus
(85) The aforementioned Grand Master is named Philibert de Naillac. 
(86) Bosius, Book V of the History of the Order of the Military Knights of Jerusalem, writes that in the year 1399, Smyrna having been taken by Temyr, the Grand Master immediately sailed with a fleet into Caria; he occupied a place there, situated between the Ceramic and Iasian gulfs, which is today called the Gulf of San Pietro, where formerly Halicarnassus had stood, and built the castle of St. Peter, concerning which Bosius speaks thus: "Which was of great glory and reputation to this Order and of great utility to Christendom"; and he adds that dogs were kept in that castle, which, tied up during the day, were sent out at night for the guarding of the castle: their sagacity was so exquisite that they distinguished Christians from Turks.
Mahomet, at the beginning of spring, having gathered the army of the West, departs from Adrianople, and having crossed Thrace, comes to Prusa. Having summoned the satraps of the East, he marched with his whole army toward the regions of Lycaonia, turning over in his mind the vengeance he desired to exact for the crimes and insolence perpetrated by Caraman at Prusa. For he had determined to avenge the insult offered to the ashes and remains of his ancestors, which his servants had mockingly dug up, and the paternal bones which Caraman had consumed in fire. When he arrived at those places, he destroyed many towns and villages by fire and, proceeding at a rapid pace, reached Iconium and took it. Caraman, fleeing for safety to the mountains of Syria, had retreated; thence, through envoys, he humbly and submissively begged for forgiveness for his committed sins and asked that he might be pardoned. Mahomet, eventually moved by his entreaties, left the province to him and gave security by oath that he would be faithful and an entirely guileless friend always, and that he would never again cross into the borders of Othman. Having abandoned the pursuit, Mahomet returned behind him to Prusa, crossed the strait, and came to Adrianople. While he was staying there, a message arrived that his youngest brother, named Mustapha (88), the son of the aforementioned Bajazet, was living in Wallachia. At first, he sent two of his chosen slaves to decapitate Cineites; but they did not find him, for two days earlier he had crossed the river and joined Mustapha, and, having given him oaths to run with him, to endure hardships together, and to establish him as ruler of the West and East. When Mahomet learned of the flight of Cineites, and not bearing the injury he was about to suffer from him, he raised an army and, leaving Thrace, entered Macedonia. There, having learned that Mustapha and Cineites had crossed the Ister and, having the Wallachians as allies and no small army of Turks, were marching toward the regions of Thessaly, he himself made his march toward them with his army. Having encountered them near the regions of Thessalonica, and—
*Notes of Ismael Bullialdus.*
(87) *Mahomet, at the beginning of spring.* This is the expedition which Leunclavius recalls, Book XII.
(88) *This is Mustapha, about whose birth there is a dispute.* The Muslim historians, whom Leunclavius follows, contend that he was an impostor, and for this reason, they call him "Dusme" in the Turkish language. Phranzes, lib. I, cap. 32, asserts that he was legitimate, and the uncle of Morates II, and by him was defeated and strangled. Laonicus, lib. IV, *Mustaphas, one of the sons of Bajazet.* Ducas likewise asserts that he was his son, and maintains this against the protestations of the Turks. Furthermore, Leunclavius and Phranzes have handed down that he became known under Morates; Laonicus, under Mahomet, the father of Morates: in which part he agrees with our author. And in detailing the beginnings of the tumult raised by this Mustapha, the transition of Cineites to his side, and the struggle of both, he is moderate.
Having then joined battle, and Mahomet having obtained the victory, Mustapha, together with Cineites, fled from him as far as the gates of Thessalonica. They resisted with a few men, aided by the citizens. When evening had already come, and they were not willing to enter the city, Demetrius Lascaris Leontarius received them with hospitality, and comforted them, saying that they should take heart regarding the changeability of fortune, and harbor no anxiety in their minds about handing them over to Mahomet, even if there were a proposal to surrender Thessalonica to the Turks. Taking heart at these promises from Demetrius, they dined without worry, and turned to sleep.
When morning came, Mahomet sent one of his officers to Leontarius, saying: "You know precisely the love I possess, and the unbroken friendship I hold with the Emperor of the Romans; do not wish, therefore, to tear this apart, and to destroy it to the end, and to cause damage to the entire race of the Romans, and to introduce an irreconcilable enmity between us and the Romans; but return to me the prey that has been hunted down by me. If you do not do this, telling me to farewell to our friendship, I shall embrace enmity, and as shortly as may be, I shall take your city, and take captive those within, and strike your life away, and have my enemies in my hands."
Then the lord Demetrius, being very prudent, replied in writing, saying: "You know, Lord leader, that I am not a master, but happen to be a servant, and not only of the Emperor of the Romans, but also of you, since you desired to be reckoned as his son. Therefore, it is a duty to fulfill and bring to an end what is ordered by you. Yet it is also my duty to make known that which has happened to my Emperor; for he who entered the Emperor's court, being pursued like a partridge by a hawk, for the sake of safety, is not one of the ordinary Turks, but your brother, as I have learned. And if he were one of the ordinary ones, I would not have handed even him over to you without the Emperor having first directed me. Therefore, I beg you subserviently, wait a little while; for at this very hour I am informing the Emperor of what has happened, and as he must order, let him order; and I shall fulfill that which is commanded."
Having heard these words, Mahomet consented that a message should be sent, having himself also written to the Emperor the things that seemed good to him, and exhorting him... D
Notes of Ismael Bullialdus
Laonicus says that he came to Therma, and that those captured were led to Constantinople: but our author's narration is fuller, and with the circumstances added, more lucid. In the margin of the edition of Laonicus, in the year of the Cologne of the Allobroges, Therma is called Thessalonica; Therma indeed is not far from Thessalonica, and lies on both sides of the Thermaic gulf. In later times it was called Thessalonica, which was once Therma: if the testimony of the author who described the catalog of some cities whose names have been changed is true: it exists in the manuscript library of the King.
regarding the matter of not being the cause of scandals from the things that had occurred. The Emperor Manuel writes to Mahomet: "I, indeed, as you know well, promised to be a father to you, and you a son to me. And if we both keep what was promised, behold, here is the fear of God and the keeping of commandments; but if we transgress them, behold, the father shall appear as a traitor to the son, and the son shall be called the murderer of his father. I, for my part, will keep the oaths, but you do not wish to keep yours. Let God, the righteous judge, be the avenger of the one who is wronged. As for the refugees (90), it is not to be said, nor to be heard by ears, that I should deliver them into your hands; for this act is not royal, but tyrannical. And if I were pursuing my own brother, and he, being pursued, fled under your wings, and you asked for him, you ought not to deliver him to me to be killed. But if you did deliver him, you would have acted worse than a human, having become a traitor and a murderer. Know, therefore, that this abominable act will never be done by me. Yet, since I was appointed to be in the manner of a father to you, I swear to you by the one God, who is worshipped by us Christians in Trinity, that the refugee Mustapha will never at all leave his prison, nor his travel companion Cineit, as long as you enjoy your sovereignty and your life itself. But after you have departed from this life, I shall decide concerning them as circumstances dictate. But if this proposal of ours is not acceptable to you, then follow your own inclination." He also writes to Demetrius Leontares, commanding him as follows: "When you have read what I have commanded you, execute it immediately. Put these refugees, Mustapha together with Cineit, and those who accompanied them, onto one trireme and send them to us with all due haste. And do not act contrary to what has been commanded."
Mahomet, reflecting in his mind on what would happen if he fell into conflict with the Emperor, and having learned that, during his own lifetime, Mustapha would not be granted freedom from imprisonment, nor would Cineit, ceased from harassing Thessalonica. Departing from there, he came to Adrianople, relieved of many cares and anxieties by which he had been tormented before, considering the manifest rebellion of Mustapha and Cineit. Lord Demetrius Leontares also prepared one trireme, and having put both captives on board, sent them to the Emperor. And the Emperor, after a short time, sent Mustapha to the island of Lemnos, ordering those there to guard him diligently and carefully; but he shut Cineit in the Monastery of the Pammakaristos, where he rested in quiet. The Emperor then sent apocrisiaries and requested from Mahomet the expenses which were to be made for the sustenance of Mustapha, in whose retinue there were thirty men; with Cineit, however, there were ten. Therefore, the Emperor received from the revenues and treasury of Mahomet three hundred thousand aspres annually, with an oath interposed that Mustapha was not to be set free so long as Mahomet should remain among the living.
Ismaelis Bullialdi notae.
(90) Manuel the Emperor, as it befits a supreme prince, one not subject to the clientage of others, a generous and magnanimous man, replied to Mehemet. For he would have committed a shameful and wicked act, and would have confessed himself to be a subject and client of Mehemet, had he, in violation of the law of asylum and hospitality, delivered up Mustapha and Cineit, who had fled to him.
For there were thirty youths with him, and ten with Cineit. Therefore, the Emperor arranged to receive annually from the treasuries and revenues of Mehemet an amount of three hundred thousand *aspers*, having taken oaths that Mustapha would not be released for the duration of Mehemet’s life. After his death, acting as was right toward the Emperor for his successors, he chose what was to his own advantage. Having thus received the agreements in writing and the oaths, the ambassadors departed. But Mehemet, nursing enmity against the Wallachians on account of the proclamation of Mustapha, sent a great army and ravaged, burned, and inflicted very great damage. After this, he began to harbor enmity against the City in secret; for he kept these things hidden in the depths, but did not manifest them openly at all.
At that time, there was a certain man from the city of Philadelphia, a Christian by race, and in rank one of the officials of the city of Philadelphia, but in his actions cunning and deceitful. During the incursion of the Scythians, being one of the leaders, he delivered up many of the Christians into the hands of the impious for the sake of the tribute, because they were wealthy, so that they might pay the tax demanded by Temyre; and since they were unable to pay, the barbarians burned them—so much so that he even drove the archbishop of Philadelphia to such trials and tortures that he abjured the worship of the Christians. This man came to Constantinople, and having met one of the men of the palace, and entering with him frequently, one of the days in the palace there was a need for an interpreter, as the matter was pressing. He entered readily and interpreted what was spoken by the Turks; for he had learned the language of the Turks to a T. From that time on, therefore, the ambassadors of the Emperor had the “Theologian”—for so he was called—with them, as he joined them for the sake of the language. Often, therefore, the embassy business did not cease, due to certain causes that arose, and the Theologian accompanied the ambassadors. Having thus familiarized himself with Bajazet, the Mesazon of Mehemet, he became his great friend day by day, receiving certain mysteries from the Romans and casting them into the ears of Bajazet, and displaying pure faith to them, while revealing only part of what he discovered from the Turks. He reached such a peak of fortune as to become the general *apocrisiarius* C of the Emperor, and a dinner companion of Bajazet, and often of Mehemet himself; for it was said and heard by many that the Theologian was not a true assistant to the Romans for their good; and they banished the aforementioned Mustapha to Lemnos out of fear, so that he would not flee from the City because of this man. And other things, I mean concerning the food allowance, and the things promised for the maintenance of Mustapha, were obstructed by the Turks for a period of time, so that they were not paid. Through other ambassadors, therefore, the Emperor complained about this but achieved nothing, until... Ismael Bullialdus’ notes: (91) The crimes and betrayals of the theologian, who was called Corax, for which he was punished with the most bitter execution, are more fully explained: of whom I find no word in others.
The things promised for the expenses of Mustafa were from time to time hindered by the Turks. And though the Emperor sent messages through other ambassadors, he accomplished nothing, until the theologian arrived and performed everything. The Romans, therefore, had evil suspicions of him. But the Emperor Manuel neither suspected him, nor even showed it, even if he held something within; however, just as the wise architect God transforms all things, and in one hour overthrows those things which are standing well, and raises up those things which are lying badly, so too the schemes of the theologian, or rather the "muddler" (for that is what *thologos* implies), even if the things said by many at that time were true, as the outcome also proved, were turned to vanity. For Mahomet, while riding in the hunt, when a wild boar suddenly burst forth from the thicket, and he himself was brandishing his spear against the beast, fell from his horse, gripped by an epileptic seizure and half-paralyzed; and having picked him up, they carried him into the palace; for he was near the hunting grounds of Adrianople. Having then summoned the most skilled physicians, both those dwelling in the vicinity and those sought from afar, they brought rapid assistance to the sick man. Meanwhile, the entire army was grieving and longing to catch sight of their leader. In the morning, a presentation taking place, according to custom they brought him out. And all, seeing him, cheered and rejoiced. B Being seized again the next day by an epileptic fit, and hindered in his voice and tongue, when evening had already fallen, he paid the debt of nature on his bed. When therefore Mahomet had passed almost all the time he reigned in peace with the Emperor of the Romans and all Christians, except the Venetians, he departed by fate, with no external force hastening him; for he expired peacefully in the palace at Adrianople, which he had built, having been troubled for a short time by illness; he was delivered from a kind of death that had befallen none of his ancestors. For while others were killed by poison, others strangled, he alone was exempt from a violent death; as I think, because Destiny looked away, out of the friendship which he had purely toward the emperors, and the compassion he showed toward the subjects of Christ. Having therefore crossed the unreturnable path to the underworld, he left his firstborn son, the one called Murat, as emperor of the Turks; he was then ruling in the borders of Amaseia. For indeed he had obtained those marches there to govern, having been given them by his father, acting as boundaries of the Perso-Turks, who were ruled by Karajulucus, a neighbor to the Lazi and the Persians, and son-in-law of Alexius Comnenus, emperor of Trebizond, whose daughter he had taken as wife. More often indeed they were agitated by seditions.

XIV, History of the Muslims, had a son named Habil, who was reduced to slavery by the Damascenes, that is, the Mizirenses or Egyptians. Laonicus, lib. V, says the sons of Carailucus were called Leucarus. Moreover, in Turkish *Kara-oiluc* is the same as the Latin "black south," and thus from the heat of the climate and the color of the earth, Mesopotamia is so called. In the same book, Leunclavius also notes that the sons of the red old man, *Kisulis Cozz*, infested the Amaseian province or Sanjakate with robberies: and that these...
Persians, and he also took to wife the daughter of Alexius, Emperor of Trebizond; for those of Amasia, being frequently unruly and inciting the Turco-Persians—since they are of the same race and live in the same manner—appeared to be moving toward defection. Mahomet, his father, who has now passed, thought it necessary to entrust that province to his son, and to establish him as lord in those borderlands, and as a head arrayed against the Persians, just as he himself had done at Adrianople against the Romans, Huns, Vlachs, Serbs, and Bulgarians, swaying the spear so that his subjects in all of Asia and Thrace might live in prosperity.
Therefore, when Murad Bey came into his inheritance, he did not enter upon the sovereignty untroubled, nor without a storm, but with great tumult and having sustained great loss, as the account will soon reveal. For indeed his father, having fallen ill, called to himself the first of his magnates, whom they call *vizier* and *pasha* in their own tongue, and whom the Romans call patrician and *mesazon*. The man's name was Bajazet, of Albanian descent, who from childhood had drawn the lot of servitude, and had been with Mahomet Bey in his calamities and afflictions. For while Mahomet was still young, being pursued by Temyr, who had slain his father, among the mountains of Galatia in the borders of the city of Ancyra—in which place also occurred that great battle which the account has already described—[Mahomet] fell into many terrible things and extreme hardships, wandering in exile and pursued by the Persians, and the aforementioned Bajazet suffered and was afflicted along with him. And how was this? Both of them were traveling on foot, and Mahomet was still a boy, and could not bear the struggle of the journey; but his feet were swollen, and being no longer able to walk, Bajazet carried him on his shoulders for many days' journey, like a Libyan ass, and brought him safely back within the borders of his father's empire. And when hunger frequently vexed Mahomet, this man, appearing in the guise of a *monochiton*—what we call a dervish—would go around entering villages, begging for bread like a mendicant so that he might provide food for Mahomet; in which he proved himself a good and faithful servant, such as no other could be found. And when he himself had reached manhood and had taken his paternal authority as an inherited estate, he also made recompense to him, according to the words of the Lord: "You were faithful over a few things; I will set you over many." Consequently, he established him as lord of his household and of all the land ruled by him. This aforementioned Prometheus, Bajazet, having administered the principality and all supervisory duties well, and as was proper,

administered the regions. This Bajazet, then—whom we have called Prometheus—rightly directed the affairs of the empire and administered Asia and Thrace, as befitted the interests of his master. He devoted his entire care to maintaining the army and procuring supplies necessary for military expeditions, and he managed the business of peace and war while Mahomet lived and ruled in peace. When Mahomet fell ill, he summoned Bajazet and declared his final will by making a testament; he decreed everything concerning his affairs. He also adjured him by God and their prophet, and by the bread and salt 98 which he had provided for him and spent on his nourishment, to be a loyal servant to his son Morat, just as he had been to him. He was to hand over to him the paternal hegemony and establish him as master of his father's house. As for his other two sons—for it happened that Morat was then of a youthful age, and the other two were boys of eight 99—he ordered in his testament that they be committed to the trust of the Emperor Manuel, so that he would be their guardian. He ordained all these things fearing that Morat might, according to their custom, destroy them by strangulation, as indeed happened later. Having thus arranged everything well by his testament, and thinking that even after death he would find matters with his children in a state of peace, he missed his mark, having cast it far from the target. For he imagined: "If my two sons are in the hands of the emperor, Morat will be, free from turbulence and agitation, the master of all subjects, and the rebels and seditious will not have the means to raise their hands. The infants will be liberated from unjust slaughter, and will have sufficient means for every kind of life, provided by the leader Prince Morat." The emperor, by holding such hostages with him, entertained the hope that he would share a sincere and unfeigned friendship with Morat, as if casting terror upon the dog with the club of Hercules. And if at some time the fortune of Morat should become exhausted and be cut off by some chance, the emperor hoped that, through his own efforts, the prince he had established would be gentle and, like a tame snake fed kindly in his bosom—which, if it should happen to strike with a bite, as the nature of evil things remains untamed, would at least not instill the poison by the pressure of its teeth—he would be safe. The emperor rejoiced, dreaming these things to himself; but the fortune of the Romans, aware of the future, groaned. When, therefore, Mahomet had died at Adrianople, as we have narrated,
in the buildings constructed by him within Hadrian’s [city], they hid his corpse for forty days in the house where it lay unburied, while no one yet knew that he had died, except for four domestic servants: Bajazet and Ibrahim, the patricians or viziers, and two physicians, who went in and out daily, babbling vain reports to the grandees that the leader was ill and that the therapeutic aid of certain necessary items was required. And it was possible to see a multitude of others sent—some to Serbia, some to Constantinople, others to the islands—to look for things useful for his medical treatment. But he who was supposed to be treated by the physicians to rid the intestines of their burden and relieve the lungs and liver, had his abdomen cut open, and all his inner contents were delivered to the earth inside the room where he lay. They anointed the body with myrrh, wrapped it in a shroud, and placed it upon a bed, as if he were still alive and sick. All these things were done by the two viziers and the servants of the palace, who did not go out, nor did they hold conversation with anyone. The purpose, therefore, was such: if the surrounding nations—the Romans, the Serbs, the Genoese, the Venetians, and the Caraman in the East—were to learn of the death of the leader, the heir Morat would not be able to come down from the borders of Persia, and there would be tumult in the government, and faction in the army; and the Caraman would mercilessly plunder all the affairs of the East, and the Christians would plunder Thrace, and the Turks would be unfortunate, while the Romans would flourish in good fortune.
Things being thus, they sent word of the father’s death to Morat by a certain courier at the time he was living in Amaseia. After the passage of forty days, the messenger whom they had sent arrived, announcing to them the arrival of Morat and that he had come down near Prusa, to a certain village called Melaina, and had handed to them letters from Morat signifying his arrival at Prusa, and instructing Bajazet that, upon receiving the corpse of his father, he should return to Prusa with the entire senate, in order to bury the father and proclaim him leader. Then Bajazet, having received the letters with as much pleasure and joy as possible, on the next day sat upon the tribunal, and with all the satraps and grandees, and with no small part of the city, he began to speak to the people as follows: "It is not necessary for me, men, to speak and harangue to you, from what state to what state you have been exalted D (2)
CHAPTER XXIII
(2) And by a certain courier. That courier was the first, and he was a *Cesnegir*, that is, a taster, by the name of Eluanbegus.
God favoring and our prophet interceding for him, we were raised to that fortune which we now enjoy. Most of you have seen these things yourselves, or have heard from your parents, that not yet sixty years have passed, or at most a little more, since the descendants of Othman crossed the strait, subdued all of Thrace with their arms, and compelled the Roman empire and the Serbs to pay them tribute; and not only them, but also the Wallachians beyond the Danube, the Huns, and the populous nations of the Albanians and Bulgarians. In a word, they reduced them all to such great slavery and oppressed them with such tribulations that their own treasury and public revenues were not enough to pay the tributes and stipends owed to us. But they were even driven to such calamity that they sent their daughters and sons to our emperors like slaves. And for what reason? To excite our clemency and pity, seeking from us a respite from their hardships and peace. Moreover, he increased the power and dignity of this empire, having wisely and prudently collected men from all nations—and for the most part, men of the lowest and most rustic status, who did not worship the one God whom the prophet preached—and led them to true piety, and made them fortunate, adorned with dignities and honors, and illustrious leaders. Of that number am I myself, as well as the greatest part of those of you who are now listening to me. Therefore, it does not befit us to lose heart, nor to be given to sloth, but rather to be sober and vigilant. And each one of us, as a natural and genuine son of Othman, must fight for this paternal inheritance; nor ought we through our own negligence allow it to be destroyed. For even the father, lord, benefactor, and bestower of goods is one, the same Mahomet, and his successor Morates, the firstborn of his children and most beloved: who now sits upon the throne of his father in the great city of Prusa. The father of our lord paid the common debt of all. Having said these things, he wailed with loud lamentations and tears, and at the same time all the grandees and the guards, with one voice, cried out with great tumult and noise and wept mournfully. Then Bajazites and D Ibraimus, bearing the corpse, placed it in the courtyard of the palace; and having followed the dead man with much mourning, they ordered the forces of the East to march the next day toward Callipolis, while the magnates followed on foot with Bajazites, accompanying the corpse. Having then crossed the strait, they carried it to Prusa and deposited it in the tomb which he had built for himself while he was alive; they mourned for eight days, and to celebrate the memory of the deceased, they performed funeral rites according to the custom of the nation: afterwards, the mourning having ended, they [acclaimed] Moratem.
Ismaelis Bullialdi notæ.
(3) The first among the nations from which the militia of the Janissaries was collected, he was the author, having indeed used wise and prudent counsel. For that fund of soldiers is inexhaustible, who depend on no one for the hope of rewards except the prince: of whom they are not only slaves, but also foster-children and sons, as it were. 
(4) They carry the body of the deceased emperor, having imitated the Roman senators who carried the funeral of Augustus on their shoulders; or the consuls, who carried the urn in which the ashes of Severus were transported on their shoulders, as Herodian notes, lib. IV Hist. post Marcum.
They proclaimed and saluted the ruler as emperor. Once the ceremonies befitting the majesty of the empire were duly performed, and the emperor had bestowed numerous and valuable gifts upon the purpurati of his court—who in turn honored him with presents—they consulted regarding the affairs of state. They immediately dispatched envoys to Karaman and to the Emperor of the Romans to inform them of the death of Mahomet and the inauguration of Murad, and to renew the treaties of peace, as is the custom for new rulers and sovereigns. For they wished to establish and secure the affairs of the East as was necessary, through agreements and oaths with Karaman, and only then, having crossed the straits, to look to the affairs of Thrace.
But the Emperor Manuel, seizing the opportunity, sent envoys to him: Palaiologos Lachynes and the theologian Korax, ostensibly to offer condolences and to congratulate him on the commencement of his rule. Furthermore, they recalled the final will of his father, and in accordance with it, requested that the children be delivered to the emperor, if indeed they desired the harmony and love that had existed between him and his father to remain intact and uncorrupted. If they refused to deliver the children and to comply with the laws of his father, the emperor had a successor at hand, whom he would shortly establish as ruler of Macedonia, Chersonesus, and all of Thrace, and before long, also of Asia and the rest of the Orient. Manuel had already disclosed this plan to the aforementioned Mustafa.
Bajazet, speaking on behalf of the new ruler Murad, gave answer to the envoys, saying that it was neither honorable nor consistent with the laws and oracles of the Prophet for the children of Muslims to be reared among the *Giavours*—that is, for the children of the faithful to be under the tutelage of infidels. "If the emperor wishes, however, let him enter into friendship with us and cultivate it according to the prior treaties, and let him be a father to these children, as many as there may be, but let him abstain entirely from the duty of tutelage. We shall count his friendship as a gain and hold it as a universal treaty confirmed by a seal; and we shall take care that no one among us attempts anything contrary to justice and equity, or transgresses these boundaries. Furthermore, let us give mutual oaths, which shall be as a wall of bronze and a fortified rampart between us. But as for your petitions, in which you ask to have the children with you, it is impossible to consent to such a request, and, in truth, even less possible to deliver them."
Dismissed with this response, the emperor’s envoys returned to him and reported everything that they had seen to be difficult. Wherefore, troubled in spirit and mindful of what had recently been arranged with Mustafa, who was abiding on the island of Lemnos—having been sent there into exile by the same emperor, as the account previously set forth—he summoned Demetrios Laskaris Leontarios, a man who was, to speak the truth, a most valiant leader of war, who had proven his strength of spirit in Lacedaemon and Thessaly while John Palaiologos lived and reigned in those regions.
For this Demetrios held the highest honors from him. Upon his death, he sent his third son, having crowned him Despot in Thessaly; and having summoned Leontarios from there, he kept him near him at Constantinople, as a man prudent and approved in military affairs. For the Emperor Manuel was blessed with six male children, of whom the first was John, who, having been crowned by his father, was proclaimed Emperor of the Romans; the second was Theodore, whom he established as Despot of Lacedaemon; the third was Andronikos, who also became Despot of Thessaly; the fourth was Constantine, who was allotted the Pontic regions bordering on Chazaria; the fifth was Demetrios, and the sixth was Thomas, who, being infants, were living with their father.
Then, as the necessity was pressing, he gave ten triremes, properly equipped, which were in the port of Constantinople, to Demetrios Laskaris, and sent him to the island of Lemnos, having ordered him to take the exile Mustapha, along with the often-mentioned Cüneyt, and to transport them to the Chersonesus with the force of the triremes. And he was to establish Mustapha as the leader of Thrace (as he was the natural son of the aforementioned Bayezid) and as the rightful heir to his father’s assets, lands, and provinces—which indeed came to pass. For it was an ancient custom among the Turks not to inquire curiously whose son this or that person is, provided only that he is a descendant of Osman. If he is not of the same root, it is impossible for them to submit to him or honor him as a leader. I shall begin from this point to narrate the plan long ago devised by the Turks, which is preserved even until now, and through which they boldly stand against the Christians, and raise trophies of victory over them, and forever carry off the prize of conquest in a way that no other race has inherited.
The Turks, having descended from Persia (7), and [the regions] lying along the Dnieper River, looking toward the more eastern and northern parts, towards Ouzia [the land of the Uz], and Chazaria, and Alania, and Cherson, and the other territories.
Having passed the borders of Armenia and having begun to plunder the regions of Upper Cappadocia and Lycaonia, they would signify by the voice of a herald, as if on behalf of their leader, that if anyone wished to make an incursion against the infidels, let him come. For the Turkish nation was, as no other, addicted to rapine and litigious—for it was so even among themselves; but if against Christians (8), what need is there to speak? And if they only heard the voice of the herald, as for an incursion, which is called in their language *Akkin* (9), then all of them, in great numbers and like a flowing river, came of their own accord, most of them without money and without a bag, and without spears and scimitars; others went on foot, forming countless camps, they rushed. There were no others, but each had a club in his hands, and rushing against the Christians, they took them captive like sheep; God having by ineffable judgments given this decree against us because of the multitude of the sins of our race. And the continuous incursion prevailing until now; holding not only the eastern themes (10), but also those of Thrace, they subdued all the provinces from the Chersonese to the Ister. Nor did they neglect the daily chances and events; for with the Serbs, having changed their plan, they made peace today, tomorrow they were plundering the lands of Attica, Lacedaemon, Achaia, and Hellas. But after the day after tomorrow, when the Romans, as it seemed, were drawing in peace, mourning and woe fell upon the Serbs; then the Bulgarians; later the Albanians. And henceforth, laying waste all the wild B [territories].
On the Themes
For the very name of the theme is Greek, and not Roman, named from the *thesis* [position]. Constantine Porphyrogenitus says in his book that the name was recently used to signify this, but it is Greek: the name of the theme itself is Greek, not Roman [that is, Latin], and it is derived from *thesis*, that is, position. The Roman Empire was distributed into those themes, which was also sometimes divided into provinces; sometimes into praetorian prefectures. But they are called oriental themes, as the same Constantine teaches, "Because it is called eastern with respect to us who inhabit Byzantium and the land of Europe."
Notes of Ismael Bullialdus
...chuntes. Hence arose the rivalries which were the first causes of the Saracens vexing the Turks with robberies, and finally they broke out into open war. (8) *But today they were turning toward peace*. Whoever reads the histories of the Turkish nation not very attentively can note that it has not hitherto wished to be entangled in two wars at the same time, but has attacked individuals while cultivating peace with the others: those whom it has even attacked in war, if peace were offered, by the benefit of which they might recover from the endured miseries, it never refused. And how great was the prudence of that nation at that time, so great can the error and blindness of the mind of the Christians be noted, who thought that their own affairs could stand against the Turks because they did not provoke all at once by war: as if a part cut off from the whole would neither be diminished nor decreased. Our people, therefore, being idle (and would that they had been idle from mutual wars, fires, and from the looting and destruction of cities and towns, and had not worn out their own strength in mutual slaughter and killing), allowed them to be oppressed one by one; by which error being admitted, the Bulgarians, the Serbs, the Greeks, and the Hungarians perished for the most part, and the Republic of the Venetians was reduced to narrower bounds, the island of Cyprus having been lost.
And this wild and savage race of barbarians has not ceased, nor does it cease even to this day; to my mind, it will not cease until such time as we receive the fear of God into our hearts. For since we behave impiously toward the divine, being baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit—of the one Godhead—yet despise this and set at naught the commandments of the one true God, we have been delivered into the hands of the impious, and we are righteously punished by them, God having ordained this rightly and justly. And they have not only reduced the countless and manifold nations living on this side of the Ister [Danube], but have utterly subdued the Vlachs beyond the Ister as well; they brought the Huns themselves, a countless multitude, into total subjection. And it is not only the neighboring Turks who make incursions—those of Thrace, of Attica, of Illyricum, of Mount Haemus, and those neighboring Serbia (for indeed, as far as I am concerned, this race is far more numerous today, from the strait of Gallipoli to the Ister, than in the regions of the East, I mean those subject to the leader descended from Osman)—but also those from the Asiatic land, and those inhabiting Phrygia. And what do I say? The Lycaonians who live on the borders of Armenia, the Amasinians, Cappadocians, Cilicians, Lycians, and Carians travel on foot all the way to the Danube, for the sake of plundering Christians. For even if ten thousand times ten thousand should invade any given province, they act in the manner of brigands, and after plundering everything, they flee. This has rendered all of Thrace as far as the borders of Dalmatia a desert; this has made the Albanians, a people beyond number, few to count. It has utterly annihilated the Vlachs likewise, the Serbs, and the Romans. With these being taken captive in this way, they dedicate the fifth [part] of the spoils to their leader, according to their new law. And they consecrate this fifth part to the authority; and these are the choicest items; then follow the leader’s own men, and those who assess the authority. Wherever they see a youth, robust from among the captives, they buy him for a very low price, and name him an inductee to the authority and a servant. And the leader calls these a newly-enrolled army, or in their own tongue, "Janissaries." He brings them over to his own impiety, circumcises them, and calls them his own household; he bestows upon them many gifts, the most brilliant offices, not mere provision, and all sorts of other good things, making them his table-companions and fellow-diners. D
And he cherishes them with a father's love, as if they were his own offspring: this includes the goatherds, shepherds, neat-herds, and swineherds, the children of farmers and cattle-breeders. For, toward such a disposition, they in return render their own lives of no account for the sake of the leader; rather, they cast them away for the sake of the glory they have attained, so that they may not fall from it, suffering in time of war on behalf of their masters, and thereby obtaining the victory. Now, the identifying mark of these men is the head-covering, which in the common language of the Romans they call a *zarcola* (14). For indeed, all the Turks in general use the same thing as a covering for the head; all of them, as many as are of the common people and as many as are of noble birth, use one dyed scarlet. But as for those from other races who have fallen under the yoke of slavery, having been registered as slaves of the leader, these wear white head-coverings made of the whitest felt—a hemisphere insofar as it covers the head, but having a projection above the crown, as much as a span high, ending in a point. B This newly recruited body of men, therefore, becomes excessively numerous each year, and is multiplied by a hundred. For even slaves acquire slaves, and the slaves of slaves acquire slaves; and all are named, and are, the slaves of the leader. There is not among them any Turk or Arab, but all are the children of Christians—Romans, Serbs, Albanians, Bulgarians, Wallachians, and Huns—who, having acted impiously, and enjoying the delights of the present life like pigs at the trough, have become like dogs diseased with rabies, always bearing deadly, implacable hatred against their own kinsmen. For as we have said above, the subject easily changes from one leader to another, provided that he is of the same Othmanic root, he who has recently begun to rule, and from nowhere else. And we have reviewed the history that even the slave race itself possesses the same impulse; for it suffices that he be a new Othmanic scion. For all the Othmanids are considered their patrons, and they are such; and they themselves hold them as their own freedmen. But when the rule flows from one to another, whether from father to son, or from brother to brother, whomever fortune may smile upon, to him the slaves most faithfully render their services. We shall begin the history again, from where the story of this narrative began. D We return again to the series of the history, from where we digressed and began this narration.
Ismael Bullialdus' Notes.
(14) They call it *zarcola*. It is a head-covering, and white wool, which the Janissaries use, the form and figure of which we have depicted in many books. The *zarcola* is surrounded by a golden fringe; and on its front part rises a cylindrical silver or bronze tube; and from the top a plume is let down onto the back, three spans in length. That head-covering for the Janissaries is white; for certain others it is red.
(15) That the subject changes. This difference in recognizing the princes is shown by the clear examples provided in the four sons of Bajazet I; in the two sons of Mehemed, Morat and Mustapha. In the sons of Mehemed II, [in] Bajazet II and his brothers: also in the sons of Sultan Suleiman: and finally in this century, in the brother of Sultan Achmet, Mustapha, and his children. 
(16) It seems that some words are missing here, *τεθνηκότα*, or perhaps just *καί* is missing.
CHAPTER XXIV
Demetrius Leontarius carries Mustapha, the son of Ilderim Bajazet, as the account has already shown, across into Thrace, and with him the aforementioned Cineites, often mentioned, having secured them first with oaths that he would never violate the imperial counsel, but would always be obedient as a son to a father, having given his own son to him as a pledge of faithfulness. And having made agreements, he would deliver to the Emperor the city of Gallipoli in the Chersonese, and the Pontic regions up to the borders of Wallachia, and those of Thessaly as far as Erissos (18) and the Holy Mountain, and certain other difficult-to-capture and impregnable gifts. Having then secured them with oaths, they hoisted their sails and sailed toward Gallipoli. And indeed, those of Murad, having ensured that he would hold the small town, and having brought the light boats and triremes into the harbor, and having stationed the fighters well upon the tower that overlooks the harbor, sat waiting for the battle. Demetrius, having brought out Cineites with a few of the Turks he had brought, and a not insignificant army of Romans, began to wage war. And indeed, the Gasmoulikon (19) of Gallipoli and the populace fought face to face, but were not capable of offering resistance to Cineites; for the man was brave and most experienced in military matters, as was no other of the Turks of that time; thus, even if unwilling, they turned their backs and the citizens turned in flight. Mustapha, therefore, seeing these things and becoming full of courage, came out with much fervor also from the triremes. And indeed, having fought until evening, at dusk Mustapha and Demetrius again went aboard the imperial trireme, and sat both of them in the stern; and he ordered those opposing him who were standing directly across from him to be summoned without fear, having given pledges that he would hold a few words with...
(17) Demetrius, having taken Mustapha... (18) Erissos... (19) And indeed the Gasmoulikon...
them which were profitable for their city. He began his speech to them in these exact words: "O men, you know precisely that I am the son of Ilderim Bajazet, and you were the bondsmen of my father. By what manner do you not render honor and respect to your master? Do you not know that he who previously held power was my brother? And he, having murdered the other of his brothers, and having seized the hegemony until now, has made me an exile and has confined me in the hands of the Romans as if in a prison. Now, by the nod of God, with fortune looking favorably upon me and running forward without hindrance, He has directed me into the paternal hegemony; but you push against me and do not allow me to proceed. If, therefore, you incline toward me, and grant me passage, and provide the way leading me to Adrianople, to the paternal house, you shall be to me from now on not bondsmen, but brothers, and I will maintain my paternal goodwill toward you, and I will heap grace upon grace, and gifts upon gifts. But if you should resist, I will indeed become master of the paternal affairs, with fortune assisting and my father the emperor laboring together with me. For the road leading to the west will not be denied to Murat; and when I become the master of my own, and take an opportunity, I will judge you." When these words had been heard in this manner, some of the leading men came over voluntarily and did obeisance, and others followed them. At daybreak, having departed from the triremes with Cineites, they mounted horses, and having sounded the war-cry, they rushed from the triremes as if for battle, together with the armed Romans and Turks. And indeed, the whole multitude of the common people, as many as were armed and as many as were spectators, immediately rendered their obeisance; and all acclaimed him as their leader and descendant of Othman; and the neighboring villages flowed together until evening, doing obeisance and acclaiming him. But those within the town did not yield; rather, they resisted, saying and acclaiming with a loud voice Murat as their leader and universal master, while heaping insults upon Mustapha. Then Mustapha, leading all his forces, departed toward the hexamilion of the Chersonese, and all those of the Chersonese and those outside ran together acclaiming him. Meanwhile, Demetrius was besieging the fortress of Gallipoli. Let us therefore return the account to the affairs of Murat, to make known to us how and by what manner he obtained the rule, and how the designs of the Romans came to nothing; and by what manner Mustapha escaped, having been sentenced to death, and how Cineites, having abandoned him, fled.
Since Murat was dwelling in Prusa, as the account has already indicated, and the better part of his subjects were daily flowing to him, as if wishing to console him for the death of his father and congratulating him on his assumption of the rule, suddenly a messenger was brought from Lampsacus, reporting that triremes, as many as...
could be, were at Gallipoli, and that shouting and disturbances, the clatter of engines, and the din on the battlements could be heard, along with other signs of a hostile incursion.
The most esteemed counselors of Morates, and the most prominent among the nobles, having long harbored envy against Bajazet—because in power he excelled the others who held offices, and he conducted himself arrogantly, holding everyone else of no account (for the man was indeed supercilious and insulting to many)—thought they had found an appropriate time and an opportunity for speaking their minds. For Morates was a youth, not yet holding the reins of the empire in his own hands, but, like a stubborn mule, kicking out everywhere and treating the boy emperor as nothing. In him there was not a spark of free speech; he cherished his satraps more, holding them excessively dear.
They spoke to him as follows: "Do you see, my lord, how diligently our regent attends to our affairs, which have already perished in the western regions? The crown of your kingdom has been placed upon the head of Mustapha. He will soon be in possession of the wealth and forces of Thrace; and before long he will grow strong even against us, unless some care is taken. Command, therefore, that Bajazet cross the strait with all the forces that are at hand here and lead them against Mustapha before the forces of the western provinces join him. For among all your satraps, there is no one more capable than Bajazet of repelling the enemy and turning them to flight; for the entire Thracian militia respects him no less than their own master, and he leads them where he wishes, just as if they were his own servants, and he has them completely obedient and submissive."
Bajazet heard these things gladly, and as quickly as he could, he arrived at the strait of the sacred mouth of the Propontis; and after crossing to the farther continent with a few soldiers accompanying him, within two days he approached Adrianople and assembled a powerful army there. For in all things, as we have said, that man was sharp and ready, and was heeded by all. Then, having shared his plans with the governors of the western provinces, he bound them by an oath never to defect, even if he should sustain any kind of defeat; and furthermore, that they would act bravely and generously against the enemy and, with God helping him to be victorious, would contribute their efforts to that end. Having done these and similar things among them, Bajazet led out a very powerful army.
And when he had entered the road which leads straight into the Chersonese, scouts sent out by him returned in haste, announcing that Mustafa, having departed from those places with a huge army, had crossed over near a village recently built by the Turks, famous for its dense population (which is called Magna Carya), and that he intended to encamp the next day in the territory of Adrianople. Having heard this, Bajazet, suspended in spirit and wavering between boldness and fear, left Adrianople and led out forces totaling more than thirty thousand soldiers. And when they had arrived at a certain marshy plain (it is near the edge of the field, so that the city of Adrianople is seen dimly from it, being planted with woods and a very humid place), in this spot he prepared for battle. For Mustafa had also arrived with those under his command, and both armies were compelled by necessity to engage, even though the location seemed unsuitable. Then Bajazet, having combined his hortatory speech with directions given from his chariot and on horseback, addressed the western leaders thus:
“Men and brothers, and all you who acknowledge your authority under my command, it is well known to you how clement and gentle toward you our late lord was. You have experienced his mild and easy spirit, for he held you not in the place of slaves, but of brothers. Truly, he did not indulge his own pleasures as much as he studied your interests; and whatever goodness he conferred upon all, he considered it as gain added to himself. He strove so that the race of the prophet might increase, and the depleted affairs of the Romans might diminish. Therefore, he added many cities and provinces to the empire of the Muslims, and he did not cease until the very day of his death to increase his powers and possessions and to make them more extensive. But now, this present false Turk, who has been raised up at this time on account of our sins, is already partitioning an authority not yet occupied by himself, and is handing over to the Romans the better part, not yet acquired, which the ancestors of our king possessed through much sweat and labor. Do you not clearly understand that this Callipolis and its strait are the keys of the East and the West, of the Aegean Sea and the Euxine? If the Romans keep this under their own dominion, the Turks will be unable to transport captives to the East, but the Romans will transport Turks, with no one to stop them. And now your troubles will begin, as the Romans assert their freedom. On this account, I urge you, that against this false”.
Mustapha, and those who assist him and share his sentiments—Romans—you must resist with all your might. For this impious man, who is an enemy of the faith, is not born of Othmanic blood. Indeed, that Mustapha, the brother of our lord—as I once heard from him—departed this life while still a mere infant. Because Manuel, the emperor, feared Moses, he declared this man, who was just one of the common Turkish folk, to be the son of Iltrim [Bayezid], to intimidate Moses. Later, when this impostor saw that the emperor was bound by oaths, and that he and our lord had entered into an agreement of mutual love and concord, he fled into Wallachia. There he remained with Mylza, who was at that time the leader of the Mysians, proclaiming himself to be the son of Iltrim and asking for aid. Having obtained some small assistance from there, he entered the regions of Thessaly as a brigand, plundering the merchants and travelers he encountered, calling himself the son of Iltrim and a descendant of Othman. Wherefore, as you know, our lord sent a respectable army against him. Having joined battle somewhere near Thessalonica, the villain, unable to withstand the assault, fled into that city. At that time, Cineites was also serving under our lord, having previously rebelled, holding the province of Asia and styling himself the sovereign ruler of Smyrna and Ephesus. Driven from thence by our king’s powerful army, he had been ordered to accompany him and live in the western provinces. Having seized an opportunity, he fled to Thessalonica and for this reason joined forces with Mustapha. When the citizens remained stubborn in their resolve not to betray this impostor, our lord wrote to their emperor, clearly signifying these things to him: "When I had gone out to the hunt, most illustrious emperor, to catch a beast, and having already driven the prey I was pursuing into the trap in my hands, this wolf burst into the sheepfold of your empire and escaped safely. I ask, therefore, that my prey be returned to me, lest it bring ruin to yours and my flocks in the fullness of time." To these things, the emperor replied: "Even if it is a wolf that has sought safety in my fold, I am of a gentle and humane disposition; nor do I take pleasure in the slaughter of others. I will be the guardian of the wolf, not his betrayer. Be content with this: I will keep him bridled and subject to my power, and I will not allow him to run forth or devour anything that is yours, but you shall reign in safety and abundance, so long as you live, and stand by the treaties which we both have sworn." Since then, the emperor kept him at Constantinople along with Cineites; and after four years, he sent him to the island of Lemnos, where he has lived until now. Now, since the emperor cannot harm us, and understands that his plans are coming to naught—for he wanted to have two royal infants in his possession, so as to strike terror into us with his own forces—he has launched this deserter Cineites and Mustapha against us, like savage dogs driven mad. Let us not show ourselves like goats or hares against our enemies; rather, let us leap upon them like lions, and direct our spears, which know not how to bend, straight at them. Let the spirit of our men be bolstered—
for they are more numerous—toward those few with him who, even now, still have the bread of my master stuck between their teeth; for they shall soon be our helpers in retrieving the straying flock. This one thing shall be enough for us, if we enter the battle promptly and eagerly.
Having said these things, and having drawn up the phalanxes in their proper order, he sounded the war-trumpet. On the other side, Mustaphas, with Cineites present, confirmed the spirits of his own men, swearing and promising them that if he should seize authority, they would be masters of all things just as he was, and that they would receive from him very many honors and gifts; offering small rewards to the lowly, and immense, measureless rewards to the nobles. And when Mustaphas saw that the wings of the battle were already shaking (that is, that they had come to the crisis of war), and that the enemies had made an onset by shaking their spears and the archers had sent forth volleys of missiles, he stood on an elevated place, abandoning the battle to Cineites—for the man was more courageous than any other, and accustomed to wars—and cried out in a loud voice:
"Men, brothers—for I do not call you slaves—to what end is this impiety? Does a slave wage war against his master? And this, indeed, from Albanians? Offspring of a barbarian race, against me, the son of Ilderim, your lord? For if my brother were alive, this impiety would have some color of excuse, as this man would be ready to sacrifice his life for him, he whose own neck is under the threat of a bloody fate. But now that my brother is dead, who is the heir begotten of him? And even if he were alive, he would have no jurisdiction in Thrace. He rules far and wide in the East. I do not invade his paternal property; I occupy only the domains of my father. Now, if anyone denies that I am the son of Ilderim, I will clearly demonstrate the truth to him. But if he wishes also to contend in war, let the son of my brother come—not my slave—with whom I may do battle. And to whomever fortune assigns the better part, let him reign. But I marvel at you, you who have proven your military virtue to all in the armies of my father, and who know the arrogance, the pride, and the disdain of this man worth three obols. If the outcome of this present struggle turns out successfully for him, who will be able to bear him? Therefore, I exhort you, do not be combatants, but rather be my allies, and come forward with fairness. And I will not withhold any of your dues—God is my witness—but instead, I will add more and increase them even further."
When these things had been said, suddenly the satrap who was guarding the right wing, having detached himself as if he intended to clash with Cineites, came with those who were with him before Mustaphas; and all of them, having dismounted from their horses, rendered to him the obeisance of servants to a lord. And immediately, he who led the left wing of the battle line...
also performed similar actions. And it was possible to see a strange transformation: Mustapha in an instant had grown wings, and was like an eagle soaring high, while Bajazet was like a jackdaw stripped of its feathers, remaining solitary and deserted by his own men. Then, having considered in his mind that a servant rarely prevails over his master, and seeing that the threads of fortune were already being spun in reverse, he endeavored to secure his own safety in haste; and having dismounted from his horse, he and his brother Hamza also approached in the manner of servants, and did him obeisance. Then the men of Mustapha, having ended the battle, and pitched tents befitting a leader, and having helped Mustapha down from his horse, acclaimed him as their leader and the ruler of all the Roman lands. But as for Bajazet, having been ordered to sit at a distance, guards were assigned to watch over him.
And Cüneyt (25) came, and saw him still alive—for he was holding the outposts so that the opponent might not escape, and having learned that he was ensnared—he said to Mustapha: "How long shall this impious one behold the sun, who is not even worthy of tangible darkness?" And Mustapha said, "Do as you wish," and ordered them to drag the wretched man a little way outside the camp and behead him. Which also came to pass, while he himself watched the beheading, and said: "Do you know, you wicked one, how to prune testicles?" For it happened that the testicles of the son-in-law of Cüneyt, Abdulla, had been cut off by the order of Bajazet. They also brought his brother Hamza, intending to behead him as well; but Cüneyt, having pity on him because he was young, said: "Let him go; for he is not like that cruel and inhuman man whom we have just put to death; nor has he yet committed any evil with his hands; let him therefore be my freedman." The wretch Cüneyt did not see that he was warming to life his own murderer, and that the one he was showing pity to, he was soon about to have his own life cruelly taken by.
The new leader Mustapha, therefore, entered Adrianople with confidence and courage with his entire army. And the citizens came out to meet him with great joy and boldness, acclaiming him with a cheerful voice. But those of the garrison of Gallipoli (24), having learned what had happened, and having abandoned all hope for the fortress, surrendered it upon oaths and covenants. Demetrius Leontarius, therefore, who had hoped to gain the city (for so among them...)
the guards of the fortress and all the supplies they had within, according to the agreements that had been made with them, he himself, having taken out from the triremes breastplates, helmets, spears, javelins, and every kind of weapon, began to bring them into the fortress. Cineites, therefore, having arrived and seeing what was happening, and seeing also the populace of the Turks disturbed and tumultuous at this unexpected and unforeseen change, began to mock and bitterly rebuke Demetrios, saying: "As it seems to me, General Demetrios, do you suppose that the struggle we waged and the dangers we underwent were for the sake of your kin and the empire of the Romans? But it is not so. That we who were shut in should be set at liberty, and that from being slaves we have become masters, this great benefit we ascribe to the heavenly God; we do not judge you Romans to be the cause of it. We consider indeed that we have used your efforts successfully, you who, having joined your labors with ours, have endured the hardships of war in this turn of events. To God alone, therefore, we offer thanks, who has kept us safe from past labors and calamities; and we send you away with gifts, such as your station permits, and with the necessary tokens of friendship. But that we should hand over cities and fortresses to you—God forbid! For you, O Demetrios, may it be enough that you return safely to Constantinople. The memory of the evils we suffered in Lemnos still clings to our minds, and how insultingly we were treated by the monks in the monastery of the Most Blessed [Virgin]. As a reward, you take home your head intact; I shall use the fable of the wolf and the stork. Ply your oars, for a gentle Eurus is blowing; reach Constantinople, salute the emperors from us, and announce to them how God has granted us dominion. May there remain between the emperor and us an integral peace and tranquility, and let there be no further question about Callipolis." The commander of the army was not a little disturbed by these words, and, becoming angry, he said: "Do you not know, O Cineites, what manner of emperor I have, how wise, experienced in affairs, and great-souled he is? Do you, after such insults that you have vomited from your mouth, send me away empty-handed? Rest assured that, as I foresee, you yourself will shortly proceed to Constantinople as a place of refuge; then you will realize what those words of yours are worth. But for the empire you have no power to command nor to dismiss me, but [rather] Mustapha the emperor, whom God and the fortune of the Romans have exalted. You indeed, being one of the crowd and the common people, refrain from words to which you have no one to pay heed." Having risen, therefore, he entered the triremes full of anger and bitterness, not knowing what to do, turning over in his mind the violation of the oaths and the promises that had been made by them. Nevertheless, he remained, waiting to see what response would be given him by Mustapha: whether, according to the treaties, he was to receive the fortress or not; and he determined to return [only] upon receiving that response. Mustapha then approached him, and after a long conversation, said to Demetrios: "I indeed, O friend, and most dear protector of mine, remember correctly those things which I promised before God and His prophet; and [I remember] that in the midst of these was also the...
fortress of Callipolis. Therefore, I have to render an account for all other things on that fearful day, if I do not stand by the agreement and fulfill it. But regarding the fortress, it is better to break an oath than to offend God, to deliver pious people into the hands of the impious, to make free people slaves, and to subject a nation dedicated and consecrated to God to the hands of infidels, and of those who do not know the one God of heaven and earth. But if I were to be plunged into such impiety, which God forbid, O Lord, the race of the Muslims would neither permit me the leadership, nor grant you entry into this place. Go, therefore, and I shall extend my gratitude to the extent of my power. But as for those things which are not under my own possession, but are allotted to the public and to my prophet, I do not wish to disturb any of the customs of the Muslims or the commands of the prophet, being a Muslim myself. For I shall persistently labor to increase the number of cities, to enlarge them, and to add the regions of the Giaours (unbelievers) to the dominion of the Muslims. But to grant the city, and Callipolis at that, which is the throat of the Muslims, swallowing the whole race of Christians, and a noose of the Christians, strangling and destroying them—never would such an absurd thought enter my mind, nor shall I bring it to pass.
When Leontarius heard these things (like a lion that has lost its prey, bearing its head low, and sweeping the ground with its tail, letting it slacken), he too, being cast down in mind by grief as if succumbing to frenzy, kept his head lowered until he had finished his absurd speech. And thereupon, lifting his eyes, he addressed him thus: We know accurately, Lord Duke, how you Muslims have been disposed toward us for many years. Indeed, one hundred and fifty years have passed since your ancestor Osman snatched the parts of Bithynia, and Paphlagonia, and Phrygia from the hands of our ancestors and subjected them to his empire. But when his son Orchan became master and heir of these same themes or provinces, he never kept to the treaties and oaths, violating and overstepping the boundaries which God and truth had established. One hundred years have passed since that time, from which he began to devastate the West. Then his grandson, your father Ilderim Bayezid, when he held the height of power and all the provinces by right of succession, he too was caught in perjury; and at the end, God delivered him and his entire empire into the hands of the Persians. To this day, almost the thirtieth year from his death is passing, and your brothers, Musulman and Musa, having violated their oaths, lost their empire and their lives with an unhappy end. Only Mehmed, who has now passed away, your emperor and brother, did not violate his oath; he therefore yielded to a milder fate, after he... D
had enjoyed the peace and the pleasures of imperial power with good fortune. But you, while acting in this way, will not laugh for long, as fortune abandons you and ceases to aid you. For God sends the unjust to Hades before their time, and utterly destroys those who set Him aside. For when you entered Thessalonica as a fugitive, if the Emperor of the Romans had handed you over to Mehmed, and your life had been ended by a noose, many would have been able to accuse and condemn the Romans as traitors, as cruel executioners of those who took refuge with them, and as people who acted contrary to justice. But now that the Romans have proclaimed you leader next to God, while you attribute all things to God—and you have spoken well in this, and I do not gainsay it—you nevertheless treat those who labored with you as enemies, and you turn your back on them. Enjoy your health and pleasures, then.
