As for us, we shall return to our own homes, and after reporting to the emperor the deception, we shall entrust everything to God and wait with patience for His just judgment." Having spoken these words, he left the harbor, unfurled his sails, and directed his course toward Constantinople.

### CHAPTER 25.
*Manuel the emperor considers concluding a treaty with Morates. Mustaphas organizes his affairs, then gives himself over to leisure and sloth. Morates seriously plots the recovery of the empire and dispatches Abraham Bassas to Manuel, who departs with his mission unaccomplished. The alum-works in Phocis are completed. New Phocaea is founded, governed by Andrea and Jacobo Calanei, and pays tribute to the Turks. Joannes Adornus, rector of Phocaea, approaches Mahomet and then Morates, promising him his services for the transport of himself and his troops. Mustaphas is saddened by the news of Morates' crossing into Europe. Cineites speaks to him and rebukes him, advising him to cross into Asia; meanwhile, he himself considers deserting Mustaphas. Mustaphas arrives at Lampsacus and advances as far as Lopadium, whose bridge is seized and destroyed by Morates.*
When the Emperor Manuel was informed of these events, he was seized by deep sorrow and filled with anger. Being at a loss as to what he should do, he decided to follow a different path in his mind and to send envoys to Morates. If he were willing to fulfill his father's wish and give the two infants as hostages—since Bajazet-Bassas had departed from the living with his task unaccomplished—he would, with God’s help, restore him to his paternal reign. In the meantime, Mustaphas—for the narrative must return to his affairs—fortified the fortress, organized it well, and admonished the populace. He appointed drungaries and counts of his own to the great fleet, and the tower in the harbor he secured well as was necessary. Having given oaths to them and rewarded them with gifts, he made his journey to Adrianople. And upon entering the palace of his brother Mehmed, who had departed, he found countless treasures and another immense preparation: garments, precious stones and pearls, beautiful women, and young male servants, outstanding in beauty, and all [manner of wealth].
And other spoils of Wallachia: then [he began] to spend his time in idleness, squandering his wealth, and daily surrendering himself to lust and drunkenness. Morates, however, still a youth, since he had not yet completed his twentieth year, was dwelling in Prusa of Bithynia, practicing the same habits, though not to the same degree; for he was stung by care, nor did his mind allow him to remain unbridled: but he was considering how and by what way he might recall to himself the paternal dominion, which his father had acquired through many labors, but which he himself had lost through no fault of his own. The chief of the magnates were with him, except for Bajazet, whom I have already said had perished through an evil fate. Having learned, then, of the surrender of the fortress of Callipolis, and that Leontarius had been sent away empty-handed, and that Mustaphas was also continuing to squander his time intemperately, not having any concern for how to keep the dominion safe, he adopted a plan similar to that which the Emperor had formed; and, having anticipated him, he sent to the Emperor a legate, a certain Abraham, a brother of Hali, of whom we have made mention, a man prudent and upright, and unaccustomed to the disgraceful words and lusts of the Turks. He, since while Bajazet was alive he was held in the second place as Bassa, upon his death obtained the first honors, and was the prince of the nobles, and the *Mesazon*—that is, the counselor—of the dominion of Morates. He arrived in Constantinople, where he said not a word of the things which the Emperor had plotted. For the Turks kept their immense anger hidden in their minds, until time should turn their affairs for the better; with placid and serene eyes, and a mind composed for fraud, he transformed the wolf which he carried within into a tame sheep without. And so, with gentle and submissive words he asks for help; he transfers the cause and blame of all that had been perpetrated onto Bajazet Bassa: he declared that he himself, and likewise the Romans, were free from guilt, using such discourse as this: "If it shall seem good to your Majesty, in a short time you will restore my master, Morates, to his paternal kingdom, just as you conducted yourself toward his father, most illustrious Emperor. For you hold the rudder in your hand, and you turn the ship wherever you please, whose steering-oar you direct skillfully. Such as you truly showed yourself to his father, who, relying on your forces, resisted Moses, so do now, and have pity on us, and do not allow him to hold the dominion who is not worthy even of a shed. For indeed, that frequently mentioned Mehemeles, while he was still reigning in Asia, when Moses had occupied Thrace after the slaying of his brother Musulman, became a hostile and capital foe to the Romans and the city (as we have warned above). That time, O Emperor, you summoned Mehemet from Prusa, and having given him safe conduct, you received him, having crossed [the straits] with his army, within the walls of Constantinople. But he, having led out his forces, once and again, and often having joined battle with Moses, being defeated, retreated to Constantinople: and again, as if from war...
During the reign of Emperor Michael Palaiologos, the first of the Palaiologoi to rule, certain Italians came requesting that the mountain be granted to them, and that they pay an agreed-upon annual sum. At that same time, the Turks were lying in wait, acting as brigands in the surrounding parts of Lydia and Asia, and were marauding as far as Sardis and even Magnesia. When the Italians perceived the incursions of the Turks, fearing for themselves and wishing to protect their own, they began to build a very small fortress, just enough for their own guard and for the fifty or more workmen they had with them. But the Romans living in the neighborhood—those in the plain of Menoemenon, and of Magnesia, and of Nymphaion—having heard of this construction, came and found them having already started the work. And then, as if by a common signal, conferring with the Latins, they promised to assist and suffer with them, and to cooperate in the erection of the fort; and not only that, but to build up what was being constructed into a great city, on the condition that if necessity should arise, they too, as lords of such a place, would be sheltered within. Both sides having agreed upon this pact, Romans and Latins began together and built what is to this day guarded by the grace of God: New Phokaia, at the foot of the mountain, near the sea, having the mountain situated on its eastern side, the island of Lesbos to the west, the Gulf of Elaia to the north, and the Gulf of Ionia to the south. The stated lords of this city were the Genoese, Andrew and Jacob of the Cataneo family; and it acquired the name from the older Phocis, calling it New Phokaia, in which I also possess a house. When, therefore, affairs passed from the Romans into the hands of the Turks not long after, those found in the city, not bearing the daily skirmishes of the Turks and the slaughters of the Christians (for the Turks had become masters right up to the gates of the city), both Latins and Romans made sworn treaties with Sarchan, the leader of Lydia, and surrendered themselves as tribute-payers.
Notes by Ismael Boulliau
(51) In the days of Emperor Michael, Phokaia had devolved to him from his ancestors, having been bestowed by the emperor, the grandfather of the emperor, for the sake of administration and the payment of certain funds. Hence, at fixed times, those succeeding to its administration were always going about renewing the payment of the allotment by imperial letters, lest the long passage of time should surreptitiously infringe upon the imperial lordship. C ... and despised the younger [Andronikos] as weakened in power: to whom, however, the Genoese later surrendered Phokaia and Mytilene. From these words of Gregoras, it is evident that Phokaia had been granted to the Cataneo family as a fief, or rather had been let by the emperor by an emphyteutic contract for the sake of receiving an annual pension or tax. But when Gregoras speaks here of the grandfather of Emperor Andronikos the Younger, it must be understood as referring to Andronikos the Elder, whom the younger succeeded. But those words show that this Cataneo did not receive it from his father or grandfather, but at least from a great-grandfather; therefore, due to the exigency of the times, Michael Palaiologos, who [as Bizaro says in book IV of his History of the Genoese] gave Smyrna and Chios to the Genoese in 1261, granted it to them. Thus, Ducas has handed down the matter accurately, as he could well have known how it was done, being one who managed the affairs of the prince of Lesbos and possessed a house in Phokaia.
They promised to pay each year to Sarchan fifteen thousand in small silver coins, equaling the value of five hundred gold coins; and that every year the governor of the city who happened to be in office should go out and pay his respects to the aforementioned chief, along with ten thousand in silver coins. And thus, the Turks and Romans lived together in peace, having no trouble from anyone; but they went out without hindrance and traded. Likewise, the Turks would enter the city without fear and receive what they needed in abundance, living together as friends. Such an agreement holds until this day, nearly one hundred and eighty years since it was first established. The governance of this same city is as follows: Since the Genoese Republic is governed democratically and no one can rule it tyrannically, it is customary every year, or sometimes after a longer interval, to send officials to the eastern parts in the cities under Genoese rule, such as on the island of Chios, in this Phokaia, in Galata, in Amisus, in Amastris, in Capha. And when the set time has passed, they send another, and the old one departs, ceding his seat to the new one; whom they call in their own language Podesta, which one might interpret in Roman terms as an official with authority.
At that time, while Mehemet was still alive, there came from Genoa one Podesta, being one of the most illustrious of Genoa, named John Adorno, youthful in years but old in wisdom, son of George Adorno, who had served as Doge of Genoa. Having been entrusted with the Podestaria for ten years, he returned from Genoa to Phokaia. And indeed, having gone out according to the ancient custom and having encountered the Emir Mehemet, and having performed the accustomed proskynesis, and having finally received the alum metal, as he did every year, he pledged to pay twenty thousand gold coins over ten years, and he returned to Phokaia, where he began to mine with great expense. Six years then having passed, the end of the aforementioned Emir came, and the proclamation of the aforementioned Mustapha took place. Cineites also happily watched for the day he had hoped for; and Bajazites saw the day that was fatal for him, and all things which I have recorded have come to pass. At that time, the aforementioned John Adorno seized the opportunity to approach the new leader, Morat, to see him and pay homage, and to receive new orders, and to pay the tribute owed for the six years; for during these years he had suffered no small loss, for during those very times there was fierce war between the Genoese and the Catalans. The Catalans intercepted the ships of the Genoese and prevented them from sailing to the parts of Italy, Gaul, Spain, and England, and the alum trade was sluggish and at a standstill; and Adorno, in all...
because he was weighed down by foreign debt and had nothing with which to relieve his affairs, conceived a noble and wise plan to secure profit for himself, though it was to the damage of very many Christians. For, having chanced upon an opportunity he had never hoped for, he sent letters—which I have transcribed—to Murad before he departed from Amasia, in which he commemorated the great friendship and intimacy that had existed between himself and his father, Mehemet, and which he now desired to renew with him. "I am," he wrote, "ready to assist in every service and to bring you help; and I shall transport you by triremes and ships from the East to the West, and I shall perform this task more promptly than any other. Only command me, and what is ordered will be quickly accomplished." Murad, having therefore listened to his words, received them gladly and wrote back, saying, "With God's help, in a few days I am about to arrive in Prusa; let one of your own most trusted intimates come there, so that we may deliberate on this matter, and what and how we shall do it." After a few days, he sent a certain Demetrios, surnamed Aga, with letters of great importance—which I have also transcribed—to Murad and to his viziers, Alibeig, Hadji-Avat, and Omur-bengin; for Bajazet had already been slain by Mustapha. Therefore, having duly arranged and settled everything with Demetrios, they sent back with him a man named Hatip, a Turk, one of the most prudent and distinguished, to give a pledge of faith to Adorno, and he also had with him fifty thousand gold coins to hire a fleet and prepare it to cross the strait of Gallipolis, as autumn was already beginning. But Mustapha, having learned of the plans and preparations of Murad and that the New Phocaea was preparing a fleet against him, felt pain in his heart, and his mind was pricked by his thoughts; he kept Phocaea constantly on his tongue, and meditated on its destruction. Yet he did not abandon his pleasures, luxury, and drunkenness; rather, like a fierce horse, he neighed and spent himself in lust, abusing both women and men promiscuously. But Ceneites, hearing these things and watching to see how they would turn out, and seeing Mustapha living in folly and mentioning nothing to him about war or any other preparation against his enemies, entered the palace of Mustapha and began to make such words of reproach to him: "Are you unaware, O Prince, that only the region which the Thracians inhabit remains in our faith? But the other provinces, lying far and wide like the sea—I mean those of the West—are wavering and awaiting the outcome of future events, to see whither fortune may lead. For it has reached the ears of those peoples that Murad is in talks with the Emperor to bring him help and restore him to his paternal rule. Now he has even struck up a friendship with the Franks (33). Everything in the West was in their hands. We, meanwhile, sitting quietly and securely in Adrianople, are doing nothing in the way of military strategy. As it seems to me, at least, before the enemies cross the strait..."
either from Lampsacus or from Scutarium, and create an uproar in the provinces of the West, and discord breaks out in the army, it is better for us to be the first to cross with the Western troops, to cross the bridge at Lopadium with speed and without hesitation, and to join battle with Murad. We, God willing, are superior to our opponents in both chariots and horses; and, once our arrival is known to them, their mind will be crushed like a reed, and their plans will be scattered, as is destined to happen to us also, if we neglect our affairs and allow them space to cross.”
After saying these things and more, Cüneyt, with Mustapha finally roused from the stupor of his drunkenness, persuaded him by such words. For Cüneyt was not planning so solicitously for Mustapha in order to install him as lord of the East; but, being a knave, and foreseeing the man’s impending ruin due to his ineptitude, drunken stupor, debauchery, and his lack of military command, he wanted to escape. And while he was in such a frame of mind, he reflected within himself that if he attempted this in Thrace or another province of the West, he would easily fall back into the hands of the emperor. And again, Lemnos or another island would await him as an exile, and bitter would be the punishment exacted from him by the Romans. But he had in mind the East, and he was being nurtured by the hope of the province which he had formerly ruled; and he felt there would be an easy escape there. But these things were hidden in the recesses of Hades.
And so, having assembled an army and having made a rapid march, they came to Gallipoli; and having crossed the strait with a great force, they stayed in Lampsacus for three days. As they were coming, the principal Phrygians of the surrounding cities were paying homage to Mustapha. But Murad, hearing of the incursion of Mustapha, set out from Prusa with a select army and came by night to Lopadium, having with him those who were skilled in knowledge and war, both Hadji-Ivaz and the sons of Temirtes-beg—Ali, and Homur, and Orudj-beg—men who were brave and excellent. There was also with them Hamza-beg, the brother of Cüneyt, who had grown up from childhood in the familiarity of Murad. Having therefore reached the bridge before Mustapha could secure it with a garrison, they destroyed it and cut off the road by which they could be reached. Mustapha, having then set out with the entire army, pitched his camp at the bank of the marsh; and Murad, likewise, in the opposite tents.
Notes of Ismael Bullialdus
(54) Although the knave Cüneyt had indeed followed the side of Mustapha of his own accord, and by his own testimony vindicated the status of his birth, asserting that he was the true son of Bayezid, when he joined Mustapha he perhaps believed him to be more energetic; but when he felt himself deceived by hope and opinion, he preferred to consult his own interests by deserting him rather than to perish with him. Cüneyt has many followers, Cicero fewer: he who, when he clearly perceived the imprudence and negligence of Pompey, but recognized Caesar as more sharp and energetic, deliberately chose, by adhering to the doomed Pompeian faction, to face the dangers hanging over the vanquished rather than to betray his loyalty.
(55) "In the authorities." He wished to write "in the powers"; but the perennial iotacism of faulty pronunciation also confuses these in writing, unless the writer is most skilled in the Greek language.
(56) It is called Ulubat. Leuncl.
(57) Clavius, book XII, calls him Chazi-Eivazem. Among the Turks, he is called a Chazi who has gone to Mecca or Medina for the sake of religion.
and set up their camps on the bank of the lake. Similarly, Morat took his position on the opposite side, and he too sat encamped, neither one having the slightest fear of the other. For the destruction of the bridge had been a wise decision; since the arriving enemies, finding the bridge broken, were prevented from continuing their march. But the forces of Morat gathered without fear; for the deep and utterly impassable river made the road to them inaccessible to the hostile forces. And if one wished to travel around the entire lake to reach the opposite side, it would not take less than three days' time, and that through narrow, rugged, and difficult mountains.
CHAPTER XXVI
The counsel of the vizier of Morat concerning the destruction of Mustapha, and how he solicits Cineites to defect through his brother Hamza. The conversations of Hamza and Cineites. Cineites deserts Mustapha and flees to Ionia. He attacks the son of Homur, Mustapha, who was of the line of Aline, and kills him in battle.
When the camps were thus situated and they looked upon each other from opposite sides, since neither could move himself or progress against the other, the counselors of Morat debated among themselves by what arts they might bring down and destroy Mustapha. This plan, therefore, entered their minds. They summoned Hamza, whom we have already mentioned, the brother of Cineites, and addressed him with these words: "If you provoke your brother against Mustapha—and we ask for nothing else than that he desert him—behold, with the approval and decree of our lord Morat, we grant him the province of Atin. We will secure it for him by a written document, that he and his descendants shall possess it by hereditary right: he shall only provide an oath that he will remain in loyalty, that he will cultivate friendship without deceit, and that he will profess himself a client of Morat. And so that it may be known throughout the entire domain that Cineites is entirely subject to the command of Morat, every year he shall send one of his sons for the sake of showing reverence and honor to the emperor, who shall accompany Morat, perform military service for him, and receive appropriate wages from the emperor in the name of that service."
These words pleased Hamza; and that night he sent one of his servants, who swam across the lake and, entering the tents of Cineites, found him sitting in a state of anxious thought during the second watch of the night. He said to him, "Your brother, my master Hamza-beg, wishes to have speech with you, which it is not permitted for another to hear. If, therefore, it pleases you, come alone around the middle hours of the night to the bank of the river near the bridge; there you from this side, and he from the other, may confer between yourselves about those secret matters." Cineites heard these words kindly, and dismissed the messenger, who swam back to the other bank. The next night, near the second watch, Hamza came to the bank near the bridge as agreed; and he [Cineites] came from the other side, alone to him alone, and having made himself known by certain signs, Hamza began to speak: "You know precisely, my lord brother, that I was born of your father, and that you are the offspring of my mother, and that I am younger in age. I would desire, therefore, that you might rule the whole world, since I would be called to a share of the empire."
Yet as I would gladly wish this, so it is hateful, undesirable, and loathsome to me that you should be in distress and danger, and in the midst of many who nourish envy against you. For I shall truly not be without a share in your misfortunes and calamities. Do you even know with whom you are riding, or with whom you are living? First, all men cry out that Mustapha is not of the Othmanian lineage; and this assertion has been mocked everywhere. Second, that even when the facts are compared, it demonstrates his incompetence in warfare and his effeminacy. For those who are descended from the line of our rulers have displayed warlike spirits, and the heroic deeds and military campaigns of each individual are known to the world. Third, if this effeminate man and barbarian layman attain the monarchy, those from of old who were the guardians of the West and of the borders of the Danube—I mean the Abranezides and the Turachanides, and every other descendant of those whom the West has recognized as the heads of the principality from the beginning—and why do I mention the Westerners? For if fortune, which God forbid, should assist Mustapha with its favor, he himself, embracing all the leaders of the East, will restore to them all their ancestral honors. But you, when these things come about, what do you expect other than the end of your life, and that a shameful one and unworthy of your courage? For all distinguished men know the readiness of your spirit and your leonine boldness for entering into battles. Envy looks at your virtues with savage and hostile eyes. Envy is followed by fear; and those who consider that you will bring destruction upon them, because they are envious, they themselves get ahead and act upon their envy against you, pre-arranging their own security and driving away their fear. Therefore, for these pressing reasons, which, when ignored, destroy the souls of heroes—to whom I consider you an equal—abandon this infamous man and come over to us. For already my master Morat, through the exhortation of the nobles of his court and myself, forgives all the failures and deeds committed by you; and all the rebellions and acts you have attempted against him and his father, and against their principality. And with a peaceful and favorable eye he looks upon you, and through me he grants you the province of Atin as a hereditary possession, so that both you and those from your loins will enjoy this as an inheritance; with the sole condition laid down, that when time demands, you shall send one of your sons to serve in his army, and that you acknowledge yourself as subject to his empire. I speak these things to you as a friend; but do you explain to me what you think. D To these things, Tzinjet began to say to Hamza: "You know accurately, brother, that from the Othmans I have seen no profit, nor honor, nor rank. But they have seen much from me in their times of distress; and these arms have performed many and countless warlike deeds. For after..."
the incursion of the Tartars, who was it that rescued this very prefecture—which Morates now promises to give me—from the hands of Homur, son of Atin? Was it not Cineites? Did I not pursue his brother Isas, and shut him up in the small fortress of Palaeopolis, and having captured him, put him to death? Did I not also kill Homur, his brother, by treacherously murdering him—both of them being the natural and legitimate heirs to that prefecture? Meanwhile, Musulman, the uncle of Morates, whom you call your master, was sitting in Thrace, indulging his own whims. But I proclaimed him lord of Ephesus and all Ionia. Later, when he cast me out, he bestowed that prefecture upon Kelpaxisi, a man of Triballian descent and a purchased slave. And in this condition things stand: that prefecture which he now grants me, the son of that Homur whose head I cut off, now possesses, having been sent into the possession of his father's domain; he has been ruling it for about a year or more, and all who are subject to it serve and obey him. If God grants me that land as a reward for my military deeds, what thanks will I owe to Morates? None at all. For the grandfather of Morates, that Ilerim Bayazit, seized and took possession of this land from the grandfather of the current Mustapha, son of Atin. Thus, I too, God willing, shall today become its master. Since, therefore, you have come for this purpose, brother, I promise you before God and his prophet that from now on I shall be a sincere friend to Morates, and when there is need of an army, one of my sons shall always accompany Morates. For C I, even without these agreements, was intending to go to Ionia to engage with Mustapha, the grandson of Atin. Since, therefore, you, my brother of the same heart and the same father, have requested that I be a friend to Morates, I promise it now, and the coming night I shall begin to demonstrate by my actions the things agreed upon with me.
When they had departed from one another, Hamzas reported the things said and agreed upon to Morates and the council, and it pleased them all, and they took courage, and conceived good hopes. On the following evening, at the first watch of the night, Cineites left his tents standing as they were, and with many lamps lit in their midst; and having gathered all things useful for this business—namely, chariots, and horses of the finest quality, and every other supply of gold and silver—he ordered his servants, purchased with money, and his friends, not a few—about seventy in number—to mount their horses. Each one carried in his clothing a suitable portion of the load, whether of gold or silver or some other precious material, which did not have an excessively great bulk, and they departed, entirely without...
noticing them. They left behind the heavy baggage and all things difficult to carry; likewise horses, camels, mules, and every other supply. Having traveled through the whole night and crossed mountains and plains, by morning they reached the borders near Lydia, in the regions towards Chliera and Thyatira, having completed a journey of two days in that one night. And towards the third hour of the day, having crossed the Hermus River, by evening they arrived at Smyrna, not being hindered by anyone at all; except that when they wished to cross at the bank of the Hermus River, some Turks who were there tried to prevent the crossing, reckoning that they were of Mustapha’s party. For indeed all of Asia was troubled by the expedition of Mustapha toward the east. Cineites, having turned and pursued them, slaughtered some with his sword, and having wounded others with arrows, he himself continued his journey without fear. The Smyrneans, seeing the orderly troop, and being puzzled as to whose it was and who was its leader, when they learned that it was Cineites, all ran out with wives and children at the sight of Cineites. For he was a Smyrnean by birth, and rearing, and grew up together with them all. Having learned from them that Mustapha, the grandson of Atyn, was residing in Ephesus and Thyra, he himself penetrated into the inner parts of the province, where Bryela, Erythrae, Clazomenae, and other villages are situated. All the Turks who inhabit these further borders are most warlike and very much accustomed to fighting, and a hereditary friendship existed between them and Cineites’ father. Having gathered, therefore, two thousand from among them, and having prepared spears from the branches of trees, and having forged lances in haste in the space of one week—making them rough and uneven—and having added to them two thousand archers armed with axes and spears, he led them on.
When Mustapha learned of the arrival of Cineites, and having assembled a multitude of troops, he went out from Ephesus and arrived at Smyrna in order to meet him. But he, having learned this, went off to meet him. And when they had met one another in a certain place called Mesaulion, and had prepared the battle lines of each side as best they could—for the place was marshy and full of wood—the war-trumpet of Mustapha sounded. For Cineites possessed neither a trumpet nor anything else of the sort. Both armies having engaged, Cineites, entering like an eagle among sparrows and scattering them hither and thither through the trees, encountered Mustapha somewhere and struck him on the head with an iron staff; and the wretch, not bearing the blow, fell forward from his horse and expired. Then all those who followed Mustapha approached and did homage to Cineites, and hailed him as leader. And immediately, with a great escort, they rode toward Ephesus, and there...
he was received with great applause as their leader and acclaimed as a friend. Mustapha’s body he finally ordered to be carried out by the noblest men with the greatest pomp, and to be buried in the little tower with his ancestors. And in this way Cineites was proclaimed leader a second time.
CHAPTER XXVII
Various discussions regarding the flight of Cineites; upon learning this, Mustapha takes to flight and crosses into Thrace. Adurnus transports Morat and his forces from Asia into Europe. Mustapha tries in vain to prevent this with great promises. Morat, having disembarked his troops onto land, puts the Mustapheans to flight, recaptures Callipolis, and makes for Adrianople. Mustapha is captured and, in a public place in the city, is suspended by a noose and strangled.
But let us return and see what happened to those whom Cineites left behind in his flight. When the nobles rose in the morning and, according to custom, came together, they discussed among themselves how a great commotion had arisen during the past night in the tents of Cineites. Some said that he had crossed to the other bank and joined Morat; others, who harbored envy against him, boasted that what had happened had been predicted by them. The army of Morat, which was sitting on the opposite bank, also learned that Cineites had truly fled. Then, in the camp of Morat, one could hear the sound of trumpets and other instruments, with shouts and signs of joy that reached up to the heavens; at the same time, riders were seen on the banks of the marsh. Mustapha, having been awakened and learning of the flight of Cineites, realized that he had surely crossed to the other bank and taken lodging with Morat. Trembling with fear, he hastened to withdraw from that place, and it was possible to see his army shivering, overcome by panic. But the enemy on the opposite side pursued them, raising a clamor, attacking them with insults, and shouting boldly in their own language, "Dur, Dur, Callan!" which means, "Stop, stop, do not flee!" For they had no way to cross and join battle, as the bridge had been destroyed. Mustapha, therefore, mounted his horse and departed toward the regions of Lampsacus, hastening to reach the opposite shore. On that day, Morat repaired and rebuilt the bridge by bringing up large timbers and beams, and, having crossed, most of Mustapha's soldiers ran to him, paying him homage and acclaiming him. Mustapha arrived at Lampsacus, truly like the jackdaw of the proverb stripped of its feathers; and in a single small boat, which he found ready, accompanied by only four servants whom he used as couriers, he crossed to Callipolis. Having gathered the light-armed infantry of Callipolis, he waited to see what would happen. Morat, having crossed the bridge, sent couriers to Phocaea to Adurnus, telling him of the events and urging him to sail with his whole fleet as quickly as possible to the straits. Adurnus, therefore, having his ships ready, boarded them, set his sails, and sailed toward the Hellespont, having the wind blowing from
astern. Sailing through the night, at daybreak he appeared between Lampsacus and Callipolis, and at that very hour Morates was on the shore. A Having arrived near—for there were seven oversized ships—Morates went into the better and larger one. Adurnus, as was fitting, paid great honor to Morates, and Morates likewise to Adurnus, and they sat together in the ship and conversed. For Morates was anxious, fearing lest the Franks, having despised their oaths, might deliver him into the hands of Mustaphas, and having taken vast treasures, might depart. Morates had with him in the ship which he boarded more than five hundred of his own servant-soldiers, along with his satraps, and Adurnus had placed in the same ship more than eight hundred brave Frankish soldiers; in the remaining ships there were as many Turkish passengers as each ship possessed as a contingent of Frankish soldiers. Adurnus, however, was keeping his oaths intact and without any deceit. While they were in the middle of the strait, Adurnus stood up, and kneeling before Morates, requested that the debt owed for the alum mine be gifted to him. And Morates, rejoicing, granted it, and a reed pen was dipped to erase the payment of the old debt; and the debt was about twenty-seven thousand coins in total count.
Mustaphas, standing on the opposite shore and observing the ships—like small towns in the middle of the sea, or like islands—was wounded in his soul, for that day was clear. And not knowing what to do, he sent one of the boats to call over one of the more intimate friends of Adurnus, pretending he had some matters to discuss. Adurnus sent his vicar, Barnabas de Cornelia, and having happened upon Mustaphas, he promised to give Adurnus fifty thousand coins, if only he would not put him out of the ship, but send him elsewhere wherever he wished. But Adurnus did not wish to listen. Morates, having heard what had happened, embraced Adurnus and said, “Be from now on our brother and faithful friend.” Then, having stood opposite Callipolis, the men of Mustaphas did not allow them at all to approach the harbor. The captains of the ships, towards the lower parts of the harbor outside the city in the sea, lowered their sails and at the same time prepared their anchors for battle in order to disembark on land. And the men of Mustaphas ran along the shore and stood opposite, preventing the landing. Adurnus, having prepared the rowboats and the skiffs and small boats of the ships—more than twenty—sent them so that they might take the land, being more than five hundred Frankish crossbowmen and javelin-men within them. Having disembarked, therefore, and sent the archers about a mile away from the shore, and while they were defending the coast, safely Morates also disembarked, surrounded by a thousand ambidextrous archers, and...
more than three thousand highly warlike soldiers. The Franks, positioned at the front of the battle line, made a path by hurling lances and throwing stones. Then those with Morates, once a trumpet blast had been sounded together with the Franks, rushed against Mustaphas, who turned his back and fled, pursued by them without ceasing until they killed many of them. Morates then marched toward the city’s small fort. Mustaphas meanwhile made for Adrianople as quickly as possible, and having entered the treasury where the treasures were kept, he took as much money as he wished, packed it, and set out toward the regions of Wallachia, urging on his horses as much as he could. Morates, having spent three days in Callipolis and having taken the fortress, cruelly slaughtered all those who had resisted him to prevent him from disembarking at the harbor. Then he set out, hastening toward Adrianople, having with him a vast army gathered from the east and the west, and John Adurnus as well, with all his ship commanders, followed by a force of more than two thousand Italian foot soldiers—sturdy men, breathing war, whose body armor was made of black bronze and whose weapons were spears and battle-axes. As he approached Adrianople, all the citizens poured out to meet him, greeting him with cheers; he addressed them all with kindness. Upon entering his father’s palace, he provided a rich banquet and feast for everyone, inviting all the Latins along with Adurnus, and they all rejoiced and praised him. Having bestowed many gifts upon Adurnus, he also granted him Peritheorion, [(44)] one of the small cities of the west, to possess and enjoy for his entire life, as well as the customs duties of Phocaea; and having rewarded the other ship captains with precious garments and other magnificent gifts, he dismissed them with thanks and in peace. They traveled to Callipolis, and having set their sails, they departed for the sea toward Phocaea. Meanwhile, Morates dispatched very swift young men and bold commanders, who captured Mustaphas somewhere near the bank of the Ister. For he had intended to enter Constantinople, but, mindful of his past deeds, his own conscience restrained him. They brought him before Morates, who passed sentence that he should be strangled in a public place [(45)] like one of the criminals, so that the public of the common people, if not all, at least the greatest part, might believe that he was not the son of Bajazet the Ottoman, but a subject.
Ismaelis Bullialdi notes
[(44)] Peritheorion. This is a fortress; it was a bishopric under the metropolitan of Trajanopolis. Regarding that place, Cantacuz. Hist. lib. II, c. 38, speaks thus while reviewing the towns restored by the younger Andronicus: "But he also rebuilt another city on the coast of Thrace, which had been previously destroyed; they claim the emperor Anastasius was the author of its foundation, and that it was called Anastasiopolis from his name. Him [Andronicus] restored it; not the whole thing, indeed, but as much area as he was able to enclose, and he called it Peritheorion." That city is situated in Thrace, near the city [of Maroneia], not far from the island of Thasos. [(45)] Strangled, Leunclavius says in lib. XIII, in a public place, so that men might believe Mustaphas was an impostor. For Muslim princes are accustomed to kill their brothers and blood relations secretly and out of the sight of men. Furthermore, regarding the note of years, observe...
people, if not all, then the vast majority of the populace, held the opinion that he was not the son of Bajazet Othman, but was a fraudulent person, invented by the Emperor Manuel Palaiologos. The truth, however, is that he was truly the son of Bajazet.
Chapter XXVIII
Morates attacks Constantinople, while the Emperor John administers the affairs of the empire on account of Manuel's old age and infirmity. Corax the Theologian is condemned for treason; wishing to avenge his death, Morates hastens to put Michael Pyllim to death for having denounced Corax; Pylles, by impiously abjuring Christ and the faith, saves his life. Manuel excites Mustapha, a boy of eleven, the brother of Morates, against him, and immediately dies. Mustapha, being captured at Nicaea, is strangled by his brother. Morates invades Thessaly and the Peloponnese. He wages war against Cineas through his pashas and defeats him; and at last destroys him and his whole race.
When Morates, after winter had already set in, had mounted the throne of his father’s principality, with the approach of the next spring, he issued a public edict and by the voice of heralds commanded the soldiers to come to arms, and gathering a great army, he prepared to lay siege to the city of Constantinople. For a long time, the Emperor Manuel had ceded the empire to his son John, and he himself, being an old man, remained at rest, occupied with the study of divine writings. Having learned, therefore, that Morates intended to wage war against him in that month—it being April—he sent an ambassador to him named Corax the Theologian, a man who originated from Philadelphia, and who, after the invasion of the Tatars into Asia, had moved his place of residence to Constantinople. He was, in fact, more cunning than any other man of that time, and most wicked in his dealings with the Turks, as well as in his calumnies. Having established a familiarity with some of the court officials, he had also become known to the Emperor Manuel. And because he practiced the Turkish language and understood it as much as was necessary, he was always sent along with the emperor’s ambassadors, serving as an interpreter and translating what was said by the ambassadors to the viziers of the then-ruling prince Mahomet. As time was often consumed in such tasks, he became known also to the prince Mahomet and to the great vizier Bajazet, and he became so intimate that if there was anything the emperor wished to communicate to Mahomet, or Mahomet to the emperor, the Theologian would instantly weave it together, and he appeared to both to be a great adjudicator of many affairs. Envy, however, which grudges at all things good, directed its sharp arrows against the Theologian. When Mahomet had passed away, and Bajazet the vizier had died, and affairs had shifted in the aforementioned [manner]—
Note of Ismael Bullialdus
It must be noted that Leunclavius, *Hist. Musulm.* lib. XIII, refers the war brought by Mustapha against Morates and all the events that took place up to his death to the year of the Hegira 825 [Christi 1423]; for he began that year of the Hegira, 821, on December 26, the sixth feria, solar cycle 2, letter E. And Phranzes reported the same year in book I, chapter 40. But the same Leunclavius in the *Turkish Annals* at the year of the Hegira, [wrongly printed in Leunclavius] 827 [Christi 1424], narrates that Mustapha Dusme was saluted as emperor, having been captured and strangled. It is necessary, therefore, to reconcile these matters by using caution; so that we may say that after the death of Mehemet, Mustapha immediately rebelled against his son Morates and acted as emperor. This war was waged for three years, and at length, Mustapha being captured and strangled, it was finished in the year of the Hegira 827 [Christi 1424]. That this Mustapha reigned for three years is testified by Laonicus in book V: "Mustapha ended his life after he had reigned for three years in Europe." More deeds indeed were done, more negotiations agitated, and ambassadors sent to and fro to conclude alliances, than could have been completed in the space of one year. Correctly, therefore, Calvisius in his *Chronology* assigns the death of Mustapha to the year of the Arabs (strictly 1424), which we also, and the *Turkish Annals*, follow. Mustapha ended his life having reigned in Europe for three years.
A ...by the help of the Romans, unto Mustapha, as aforesaid, does the sum of affairs devolve. And the sweet friendship which had been cultivated between them was transformed again into hatred and rivalry upon the empire shifting once more to Morates. And since the Emperor had determined to mitigate and appease this bitterness, he sent as envoys to Morates, Palaeologus Lachanas and Marcus Jagaris, men distinguished for their nobility and prudence, that they might satisfy him with plausible arguments that the Emperor was not the cause of those things which had befallen Morates, but rather Bajazit, who was then administering the affairs of the state; for he had been unwilling to hand over the infants to the Emperor, as he had been commanded by the will of their father, though he had been admonished by the entreaties of Bajazit: nay, he had even dismissed with contumely the envoys who requested them. But Morates would neither see nor hear these envoys, but kept them held apart for a few days, until he had gathered what was necessary for him for this military expedition to assault the city of Constantinople. Afterwards he dismissed them, having given this reply: "Depart and announce to your Emperor that I shall arrive shortly." A few days later, having gathered all his forces in one place—a vast army of two hundred thousand soldiers or more—he marched against Constantinople.
For this reason, the citizens were brought into suspicion regarding some atrocious act concerning the Theologian, saying that he had engineered fraud and treachery against the city, bearing it ill that he had not set out with the envoys. For the Theologian was, for the most part, disposed kindly toward the Turkish commanders, and loved their emperor. Manuel, having learned of the envy of the tumultuous crowd against the Theologian, sent him to Morates as if to negotiate peace; for Morates had already encircled and entrenched the city, and had pitched his tents within the sanctuary of the Fountain (the Pēgē) near the walls of the city. The Theologian, having gone out of the city and met with Morates and his high-ranking men, and having labored much and spoken concerning peace, was unable by any means to persuade the tyrant. But, it was reported in the opinion of the many, he had wished to come to terms with the Turk on this condition: "If," said he, "you bind your faith with an oath that you will not make me prefect of the city, I will hand it over to you"; which words one of his most faithful friends, who was present, overheard. Having made such a pact, he returned to the city, so that on the day agreed upon and appointed when the Turks were to assault the city, he would stand at the Gate of the Fountain, surrounded by his men, and introduce them. The Theologian immediately met with the Emperor, to report the account of those things which the envoy had negotiated. But he, having heard word of the matters recited above from another, reported it to the crowd and revealed the betrayal which the Theologian was meditating, and secured belief for his words by certain pieces of evidence. When the Theologian had gone out from the monastery—for the Emperor, being old and infirm, was then living in the monastery of the Peribleptos…
While the elder [note: referring to the previous context, the ailing Emperor John Ⅷ] was dwelling in the monastery of the revered Virgin, the Theologian departed. Emperor John, who was intent on repelling the attack of the enemy, had some of the city's leading men and light-armed soldiers simultaneously shouting humiliations and insults against him. Having become aware of this tumult, Manuel inquired what had happened; then those present brought before him the man who had revealed the betrayal. Manuel wished to calm this tumult and ordered the Theologian to be held in custody, along with his accuser, so that on the next day the matter might be clearly understood. The Cretans, who were on guard at the Emperor's gate, having heard the rumor of the betrayal, gathered together and approached him (the Cretans had always rendered the most faithful service in every way, were burning with divine love for the temples of the saints and their relics, and ardently desired the imperial majesty of the city to be safe); they therefore said: "Emperor, it is not fair that we should prefer this city to our own homeland and be lavish with our own blood for the protection of this imperial city, while the natives, and those who have renown and authority in it, wish to betray the divine mysteries and your empire. Command, therefore, that the Theologian be delivered into our hands, that we may examine the whole matter accurately." The Emperor Manuel replied that he feared lest the man be in danger of his life due to envy, and to these he added such words: "If I had truly known he was guilty of any crime, I would have immediately punished him with the most shameful death. Therefore, take him in chains and examine him, and conduct the inquiry. If he should be innocent, absolve him. If he is proven guilty, let him pay the penalty." Diligent inquiry was therefore made concerning the Theologian, who was in chains, with torments being applied; certain proofs became evident to those investigating exactly, when there were found in his house very many gold and silver vessels, garments also woven with gold, and documents undoubtedly composed against the Emperor. These vessels had indeed been given to him by the Emperor to bestow later upon the Turk, which he, having committed theft, was concealing for himself. Then the Cretans, having dragged him through the main street to the imperial gate, there put out his eyes with inhuman and altogether bestial cruelty; they gouged them out in such a way that not even traces of eyelids or skin appeared. Being then thrown into prison, he died after three days; and his house, having been plundered of the many treasures which were in it, was destroyed by fire. When Mourat heard of the death of the Theologian, and the cause of the slaughter, he was inflamed with anger and grief; certain men suggested to him that no one else was the author of this slaughter but Michael Pyllis. This Pyllis was an Ephesian, a Roman by race, Christian in rite, and born of a noble family of that city. He was skilled in the Roman and Arabic tongues and worked as a scribe in the prefect's palace. However, he was corrupt and wicked in his morals, wallowing in luxury and intemperance, and was altogether profane. Him, then, they brought to the tyrant's court, and accused him to Emperor Manuel of having revealed by letter that Corax the Theologian was about to betray the city; and his
fate was to be condemned to death. Then they bound him and harassed him with fierce tortures, for he was hateful to all; finally, having kindled a pyre, they placed the wretch upon it. And they asked him if he wished to abjure the Christian faith, so that he might be saved; otherwise, the fire would consume him. Then he, who in his character and deeds had already been a Turk before his formal abjuration, betrayed the Christian faith by renouncing it; having been circumcised, he was then led away with much pomp. After many years had passed in that execrable profession, having paid his debt to nature, he cast off his soul.
Meanwhile, Emperor Manuel, who, as one might say, had death before his eyes every single day, lying bedridden, devised a plan against Morates. Of the two sons of Mehemet, the brothers of Morates, he had already throttled one with a noose, according to the cruel and wicked custom that prevailed among them. As for the other, who was also named Mustapha, after the death of their father, a certain one of the magnates of his father, named Eliez—who performed the office of cupbearer, called in the Turkish tongue Siaraptar—having stolen him away after the father's death, transported him to the parts of Anatolia toward Cappadocia. To this Siaraptar Eliez, the Emperor wrote letters in secret, in which he invited and urged him to bring that boy to Prusa. At the same time, he sent a great sum of money so that he might hire soldiers for pay, raise a new army, and introduce the boy into the province of Bithynia. Morates was occupied meanwhile with constructing engines for the purpose of tearing down the battlements of the walls, and was wearing out those besieged with skirmishes, being desirous of possessing Constantinople; when, after a few days, one of the couriers arrived, bringing news to Morates that his brother Mustapha had entered Prusa, and had been received kindly and with applause by the citizens as their prince. And that, having departed from Prusa with Siaraptar Eliez, he had proceeded to Nicaea. Having learned these things, Morates reflected within himself: "The Emperor of the Romans has another Mustapha at the ready, through whom he will bring me troubles." Moved by this new state of affairs, Morates desisted from his hostile actions; he dismissed his immense army, giving them the opportunity to depart. Leaving aside his towers and engines for the storming and defeating of the city, he returned to Adrianople.
While these things were happening, Emperor Manuel, having become paralyzed and drawing his final breaths, was lying and within three days he paid his debt to nature. He was most wise and virtuous, illustrious in temperance and modesty; he left the empire to his son John, the last Emperor of the Romans, who in truth surpassed all others in virtues worthy of the empire. D Morates, therefore, proceeded with his armies against
the city for three months. After he had recovered and entered Hadrianople, he came to Callipolis after three days. Having crossed over with a sufficient force of foot soldiers and a few horsemen—with no one knowing where he was going—he arrived at Nicaea, after traveling for one day and a night, early, while it was still dark, and signified his arrival to those who remained in the faith. Through them, a commotion was stirred up in the middle of the city, the gates were opened, and as the sun was rising, Morates was received within the walls. He found the boy, Mustapha, about six years of age, and strangled him, and slaughtered his guards. When he saw the child dead, he ordered him to be taken to Prusa and delivered to the tomb near their father. In that same year, three princes who bore the name Mustapha died: one, who was considered by many to be the supposititious son of Bajazet; a second, the brother of Morates; and a third, the grandson of Atin, whom Cineites killed; and in the same year, the Emperor Manuel died. After Morates returned to Hadrianople, he did not cease day and night from searching for some pretext by which he might attack Cineites. He therefore sent a message to him, saying: "You remember well the conditions upon which you agreed with me. If you wish to be my friend, send me your son at once, for I intend to cross the Ister. But if you are not so disposed toward me, and refuse my commands, I shall act toward you as God wills." Cineites answered him: "Do as you please, but leave the outcome to God." C He therefore sent Akincidas in that year into Walachia and Serbia, revealing his proclamation as king. Legates came from all sides, wishing him well in the beginning of his reign, both from the Despot of Serbia and from the Voivode of Walachia; he therefore made peace with them. With the Emperor John, however, there was no possibility of reconciliation; for he nourished an implacable hatred. Since he could not accomplish anything against the city of Constantinople, he turned his mind toward the regions of Thessaly, the approach to the Peloponnese, and the coastal areas along the Strymon. He sent sufficient forces, blockaded Thessalonica, and ravaged the surrounding areas. He raided Zetunium and its environs. At that time, Cantacuzenus Stravometis had been sent to the governorship of Zetunium—a courageous man, if he should be called a man—who had inflicted great damage on the Turks living in those parts and was protecting the areas around Zetunium and the small town securely. Having prepared the army of the East, he sent as commander a certain Halilin, Roman by birth, the husband of the sister of the aforementioned Bajazet, whom Cineites had killed while he was with Mustapha. Having taken all the forces, he approached the regions of Philadelphia. But Cineites [the rest of the text is missing from the scan].
territory of Thyatira to meet Halil. Both encamped in such a way that they could see one another, and they were no more than five stades apart. When day broke, the clarion sounded on both sides; and when the phalanxes had been drawn up in due order, the younger of the sons of Cineites, who was also surnamed Curtis—that is to say, Wolf—rode out with his shield-bearers and the other squadrons which he led, and charged into the enemy. Like a wild boar, he hacked a path for himself through the center of their line. But the legions and troops of Halil, as they retreated, opened their ranks from the front to the rear, so that he passed through without inflicting any great damage. Then Halil, having detected that this man was unskilled and ignorant of military affairs, immediately led his forces into a narrow place and ordered them all to conceal their white head-coverings, thinking that Curtis would return by the same road. Cineites meanwhile stood ready to attack the first line of Halil, while at the same time waiting for Curtis to attack the rear on his return. For he feared that if he himself pursued Curtis straight into the enemy lines, the rest of the ranks might disperse and join themselves to Halil; for this reason, he would not move from his position while awaiting Curtis. But the latter, insolently proud, was returning at a slow pace with his cavalry and other fellow-soldiers. And having quickly completed a journey of ten stades and slaughtered those who met him, he returned by the direct road he had taken. Upon seeing a large body of soldiers in an elevated place, and hearing the sound of trumpets, and catching sight of standards similar to those that were in his father’s army, he supposed that his father had pressed upon the enemy from the rear and had put Halil to flight. When he had approached the place, however, and recognized that they were his opponents, he turned his reins and, driving backward, fled like a hare; but he was pursued by the light-armed troops, who were equal in speed to flying dogs, as one might say. In a short time, the Wolf was caught and brought to Halil. Cineites was impatient of this delay, because he had been standing idle in the meantime. But when he learned that his son had fallen into the hands of the enemy, he retreated with the remaining forces to the mountains that look toward Smyrna and traveled through steep and difficult roads until he arrived at a certain small fortress named Hypselen. For he had provided it in advance with everything necessary, and had fortified it with chariots and ships, and had also brought along all kinds of provisions. This fortress was situated on a certain gulf of Ionia, opposite the island of Samos, on the very shore of the sea. Meanwhile, Halil sent his son Curtis, bound in iron chains, to the Emir at Adrianople, as the first fruits of the Cineites who would soon be cut down by the sickle. The Emir Murad sent him and his uncle Hamza, mentioned above, bound to Gallipoli; and there, having put iron manacles on them, he threw them into the tower. Halil then, having crossed the river Hermus, and
fifty thousand; those within numbered barely a thousand, including those of the Caramanian. A Hamzas, therefore, observing that he had no power against it by land—for it was a very strong fortress, situated in a high place—sent word to Murad that they should provide for ships from the Genoese for assistance; for the fortress opened toward the sea, and showed the whole interior position to the sea, and left everything exposed. One of the Genoese known to Murad, named Persivas Palavicinus, agreed with the leader to depart and take the fortress; for Adorno had already died. He, having come to the island of Chios, and having hired three very large ships, came by sea to Hypsela. Those within, along with Cüneyd, seeing the ships, were struck with fear, and having fought on the first day, they realized on the day after that they would be surrendered. For the five hundred Caramanian soldiers, having opened the gates of the fortress during that same night, fled; some escaped safely, while others were cut down by those outside. For the subjects of the Ottoman Empire and those who followed the party of the Caramanian were always in a state of mutual hostility. In the morning, Cüneyd, seeing the crowd in an uproar, and fearing lest they might all flee in the coming night, leaving him behind, sent one of his own men to Khalil—for he was the one besieging the fortress that week; Hamzas was staying in Ephesus. He sent word to Khalil: if he would give pledges to Cüneyd that he would not kill him, but would take him alive and bring him to Murad, or send him, he would come out and surrender, and leave the city to him. Khalil having given sworn pledges, Cüneyd came out with his brother Bajazit, and they did obeisance to Khalil. He therefore gave them tents, and they rested. But Hamzas, having arrived toward evening, and having learned from his brother-in-law Khalil what had been done, sent four executioners—for he [Cüneyd] was sleeping and snoring from much wakefulness during previous nights—who crushed his head as he slept. In like manner, they cut off the head of Bajazit, and of his son, and of his descendants. They did not spare even the infants of his lineage. They sent the heads to him swiftly to Adrianople to the ruler. And the ruler sent to Gallipoli, ordering the heads of those imprisoned there to be cut off, namely Curti and his uncle Hamzas. And so it was done. And by such an event the race of Cüneyd was utterly destroyed, root and branch.

### Chapter XXIX.
John preserves peace with Murad. Murad firms peace with other princes, from which the Venetians are excluded on account of the occupation of Thessalonica: the causes are related in passing through which Thessalonica came into the power of the Venetians. Thessalonica is besieged and taken by storm and pillaged by Murad, and new inhabitants are sent into it. The Venetians, fearing worse things, enter into peace with Murad. The princes of Wallachia overturn one another from the royal throne; Draculius, having killed the others, survives as voivode of Wallachia. On account of a horse refused to him by the Caramanian, Murad brings war upon him: and between the two peace is soon after established.
John therefore the emperor, having settled affairs, and with Murad the peace having been established and strengthened, to the cities and Ismael Bullialdi note.
villages which the Pontic Sea possessed, except for the strongholds which he was unable to take in battle, such as Mesembria, Dercos, and others, and Zetunium together with the remaining regions of the Strymon, and a yearly tribute of three hundred thousand aspers, he sat in peace as much as possible. Murad, however, as fortune looked upon him with a smiling face, and he had utterly destroyed all his enemies, and had no one remaining to cause him fear or to oppose him, wandered through Thrace and arrived at Prusa. Departing thence, he crossed the bridge of Lopadium and descended into Pergamum. From Pergamum he arrived at Magnesia; from Magnesia to Smyrna, and from Smyrna to Thyrea and Ephesus. The B envoys of the neighboring princes, and also those from afar, flocked to him. For the emperor had sent his lord, Lucas Notaras, his minister, with many gifts. In like manner also Lazarus the Despot of Serbia, and Danus the prince of Wallachia, and the lord of Mitylene, and the Chians and Rhodians, all sent envoys to congratulate him on his happy and auspicious success. They all received pledges from him, and they themselves gave them, that they would be at peace and full of friendship with him, and he with them, except for the Venetians, for a reason which I shall presently recount. The Despot Andronicus, who after the emperor John and Theodore was the third son of the emperor Manuel, and who was afflicted by the sacred disease, was ruling over Thessalonica. At the time of Murad’s war—I mean the war before the city—after Mustapha had departed from Lemnos, Thessalonica was troubled by war; and all the leaders of Thessaly, Aetolia, Phthia, Thebes, and those stationed beyond Ioannina, that is to say the descendants of Abranezis, Turachanes, and many others, surrounded Thessalonica with a close siege. C The Thessalonians, therefore, being indignant at the daily incursions of the Turks and hoping that it would be liberated by none of their own people, because the city was being squeezed by internal calamities and could not endure the pressing famine and the shortage of all necessities, held a council; and the Despot willing it or not, they sent some of the leading citizens to the Venetians to surrender Thessalonica to them. The Venetians, having received the message gladly, agreed to guard and to nourish and to make the city prosperous, and to transform it into a second Venice. And the Thessalonians themselves consented to be faithful in the community of the Venetians, just as those who were born in Venice itself, and…
had been reared there. Having therefore established these conditions, they brought the duke with ten triremes to Thessalonica, and introduced him within, and escorted out the despot Andronicus. And the triremes, having offered praises to the new duke, sailed back to Boeotia. From then on, there was a multitude of wars; for the Turks said, "This city belongs to us; for if we had not shown it to be weak, it would not have turned to you." For in this frame of mind a hard battle took place, and the Turks held the upper hand, while the Thessalonians were famished. But the Latins, fearing lest the Romans, being hard-pressed, should make a revolt and bring in the Turks and drive out the Venetians—for the city had also been predisposed by the Turks—began to move the families of the noble Romans, some to Euboea, others to Crete, others to Venice. The pretext alleged for this, which was commonly bruited about, was the shortage of necessities, such as grain, barley, legumes, meats, and any other food. Therefore, so that fewer and more sparse families might remain in the city, and the citizens might be freed from these straits, the leaders changed their abodes and transferred them elsewhere, with the intention of returning later, God helping. Thus they moved most of them here and there; many were cast into the deep sea; others they punished as traitors; and those who were left behind they vexed with countless outrages and indignities.
After Murad had returned from Asia to Thrace, the Venetians sent envoys to him seeking peace. But they received no other response from him than this: "That city is my ancestral possession, and my grandfather Bayezid took it by force and hand from the Romans. If the Romans were the ones holding power there, they could justly complain that I am doing them an injury. But you, being Latins and having arrived from Italy, by what right do you meddle in the affairs of these regions? If it seems good to you, return to your own lands; otherwise, I shall be there shortly." Having therefore returned without success, they wrote this response to Venice by the guard—that is to say, the scout—triremes. Then, as spring began, Murad departed from Adrianople and came to Serres (59). Having gathered there his army from the West, he wrote to Hamza to bring the forces of the East with him, and having crossed the strait, to enter the borders of Thessaly. Having then united together, he sends him to Thessalonica with all his forces. Meanwhile, Murad remained in Serres, indulging in the good things there; for he was fond of banquets, being a young man at that time, of about twenty-five years of age. Hamza, however, was surrounding Thessalonica with a rampart, intent on the siege daily. Those who defended themselves within the walls, if their number were compared with those of the besiegers, were as one to a hundred. Then, having constructed ladders, and...
siege engines, he urged Morates to come so that they might undertake the storming of the city. Meanwhile, those who were held besieged within the city were awaiting the triremes from Venice. Consequently, Morates arrived, and he found everything skillfully prepared, and the triremes did not appear. Then Morates, through a trumpeter, announced these things to the soldiers: "Behold, I grant to you all that is in this city: men, women, children, silver, and gold; I wish only that the city be gained for me." When these things were proclaimed by the trumpeter, the blare of the trumpets was sounded, and the ladders were moved toward the walls. (What, I ask, could five hundred, or a thousand, or even two thousand men accomplish in such a great city, when scarcely one archer was present in every ten towers?) By means of the ladders, therefore, they climbed upon the walls, and at the same time they threw themselves into the city; and through one of the gates opened by them, the whole army entered like a swarm of bees. A spectacle then appeared to the eyes like a wondrous prodigy. Individual horsemen, holding chains in their hands, were dragging after them men, women, boy and girl children, and infants. Those who were dragged forth were uttering only this one cry: "Woe," and there was no one who was touched by their miseries, or who extended a helping hand. A bad omen, and a miserable precursor of the calamities that were impending over the imperial city. B Houses were stripped, temples were left desolate; the ornaments of the churches and the sacred vessels were handled by the polluted hands of the impious: venerable virgins came into the embraces of the lewd; noble women became the slaves of ignoble men; in the end, every evil overwhelmed them. What is this? How and why did it happen? Because of our sins. Thus, in the space of one day, so great a city, deprived of all its inhabitants, stood utterly desolate. But Morates the emperor brought into it from the neighboring villages and towns new Turkish colonists with their wives and children; furthermore, he proclaimed that if any of the Romans, having paid the price of redemption, should return after the war into liberty, he might come into the city and dwell there securely. The principal monasteries, whose fame was celebrated everywhere, he consecrated as temples of his own religion, except for the church of the great martyr Demetrius. For although he had entered that temple and sacrificed a ram with his own hands and had prayed to God, he nevertheless ordered it to be restored later to the Christians. However, the Turks stole all the ornamentation of the sepulcher and the shrine of the martyr, and of the temple and the sanctuary, leaving only bare walls. Then Morates departed from Thessalonica and returned to Adrianople. A few days later, the Venetians sent envoys to him, who concluded a peace, being moved by the fear that Euboea might also be snatched away from them.
During this time also, amidst the illegitimate sons of the Vaivode of Wallachia, Mylcas (such as many, being very much given to Venus,
dissipation, were living), departed from Constantinople—for he had been residing there in the palace of the Emperor John in military garb, and conversing daily with the youth, being skilled in warlike and insurgent matters. There were also certain Wallachians to be found at that time in Constantinople. Taking him, they departed to a certain corner of Wallachia; and having gathered there in significant numbers daily, a powerful force was formed. For the race of the Wallachians was unruly and of a fickle disposition, inclined toward plotting against their princes.
Now the Vaivode at that time was a nephew of Mylcas, the son of a brother named Danus. Having learned, therefore, that Mylcas was dead—though he himself was residing with Murat when he campaigned against the city [Constantinople], and being as one prepared for the onset of battle—he also, having run with the Turks into an ambush, managed to enter the city. And having made himself known to the Emperor, he went out with the Romans and performed valiantly against the Turks. When, therefore, Murat departed from the city, having not attained what he was hoping for, but instead having failed in his purpose, Danus, having done obeisance to the Emperor, sought his freedom and a direct path to return to his own lands. The Emperor, having acted generously and having placed him upon one of the greatest ships, sent him from the Pontic sea to Asprocastron. There, the nobles of Wallachia who were present acclaimed him as their prince and restored him to his ancestral principality.
Ismael Bullialdus’s Note
The narrative which has been pursued here concerning the Wallachians is to be understood correctly; we shall append the genealogical series of these princes, such as we have gathered it from his own text.
[N] 
Mylcas, or Mirkes, concerning whom see chapter 19, and this chapter 29.
 [N] 
Danus.
N. illegitimate son, killed by Danus, son of Dan.
Dracula, another illegitimate son, who killed Danus, son of Dan.
Danus killed by Dracula.
N. sent by Murat into Wallachia to rule over it: and defeated and killed by Dracula.
N. blinded by John Hunyadi. (Hist. Hung.)
Regarding Mirkes and Danus, John Thwrozius in the Hungarian Chronicles, year 1415, chapter 17, makes mention that they were born of the same blood, yet were not brothers: of whom the latter implored the aid of the Turks, the former the help of Sigismund. Likewise Anthony Bonfinius, *Rerum Hungaricarum*, decade 3, book 3, year 1415, speaks thus: "In the cause of the Wallachians there were two princes, the one Danus, the other called Mirkes, both born of the same lineage; discord arose for the sake of ruling. When Danus noticed that he was inferior in strength, he was drawn by a precipitous plan to flee for the aid of the Turks: from whom he easily obtained the auxiliaries he requested, since they thought this an excellent opportunity to occupy Dacia. Wherefore, in order to drive out the kinsman who was hostile to his kingdom, he introduced profane legions. Mirkes, lest he allow the Turks to invade Dacia, or to be cast out of the kingdom by the wealth of a wicked race, fled to the help of Sigismund, etc. Losoncius, sent with an army to protect Mirkes, was cut down by the Turks and Wallachians." Laonicus, book IV, makes words about Mirkes and Danus, whose wealth and help Moses used against the Muslim; in book V [he relates] that Dracula was defeated by Hunyadi, and Danus restored to the possession of Dacia or Wallachia.
It was asserted that he had been set over them: he killed all of Dracula's kinsmen and allies: who were the illegitimate sons of the leader Myrxas, says Laonicus. But from John Thwrozius we learn that after the rout at Varna was accepted by the Hungarians, John Hunyadi Corvinus, seeking safety in flight, escaped into Wallachia, and was there captured by the Vaivode Dracula and detained for some time. Having received such an injury, Hunyadi, incensed with anger, moves against Dracula in the year 1446, and having captured him along with his firstborn son, kills him by the sword. He also deprives the son of the Vaivode Danus of his sight. Laonicus, book VIII, also discourses on the capture of Dracula by Hunyadi: and that he moved against the Dacians in order to send Danus into possession of Wallachia. The outcome of the war was this: the Dacians abandon Dracula and go over to Danus. Dracula, deserted by his own men, betakes himself to flight, from which he is dragged back by Danus, who had pursued him, and is killed by him along with his son. Therefore, either Laonicus writes falsely concerning this Danus, or it is necessary that there were two: one, according to Hungarian history, blinded; another who, according to Laonicus, killed Dracula. Regarding these, Mirkes and Danus, Leunclavius speaks few words in *Pandectae*, number 71, but they are of no moment.
Having obtained the dominion, he sent envoys to pacify Morates, who succeeded in winning him over. For Morates was of a gentle character and possessed of praiseworthy manners; thus, with the annual tribute paid, Danus held power over Walachia in peace. But let us return to Draculius—for it was by this name, which carries the notion of perversity, that this wicked man was called. Having then waged war against Danus, he cut off his head and became master of his father's principality. Morates, having learned of the deed, took it heavily; for he had in his hands another brother of Danus, and wishing to establish him as ruler in place of the brother who had been murdered, he sent him with a force into Walachia. Draculius, having raised a fierce war against the invaders, routed them, destroyed them utterly, and with Danus's brother slain, secured the principality.
In that same year there came one of the servants of Caraman, reporting to Morates that among his horses there was one of the Arabian breed, which, in action, in age, in color, and in the symmetry of its limbs and joints, was as superior to any of those raised and trained with care and diligence among the Arabs as could be. Morates, therefore, falling into a desire for the horse, sent one of his honored servants to request it, hoping that Morates would obtain the horse upon his first message, whether for the sake of friendship or in exchange for some price. For Morates was always threatening him, having been, from his father and grandfathers, fortunate in his wars against the principality of Caraman. He was confident, therefore, on many accounts, that he would obtain the horse.
But Caraman, thinking otherwise, answered the servant of Morates: "Is your master able to mount this horse?" pointing with his finger to the horse. And he said, "Whether he is able or not is not for me to say; he has, indeed, the answer to your words. But return to me the answer that I may report to my master." Caraman said, "Announce to your master that he will not be able to sit upon this horse while he stands haughty; for I myself can barely manage to mount him, and for this reason, I do not send him to you." Morates, having heard these words, was hardened; and having gathered his armies with haste, and crossed the Strait, he arrived at Prusa, and remained there a short time until the forces of the East could assemble.
And the aforementioned Draculius, the Vaivode of Walachia, having also crossed the Strait, arrived at Prusa and met with the Emir Morates. He paid him homage and professed himself a subject, and gave his oath to Morates that whenever he should desire to move into Hungary, he would grant safe passage and point out to him the way as far as the borders of Germany and Russia. Moved by such promises, Morates admitted him as a guest and companion to his table; and having honored him with many gifts, he took leave of him and his more than three hundred followers in a friendly manner. Prusa then, having proceeded to Cotyaeum and advancing from there, he moved toward the borders of his domain.
