And having seized two cities, one of which is called in the Turkish language Aksiari, and the other Pegsiari 64; this latter city was near A Iconium, being a two days' journey away. Then Caraman, having nothing else to do, sent to him ambassadors—the most honorable of his lords—carrying a large sum of money, his horse, and the two cities he had taken, along with their fields and villages, solely for his turning back. His sister, whom Caraman had married—for Caraman was brother-in-law to Morates through his sister—also sent him letters of entreaty; and being swayed by their entreaties, he made peace with oaths, and returned.
After he came to Adrianople and learned that the Despot of Serbia, the son of Lazar 65—the brother-in-law of Bajazit, whom the narrative mentioned in the events of Bajazit’s time, namely the Ilerem—had died, he having died childless and without an heir, he sent ambassadors to his successor, demanding the whole of Serbia. Now he had a nephew through Maro, the daughter of Lazar and sister of the late Stephen. For George was the son of Vulko and son-in-law of Lazar. When he saw the ambassadors, he honored them as was fitting; and he reflected in his mind upon the deceits of the dragon, knowing that if it eats and is satisfied even a little, it will be quiet; but otherwise, if no morsel is cast into its mouth, it will devour all of Serbia, and Bulgaria, and his own ancestral lands with gaping jaws. Therefore, he maneuvered to buy time, and pledged his daughter in marriage to him, and conceded the greater part of Serbia under the name of a dowry, with this sole condition appended, that peace should quickly...
Ismaelis Bullialdi notes.
64 Aksiari, Pegsiari. Leunclavius in his 15th book calls these cities Acscheherem and Beg-Scheherem, and in the same book calls them Buscara. In the common geographical tables, Sari, which is perhaps Acsiari, is situated to the north of Iconium; Bogas, which is Begsiari or Boscara, lies to the east and south of Iconium. Ortelius is mistaken, who makes Leunclavius's Ac-Serai into Anazarbus; whereas Anazarbus was once in the eastern borders of Cilicia, which is a journey of many days from Iconium.
65 Now the Despot of Serbia, son of Lazar. That it may be clearer to the readers of the History of Ducas regarding those things that pertain to the despots of Serbia, we repeat here from Mauro Orbino, who wrote in Italian of the kingdom of the Slavs, two genealogies: one from the side of the family, namely of the Nemagna; the other of the Privazii.

Uroscus, the last king of the Nemagna family; whom Cantacuzenus, Book IV, Chapter 43, calls the son of the king: who waged war against his uncle Simon, the prince of Acarnania.
his daughter in marriage, and the greater part of Serbia as dowry; who could number the talents of gold and silver that he paid to satisfy the peace with an oath? He then sends ambassadors, who win over the prince to the conditions of this peace. He sends the Saritzas, one of his viziers, to betroth the maiden and to give oaths to George and receive assurances from him in return. The Saritzas, therefore, having met with the Despot George and completed the marriage agreement, returned. Having requested leave to build a small town on the bank of the Danube, he was granted it by Murat, and a decree was issued to him, and the Despot began to build Smederevo. And Murat, when summer was now near at hand, moved against Hungary, and having crossed the Danube toward Nicopolis, he was met by Draculus, who pledged to pay tribute and to be ready to carry out his orders. Murat, therefore, through Sarazias Bassa, demanded that not only tribute, but also Maria, the daughter of George, be given to him as a wife. As George was prepared to pay the tribute, so he was averse to that marriage. Yet, overcome by the pleas of his wife Jerine—or Irene—who hoped that by this marriage Murat would be reconciled to the Serbs, he entrusted his daughter to Chalil Bassa to be brought to Murat.
From this it is evident that Ducas, in chapter 111 of this history, was in error when he asserted that Lazarus was the son of Stephan—who in this genealogy is the son of Dusan; he likely believed that there was another son besides the son. Stephan Crala did not succeed… [Here follows the *Genealogia gentis Pribaziæ* table:]

### [Genealogy of the Pribazian race from which the last Despots of Serbia came.]
[PRIBASIUS. 1. Despot Lazarus, slain in the battle at the field of Kosovo: he took parts of the empire from Uroscus, son of Stephan Dusan, by force of arms.]
[STEPHAN, Despot of Serbia.] [MARA or MARIA, wife of Wki Branchovik.] [JELINA or HELENA, wife of Nikolai de Gara.] [DESPINA, wife of Balsa.] [WCOSAVA, wife of Milos Kobilich, who killed Murat.] [MILJEVA, wife of Wk. Baiazitis primus.]
[STEPHAN.] [GEORGIUS, Despot of Serbia, succeeds his uncle Stephan. His wife Irene Cantacuzena.] [GREGORIUS.] [JOANNES.] [LAZARUS.] [MARIA, wife of Murat II.] [NN, two sons blinded by Murat.]
[GEORGIUS.] [Wk.] [MARIA, wife of Bonifacius, Marquis of Montferrat.] [CATARINA, wife of Count Ulrich of Cilli.] [JOANNES.] [MARIA, wife of Ferdinandi Frangipani.] [MARIA, wife of King Stephani Bozina.] [IERINE or IRENE, wife of Joannes, Duke of S. Petri in Galatina.] [MILIZA, wife of Leonardo, Despot of Lartensis.]
From this genealogy and from the consensus of Leunclavius’s history, the error of those who assert that the daughter of Despot George was the wife of Bajazit I is refuted; and the genealogy which was exhibited in the *Pandects*, no. 54, is entirely false. Lazarus's son, who died in the year 1421 with no surviving children, is Stephan, whom George Brancovich succeeded, as the grandson of Lazarus through Mara, whom Ducas calls Maro. What our writer says, that George was the son-in-law of Lazarus and not his grandson, is written incorrectly; and he certainly should have written: *vid. Voulkou, son-in-law of Lazarus*. For if Despot Stephan had died while his nephew (who succeeded him) through his sister Maro—or Mara—survived, there could be no other person than George, from whom Murat sought to reclaim Serbia under a new right, because his uncle Stephan had died without children. Murat did not have Milieva as a grandmother, daughter of Mahomet and granddaughter of Bajazit; for no author has handed down that Bajazit had children from her.
Joyfully exulting, he greeted him; and having joined the forces he was leading, he attached himself as a companion on the march to Morates. And when he had led him four days' journey within the borders of Hungary, they found the region deserted; for the Hungarians, having learned of the approach of Morates, had transported the inhabitants from the villages, hamlets, and minor camps to another place. Wherefore the Turks proceeded through the deserted region, having gained nothing except one very small castle, and that taken even beyond their expectation. For when the garrison had gone out to seek the things necessary for their needs, and were remaining outside the city, the Turks, passing by in the morning by chance, found the gates open, and entered without any resistance, and having plundered everything, they departed. But having advanced as far as Zipinium, which is one of the famous cities of Hungary, they did not dare to approach it closely. When therefore its inhabitants saw the invading Turks with indignation, they engaged in battle with them at the open gates of the city and slew many of them. Wherefore the Turks retreated, always having Draculius as their guide, from whom Morates feared that ambuscades might be laid against him. When they arrived at the bank of the river, they crossed him over again. At this time the King of Hungary was still an infant, nor did he have a regent to administer military affairs. Wherefore, the audacity of the Turks having become known, the Queen appointed one of the nobles as prefect general over the armies; a man, indeed, bold and spirited, and in military matters another Achilles or Hector. Morates, having crossed the river and arrived at Adrianople, sends Saricias as a bridesman, in order to bring to him his betrothed from Serbia. And when he arrived, the Despot received him kindly and magnificently, for he had been crowned that very winter. For Emperor John, having sent the signs of the principality through George Philanthropinus, had named him Despot of Serbia. That bridesman at length departed from Serbia, having abducted the young virgin, who was carrying away immense treasures and garments woven with gold; she was also taking her two brothers with her. When they arrived in Adrianople, the marriage was celebrated with the greatest joy. Morates had previously taken another wife, the daughter of Spentiar; yet he burned more for this one, because she excelled in outstanding beauty and keenness of intellect. The nuptials having been completed, he generously bestowed many gifts upon his brothers-in-law and dismissed them kindly; afterwards, as autumn began, he lingered in Adrianople, passing his time now in hunting, and at other times occupying himself with spectacles and drinking bouts.
